en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa; salutations to Śrī Sarasvatī;
salutations to Śrī Rāmacandra.
Now begins the first part of the *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa*:
Salutations again and again to the Self-born One, who consists of *sattva* during the dissolution, creation, and maintenance;
salutations to Him who is the threefold form of *rajas*, *tamas*, and *sattva*.
Victory has been won by the Blessed One, by that Hari, the sustainer of the world;
by the Unborn, whose form is the universe, who is devoid of qualities yet whose very self is the qualities.
To Brahmā, the creator of the world, the omniscient and unconquered,
the Lord of the past, the future, and the present, the true Master.
The unsurpassed knowledge, detachment, sovereignty, and virtue of that Lord of the World— this fourfold set is to be cultivated by the virtuous.

The Lord, being free from the twenty-fold [tendencies], again [created] these states of man, which consist eternally of both the existent and the non-existent, for the sake of the manifestation of action.
The creator of the world, who knows the true nature of the world, being a knower of yoga,
resorted to yoga and created all beings, both the stationary and the moving.
Desiring to know the ancient accounts, I go for refuge to the omnipresent Lord Viśvakarman, the protector of the good and the witness of the world.
The Blessed Lord Prajāpati praised the Purāṇa— which contains the essential truth of the world, is inexhaustible, and is equal to the Vedas— to Vasiṣṭha.
The venerable sage Vasiṣṭha taught the meritorious nectar of the knowledge of reality to Parāśara, the son of Śakti and grandson of [Vasiṣṭha].
And in ancient times, the venerable Parāśara taught that divine Purāṇa, which is equal to the Vedas, to the sage Jātūkarṇya.
Having attained that ancient, supreme, eternal Brahman, Jātūkarṇya, the knower of distinctions, imparted it to Dvaipāyana.
Then the self-controlled Dvaipāyana, being pleased, bestowed that most wonderful work upon his five disciples for the purpose of establishing the true principles of the world.
For the sake of making it renowned in the worlds, for its manifold meaning, and in accordance with the Vedas,
[he honored] Jaimini, Sumantu, and Vaiśampāyana.
The fourth among them was Pailava, and the fifth was Lomaharṣaṇa;
he was a Sūta of wonderful deeds, humble, righteous, and pure.
Having studied the Purāṇa, the humble Lomaharṣaṇa—
endowed with perfected wisdom and highly righteous— was questioned by you, O Sage.
Vasiṣṭha, too, having bowed his head to the sages and performed a circumambulation, was endowed with the highest devotion.
Having acquired knowledge and being well-pleased, he went to Kurukṣetra,
where at a well-conducted sacrificial session there were pure ṛṣis acting as sacrificers.
Having approached the sacrificial session with humility,
he surpassed even the hair-raising ritual by means of his wisdom, according to the prescribed injunctions and the scriptures.
And all those sages, having seen that hair-raising sight at that time, were exceedingly thrilled, delighted, and well-disposed.
Then, having saluted all the sages and received the king’s command, they honored them with hospitable offerings such as water for the hands and feet.
Permitted by those sages and questioned regarding his well-being,
he approached all the munis, who were the eternal Brahman and spiritual luster; then,
with the consent of the assembly, he sat down upon a beautiful, well-spread seat.
When he had thus sat down, the sages of celebrated vows,
filled with joy, remained composed and humble, according to the prescribed rule.
All those sages, surrounding that one of great vows and filled with supreme joy, spoke thus to the son of Sūta: ||| BndP_1,1.23 |||
Welcome to you, O highly fortunate one! By good fortune we behold you, O wise one, free from ailment, established here, a best of sages of excellent vows.
O Sūta, today my [ears] have become non-empty by virtue of you, a man of meritorious deeds;
for you are the son of that great-souled sage Vyāsa.
O Lord, a wise disciple who possesses the qualities of a disciple and has a firm intellect regarding reality should always be favored by you through such favor.
O wise one, having attained vast knowledge and having severed all doubts on every side,
you ought to explain everything to us who always question you.
Therefore, we desire to hear that divine, ancient narrative, which is consistent with the Vedas and endowed with righteousness and purpose; for you have heard it from Vyāsa.
Thus addressed by the sages, the charioteer,
endowed with humility and possessing supreme wisdom, spoke this most excellent and modest reply.
Whatever service I rendered to the sage, and whatever wisdom I possess—all that was for the sake of serving him; this is my firm conviction regarding the truth.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, you should now deign to learn that which I am able to say regarding the matter of the destination,
wherein you have a desire to know.
Having heard these sweet words spoken by him, the sages replied once more to Sūta, whose eyes were clouded with tears.
"You are skilled in discerning distinctions and have seen Vyāsa in person;
therefore, reveal this entire origin of the world."
"Whosoever and whomever we desire to know in their respective lineages,
as well as the diverse prior creation of those lords of progeny—
being thus respectfully questioned, that high-souled Romaharṣaṇa [began to speak]."
The best of men related it in detail and in proper sequence.
Sūta said:
"O best of the twice-born, this is the story which Dvaipāyana, being pleased with me, indeed told."
O Brahmins, I shall indeed relate in due order that meritorious account which was spoken by Mātariśvan; I shall fully proclaim this Purāṇa.
Formerly, when questioned by the high-souled sages of Naimiṣa, [he recounted] the primary creation,
the secondary creation, the genealogies, and the periods of the Manvantaras.
The lineage and the deeds of ancestors constitute the Purāṇa with its five characteristics;
the first quarter is the formal introduction, which serves as the framework for the narrative.
The Anuṣaṅga, the Utpoddhāta, and the Upasaṃhāra—
thus have the four quarters been briefly proclaimed by me.
I shall describe them to you hereafter in detail and in their proper order;
first, however, is the Purāṇa heard by Brahmā from among all the scriptures.
And immediately thereafter, the Vedas issued forth from his mouths,
as well as the auxiliary sciences, the Dharmaśāstras, the vows, and the observances.
"That which is the unmanifest cause is eternal, consisting of both being and non-being;
it is my firm resolve that I shall create [the universe] beginning with Mahat and ending with the specific elements. (Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 1.1.42)
The egg was indeed golden, the supreme birthplace of Brahmā;
its outer covering was the ocean of waters, which in turn was enveloped by fire.

By the wind, that [wind] is covered by space; by space, the source of the elements (bhūtādi); and by the great principle (mahat), the source of the elements is covered; and the great principle is covered by the unmanifest (avyakta).
And the egg itself is described as being within the elements;
herein, the manifestation of the rivers and the mountains is recited.
Therein is the description of all the Manvantaras and the Kalpas;
the glorification of the Tree of Brahman, and the proclamation of the birth of Brahmā, is set forth.
From this point forward follows the description of the creation of beings by Brahmā;
herein are also proclaimed the various states of Brahmā, who is born from the unmanifest.
The origin of the kalpas as well as the establishment of the world, the reclining of Hari upon the waters, and likewise the lifting up of the earth; BndP_1.1.48 //

It contains the specific classification of cities and other settlements according to caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama), as well as the locations of the constellations, the planetary positions, and the abodes of the Siddhas.
Likewise, there is the extensive account of their movement for many *yojanas*,
as well as the classification of the celestial abodes for those beings who have practiced virtuous conduct.
The enumeration of trees, medicinal herbs, and creepers, as well as that of the deities and the ṛṣis—these two paths have been proclaimed. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.1.51)
The creation and the manifestation of trees such as the tamarind,
as well as the origin of animals and human beings, have been fully described.
Likewise, the etymological derivation and the adoption of the Kalpa were proclaimed;
furthermore, the nine creations of Brahmā, preceded by his conscious intention, were declared.
Those three [views] which are preceded by intellect, as well as the conception of the world,
and the emergence of dharma and the other principles from the limbs of Brahmā— [these are the views of the Sāṃkhyas].
Those twelve who are born again and again in every cycle of creation,
as well as that which is called the reconnection between those two cycles, have been declared.
Due to being enveloped by the quality of darkness (tamas), unrighteousness arises from Brahman;
and due to the body being predominant in goodness (sattva), the Puruṣa comes into existence.
Likewise, from Śatarūpā, they subsequently begot two sons,
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, who were auspicious in form and character.
Those who are established throughout the three worlds and celebrated as cleansed of all evil were born as a pair from Ākūti, the daughter of the progenitor Ruci.
Furthermore, there was the auspicious birth of the daughters of Dakṣa;
and from those daughters of Dakṣa, known as the Dākṣāyaṇīs, beginning with Śabdalā and others, there arose the offspring of the Great-Souled One.

The creation of Dharma is proclaimed as being characterized by goodness (sāttvika) and resulting in happiness; likewise, the creation of Adharma through violence is characterized by darkness (tamas) and is inauspicious.
Therein is the description of the creation of progeny by the sages beginning with Bhṛgu,
as well as the proclamation of the lineages of the Brahman-sage Vasiṣṭha.
The origin of Agni’s progeny in Svāhā, where it is proclaimed, and immediately thereafter that of the two classes of Pitṛs in Svadhā; BndP 1.1.62.
In connection with the lineage of the ancestors, the curse of Dakṣa upon Maheśvara, as well as that of Satī and the wise Bhṛgu and others, is recounted.
The curse of Dakṣa upon Rudra of wondrous deeds,
and the prevention of their enmity through the perception of its faults, are proclaimed.
In connection with the description of the Manvantaras, the exposition of Time is proclaimed,
as well as the auspicious characteristics of the daughter of the Prajāpati Kardama.
In this [chapter], the detailed account of Priyavrata’s sons is told,
as well as their respective assignments over the islands and regions.
Then follows a detailed recitation of the creation of Svāyambhuva,
as well as of the regions, the rivers, and all their various divisions in every respect.
The inclusion of thousands of different islands within the seven [great continents],
as well as the detailed extent of Jambūdvīpa and the ocean, [are described].
The measurements in yojanas are proclaimed along with the mountains:
Himavat, Hemakūṭa, Niṣadha, and Meru itself;
Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgin—these seven mountains are proclaimed.
Their internal diameters, heights, lengths, and breadths are as follows.
And those inhabitants who dwell there are described by their extent in yojanas,
as well as the regions such as Bhārata, along with their rivers and mountains.
The continents, beginning with Jambūdvīpa, are situated upon these elements— both mobile and stable— and are surrounded by seven oceans.
Beyond that, the golden earth and the Lokāloka mountain are proclaimed;
these worlds, along with the earth consisting of seven continents, are described with their specific measurements.
Form and the other [elements] are proclaimed along with the instruments by those who follow the primordial nature (prakṛti);
all of this is but a partial transformation of the Pradhāna.
And the measurement of these in their various aspects is here proclaimed in brief,
as well as that of the sun and the moon, and of the earth, without exception.
According to the current measurements of those who possess such pride,
the auspicious and meritorious mountains beginning with Mahendra are situated upon the summit of Mānasottara.
Therefore, the upward motion of the sun is described as being like a whirling firebrand (alāta-cakra);
furthermore, the characteristics of the Nāgavīthī and Akṣavīthī are proclaimed.
Through the conjunctions of the two treasuries (koṣṭha), the two lines (lekha), and the circles (maṇḍala), as well as the twilight of the Lokāloka mountain, the day, and the equinox; BndP_1,1.78.
The world-protectors are stationed above, and they are proclaimed in the four directions;
the paths of the ancestors and of the gods lie to the south and the north.
For householders and renunciants alike, it is said to be the refuge of passion (rajas) and goodness (sattva);
and it is celebrated as the station of Viṣṇu, wherein dharma and the other [qualities] abide.
The movement of the sun and moon, as well as that of the planets and luminaries,
is proclaimed [by him] through his sustained power, as is the auspiciousness and inauspiciousness of living beings.
Created by Brahmā himself for the purpose of providing a seat,
that lordly sun is celebrated as he moves from heaven toward its setting place.
That chariot was presided over by the gods, the Ādityas, and likewise by the ṛṣis,
as well as by the Gandharvas, Apsarases, Grāmaṇīs, Sarpas, and Rākṣasas.
And likewise, the essence of the waters is said to flow as sap;
furthermore, the waxing and waning of the moon are proclaimed to be caused by Soma.
The movement of the sun and other celestial bodies proceeds from Dhruva alone;
it is proclaimed that Dhruva is situated at the tail of the Śiśumāra (the celestial crocodile).
All the stars in the form of constellations, together with the planets,
are proclaimed there as the dwellings of the gods of meritorious deeds.
And there is a thousandfold solar radiance, manifesting as rain, cold, and heat;
furthermore, there is the differentiation of the rays according to their names, functions, and spheres of influence.
The dimensions and movements of the planets have been described as dependent upon the sun;
from the form of the courtesan, the dimension of Pradhāna arises as the Great One (Mahat).
The glorification of the greatness of Purūravas, the son of Āyu;
or the greatness of the two kinds of ancestors, and of the deceased.
Thereafter, the lunar phases (parvans) and the junctions (saṃdhis) of those phases are proclaimed,
as well as [the accounts] of those who have gone to the heavenly world and those who have attained a downward course.
Through the Śrāddha rite, there is great benefit for the two classes of ancestors;
furthermore, the duration measured by the number of Yugas is proclaimed as the Kṛta Yuga.
In the Tretā Yuga, due to the decline [of righteousness], the practice of agriculture was introduced,
as well as the establishment of the social classes (varṇas) and the stages of life (āśramas) according to dharma.
Furthermore, the turning of the vajra and the dialogue therein which is proclaimed—
the descent of the sages together with Vasu, and the subsequent downward journey of Vasu;
and the state of sound arising from Pradhāna, except for the Svāyambhuva Manu.
The praise of austerity has been spoken, as well as the conditions of the ages (yugas) in their entirety;
and there is also a brief proclamation concerning the Dvāpara and the Kali ages.
The number of a *manvantara* has been proclaimed according to human reckoning;
this indeed is the defining characteristic of all *manvantaras*.
The past, the future, and the present are proclaimed,
as well as the characteristic of the transition between the Manvantaras.
Then, in the Svāyambhuva [Purāṇa], the course of the past and the future was proclaimed;
likewise, the destiny of the sages and the course of the knowledge of time were declared.
The number and measurement of the fortresses, the occurrence of the Yuga-era,
and indeed the characteristics and births of the universal emperors (*cakravartin*) during the Tretā age.
Likewise, the birth of Pramateśa and indeed that of the Kali Yuga, as well as what is said regarding the diminution of living beings by finger-breadths, [are described].
The enumeration of the Śāsanās, the preeminence of the disciples,
the sevenfold statement, and the proclamation of the lineages of the Ṛṣis.
The characteristics of the sons of the Sūtas were described by Brahmā in their entirety,
as was the decline of the Vedas by the high-souled Vedavyāsas.
In this [chapter], the glorification of the gods and the lords of creatures during the Manvantaras is recounted,
as well as the sequence of the Manvantaras and the knowledge of time.
And Dakṣa’s granddaughters, the beautiful daughters of his beloved daughter,
were begotten by Brahmā and the other gods, as well as by the wise Dakṣa himself.
Herein are glorified the Sāvarṇa Manus who reside on Mount Meru,
as well as the description of the creation of progeny by Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda.
This is the account of the creation of beings during the Manvantara of Cākṣuṣa Manu,
and how the earth was milked by the lord Vainya.
This was the specific distinction regarding the vessels, the milks, and the calves;
furthermore, this earth had already been milked by Brahmā and the others in the past.
And from the ten Pracetas, sons of the wise Prajāpati Dakṣa, the birth of Dakṣa himself is proclaimed to have occurred through a portion of that same [Brahmā] in the womb of Māriṣā.
The lordship over the past, the future, and the present is proclaimed for the great Indras;
they shall become Manus and others, surrounded by many narratives.
The detailed account of the creation of Vaivasvata Manu is proclaimed,
as well as the origin of the sheath of Brahmā and the birth of Bhṛgu and the other sages.
Having extracted it during the creation of progeny under the auspicious Cākṣuṣa Manu,
the creation of Dakṣa is now proclaimed from within the Vaivasvata interval through meditative reflection.
Nārada, the mind-born son of Brahmā, having engaged in conversation with the exceedingly powerful sons of Dakṣa, caused them to perish through a curse.
Then Dakṣa begot daughters renowned by the name Vairiṇīs;
and the birth of the Maruts occurred from the goddess Diti within the flow of the Maruts.
And here the hosts of the Maruts are celebrated; they consist of seven groups of seven.
Their divinity resides in the dwelling of Indra, and their hermitage is in the regions of Vāyu.
Of the Daityas and Dānavas, of the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas,
of all beings, Piśācas, Yakṣiṇīs, birds, and plants.
The births of the Apsarases are recounted in great detail,
as well as the entire solar disc and the birth of the elephant Airāvata.
The birth of Vainateya, as well as his consecration to the kingdom,
the detailed account of the Bhṛgus, and likewise that of the Aṅgirases, has been told.
In this [section], there is the detailed account of the progeny of Kaśyapa, Pulastya, the high-souled Atri, and the sage Parāśara.
Three daughters are well-renowned, upon whom the worlds are established;
thereafter, the expansion of Icchā and Āditya is described.
What conduct was proclaimed as the cause of Dhruva’s downfall?
And in brief, who were those of great strength, beginning with Ikṣvāku and the others? Thus it was proclaimed.
In this section, the [misdeeds] of kings such as Niśya and others, including their theft of onions and so forth,
are recounted in detail, as well as those of King Yayāti.
The summary of the Yadu lineage and the detailed account of Haihaya were told immediately after Krodha, as was the further expansion of that dynasty.
The greatness of Jyāmagha and the creation of progeny are also glorified,
as well as those of Devāvṛdha, Andhaka, and the high-souled Dhṛṣṭi.
The lineage of Animitra, the false accusation against Viśvāmitra,
and the acquisition of the wise jewel by Viśvāmitra.
The birth of Śūra, the son of the royal sage Devamīḍhuṣa, as well as the life-story of that high-souled Satrājit during his creation of progeny, has been told.
And the wickedness of Kaṃsa, as well as the birth from a single lineage of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor as Vāsudeva in the womb of Devakī— [all this has been told].
Immediately following this is the creation of the Ṛṣis and the description of the creation of progeny;
then, when the war between the gods and demons had arisen, Viṣṇu performed the slaughter of women.
In ancient times, while seeking to protect Śakra from being slain, he incurred a curse from Bhṛgu;
yet Bhṛgu then restored Śukra’s divine mother to life.
The twelve steps of the gods and the sages,
beginning with Nṛsiṃha and others, are proclaimed as destroyers of sin.
Therein is the propitiation of Sthāṇu by Śuka through fierce austerity, as well as the granting of boons and the hymn of praise offered to Śarva.
And immediately thereafter, the activities of the gods and asuras were described,
wherein Śuka [was born] from Śakra together with Jayantī into that great-souled one.
The wise Bṛhaspati, of great splendor, deluded the Asuras by assuming the form of Śakra; he then cursed that Śuka.
And the majesty of Viṣṇu has been declared; it is proclaimed at the birth of Viṣṇu that Turvasu was the younger grandson born here of Yadu.
Anurudra and all the others, as well as their sons who were kings,
were high-souled descendants of that lineage, the best among monarchs.
In this [section], the [exploits] of Vibhrāja, the son of Ātithya, who possessed abundant wealth and splendor, are recounted in their entirety through seven divisions based on his recourse to dharma.
And where the curse of Bārhasvatya was withdrawn by the wise ones;
where there was the touch of the fame of the lineage of Hara, and the proclamation of the heroic power of Śantanu.
Likewise, there is the mention of future kings by way of summary,
as well as the description of future Saṅghas and their leaders.
At the end of the Bhautya Kali age, when it has waned, the description of dissolution is given;
these are known to be occasional (naimittika), elemental (prākṛtika), and absolute (ātyantika).
The dissolution of all beings is described as manifold:
the disappearance of the sun, and the terrible fire of universal destruction.
In that [chapter], the characteristics of Sāṃkhya were indicated; thereafter, Brahman was described in detail, along with a description of the seven worlds beginning with Bhūḥ.
The characteristic of Brahmā is proclaimed by others as being half of an aparārddha; this is the determination of his measurement in terms of yojanas.
And herein are described the hells, such as Raurava and others, for those who have committed evil deeds,
as well as the determination of the transformation of all sentient beings.
From the reabsorption into Brahman follows the description of the entire cycle of worldly existence;
the upward and downward destinies are declared to be based upon dharma and adharma.
In age after age there is the destruction even of great beings;
there are innumerable sufferings, and even Brahmā is impermanent.
The wickedness of enjoyments, the misery of their destruction,
and the rarity of liberation— [all these arise] from dispassion through the perception of faults.
Having abandoned both the manifest and the unmanifest, the pure being established in Brahman turns away from that [world] through the vision of its manifoldness.
Then, fearing the threefold affliction, the stainless one who seeks the goal of the true form attains the bliss of Brahman and fears nothing whatsoever.
Furthermore, the creation of another Brahmā is proclaimed as before;
herein, the transformations of the world’s creation and dissolution are proclaimed.
The activities of living beings and the fruits of their actions are proclaimed, as well as the creation of the host of sages, which destroys all sin.
The manifestation of Vasiṣṭha and likewise the birth of Śakti,
as well as his taking up the bones of Saudāsa, which was brought about by Viśvāmitra.
Likewise, O Lord, the birth of the powerful Parāśara from Adṛśyantī, the daughter of a Pitṛ, occurred; and thus the great sage Vyāsa was born as well.
Likewise, the birth of Śuka along with his wise son,
and the hostility of Parāśara toward the sage Viśvāmitra.
O Brahmin, by divine ordinance, Vasiṣṭha gathered the fires with the intent to destroy Viśvāmitra, acting as one who desired the welfare of Viśvāmitra.
For the sake of the continuity [of the world], the wise Lord, having swallowed the Vedas with his all-pervading body,
divided that single Veda consisting of four quarters into four parts once again.
Likewise, by the grace of Śiva, the venerable Vyāsa divided [the Vedas];
and by his disciples and grand-disciples, branches numbering ten thousand were established for the Vedas.
In their practice, they were never at all negligent, just as was seen by the Self-Existent One;
those distinguished sages, desiring the Dharma, questioned him.
For one desiring a meritorious region, the Lord, who seeks their welfare,
[bestows] that which has a beautiful navel, possesses a divine radiance, consists of seven parts, and proclaims auspiciousness.
"This wheel, which is beyond compare, is turning; follow it unweariedly and with self-restraint, and you shall then attain the state that has been opened."
"That region where the rim of that wheel breaks as it travels should be considered meritorious," the Lord then replied.
Having spoken thus to all the sages, he vanished from sight;
so too did Gaṅgā, Garbha, Yavāhāra, and the inhabitants of Naimiṣa.
And at that time, the sages presided over a sacrificial session in Naimiṣa.
When Śaradvatī had died,
the sages of Naimiṣa, filled with supreme compassion, performed her restoration to life.
Having made this earth boundless, he brought forth King Kṛṣṇa;
and then, having performed the rites of hospitality according to the rules, he showed great affection toward the king.
Then, while the king was fleeing, the cruel Asura Svarbhānu, seizing the royal power within the creation, took it away; thereafter, O sages, the kingdom passed to Anu.
Having seen that the banner of Kalāpagrāma was protected by the Gandharvas,
there was again an assembly of great seers for his sacrifice.
Seeing everything made of gold, a dispute arose between him and them at that time during the twelve-year sacrificial session of the Naimiṣeya sages.
While they were thus disputing, Yadu was established by them;
having quickly produced a son in the forest, he [Yadu] then begot Ayuta.
Having completed that sacrifice, they worshipped Vāyu;
thus is the summary of duties described as a portion of the Purāṇa.
In this very sequence, the Purāṇa is revealed;
even its vast meaning is easily perceived in brief.
Therefore, with reference to the entire collection, I shall explain it to you in detail:
he who, having conquered his senses, correctly studies this first quarter [of the work].
By him, O twice-born ones, the entire Purāṇa has been studied; there is no doubt about this—[he who knows] the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs and Upaniṣads.
One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
for the Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, "He will strike me."
By practicing this chapter, which was spoken directly by the Self-Existent One himself,
one shall not be deluded upon encountering adversity and shall attain the desired goal.
Because this existed in ancient times, it is therefore remembered as "Purāṇa";
he who knows its etymology is liberated from all sins.
Therefore, listen to this summary: Nārāyaṇa is all this from of old;
even at the time of creation he brings forth the path, and at the time of dissolution he does not exist again.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Enumeration of Duties," in the first section (Prakriyā-pāda) of the Vāyu-prokta Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Then those ṛṣis, whose wealth is their austerity, spoke again to Sūta:
"Where did the sacrificial session of those performers of wondrous deeds take place?"
And for how long did that time last, and how did it proceed?
He related the Purāṇa and how that occurred together with the wind.
"Tell us in detail, for our curiosity is great.

Listen to where those wise ones conceived that supreme mantra,
for how long a time it existed, and how it came into being.
Desiring to create the universe, he indeed performed a sacrifice and released it in the past;
for your sacrificial session (*sattra*) was most meritorious and lasted for a thousand years.
Wherein Brahmā himself became the householder of Tapas,
wherein he assumed the role of wife to Iḍā, and wherein the wise one performed the office of the Śamitṛ.
The highly effulgent Mṛtyu performed the sacrifice of those great-souled ones;
and there the gods remained for a thousand years.
Where the rim of the revolving wheel of Dharma was shattered,
that place, honored by sages, became renowned as Naimiṣa because of that deed.
Where that meritorious Gomatī flows, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
there Rohiṇī became that Gomatī in an instant.
The eldest daughter of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, who possessed supreme splendor, was Śakti;
she was given as a bride to Ruṃdhatī’s son.
Where King Kalmāṣapāda and Śakra [fought] with the spear,
and where the enmity between Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha arose.
In Adṛśyantī was born the sage Parāśara,
by whose knowledge he indeed brought about the humiliation of Vasiṣṭha.
There, those exponents of the Veda considered it to be Śaila in Naimiṣa;
because they were born in Naimiṣa, they are therefore known as the Naimiṣīyas.
That sacrifice of those wise ones lasted for twelve years,
while the valiant Purūravas ruled over the earth.
Purūravas traversed the eighteen islands of the ocean, yet he was not at all satisfied; for we have heard that it was due to his greed for jewels.
Urvashi, urged by a messenger from the gods, desired him;
and having united with Urvashi, he completed that sacrificial session.
While that lord of men was presiding over the sacrifice, the sages of Naimiṣa performed the rites for the embryo which Gaṅgā had borne from Agni, blazing with radiant splendor.
An amount of gold equal to that was placed upon the mountain;
from that, he then constructed a golden sacrificial enclosure for those great-souled ones.
Viśvakarman, the self-existent god, the creator and sustainer of the worlds,
then entered that sacrificial session of those beings of immeasurable splendor.
While wandering on a hunt, Purūravas, the son of Iḍā, reached that region;
there he beheld that most wonderful sacrificial enclosure made of gold.
With his consciousness destroyed by greed, he proceeded to seize it;
thereupon, the inhabitants of Naimiṣa became violently enraged at that king.
And the wise sages, established in austerity and impelled by the gods, being enraged, struck that king with kusha-grass darts as if they were thunderbolts.
Crushed by Kuśavajra, that king abandoned his body;
thereafter, the king fought on the earth with the sons of Urvaśī.
That righteous king, whom they call the high-souled father of Nahuṣa, was present at those very final ablutions.
At this sacrifice, the Supreme among Men brought about the highest attainment of life and prosperity for the king as well as for those who know Brahman, having thus pacified them.
Those whose very forms were like the offspring of the Earth began to perform a sacrificial session (sattra);
during that sacrifice of those high-souled ones, there was the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya).
Like the creators of the universe in the past when they desired to bring forth the world,
he was accompanied by his dear friends, the Vaikhānasas, the Vālakhilyas, and the Marīcis.
He, possessing the splendor of the sun and Vaiśvānara, was born amidst the unborn sages,
the gods, the Apsarases, the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Cāraṇas.
The king shone with the Bhāratas like Indra among the gods;
he honored the gods with hymns and sacrificial recitations, and the ancestors with ancestral rites and offerings.
They honored the Gandharvas and others according to their respective classes and in accordance with the prescribed rites;
thereafter, he remembered them during the intervals between the ritual acts for the sake of propitiation.
The Gandharvas sang the Sāman hymns, the hosts of Apsaras danced,
and the sages uttered auspicious speech with its varied syllables and words.
There, the learned ones recited mantras and so forth to one another,
and they struck down their opponents with words of sophistry.
The learned sages, who were experts in grammar, semantics, and logic,
as well as the Brahma-rākṣasas, entered there without losing anything at all.
Neither Daityas who seize sacrifices nor Vājamukha birds were present there,
nor did poverty or the need for expiation arise in that place.
The ritual procedure was performed with blessings through the movements of power, wisdom, and action;
and thus the sacrificial session of the wise continued for twelve years.
For the sages of Naimiṣa, that was as if it were for the wielder of the thunderbolt himself;
the heroic priests, led by Vṛddha and others, performed the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices individually.
They followed behind him, bestowing ten thousand-fold sacrificial fees upon all;
where Vāsudeva, the great lord, stood at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
They questioned the one of immeasurable soul: "Since I, a twice-born, have been urged by you for the sake of my own lineage," and the Lord spoke to them.
The disciple of the Self-Existent Lord was a deity who perceived everything directly and possessed self-mastery;
he was endowed with the eight subtle limbs beginning with *aṇiman*.
He who supports all the worlds with his rains against the transverse winds and other forces,
possesses seven trunks as branches that sustain all the waters, undecaying and ageless.
The immensely powerful one, for whom the Maruts are stationed in groups of seven by the objects of the senses, performed a sacrificial session (*satra*) consisting of three arrays of charioteers.

Moreover, through its own functions, the fivefold vital breaths—prāṇa and the rest—maintain here for embodied beings both the element of fire and the means of sustenance. (Bṛhad-yogiyājñavalkya-purāṇa 1.2.42)
Being filled, it performs the support of bodies;
its source is space, it possesses the two qualities [sound and touch], and it is endowed with sound and touch.
She was declared by those expert in the science of grammar to be the fire-drill for speech;
with her gentle voice, she seemed to gladden all the sages.
In ancient times, the all-pervading Lord spoke this story to the pure-minded brahmins who were well-versed in the Purāṇas, devoted to the Purāṇas, and disciplined in their observances.
O best of the twice-born, this entire narrative as it occurred,
as well as this supreme and unsurpassed truth concerning the world of the sages, has been told.
This supreme, ancient knowledge was proclaimed by Brahmā in the past;
it liberates both gods and sages from all sins.
I shall explain its sequence in detail and in proper order.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Naimiṣa Account," in the first section (Prakriyā-pāda) of the Pūrva-bhāga of the Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa, as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Listen to their divine story, which liberates one from all sins.
Listen to this wonderful narrative, rich in meaning and in harmony with the Vedas, as it is being told by me.
Whoever would constantly uphold this, or listen to it repeatedly,
having ensured the preservation of his own lineage, is glorified in the heavenly world.
Listen to the account of Viśvātārā and the five others, exactly as it occurred and as it was heard; this narration increases the fame of the ancients.
The recitation of the names of all those of meritorious deeds and steadfast fame brings wealth, renown, long life, heaven, and even the destruction of enemies.
Because he forms the kalpa through the entire kalpa for the sake of purity, being himself pure—
to that Hiraṇyagarbha, the Puruṣa, and the Īśvara.
Having paid homage to the self-existent Brahmā, the first-born, the most excellent, the creator of progeny, and the sustainer of the world-system; BndP_1.3.6.
That which begins with the Great Principle (mahat) and ends with the specific elements (viśeṣa), together with their various forms and characteristics,
consisting of five measures and ending in the sixfold [evolutes], is presided over by the Puruṣa.
Out of a desire for self-restraint, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed creation of beings;
that which is the unmanifest cause is eternal, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent.
Those who contemplate the principles call it Pradhāna and Prakṛti;
it is devoid of smell, form, and taste, and is free from sound and touch.
The primordial source of the world, the great element, the supreme and eternal Brahman—
the unmanifest, indeed, became the body of all beings.

Brahman is without beginning or end, unborn, subtle, composed of the three qualities, the source of origin and dissolution, not of the present moment, unknowable, and that which is beyond both being and non-being.
By his own self, all this was pervaded; it consisted of darkness. At that time, while the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas) prevailed, it was undifferentiated and composed of darkness.
At the time of creation, when the primary matter (pradhāna), presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña),
was manifesting through the state of the gunas, the Great Principle (mahātattva) indeed came into being.
That Great One (Mahat) is initially subtle and enveloped by the unmanifest;
at first, it is an intensification of *sattva*, manifesting as pure *sattva* alone.
That Great One (Mahat) is to be known as the single being, arisen from that cause;
the subtle principle (liṅgamātra) has emerged, presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
Volition and determination are known as its two functions;
free from egoism, it performs the great creation out of a desire to create.
The elements, beginning with *dharma*, are the causes for the true nature of the world;
the mind arises from the Great Self (*mahātman*), and the deluded notion of "Brahmā" arises from the Lord (*īśvara*).
The junction of wisdom is his entire essence; through the rays of the spheres of perception, he perceives all beings, and therefore the omnipresent Lord yields fruitful results.

The enjoyer, the protector, and the one whose self is manifold—this is called the mind (manas). Because it encompasses the principles (tattvas) and because it is great in its magnitude, it is [called] Mahat.
Like the Mahat [principle] from the remaining qualities and principles (guṇa-tattvas), it is known as the subtle body (tanu);
it conceives of differentiation, or rather, it perceives division. (Bṛhad-yogiyājñavalkya-purāṇa 1.3.20)
He is remembered as Puruṣa because of his connection with experience (bhoga), and by that [connection] he exists;
he is called "Bṛhat" (the Great) because of his vastness, his nourishing nature, and because he is the support of all beings.
Because he causes all beings to flourish, he is therefore defined as Brahmā; and because he fills all bodies with his favors, [he is called Viṣṇu].
And herein the Puruṣa perceives all entities individually;
yet within him, the instrument of action was perfectly established by Brahmā in the beginning.
O Goddess, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who is equal to Brahman, [perceives] my primordial state;
he is indeed the first embodied one, called Puruṣa in ancient times.
He is the first creator of beings, Brahmā who existed at the beginning of all that comes into being.
He is Hiraṇyagarbha, who manifested within this egg as the four-faced one;
in creation and in re-creation, he is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), Brahmā, firmly established.
Together with their instruments, they are questioned, they abandon them through withdrawal (pratyāhāra),
and they assume bodies again at the junctions of the cycles of aggregation.
Even the waters of the Garta-tīrtha, along with the Budā, shall carry away to death that great-souled one who uproots Meru, which is made of gold.
In that egg these worlds are firmly established,
together with the earth and its seven continents, as well as the seven oceans.
By means of immense mountains and thousands of rivers,
these worlds are situated within him, and this entire universe is contained within him.
The moon and the sun together with the constellations, the aggregate along with the wind, and whatever exists in that egg, including the Lokāloka mountain— all are established therein.
The waters, increased tenfold, are indeed enclosed on the outside by fire;
and fire, increased tenfold, is enclosed on the outside by air.
The wind, possessing tenfold qualities, is enveloped on the outside by space;
likewise, all of space is enveloped on the outside by the primordial element (bhūtādi).
The Great Principle (mahat), which is the source of the elements, is itself enveloped by Pradhāna;
thus the cosmic egg is surrounded by these seven primordial coverings.
By their own will, the primary elements remain in a state of mutual destruction;
having remained thus at the time of cosmic dissolution, they devour one another.
In this way, they sustain one another;
through the relationship of the container and the contained, those modifications exist within the modified.
The unmanifest is called the field (kṣetra), and Brahman is called the knower of the field (kṣetrajña);
thus is the creation of primordial nature (prākṛta-sarga) presided over by the knower of the field.
The first [mantra] appeared spontaneously, like lightning;
he who knows this mantra of Hiraṇyagarbha in its true essence will,
without a doubt, be long-lived, famous, fortunate, and wise.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Hiraṇyagarbha," in the first section (Prakriyāpāda) of the Purvabhāga of the Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa, as narrated by Vāyu.
The Son said:
When the manifest [universe] was established within the Self and all modifications had been withdrawn, [the Lord remained].
Then the primary matter (pradhāna) and the spirit (puruṣa) abide in a state of similarity.
These two qualities, tamas and sattva, exist in a state of equilibrium; because they are neither predominant nor subordinate to one another, they are said to be mutual companions.
When the qualities are in equilibrium, dissolution is to be known; when they are in excess, creation is said to occur.
When sattva increases, stability arises; thus, O Lotus, the state of permanence is firmly established upon the crest.
When rajas is present within both darkness (tamas) and goodness (sattva), it acts as the impeller;
it is like water [that causes germination] within seeds.
When the qualities (guṇas) have reached a state of imbalance and become established through mutual attachment,
three [entities] are to be known with reverence as arising from those qualities being agitated.
They are eternal, supremely secret, the self of all, and embodied beings;
Viṣṇu is the quality of goodness (sattva), Brahmā is passion (rajas), and Rudra Prajāpati is darkness (tamas).
Viṣṇu, the illuminator of the quality of passion (rajas), attains the state of Brahmā as the creator;
and from whom, the one of great luster, this creation of the worlds arises.
Viṣṇu, as the illuminator of darkness, is established as Time (Kāla);
Viṣṇu, as the illuminator of goodness (sattva), is established as Maintenance (Sthiti).
These indeed are the three worlds; these indeed are the three qualities (guṇas);
these indeed are the three Vedas; these indeed are the three fires.
For these are mutually interconnected and follow one another;
they exist through mutual dependence and impel one another.
For these are indeed pairs with one another, subsisting upon one another;
there is no moment of separation for them, as they do not abandon each other.

At the time of creation, it proceeds from that primordial cause— which consists of both the existent and the non-existent— due to the prior unseen force (adṛṣṭa) presiding over it and the inequality of the primary qualities (guṇas).
Brahmā indeed came into being simultaneously with the pair consisting of intellect (buddhi) and its object;
therefore, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who is composed of darkness (tamas) and the unmanifest (avyakta), is designated as Brahmā.
Having accomplished his task, he stood before Brahmā;
wise and incomparable in splendor, he was unmanifest yet the illuminator of all.
He was indeed the first of embodied beings, established in the state of a sustainer;
through incomparable knowledge and detachment, he attained seventy [divine years] here in this world.

Because of his mastery over the three qualities (guṇas), because of his dependence on the state of being, and because of his mental disposition, he attains unmanifestness through that mind by whatever he desires. (Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 1.4.16)
As Brahmā he has four faces; as the Destroyer (Kāla) he is the end-maker;
and as the Puruṣa he has a thousand heads—these are the three states of the Self-born One.
All passion (rajas) exists in the state of Brahmā; both passion and darkness (rajas-tamas) exist in the state of Time;
and goodness (sattva) exists in the state of Puruṣa—such is the manifestation of the qualities (guṇas) of the Self-born One.
In the state of Brahmā he creates the worlds; in the state of Time (Kāla) he also destroys them;
in the state of the Puruṣa he remains indifferent—these are the three states of the Self-born One.
Brahmā, with eyes like lotus petals; Kāla, with the luster of fine black collyrium;
and Puruṣa, with eyes like white lotuses—these were the forms of the Supreme Self.
The Lord of Yogis makes for himself bodies— onefold, twofold, threefold, and again manifold— and he transforms them as well.
Because it assumes, by its own play, various forms, actions, and appearances,
and because it exists in the world in three ways, it is called the tri-guṇa (possessing the three qualities).
Because he is divided fourfold, he is proclaimed as the Fourfold Manifestation (Caturvyūha).
When he sleeps, then he is half-asleep; when the Lord enjoys sense-objects, then he is awake.
Because it is that which exists eternally as the state of being well-established, it is therefore called the Self (ātman);
the seer (ṛṣi), omnipresent and the Lord, has entered here into this body.
Viṣṇu is the master of all because he enters into everything;
he is the Blessed One (Bhagavān) because of his preeminent existence, and he is the Nāga because he is the refuge of the Nāgas.
He is the Supreme because of his extreme delight; he is the deity remembered as "Om";
he is the All-Knowing because of his complete knowledge of all things; he is the All because everything proceeds from him.
Because he causes men to sleep (nārāṇām svāpanam), he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa;
having divided himself threefold, he proceeds in his entirety.
He himself, being the Lord, manifested in the beginning as Hiraṇyagarbha; by means of these three [powers], he creates, consumes, and indeed protects.
For he is the first, independent, and because he is unborn, he is remembered as the Unborn (aja);
therefore, he is designated as Hiraṇyagarbha in the Purāṇas.
The duration of the period of the self-existent one who has withdrawn, which precedes the [period of the] castes,
cannot be calculated even by hundreds of human years.
The period of Brahmā’s life is recorded as a parārdha, which consists of the cessation of the count of kalpas;
his other time is of that same duration, and at its end, he awakens.
Those thousands of millions of years which have passed as householders,
and those remaining from the kalpas that are yet to come— [may they all pass].
Understand that the Varāha Kalpa is currently proceeding;
among those [fourteen], it is indeed the first Kalpa that is now occurring.
Indeed, for a full thousand yugas, it is to be protected by the lords of men.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Formation of the World," in the first section (Prakriyā-pāda) of the *Vāyu-prokta* *Śrī-Brahmāṇḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*.
Śrī Sūta said: In the beginning, the waters were all-pervading, reaching to the very edge of the earth's surface.
When this had dissolved away through the peaceful winds, nothing at all could be discerned.
Then, when that single ocean has arisen and all things mobile and immobile have perished,
that pervasive Lord Brahmā becomes manifest, possessing a thousand eyes and a thousand feet.
The Puruṣa with a thousand heads, golden-hued and beyond the senses—
known as Brahman Nārāyaṇa— then slept upon the waters.
Due to the predominance of the quality of goodness (sattva), he was forbidden [from entering] and beheld the world as empty;
and in this regard, they cite this verse concerning Nārāyaṇa: BndP_1,5.4 //
The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara;
they are said to be his place of movement (*ayana*), and therefore he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
While he dwells for a period equal to a thousand yugas performing his service,
he fashions a golden leaf for the purpose of manifesting the nature of Brahman.
But Brahmā, having become invisible and moving here and there within that water at that time,
was like a firefly at night during the rainy season.
Then, having understood through inference that there was something great within those waters, he remained undeluded regarding the support of the earth.
Then, as in former ages at the beginning of the kalpas, the Great-Souled One mentally conceived another body, one whose form was divine and which had originated from the syllable Oṃ.
Seeing the earth submerged in the water, he reflected:
"But having assumed what form shall I lift the earth out from the water?"
He recalled the form of the Boar, which was appropriate for sporting in the water,
visible to all beings, consisting of speech, and known as Brahman.
Ten yojanas in width and a hundred yojanas in length,
it resembled a dark blue cloud and possessed a sound like the thundering of clouds.
He possessed the stature of a great mountain, with white, sharp, and fierce fangs;
he resembled lightning and fire, and his splendor was equal to that of the sun.
With broad, rounded, and long shoulders, he possessed the stride of Viṣṇu;
his waist was thick and elevated, and he was honored with the auspicious marks of a bull.
Assuming his incomparable and immeasurable boar-form,
Hari entered the subterranean realm (rasātala) for the purpose of lifting up the earth.
He whose fangs are the concluding sacrificial offerings, whose tusks are the rituals, and whose mouth is the *juhū* ladle;
he whose tongue is fire, whose hair is *darbha* grass, whose head is the Veda, and who possesses great ascetic power.
The Veda is his trunk; he possesses the fragrance of oblations and the momentum of offerings to gods and ancestors;
the *prāgvaṃśa* hall is his body, and he is resplendent, endowed with various initiations (*dīkṣā*).
The yogi has the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as his heart; he is all-pervading, composed of faith and the quality of goodness (sattva);
he delights in the preparatory rites (upākarma), and his ornaments are the whirlpools of the Pravargya ceremony.
His path consists of various meters and modes of movement; his seat is the secret Upaniṣads;
he is indeed accompanied by Māyā as his consort, and his height is like that of a mountain peak.
Day and night are his lower lip; the Vedāṅgas and the Śrutis are his ornaments;
he has the fragrance of clarified butter and the sacrificial ladle for his snout; and he is great, with the sound of the Sāman chants as his voice.
Consisting of truth and dharma, glorious, honored for his ritual prowess and valor,
with expiatory rites as his claws, he was the terrible Great Sacrifice (Mahāmakha), whose knees were the sacrificial animals.
In this sacrifice of the inner self, the Udgātṛ priest is the seed of fruit; the oblation is the medicinal herbs;
and there is no flesh or blood for it.
The devotees, ending with Yajñavarāha, entered the waters again,
seeking Prajāpati, who desired the earth to become level after it had been covered by fire.
Having approached them, he offered these oblations today and yesterday;
he cast the oceanic waters into the oceans and the river waters into the rivers.
Having leveled those separately, he piled the mountains upon the earth.
At the time of the prior dissolution, when they were being consumed by the Saṃvartaka fire,
those mountains on earth were completely melted away by that fire.
In that single ocean, whatever was gathered together by the wind through Truth,
wherever it was poured down, there the mountain came into being.
Then, when those [elements] have been scattered, Viśvakarman distributes the mountains of the world-ocean again and again at the beginnings of the kalpas.
He fashioned this earth with its oceans, its seven continents, and its mountains,
as well as the four worlds beginning with Bhūr, again and again.
Having fashioned the worlds,
the self-existent and blessed Lord Brahmā, desiring to create various kinds of beings, indeed brought forth the creation of progeny.
As in former kalpas, he emitted that created form;
then, as he meditated upon creation, it indeed came forth preceded by his conscious intent.
Simultaneously with the emergence of Pradhāna, that which consists of darkness appeared:
namely, Tamas, Moha, Mahāmoha, Tāmisra, and that which is designated as Andhatāmisra.
This fivefold ignorance manifested from the Great Soul;
as he meditated with self-conceit, the creation became established in five ways.
Enveloped on all sides by darkness and covered with seeds, jars, and creepers,
it was without light both inside and out, and likewise utterly devoid of consciousness.
Because their intellect has been formed [by this] and they possess the instruments of suffering,
therefore those self-restrained ones are proclaimed as the foremost among the mountains.
Then, having seen that which had arisen during the primary creation, Brahmā, born from the Self,
became dejected in mind and reflected upon its origin.
As he was thus meditating, another stream, the Tiryak-srotas, turned outwards;
because it turned outwards (tiryak), it is therefore known as the Tiryak-srotas.
Because of their abundance of darkness (tamas), they are all considered to be full of ignorance;
though they produce and grasp [false notions], they imagine themselves to possess knowledge in their ignorance.
The ego-maker (ahaṅkṛta) and the ego-inflation (ahaṃmāna) consist of twenty-eight kinds:
the elevenfold forms of the sense organs, as well as the ninefold forms of the self (ātman) and so forth.
The eight [beings] beginning with Tāraka are recorded as those whose powers were destroyed;
they were all luminous within, yet again, enveloped on the outside.
Those who have mastered their selves and possess the three-fold perception are called those with horizontal currents.
Having indeed created the second universe with horizontal currents, the Lord, seeing that such a creation had arisen according to his intention, [proceeded further].
As he was meditating, a third [son] was born from his final [thought], characterized by sattva; he was the "Upward-streamer" (Ūrdhvasrotas), and he indeed established himself above.
That from which they turned back is known as the Ūrdhvasrotas;
they were full of happiness and joy, and were veiled both within and without.
Those who shine both externally and internally are known as the Ūrdhvasrotas progeny;
they are the nine Dhatas and others, who are remembered as wise ones with contented souls.
The third, who is remembered as the Ūrdhvasrotas, is entirely divine;
when the Ūrdhvasrotas gods were created, he was then the Lord among them.
Then Brahmā became filled with joy and no longer considered anything else; the Lord, desiring to bring about another creation, again made him his instrument.
As he was then meditating upon creation with true intent, the elemental creation appeared; that was the downward stream, which is the means of accomplishment.
Because their speech flows downward from there, they are called arvāksrotas;
they abound in light, are untouched by darkness, and have an excess of passion (rajas).
Therefore, those humans who perform [the rites] repeatedly will have much suffering;
they shall be manifest both externally and internally, and they shall be practitioners.
Established in eight ways by those characteristics beginning with the hell-beings,
those perfected souls among humans share the same nature as the Gandharvas.
The fifth is the creation of grace, which is established in four ways:
through error, through power, through the perfected, and likewise through the primary [beings].
Those who have ceased and those who are currently existing are born again and again;
this is called the sixth creation of beings beginning with the elements.
They should be known as being both gluttonous and lacking in moral conduct, as well as consisting of the elements and so forth;
this is to be understood as the first creation of Brahmā, namely that of Mahat.
The second creation is said to be that of the elements from the subtle essences (tanmātras);
the third is called the creation of the sense organs, which is the transformational (vaikārika) creation.
Thus these primary creations have arisen as preceded by intelligence;
the fourth is the primary creation (mukhya-sarga), and the immobile beings are indeed known as the primary ones.
The fifth creation is that of the animal realm (tairyagyonya), characterized by horizontal flow;
likewise, the sixth creation is said to be that of the gods, characterized by upward flow.
Among those, the seventh creation is that of the *ūrdhvasrotas* (those whose stream flows upward), which is human;
the eighth is the *anugraha* (grace) creation, which consists of both the *sāttvika* and the *tāmasa*.

These five are known as the modified (vaikṛta) creations; the first three are remembered as the primary (prākṛta) ones. The primary and the modified, and the ninth is remembered as the Kaumāra creation.
The three types of creation, however, are preceded by intelligence and are modifications; those groups of Brāhmaṇas indeed proceed from that which is preceded by intelligence.
And listen as it is described in detail how he also abides in all beings in their entirety, in four ways.
Through error, power, intellect, and likewise through perfection—
there is error among stationary beings, and [error] among those born as animals by virtue of their power.
Human beings were perfected in soul, while nourishment was complete among the gods;
then Brahmā indeed created from his own mind other beings equal to himself.
But by means of irreversible knowledge, those of great majesty have turned back; and having fully awakened to the meaning of the name, those three have indeed returned from the cycle of rebirth.
Without having yet brought about the creation or the secondary creation of beings here and there,
Brahmā then created other progenitors among those who were dispassionate.
Furthermore, hear from me concerning the gods who pride themselves on their stations, the instruction of Brahmā, and the state of the creation of unreal beings— those who dwell in those stations.
Water, fire, earth, wind, the intermediate space, and likewise heaven, the directions, the oceans, the rivers, and the lords of the forest; BndP_1.5.66.
Likewise, he is the self of herbs, and the self of trees and creepers;
he is the climbing plants, the woods, the digits, the moments, the twilights, and the nights and days.
The half-months, months, solstices, years, and yugas—these are known as the "Stationary" (Sthāna) currents, which are formidable in their respective stations. ||| BndP_1,5.68 |||
Having first created those who consist of the principle of space (sthāna), he then created others—
the gods and the ancestors— by whom these offspring were increased.
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Marīci, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha— these nine he created from his mind.
"These nine Brahmās are established as such in the Purāṇas;
they are like the very self of all those who are Brahma-yogins."
Then Brahmā again created Rudra, born from his own wrath,
as well as Saṃkalpa and Dharma, for all of them indeed, O Mountain.
Then Brahmā made a resolve for a being whose nature was happiness;
from that very resolve, he who has the unmanifest as his source was born as Saṃkalpa.
From his breath Dakṣa created Speech, and from his two eyes Marīci;
and from his heart the sage Bhṛgu was born, whose source was the waters.
From his head came Aṅgiras, from his ear likewise Atri,
Pulastya from his udāna breath, and Pulaha from his vyāna breath.
From Samāna he created Vasiṣṭha, and from Apāna he created Kratu;
these are remembered as the twelve most excellent sons of Brahmā.
Dharma and the others who were born first are known as those who spoke the Veda;
however, those such as Bhṛgu who were created later are not considered speakers of the Veda.
O twice-born ones, those sons of Brahmā known as the Gṛhamedhipurāṇas are twelve in number; they are born together with Rudra.
Kratu and Sanatkumāra—these two are perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas).
Indeed, in their prior birth, these two were the first-born of all.
When seven kalpas have passed, those two ancient ones, the accomplishers of the world,
having withdrawn their own splendor from this world, indeed become free from passion here.
Having established themselves in the dharma of yoga by means of their own selves, those two of great splendor continue to pursue the duty of progeny and the fulfillment of desire.
Because he was born exactly as he was, he is called "Kumāra" (the Youth) here;
from that, the name Sanatkumāra became established for him.
Those twelve lineages of theirs were divine, accompanied by hosts of gods; they were observant of sacred rites, possessed of progeny, and adorned by great seers.
Having indeed seen those twelve sattvic beings born from his vital breaths, the Lord Brahmā then created the asuras, the ancestors (pitṛs), the gods, and human beings.
From his mouth he generated the gods and the ancestors;
from his chest, indeed, the humans; and from his hips he fashioned the asuras.
At night, Brahmā, the god of gods, again created from his human-like self the moonlight,
as well as nectar and the ancestors.
Then, once again, he cleansed the principal and subordinate gods and asuras,
as well as the Manus, humans, and the great Pitṛs, like a father.
For the successful accomplishment of sacrifice, he created lightning, thunderclouds, and red rainbows, as well as the Rig, Yajur, and Sama Vedas.
From that Great One, Brahmā, were born various beings, high and low;
indeed, from Brahmā came the creation of progeny consisting of gods, sages, ancestors, and humans.
Again he creates all beings, both moving and stationary,
as well as yakṣas, piśācas, gandharvas, and apsarases in every way.
Hell-beings, kinnaras, and rākṣasas; birds, domestic animals, wild beasts, and serpents; the imperishable and the perishable—this twofold world of the stationary and the moving.
Their karmas, which were created by the Self-Existent One in the past,
those very same ones they encounter as they are created again and again.
Regarding the violent and the non-violent, the mild and the cruel, dharma and adharma, and the performed and the unperformed—
the wise know that among these very things, three are distinct, while one is undivided.
Those established in being and possessing equal vision declare that action regarding its own object is neither thus, nor not thus, nor both, nor neither.
By means of the word "div," the Great Lord fashioned these five— the name, the self, the five elements, and the manifoldness of created things.
The Lord bestowed upon them the names of the Ṛṣis and the creations that exist among the gods,
which do not come forth again during the night.
Thus, from this cause, the creation of the world arose from the Self-existent;
the transformations beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas are themselves of the nature of Prakṛti.
The world, adorned with the sun and moon, and graced by the circles of planets and constellations,
[is filled] with rivers, oceans, and thousands of mountains.
In this forest of Brahman, filled with various delightful cities and prosperous provinces, the omniscient, unmanifested Brahmā moves about.
Having its origin in the seed of the Unmanifest, it stands supported by that very [Unmanifest];
it consists of the trunk of the intellect and has the cavities of the sense organs as its hollows.
It has the great elements as its light and is possessed of specific qualities as its leaves;
it has merit and demerit as its beautiful flowers, and the arising of pleasure and pain as its fruit.
The eternal Brahma-tree is the livelihood of all beings;
it is both the forest of Brahman and that very tree of Brahman.
Those who contemplate the principles of reality call that which is the unmanifest cause— eternal and consisting of both being and non-being— the Pradhāna, the Prakṛti, and Māyā.
Thus, this path of grace is known as the occasional creation of Brahmā;
the three natural creations of Brahmā are those that occur without prior conscious intent.
But the six creations beginning with that of Sukha are modified (vaikṛta) and preceded by intelligence;
they proceed from the volitional choice of Brahmā, and they are characterized by his self-conceit (abhimāna).
Thus, these nine creations—both primary (prākṛta) and modified (vaikṛta)—are recorded as having arisen from one another; they are considered by the wise to be the cause.
Know that he whose head the Vedas proclaim, whose navel is the sky, whose eyes are the moon and the sun,
whose ears are the quarters, and whose feet are the earth— he is the inconceivable Self, the leader of all beings.
From his mouth the Brāhmaṇas were produced; from the chest and the front part [of his body] the Kṣatriyas;
from his thighs the Vaiśyas, and from his feet the Śūdras—all the castes were produced from his limbs.
Beyond Nārāyaṇa is the unmanifest; from the unmanifest arises the Egg, known as the Unmanifest.
From that Egg was born Brahmā himself, and by him the worlds were created.
Having remained there for ten kalpas, they then proceed to Truth;
those worlds indeed lead to the world of Brahmā, a state from which there is no return.
Indeed, even without sovereign authority, they become equal to him in power;
they are equal to Brahmā in form and in their objects of enjoyment.
There they indeed abide, filled with joy and united with their own [nature];
by means of that which is necessarily destined to be, they themselves expand the primordial matter (prakṛti).
Not connected with diversity, those states existing at that time arise like the unconscious awareness of one who is sleeping.
When cultivated at that time, their knowledge proceeds in such a manner through the various forms of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), but not for those who are merely boastful.
And together with them proceed both effects and causes for those inhabitants of the world of Brahmā who perceive diversity.
For those whose transformations have ceased and who abide by their own nature,
they are established as having identical characteristics— pure in essence and stainless.
In the primordial state (prakṛti), endowed with the instruments of action, they are established within their own selves;
having thus projected the self, this is indeed the reality of prakṛti.
When perceived as being many and distinct from the Puruṣa, [the world] does not proceed; however, the creation of those whose nature consists of both form and cause proceeds once more.
Union is to be known as the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) for those who see reality and have become liberated; therein lies their final liberation, as they proceed to a state of no further rebirth.
Furthermore, truth exists by virtue of non-existence, like the stillness of extinguished flames;
when those whose souls were filled with joy have departed from the three worlds upward, [truth remains].
Together with them, that great world was indeed not attained;
for those who are his disciples remain when the conflagration at the end of the eon has arrived.
Gandharvas and others, Piśācas, humans beginning with Brahmā,
as well as beasts, birds, immovable things, and reptiles.
While those sons remain at that time dwelling upon the surface of the earth,
that thousand of rays belonging to the sun which perishes here—
Having become those seven rays, each one arises as a sun;
in due course, numbering a hundred, they utterly consume the three worlds.
Mobile beings and immobile things alike, as well as all rivers and mountains,
were scorched by those very fires when previously dried up by drought.
Then all of them, both mobile and immobile beings, as well as merit, demerit, and the rest, being rendered helpless, were utterly consumed by the rays of the sun.
Then, at the end of the age, their bodies consumed and their sins shaken off,
they became renowned for their ascetic heat, liberated by that exceedingly auspicious [state].
Then those people are reborn among beings of similar form;
and having dwelt there for a night of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, they pass away.
Furthermore, at the time of creation, the mental progeny of Brahmā come into being here;
thereafter, when those inhabitants of the three worlds have arrived, they populate the realms with people.
And when the worlds have been consumed by the seven suns, and the earth has been flooded by rain, or when the oceans have become desolate; ||| BndP_1,5.130 |||
The oceans, the clouds, the waters, and the earthly elements,
as well as those called water and the mountains, all move along while being carried away.
And when the vast waters, arriving again and again,
had completely covered this standing earth, it then became known as the ocean (arṇava).
Because it shines forth from its radiance— and since the word *bhā* denotes beauty and brilliance—
all that has been attained by these months is manifested through their splendors.
Because it extends throughout the entire earth from within, the element (dhātu) spreads out its expansion; therefore, they are known as *apatana* (those without falling).

The verbal root *śār* is said to have various meanings when it means "to be shattered" (*śīrṇa*). However, in the single ocean, the waters do not become shattered; for that reason, those people are called *śāra*.
When that day of Brahmā, consisting of a thousand yugas, has come to an end, and during the night of equal duration as he exists in the form of water; BndP_1.5.136.
Then, upon that surface of the earth, the fire having vanished into those waters,
the wind was stilled and there was darkness on all sides, without any light.
Indeed, by whomsoever this was presided over, that Lord Puruṣa, the Brahman,
desired once again to effect the division of this world.
The root *śār* is said to have various meanings when it signifies "to decay.
Then, when that single ocean has vanished and all things mobile and immobile have perished,
he becomes Brahmā, possessing a thousand eyes and a thousand feet.
The Puruṣa with a thousand heads, golden-hued and beyond the senses,
known as Brahmā Nārāyaṇa, then slept upon the waters.
But awakened by the predominance of the quality of goodness (sattva), he beheld the world as empty;
by this first quarter-verse, the Purāṇa is proclaimed.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Formation of the World," in the first section, the Prakriyā-pāda, of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Thus has the first section, concerning the subject matter of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), been fully described.
Having heard this, Kāpeya, with a joyful mind, spoke out of doubt.
Having gratified the Sūta with his words, he who knows the Kalpas then began to relate another discourse concerning its meaning, starting from the point of reconnection.
I wish to know correctly this interval between the past eon and these two present eons, and that point of reconnection which exists between them; for you are indeed skilled in this.
Thus addressed by Kāpeya, Sūta, the best among eloquent speakers,
began to relate the entire origin of the three worlds.
Sūta said:
O you of excellent vows, I shall here describe, exactly as it is,
the past kalpa, the future one, and the transition between the two.
O you of excellent vows, those various Manvantaras that exist within the Kalpas, as well as this auspicious Vārāha Kalpa which is currently proceeding; // BndP_1.6.6 //
Learn now of the intermediate state between this present kalpa and that eternal kalpa which passed before it.
When the previous kalpa has returned and the sinless ones have passed away without rebirth,
another kalpa proceeds once more, beginning with the world of humans and so forth.
But with the cessation of rebirth, one kalpa follows another;
at the end of the kalpa, all living beings are then completely annihilated.
But from that kalpa to the next kalpa, no point of transition is found;
however, within a manvantara, the transitions between the ages (yugas) remain unbroken.
These past kalpas, which have been described in brief for the sake of explaining the process of manifestation, proceed from one another along with the periods of the Manvantaras and the Yugas.
Of those intermediate kalpas, that which was the last among the former ones— indeed,
that which occurred when the kalpa had passed— is the one beyond the half (the final one).
O twice-born ones, there will be other kalpas which are multiplied by the number of the second half; among them, O brahmins, the first is the present kalpa that is currently occurring.
In this first half of the supreme age (para-ardha), the second half is spoken of;
this duration of time established therein is traditionally known as the withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
Prior to this present kalpa, there passed a former, ancient kalpa,
along with its four thousand yugas and its manvantaras of old.
When that eon had waned and the time for its conflagration had arrived,
at that time there were those gods who dwell in celestial palaces.
The constellations, planets, and stars, including the moon, the sun, and so forth—
these twenty-eight [deities] belong to those of virtuous nature, numbering indeed twenty-eight crores.
Just as it is in one Manvantara, so it is in all fourteen;
there were three hundred and ninety-two crores [of Manus].
Furthermore, it is traditionally remembered that in each individual kalpa, there were formerly twenty-seven thousand gods belonging to the celestial mansions (vaimānika).
Then, during the fourteen Manvantaras,
the gods, the ancestors, and likewise the sages who drink nectar dwelt in the sky above.
Their followers, as well as their wives and sons,
and those who were outside the system of castes and stages of life, as well as the gods in the sky at that time, [all vanished].

Then, when the dissolution of all beings (ābhūtasaṃplava) had arrived, they all attained an equal state of perfection together with those who had gone to union (sāyujya) within that [supreme] reality.
Then, because their intellects were subject to inevitable change,
those gods dwelling in the three worlds here became full of self-conceit.
When that period of stability has then reached its full measure and the final northwestern [age] is near,
those gods who exist at the end of the eon will indeed encounter that calamity.
Then, filled with anxiety and having abandoned their respective places out of despair,
they set their minds upon Maharloka.
They were all disciplined, possessed of great physical vigor,
abundant in purity, and established in mental perfection.
Then, together with those inhabitants of the Kalpa, he attained greatness along with the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and other people born therein.
Having gone to Mahārloka, those fourteen hosts of gods then,
filled with anxiety, set their minds upon Janaloka.
By this sequential process, those who dwell for a kalpa pass away;
in this manner, thousands of divine ages (devayugas) succeed one another.
All were abundant in purity and established in mental perfection;
indeed, the people attained [their goal] together with those who dwell in the Kalpa.
Having remained there for ten kalpas, they indeed go once more to Truth;
having gone to the world of Brahmā, they attain a state from which there is no return.
They indeed possess sovereignty in their celestial palaces through their lordship;
they become equal to Brahmā in form and in their sensory domain.
There they indeed abide, endowed with joy and practicing self-restraint;
having attained the bliss of Brahman, they are liberated together with Brahman.
Then, by the power of an inevitable destiny, you yourself were bound by those very common people with honors and worship, being influenced by the circumstances of that time.
Just as one who is sleeping becomes conscious through a deliberate act of will, so too,
when service is cultivated through meditation, bliss arises in that same manner.
But for those whose vital breaths have been withdrawn and whose bodies are severed,
their functions and organs increase along with those [breaths].
But for those inhabitants of the world of Brahmā who perceive diversity,
whose offices have ceased, and who abide by their own nature, [the state is different].
Established as having identical characteristics, pure in essence and stainless,
they are endowed with their natural faculties and remain firmly established in their own self.
Having thus manifested itself, this primordial nature (prakṛti) proceeds in reality by being perceived as distinct from the many puruṣas.

Furthermore, when creation proceeds again, for those whose selves possess forms and causes, Prakṛti is to be known as the cause of their conjunction; however, for those who have seen the truth and are liberated, she is not.
There, for those who had attained liberation and were no longer traveling on the path, there was no further rebirth,
just as there is no re-emergence of extinguished flames.
Then, after those great-souled ones had ascended through the three worlds,
Maharloka was indeed reached by them together with these [others].
When the conflagration at the end of the aeon has arrived, they will indeed become his disciples—
gandharvas and others, piśācas, humans, brahmins, and so forth.
While those dwelling upon the surface of the earth— beasts, birds, stationary things, and reptiles— remained there at that time, [the world was filled with light].
That thousandfold mass of rays which is manifested by itself becomes seven rays each, and thus each one arises as a sun.
Rising up in succession, they burn the three worlds—
both the moving and the stationary, as well as the rivers and all the mountains.
Previously dried up by drought and now scorched by the suns,
they were all rendered helpless and utterly consumed by the rays of the sun.
Indeed, both the mobile and the immobile beings, consisting of dharma and adharma,
have their bodies consumed and are cleansed of sin during that interval between yugas.
Freed from the heat of their fame and bound by an exceedingly auspicious bond,
those people are then reborn among people of similar form.
