Having dwelt there for one night, those who were the mind-born sons of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, become [beings] here again at the time of creation.
Then, when those inhabitants of the three worlds had been reborn there and the worlds had been consumed by the seven suns, [the dissolution proceeded].
When the earth has been flooded by rain, and within the solitary oceans,
all the waters— both those of the sea, those of the clouds, and those belonging to the earth— [merge together].
Those known as waters, along with their followers, continue to flow even as they are being consumed;
yet when that water has become so abundant that it reaches the point of overflowing its source, [the process continues].
Having covered this earth that stood there, it then became what is called the ocean (arṇava);
for it shines with its own radiance, and the word *bhā* denotes both pervasion and light.
Through their universal attainment, water is manifested within them;
because it expands from within them, it subsequently pervades the entire earth on all sides.
The root *dhātu* signifies expansion; however, these [elements] are not considered "subtle" (*tanu*).
As for the root *śara*, it is said to mean "to be shattered," though it is also declared to have various other meanings.
When the world becomes a single ocean, the waters are not swift;
therefore, those men [remain] there when the day of Brahmā has come to an end after a thousand yugas.
While that night was still proceeding, he [entered] into the form of water;
then, upon the surface of the earth, those fires were extinguished within that water.
In a windless, dark, and entirely lightless space, this was indeed presided over by him; he is Brahmā, that Lord, the Puruṣa.
Then, when that single ocean had arisen and all things mobile and immobile had perished, he desired once more to effect the division of this world.
Then he becomes that Brahmā, the thousand-eyed, the thousand-footed, the thousand-headed Puruṣa, golden-hued and with senses subdued;
and in this regard, they cite this verse concerning Nārāyaṇa: BndP_1,6.61 //
"We have indeed heard that the waters are called *nārāḥ* because they are his bodies;
since he dwells within them as they swell, he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa. (Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 1.6.62)

With a thousand heads, gracious-minded, with a thousand feet, a thousand eyes, faces, and deeds, possessing a thousand arms, he is the first Lord of Creatures; this Puruṣa is declared to consist of the three Vedas.

Resplendent as the sun, the protector of the world, indeed the one formless, primordial Virāj, the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha), the Great-Souled Puruṣa—he truly exists beyond the mind. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.6.64)
At the beginning of the kalpa, the Lord Brahmā, being predominant in rajas, became the earth and created [the world];
at the end of the kalpa, being predominant in tamas, he became Time (Kāla) and swallowed it again.
Having indeed become Nārāyaṇa, overflowing with the quality of goodness (sattva) within the ocean,
he divides himself threefold and proceeds throughout the three worlds.
He himself creates, devours, and observes by means of these three;
at that time, when all mobile and immobile beings have perished in that single ocean.
At the end of a thousand cycles of four yugas, when everything was enveloped in water,
he who is called Nārāyaṇa appeared himself as Brahmā within that existence.
All four classes of beings, shrouded in darkness by the power of Brahmā,
behold him as Time sleeping in Maharloka, O great seers.
At that time, the great sages such as Bhṛgu who were previously mentioned,
as well as the eight great sages beginning with Satya, were dissolved when the Kalpa had ended;
then, by those being withdrawn, the Great One (Mahat) was enveloped in the Supreme.
The derivation of the name is explained from the root *ṛṣ*, which means "to go";
because they have gone (*ṛṣita*) by means of their being great, they are therefore called Great Sages (*maharṣis*).
Then Kāla was seen by those residing in Maharloka while he was asleep;
they were the seven great sages, beginning with Sattva, who had existed in the kalpa that had passed.
Thus, during those various nights, the great seers, having witnessed him thousands of times, perceived that Brahmā had been brought back to sleep for the duration of time.
Because at the beginning of a kalpa there are fourteen very numerous creations, Brahmā measures [time] by means of the kalpas; therefore, it is called a kalpa.
He is the creator of all beings again and again at the beginnings of the kalpas;
Mahādeva is both manifest and unmanifest, and this entire world belongs to him.
Thus has this connection between the two Kalpas been proclaimed; now, indeed, the prior state that existed between them shall be described.
This has been recounted in brief exactly as it occurred in the previous kalpa; now I shall fully proclaim this present kalpa—listen to it.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narratives of Kalpas and Manvantaras," in the second section (Anuṣaṅga-pāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Having observed the period of night, which is equal to a thousand yugas, he...
At the end of the night, Brahmā indeed performs [his duties] for the purpose of emission.
But Brahmā, having become the wind,
moved through that water while that ocean of darkness existed, in which all things mobile and immobile had perished.
Having completely inundated the surface of the earth with water on all sides,
[the dissolution occurs] either through the differentiation among beings or when they remain as mere existence.
Then, at that time, like a firefly in the night during the rainy season,
he was himself swiftly overcome by passion, despite his own intelligence.
Seeking a means for establishing [the earth] at that time,
he then perceived the earth submerged within those waters.
Perceiving another who was blind, the Lord, capable of uplifting him from the earth,
then remembered him from the beginning of previous kalpas.
Having assumed the true form of a boar and entered beneath the waters,
that Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) desired to recover the earth submerged by the waters.
Then, having lifted up the earth, he deposited it along with its offspring;
he placed the waters of the oceans in the oceans and the waters of the rivers in the rivers.
Having leveled the distinct regions upon the earth, he piled up the mountains,
after the previous creation had been consumed by the fire of universal destruction (saṃvartakāgni) in the past.
By that fire, those mountains were completely melted upon the earth;
yet those which had been gathered together by the wind in that single ocean remained as solid rock.
Wherever they were poured out, there the mountain became fixed;
because of the immobility of their shoulders (*skandha*), they are called *acala* (immovable), and because of their joints (*parvan*), they are known as *parvata* (mountains).
For they were called *girayaḥ* because they had swallowed [the earth], and *śiloccayāḥ* because they were accumulations of stones;
then the Lord, having lifted them up from beneath the waters, established them upon the earth.
Having leveled the uneven regions with rocks on all sides up to the mountains, he dwelt for seven times seven years upon those seven islands.
In those continents, there are likewise forty regions (varṣas),
and an equal number of mountains situated at the boundaries of those regions.
In heaven and other realms, they are endowed with splendor by their very nature and not otherwise;
likewise, the seven continents and oceans exist as successive circles surrounding one another.
The four worlds, beginning with Bhūḥ, along with the moon, the sun, and the planets, are situated by their very nature, mutually encompassing one another.
As before, Brahmā created all the stationary beings here;
and at the beginning of this kalpa, Brahmā also created the gods who dwell therein.
Water, fire, earth, wind, the atmosphere, and likewise heaven;
the celestial realms, the directions, the oceans, all rivers, and all mountains.
He [knows] the herbs and himself, himself and the trees and creepers;
the moments, the twilights, the divisions of time, the muhūrtas, the junctions, and the nights and days.
And [he created] half-months and months, solstices and years, as well as the Yugas;
and the presiding deities of the various stations, and those stations themselves, each distinct from the other.
Having created the self of the world-places, he fashioned the states of the ages:
the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and likewise the Tiṣya age.
At the beginning of the Kalpa, in the Kṛta Yuga, he first created progeny;
those very same progeny whom I previously described to you were created in the former Kalpa.
While that kalpa was thus dissolving, those beings who were on earth— briefly stated— were consumed by that fire before they could reach the world of heat (tapoloka).
For they indeed return at the time of creation for the purpose of observation;
having remained there for the sake of observation, they become the cause of creation once again.
Thus, those women being created indeed serve for the purpose of progeny;
they are remembered here as the means by which dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are accomplished.
The gods, the ancestors, and likewise human beings, being endowed with austerity, filled their respective stations in succession in ancient times.
Those Brahmins were indeed men who had perfected their souls;
through actions free from attachment and aversion, they have gone to heaven.
Revolving within the body, they come into existence age after age;
by virtue of the remnants of the fruits of their own karma, they are renowned and identified as being of that very nature.
The worlds of living beings arise, bound by the arrival of the kalpas;
he who is the cause of them in the waters awakens them indeed through karma.
By means of those auspicious and inauspicious actions, they are born from the Janaloka;
they take up bodies of various forms within the various wombs.
From the gods down to the immovable beings, they indeed encounter one another;
among them, they generally adopted pure actions. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.7.31)
Therefore, those very names and forms which they attained,
by means of those names and forms they are born again and again throughout the kalpas.
Then, indeed, from Brahmā who desired to create, there arose the secondary creation (upasṛṣṭi);
those creatures appeared as he meditated with true intention at that time.
Indeed, a thousand pairs of humans emerged from his mouth;
they were born endowed with the quality of goodness (sattva), possessed of great splendor, and full of vigor.
From his eye, he indeed created another thousand pairs;
they were all overflowing with passion, impetuous, and irascible.
He further created another thousand arms, which were devoid of virtue;
because they were increased by passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas), they are traditionally known as the householders (gṛhaśīla).
At the end of their lifespan, pairs are indeed born;
and for those about to die, both *kūṭaka* and *akūṭaka* insects arise from their bodies.
Having produced families from them, they abandoned their bodies;
from that time forth in this kalpa, the occurrence of sexual union began.
Through meditation and mental application for the sake of those beings,
there arises for each of them a pure sensory object— sound and so forth— possessing five characteristics.
Thus, through these mental dispositions, those who are childless abide with their Beloved; yet others are born into lineages by whom this world is filled.
At that time, those who possess little contentment indeed frequent rivers, lakes, oceans, and even mountains during that war.
The earth was named Rasavatī, and they spoke of it as food;
those creatures moved according to their will, desiring the perfection of the mind.
In the Kṛta Yuga, their lifespan, happiness, and form were equal;
at the beginning of the Kalpa, in that first age, neither dharma nor adharma existed.
According to their respective offices, they were born age after age;
[the duration of each] is four thousand years by divine reckoning.
They say that at the beginning there was the Kṛta Yuga, along with its two junctions (saṃdhyā and saṃdhyāṃśa), each consisting of four hundred [years];
thereafter, those thousands [of years] became renowned here among the progeny.
There is no obstruction for them, nor conflict, nor even a sequence;
for they dwell upon mountains and in oceans, having no fixed abode as their refuge.
The subjects were free from sorrow, full of strength, and exclusively happy;
they constantly indulged in their desires and were always joyful in mind.
At that time, there were no domestic animals, no birds, and no reptiles; there were neither small creatures nor fierce beasts—such was the state of Dharma.
For the sake of sustenance, they took fruits, flowers, and roots entirely without exception;
indeed, it was a time of absolute happiness, being neither excessively hot nor cold.
The desires cherished by their minds arise everywhere and at all times upon the earth; indeed, they emerge for them from the subterranean realm (rasātala) through meditative concentration.
It bestows strength and complexion upon them and destroys old age and disease;
with bodies that require no further refinement, those subjects possess enduring youth.
Yet, even without intentional conception, offspring were born from their perspiration;
they were equal in birth and appearance, and they took delight together as equals. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.7.52)
Then truth, freedom from greed, contentment, happiness, and self-restraint were present;
and they were all indistinguishable from one another in their appearance, lifespan, skills, and conduct.
The activity of living beings occurs spontaneously without prior conscious intent;
likewise, there is non-activity when the gateway for both auspicious and sinful karma has been closed.
At that time, the regulations for the castes and stages of life did not exist, nor were they practiced;
people conducted their mutual affairs free from desire and aversion.
In the Kṛta Yuga, all beings are born with identical forms and lifespans, free from the distinctions of low or high status; they abound in happiness and are devoid of sorrow.
Whether gain or loss, friend or foe, pleasant or unpleasant may occur,
the mind of those who are free from desire engages with these objects.
At that time, they do not harm one another, nor indeed do they praise one another.
In the Kṛta age, supreme knowledge is said to be the highest; in the Tretā, sacrifice is proclaimed as such;
in the Dvāpara, it is battle; and in the Kali age, it is indeed theft.
Sattva is established in the Kṛta age, Rajas in the Tretā, and Rajas-Tamas in the Dvāpara; Tamas alone is to be known as the Kali age—such is the conduct of the qualities among the ages.
Such is the duration of time in the Kṛta Yuga; now learn of its twilight (sandhyā).
That Kṛta Yuga consists of four thousand years.
The two portions of his [life] to be accomplished consist of eight hundred divine years,
and specifically four thousand human years.
Then, among them, there will quickly be no more outcries or reversals;
thereafter, when that Kṛtayuga, along with its transitional periods (saṃdhyāṃśa), has passed away.
The Dharma of the Yuga remains in its entirety as only one quarter;
when the twilight period has passed, that is the time of the Yuga's conclusion.
With the remainder [of the Veda] mixed with only a quarter remaining, and through the repeated performance of the twilight rituals (*saṃdhyā-dharma*),
it thus disappeared entirely during that Kṛta Yuga.
And when that junction had passed away, the offspring became mind-born;
in that subsequent age called Tretā, which followed the Kṛta, perfection was attained.
Those eight mental [perfections] which were indeed proclaimed by me at the beginning of creation—
those eight perfections come to an end through the process of sequential progression.
At the beginning of the kalpa, there is indeed one mental perfection (siddhi) in the Kṛta age;
[this occurs] in all the Manvantaras according to the divisions of the four yugas.
Then, by the power of a portion of what was performed during the twilight rites, the accomplishment of karma arising from the conduct of the castes and stages of life was brought about in brief.
For these [ages], having taken up three parts of the twilight period (saṃdhyāṃśaka) among themselves,
the characteristics of the yugas— namely austerity, sacred learning, strength, and lifespan— decline.
O best of sages, when the Kṛta age had been completed and had passed away, the emergence of the Tretā Yuga followed immediately thereafter, along with its constituent parts.
When that [period] had been exhausted and its purpose fulfilled, while those seven [rivers] remained,
at the beginning of the Kalpa, during the initial happiness of the Tretā age, then—
Then, through the conjunction of time, that accomplishment perished; it could not have been otherwise.
When that accomplishment had vanished, another accomplishment arose.
Then, having both returned to the state of water, they indeed became clouds;
from those thundering clouds, the emission of rain began.
Once the surface of the earth was fully perfected by that rain, living beings came into existence;
thereafter, for them, trees were designated as houses.
All their enjoyment, however, was produced from those [trees];
at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, living beings sustained themselves by means of them.
Then, after a long time, due to a reversal of those very [qualities],
a state consisting of passion and agitation suddenly arose.
That which occurs for women at the end of life is their menses;
at that time, it indeed does not occur again, even by the power of yoga.
Furthermore, their monthly menses then set in;
consequently, through that very same process, sexual union then took place.
Because they had cultivated that state at that time, as they approached [their wives] month after month,
conception occurred even when it was not the proper season due to the emergence of the menses.
But by the reversal of that [state], they were brought about for a time;
then all those trees designated as houses perished.
Then, when those [means] had vanished, they, bewildered and with their senses agitated,
meditated upon that perfection, for they were then intent upon the truth.
Then there appeared for them trees designated as houses,
which produced garments, fruits, and ornaments.
In that very same way, for those Gandharvas, there arises within every single leaf-cup honey endowed with flavor, possessing great potency, and characterized by analytical insight.
By that means they sustained themselves at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga;
nourished by that accomplishment, those subjects were free from all distress.
Then, after some time, the subjects, again overcome by greed,
seized those trees by force for the sake of honey or bee-wax.
Due to that misconduct of theirs, indeed brought about by greed,
the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) perished here and there along with their Lord.
When that very perfection had become diminished due to the power of time,
the dualities among them arose with great intensity.
Then, due to intense cold, wind, and heat, they were exceedingly distressed;
being tormented by those pairs of opposites, they cried out or covered themselves with their garments.
Having established dwellings recognizable by pairs [of opposites], those who were previously homeless and free to roam at will became distracted in mind.
In former times, they dwelt in various dwellings according to their inclination and pleasure,
on mountains and by rivers where honey-dripping bees abounded.
And they take refuge in fortresses— whether in arid regions, mountain retreats, or by the water—
as they please and according to their desire, both on level ground and on uneven terrain.
They indeed began to construct those dwellings to ward off cold and heat;
thereafter, they built villages and cities.
And likewise the villages and the cities according to their respective portions, as well as their lengths,
breadths, and the intervals between their settlements.

Then, according to their knowledge, having measured [the world] by means of their own qualities, they established the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the purpose of measurement; from that time forward, they were so employed.
Three finger-breadths (aṅgula) make one cubit (hasta), a fathom (kiṣku), or a bow (dhanus). Ten finger-joints (parvan) are designated as a span (prādeśa).
The span from the thumb to the forefinger is called a *vyāma-prādeśa*;
a *tāla* is defined by the middle finger, and a *gokarṇa* by the ring finger.
A *vitasti* is measured by the little finger; it is said to be twelve *aṅgulas*.
A *ratni*, however, consists of twenty-one finger-joints (*parvan*) in number.
Twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) constitute one cubit (hasta);
a span (kiṣku) is traditionally held to be two cubits, or forty-two finger-breadths.
A bow-staff was four hastas long, as were the nālikā and the yuga;
at that time, two thousand bows were made to constitute one gavyūti.
Eight thousand bows constitute one yojana as defined by them;
by this measure of a yojana, the settlements here were established.
Now, of the four types of forts, three arise naturally and the fourth is artificial; I shall explain the definitive characteristics of that [artificial] fort.
It had walls with elevated openings and was surrounded on all sides by moats;
it possessed jeweled gateways at every door, as well as a secluded inner apartment for the princesses.
A width of two cubits is best for the foremost of streams;
ten cubits is best for a stream of a single cubit's width, as are nine and eight cubits respectively.
And of all the hamlets, cities, and villages in every respect,
as well as the three kinds of fortresses— those on mountains, those by water, and those protected by archers.
Regarding artificial fortresses,
their width and length should be such that the width is half a yojana and the length exceeds that by one-eighth.
The city has a length of half of the supreme half-measure (paramārddhārddha), slopes toward the east and north,
has its corners cut off or irregularly shaped, and is situated in the form of a fan.
A city that is circular, shaped like a thunderbolt, or elongated is not praised;
however, a divine city endowed with four corners is highly commended by them as the ideal form.
The smallest [vāstu] is twenty-four [cubits], while the largest is one hundred and eight;
among these, the middle size is praised, and the smallest is devoid of wood.
Now, they say that eight hundred *kiṣkus* constitute a primary settlement (*niveśana*);
half a *viṣakambha* from the city is a *kheṭa*, and beyond that is a *pāna*.
A *kheṭa* is one *yojana* from a city; a village is half a *yojana* from a *kheṭa*.
Two *krośas* is the maximum boundary for land, while the boundary of a field is four *dhanus*.
A path for the cardinal directions was made by them twenty *dhanus* wide;
a village path is twenty *dhanus*, while a boundary path is ten.
A magnificent royal highway, ten *dhanus* in width, was constructed,
providing a passage free from congestion for men, horses, chariots, and elephants.

The crossroads are measured by those [crossroads] at four *dhanus*, the side-streets (*śākhārathyā*) are three *dhanus*, the main streets (*rathyā*) are two *dhanus*, and the minor streets (*uparatyakā*) are one *dhanus*.
The *jaṅghāpatha* consists of four feet, the *gṛhāntara* of three feet, and the *dhṛtimārga* of six feet; these are known as the *padika* measures in successive order.
Surrounded by a moat one cubit deep on all sides,
once those sites have been prepared, the actual houses shall indeed be built.
Having reflected again and again, they began to act so that those trees which had previously been situated as houses might become as they were before.
The branches of the tree extend downward from here, others go in another direction, some go upward,
and others likewise extend horizontally.

Having investigated by means of the intellect according to the proper method, just as they had gone forth upon the branches of the tree, and because those branches were fashioned by them, they are therefore remembered as *śālās*.
In this way, houses were established from branches and from the śāla tree;
therefore, they are remembered as śālās, and the nature of being a śālā is traditionally attributed to them.
Because they find delight in them, it is therefore designated as "prāsāda";
for that reason, houses, halls, and palaces are all so named.
Having struck those [trees] with pairs of blows, he pondered a means of relief when the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) had perished along with the honey.
Those creatures who had been created were indeed shown to be agitated by despair;
then, at that time in the Tretā Yuga, their perfection (siddhi) manifested.
For another rain, which accomplishes all purposes, falls from them according to their desire;
and whatever waters of that rain fall here, they become sweet.
In this manner, the process proceeded during the second creation of rain; those drops of water which subsequently fell upon the surface of the earth— BndP_1,7.125.
From the conjunction of water and earth, herbs then came into being;
indeed, those herbs were born possessing flowers, roots, and fruits.

Fourteen kinds of trees and shrubs— both those of the village and those of the forest— which do not require plowing or sowing, and which bear flowers and fruit according to the seasons, came into being.
In the Tretā age, however, [the means of subsistence] appeared through illusion or through medicinal herbs;
at the beginning of the Tretā, people then lived by means of those herbs.
Then, moreover, passion and greed arose among them constantly,
due to the inevitable nature of things and by the power of the Tretā Yuga.
Then they seized the rivers, fields, and mountains,
as well as the trees, shrubs, and medicinal herbs, by force according to their strength.
Those perfected souls who were previously described by me for your sake are indeed the mental sons of Brahmā, those beings who have arisen here from the beginning of creation.
Those who were peaceful as well as powerful, and likewise those who were active and suffering,
returning from there, were born again in the Tretā age.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and likewise people of mixed castes,
are conditioned by their previous births according to their renown for virtue or vice.
Then those who are powerful, possessed of the nature of truth, non-violent,
free from greed, and self-controlled, indeed dwell in the Smṛtis.
Those who, having arrived, say "We do not accept [anything]," yet perform services for them, as well as those who are weak, [should be avoided]. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.7.135)
They engage in acts of service, while others of lesser luster remain;
thus they become entangled with one another in their mutual misdeeds.
Because of that very fault, the medicinal herbs were then utterly exhausted;
though grasped with both hands, they vanished like grains of sand.
Then, by the power of that age, fourteen species of domestic and wild animals again began to gather fruits, flowers, and likewise roots for him.
Then, when those [plants] had perished,
all those creatures, bewildered and overcome by hunger, went indeed to the Self-born One.
For at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, those women were desirous of obtaining a means of livelihood;
the blessed Lord Svayambhū Brahmā, having understood their intention, [acted accordingly].
Having investigated through direct perception the fact that the plants had been swallowed by the earth, he understood this and caused them to grow back again.
Having made Mount Sumeru the calf, he milked this earth;
then, by him, these seeds were milked from the cow upon the surface of the earth.
Those seeds were born; the Lord [created] those plants of the villages and the forests, which ripen with fruit and are subject to the seven stages of growth.
Rice, barley, wheat, chickpeas, sesame seeds,
and noble millet— these are the *koraduṣṭa* grains along with the *vāmakas*.
Māṣas, mudgas, masūras, nīvāras, along with kulatthakas,
harikas, carakas, and gamas— these are recorded as the seventeen [types of grains].
Thus, these are recorded as the species of cultivated plants:
śyāmāka, nīvāra, jartila, and gavedhuka.
Kuruviṇḍa, veṇuyava, tāmrā, and īṣikā are recorded;
these are remembered as the fourteen medicinal plants belonging to both villages and forests.
These fourteen kinds of cultivated and wild plants, all grown without the use of the plow, appeared at the beginning of the first Tretā Yuga.
Trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants,
and species of grasses receive nourishment through their roots, fruits, and sprouts, thereby attaining growth and fruitfulness.
When the earth was milked by the Self-born One,
those seeds which were [milked] then became the medicinal herbs here, possessing seasonal flowers and fruits.
When the plants that had been released did not spread here again,
he then established the means of livelihood for the sake of their cultivation.
To them, the Blessed Lord, the Self-Existent One, granted the mastery of their own hands through their own karma;
and from that time forward, medicinal herbs grew ripe even without being cultivated.
Then Prajāpati, having established his body for the sake of sustenance,
fixed the boundaries for them by which they protected one another.
Those who were their powerful husbands remained as protectors; he established the other Kṣatriyas as those for whom protection had been provided.
As many as have been emanated, so many attendants shall stand by you;
speak the truth as it truly is, and may the eternal Brahman be yours.
And those others who were weak remained engaged in the task of guarding them;
established upon the earth, they caused the purchased goods to perish.
They call those very ones Vaiśyas— those who are tillers of the soil, who provide their livelihood through labor,
and who are devoted to service, running about and attending to others.
To those Śūdras, who were devoid of splendor and possessed little vigor, the Lord Brahmā spoke;
indeed, the Lord Brahmā ordained their duties and their religious laws.
Once that social order had been established by him for those belonging to the various classes,
the subjects again, out of delusion, did not follow that dharma.
And those who lived by the duties of their respective castes were obstructed from one another;
but the Lord Brahmā, having awakened, understood all that exactly as it was.
He ordained that for Kṣatriyas, strength, punishment, and warfare constitute their livelihood;
whereas for Brāhmaṇas, he prescribed officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and likewise the giving and receiving of gifts.
The Lord assigned these duties to those Brāhmaṇas;
and he gave cattle-rearing, trade, and agriculture to the Vaiśyas.
Furthermore, he assigned common occupations for the Śūdras who subsist by their crafts,
as well as for the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
Sacrificing, teaching, and giving are common to all, as well as to others;
however, one should not adopt the livelihood of performing rituals for one another among them in this world.
He further established for them abodes on the summit of Lokāloka;
the station of the twice-born who perform ritual acts is remembered as that of Prajāpati.
The station of Indra belongs to Kṣatriyas who do not flee in battles;
the station of Marut belongs to Vaiśyas who subsist by their respective duties.
The Gāndharva [Veda] is for those of the Śūdra caste, as well as for those who remain in service; these are the stations of the social classes for virtuous people who practice appropriate conduct.
When the social order of the four castes had been well established,
those castes remained fixed in their respective duties through the fear of punishment;
then, once the castes were settled, he indeed established the stages of life (āśramas).
The householder, the student, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—
the Lord established these four stages of life (āśramas) as before.
Whatever duties of the social classes (varṇa) there may be, for those here there are four stages of life (āśrama);
having performed their duties and established their dwellings, they enjoy the fruits from these stages.
Brahmā established those hermitages for them as they wandered;
thereafter, Brahmā instructed them and proclaimed the duties of dharma.
Their various paths, as well as the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), were established;
first, the stage of the householder belonging to the four castes was set forth.
I shall indeed explain, in due order, the sources of livelihood for the three stages of life, as well as their vows and observances.
Wife, sacred fires, guests, the performance of *śrāddha* rites, and progeny—
this, indeed, is the summary of the duties of a householder.

Carrying a staff and wearing a girdle, sleeping on the ground and likewise clad in an antelope skin, the student seeking knowledge must serve his teacher and subsist on alms. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 1.7.175)

For those dwelling in the forest, their clothing shall consist of bark, leaves, and skins; they shall subsist on wild roots, fruits, and herbs; and they must perform ablutions at both twilights as well as the fire-oblation.
When the pestle has been set aside, there is alms-seeking, non-stealing, and indeed purity; vigilance, celibacy, compassion toward all beings, and forgiveness. (Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 1.7.177)
Hearing [the sacred teachings], service to the guru, and truthfulness are recorded as the tenth;
for this tenfold dharma was proclaimed by the Self-Existent One himself.
There are five vows for a monk, as well as the vows of mendicancy and the Vedas; he explained the locations where those who remain established in them abide.
It is recorded that there are eighty-eight thousand sages who have drawn up their vital energy;
the very abode of those [sages] is also the abode of those who dwell with their teacher.
The place that is remembered as belonging to the Seven Sages is indeed for forest-dwellers;
that of the Prajāpatis is for householders, and the abode of Brahmā is for renunciants.
For yogis, there is no state that has not been attained;
yet those states belonging to the stages of life are indeed situated within the state of Brahman.
Four paths alone were fashioned as the ways of the gods;
likewise, those four paths of the ancestors are said to be fully established.
In the beginning, during the first Manvantara, according to the cosmic order of the worlds,
the Sun is traditionally known as the gateway for those paths that lead to the gods; likewise, the Moon is said to be the gateway for those paths that lead to the ancestors.
Thus, when the division of the castes and stages of life had been established,
yet the progeny did not increase, being fully devoted to the duties of their respective castes.
Then, in the middle of the Tretā age, he indeed created other mental offspring from his own bodies; they were equal to himself in nature.
When that first Tretā Yuga had gradually reached its midpoint,
he then proceeded to create other mental offspring.

Then the Lord created beings in whom the qualities of *sattva* and *rajas* were predominant— those who are the achievers of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, as well as the means of livelihood.
The gods, the ancestors, the seers, and likewise the Manus— by them,
in accordance with their respective ages and through righteousness, these subjects have been nourished.
Then, when that host of created beings had appeared before the Self-born One, Brahmā meditated upon his own mind-born progeny of diverse powers.
Those whom I have previously described to you as having resorted to the multitude of people were,
in a past age long ago, the progeny here, beginning with the gods.
As he was meditating here, those [goddesses] who had appeared for the sake of his procreation were,
according to the sequence of Manvantaras, first joined with him by the youngest.
They are known by their ancestors, who were previously manifested here;
they are then joined with those roots—both wholesome and unwholesome—which have not yet been exhausted.
Indeed, due to the defects resulting from the fruits of those actions, afflictions arose among the gods,
asuras, and ancestors, as well as among the yakṣas, gandharvas, and humans.
He created those *rākṣasas*, *piśācas*, beasts, birds, reptiles,
trees, hell-beings, insects, and all such [beings] endowed with various forms of consciousness, for the sake of providing food for all living beings.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Knowledge of the World," in the second section (Anuṣaṅgapāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Then, as he was meditating, mental offspring were born to him.
Together with those effects produced from that body and their respective causes.
The knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) came forth from this wise field;
from them arose the fourfold classes: gods, asuras, ancestors, and humans.
Desiring to create, he joined himself with tens of thousands [of forms];
from him, whose self was thus joined, there arose the manifestation of the constituent of darkness (tamas).
Then, as the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) was meditating upon creation, an effort arose within him;
consequently, his sons, the Asuras, were first born from his hindquarters.
The wise have remembered that *asu* means breath; since they were born from that, they are called Asuras.
That body by which he created the Suras, he cast it aside.
That discarded body instantly became night;
because it was full of darkness (*tamas*), night therefore consists of three watches (*tri-yāmikā*).
Because living beings were enveloped by darkness at night,
he himself then created the Asuras once more and thereafter assumed another body.
Then he applied himself to that unmanifest [nature], which abounds in the quality of sattva;
as he was thus engaged, it became dear to the Lord.
From the mouth of that one as he was gambling, the deities were born;
because they were born from him while he was gambling, they are celebrated as the Devas (the Shining Ones).
The verbal root *div* is said to mean "to play," and that is how it is understood here;
therefore, from that divine body, the deities were born.
Then, having created the gods, he cast off his divine body;
that body, once discarded by him, then became the day.
Therefore, the deities devoted to the rites of the day worship him;
then, having created the gods, he assumed another body.
Then that Lord, meditating upon them as his sons, indeed united with another woman who consisted solely of the quality of goodness (sattva), just as a father would.
For they became the Pitṛs (Ancestors) separately during the day and night of that [Brahmā];
therefore those gods are the Pitṛs, and their status as Pitṛs is traditionally remembered as such.
He cast off that body by which the Pitṛs had been created;
that discarded body immediately became the twilight (saṃdhyā).
Therefore, that which is the day is known as the deity of the gods, and that which is the night is remembered as belonging to the Asuras;
between those two, however, that form which belongs to the ancestors is the most venerable.
Therefore, the gods, asuras, sages, and likewise human beings,
being disciplined, worship that body during the interval between dawn and sunrise.
Therefore, the twice-born worship the junction of night and day;
thereafter, Brahmā again enters into another body.
The Lord created that which consists of the subtle element of passion (rajas) by means of his mind;
and from his mind, through procreation, his daughters were born as progeny.
And because they were produced through thinking (*manana*) and from Manu, they are celebrated as "creatures" (*prajā*).
Having created the creatures again, he then cast off his own body.
That body was cast away by him and immediately became the moonlight;
therefore, living beings become joyful at the rising of the moonlight.
These bodies were indeed cast off by that Great-Souled One;
immediately thereafter, night and day, as well as the twilight and the moonlight, were born.
Moonlight, twilight, and day—these three consist of the quality of *sattva*;
night consists of the quality of *tamas*. Therefore, it is indeed the night that acts as the restrainer.
Therefore, the gods were indeed created from happiness by means of their divine bodies through contentment;
since their birth was during the day, they are strong by day.
When the Lord, having struck down the Asuras with his body during the night, released them from their vital breaths, they were born from the night; therefore, they are invincible at night.
These very same [elements] belong to the future gods together with the asuras,
and to the ancestors and humans, both those who have passed away and those yet to come.
Indeed, in all Manvantaras there are four causal signs:
moonlight, night, day, and twilight. These are those four.
Because they shine, therefore He shines; the word *bhā* [is used] in the senses of pervasion and radiance.
Having created these waters, as well as the gods, demons, and humans... [Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.8.28]
He likewise created the ancestors and various other kinds of progeny;
then, having emitted that moonlight, the Lord proceeded to create another.
Then he directed that form, which was dominated by rajas and tamas;
thereafter, he created other beings who were shrouded in darkness and possessed by hunger.
Once created, they were overcome by hunger and prepared to seize the waters;
however, those among them who spoke, saying, "Let us protect these waters," [remained].
Therefore, those night-stalkers who said, "We shall devour the waters," are known as Rākṣasas, whose very nature is hunger; they were seen by one another.
By that karma, you have become yakṣas and guhyakas of cruel deeds;
furthermore, this verbal root *rakṣ* is understood to mean "protection" (*pālana*).
That which is indeed the element of earth (kṣiti-dhātu) is called *kṣapaṇa* because of its destruction;
it is called *rakṣas* because of protection, and it is called *yakṣa* because of its power to destroy (*kṣapaṇa*).
Upon seeing them, the hair of that wise one fell out due to his displeasure;
once fallen, it rose up again and again, piercing him repeatedly.

Those who are deficient in head, foolish, and lacking in wisdom, who crawl away like children—such serpents are known as *bālātman* (child-souled); because of their deficiency, they are known as *ahayaḥ* (snakeless).

Because they have fallen away from wisdom, they become serpents; and because of their slithering away, there is the dissolution of those [beings] into the earth, as well as into the sun, the moon, and the clouds.
That most terrible fire born of his anger,
whose essence was poison, entered those snakes that had arisen simultaneously with him.
Then, having created serpents, he produced from his wrath beings of a wrathful nature;
fierce and tawny-colored, those creatures were eaters of raw flesh.
Because they had become beings (*bhūta*), those beings became immortal; because they ate flesh (*piśita*), they were Piśācas.
Then, as he sang of the Earth (*gāṃ*), the Gandharvas were born as his sons.
The root *dhā* is recited by poets in the sense of drinking;
because they drank [the essence] and produced speech (*vāk*), they are remembered as Gandharvas.
When these eight divine wombs had been created, that Lord,
according to his will, created the Vedas from his will and the birds from his vital energy.
Having indeed created the birds, he then created the herds of cattle;
creating the goats from his mouth, he then created the sheep from his chest.
From his belly he created cows, and from his two sides he brought forth Brahmā;
from his feet he produced horses, elephants, donkeys, gayals, and deer.
From his body hair were born camels, boars, dogs, and other species, as well as medicinal plants bearing fruits and roots.
Having thus created the five medicinal herbs, he indeed employed them in sacrifices at the beginning of this kalpa,
long ago, at the onset of the Tretā Yuga.
The cow, goat, man, sheep, horse, mule, and donkey—these seven are the domestic animals; there are likewise seven others that are wild.
Beasts of prey, leopards, elephants, monkeys, and birds as the fifth;
aquatic animals as the sixth, and reptiles as the seventh.
Buffaloes, gayals, and camels; cloven-hoofed animals, the śarabha, and deer; and the monkey as the seventh among these—these indeed are the wild animals.
From his first mouth, he fashioned the Gāyatrī meter, the Ṛg-veda, the Trivṛt-stoma, the Rathantara-sāman, and the Agniṣṭoma among sacrifices.
From his mouth, he emitted the Yajus formulas, the Triṣṭubh metre, the fifteen-fold Stoma, and likewise the Bṛhat Sāman; thus it was declared. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.8.51)
From the western sacrifice, he created the Sāman chants, the Jagatī meter, the seventeenfold Stoma, the Vairūpya chant, and the Atirātra rite.
From his fourth mouth, he likewise created the Ekaviṃśa, the Atharvāṇa, the Āptoryāma, the Anuṣṭubh, and the Svarāja.
Having created lightning, thunderclouds, red clouds, and rainbows,
that Blessed Lord created the deity renowned as Parjanya.
He fashioned the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas for the successful accomplishment of sacrifice;
from his limbs were born beings of various kinds, both high and low.
Indeed, as Prajāpati Brahmā was engaged in the creation of progeny, he first created a fourfold group: the gods, the ṛṣis, the ancestors, and human beings.
Then he created all beings, both moving and stationary;
having created them, he then produced the yakṣas, piśācas, gandharvas, and apsarases.
Hell-beings, kinnaras, and rakshasas; birds, livestock, wild animals, and serpents; the imperishable and the perishable—this pair of the stationary and the moving.
Whatever actions those beings performed in previous creations, those very same actions they encounter again and again as they are created once more.

Creating both the violent and the non-violent, the cruel, righteousness and unrighteousness, truth and falsehood, beings are permeated by those qualities and enter into them; therefore, each finds pleasure in that which corresponds to its own nature.
The Creator himself ordained the diversity among the great elements, their forms as objects of the senses, and the specific functions of those elements.
Some men, O Brahmins, speak of human effort and action; others say it is destiny, while those who contemplate the elements speak of inherent nature.
Human effort and destiny exist as the fruit, the activity, and the inherent nature [of things];
however, the wise do not recognize them as having a separate existence beyond that.
"Thus it is, and not thus; neither both, nor neither;
those established in being and possessing equal vision declare their own sphere of action to be such."
In the beginning, that Maheśvara fashioned from the words of the Veda alone the manifold forms of beings and the elaboration of their actions.
And the names of the seers, as well as the insights found among the gods,
the Unborn One bestows upon those born at the end of the night once again.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Mental Creation," in the second section (Anuṣaṅga-pāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
[He created] Rudra, Dharma, Manas, Ruci, and likewise Ākṛti.
Then indeed, that Lord mentally emitted five creators.
All these mighty-armed ones are the causes for the stability of living beings;
Rudra, having withered away, repeatedly restores the medicinal herbs.
When the medicinal herbs had perished, the God was duly worshipped by those seeking rewards with only three skulls, each possessing the fruit of the herbs.
Because he is worshipped by sages, he is therefore called Tryambaka;
moreover, Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī are remembered as those [metres].
I have described the wombs of the Ambikās belonging to Svanaspatis;
through those three kinds of wombs, which have become one with him by his own power, [he exists].
The sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) has three modes of preparation and is known to be on three potsherds;
that sacrificial cake has three eyes, and for that reason it is remembered here as Tryambaka.
Dharma supports all creatures; Manas is known as the producer of knowledge.
Ākṛti is the form of Suruci, and Ruci is known as the producer of faith.
Thus these protectors of subjects are the causes for the stability of living beings; now, as he was creating this world, it was for the sake of the increase of his progeny.
Those created beings did not multiply for some reason;
therefore, he formed an intellect directed toward the determination of the goal.
Then, within himself, he beheld the mere quality of darkness (tamas) moving about,
existing by its own activity while having abandoned both passion (rajas) and goodness (sattva).
Then, because of that suffering, the Lord of the World felt grief;
he first dispelled darkness, but afterwards he was completely enveloped by passion.
That darkness was indeed dispelled, and a pair was procreated;
from his practice of unrighteousness, violence and sorrow were born.
Then, when that couple consisting of Varuṇa had been produced,
the Blessed One became pleased and took refuge in him.
Thus, from the half of his own body, there emerged a woman of supreme auspiciousness, enchanting to all living beings, as he was filled with joy.
For she was created from Prakṛti by one whose nature was desire; she was of beautiful form and was called Śatarūpā, and so she has been described again and again.
Then the subjects were produced, just as I previously described to you during the discussion of the great-souled one in the midst of the Tretā age.
When those creatures created by the wise one did not multiply,
he then created other sons from his own mind who were like himself.
He created as his mind-born sons Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Marīci, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha.
"These are the nine Brahmās," so it is determined in the Purāṇa;
for among all those born from the Self who have restrained their souls, Brahmā is the source.
Then Brahmā again created Dharma, which brings happiness to all beings,
as well as Prajāpati and Ruci, who were the first-born of the former [creatures].
From his intellect (buddhi), he created Dharma, which brings happiness to all beings;
and from his mind (manas) was born Ruci, who was born from the Unmanifest (avyakta).
But from his heart was born the sage Bhṛgu, who originated from the *sāla* tree;
and while creating Dakṣa from his vital breath, Brahmā created Marīci from his two eyes.
He created from his head Rudra, who is blue-and-red and characterized by self-conceit (abhimāna),
and likewise Aṅgiras from his head and Atri from his ear.
From Udāna he likewise created Pulastya, and from Vyāna, Pulaha;
Vasiṣṭha was born from Samāna, and from Apāna he fashioned Kratu.
Thus these twelve are remembered as the sons of Brahmā at the beginning of creation;
among them, Dharma is indeed recorded as the first-born of the gods.
Those such as Bhṛgu and others who were created are known as the Brahmarṣis;
they were the ancient householders, and by them dharma was first set in motion.
These twelve give birth to offspring again and again in every kalpa;
their twelve lineages are divine and endowed with celestial qualities.
Even as the creatures were being created by that wise one, they did not multiply;
he became shrouded by the quality of darkness (tamas) and was indeed overcome by grief.
Just as that Brahmā was enveloped by the quality of darkness (tamas), so too another portion of the quality of darkness emerged from his sons. 1,9.30.
For unrighteousness consists of moving against the current, and violence is of an impure nature;
therefore, when that which is of the nature of an obstruction is struck down and understood, [the path is clear].
Then Brahmā cast off his own radiant body;
having divided his own form into two, he became a male with one half.
With the other half, Śatarūpā was born as his wife;
she was the primordial nature (prakṛti) and the sustainer of all beings, created from the desire of the Lord as he was engaged in creation.
Having pervaded both heaven and earth with her majesty, she remains firmly established;
she is the primordial body of Brahmā, standing encompassing the heavens.
But the female half that was created, Śatarūpā, was born;
that goddess, having performed austerities most difficult to practice for a million years, [attained her state].
She obtained as her husband a man of radiant fame;
he was indeed the first Puruṣa, called Svāyambhuva Manu.
His period of authority here is said to be seventy-one yugas;
having obtained Śatarūpā as his wife, who was not born from a womb, the Puruṣa [proceeded].
He took delight with her; therefore she is called Rati.
That was the first union, which came into being at the beginning of the kalpa.
Brahmā created Virāj; he became the Puruṣa Virāj.
He was the sovereign Samrāṭ together with Śatarūpā, and is remembered as Manu Vairāja.
That Puruṣa Manu, Vairāja, brought forth the creation of beings;
from that Vairāja Puruṣa, Śatarūpā gave birth to two heroes.
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were two sons, the best among those who possess sons;
they had two daughters of great fortune, from whom these progeny were born.
O auspicious one, their names were Devī, Tathā, Kūlī, and Prasūti.
The Lord Svāyambhuva bestowed Prasūti upon Dakṣa.
He bestowed Ākūti upon Ruci Prajāpati;
from Ākūti, a pair of auspicious offspring was born to the mental Ruci.
Yajña and Dakṣiṇā became twins;
and from Yajña and Dakṣiṇā, twelve sons were born.
The gods other than those of Svāyambhuva are designated as the Yāmas; because they are the sons of Yama and of Sacrifice (Yajña), they are therefore remembered as the Yāmas.
The Ajitas and the Śukras are known as the two hosts of Brahmā;
the Yāmas have already been described, who are designated as the Divaukasas.
Upon Prasūti, the daughter of Svāyaṃbhuva and mother of the worlds,
the lord Dakṣa begot twenty-four daughters.
All of them were highly fortunate, all had lotus-like eyes;
they were all wives of yogins, and all of them were mothers of yogins.
And all were expounders of Brahman, all mothers of the universe:
Śraddhā, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Medhā, and likewise Kriyā.
The Lord Dharma accepted these thirteen daughters of Dakṣa— Buddhi, Lajjā, Vasu, Śānti, Siddhi, and Kīrti— as his wives.
These were the gates ordained for him by the Self-Existent One;
and there were eleven younger, beautiful-eyed sisters who followed after them.
Satī, Khyāti, Sambhūti, Smṛti, Prīti, Kṣamā, as well as Sannati, Anasūyā, Ūrjā, Svāhā, and Svadhā. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.9.52)
Then other great sages accepted them once again:
Rudra, Bhṛgu, Marīci, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, and Kratu.
Pulastya, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, the Pitṛs,
and Agni likewise gave Satī to Bhava, and Khyāti to Bhṛgu.
He gave Saṃbhūti to Marīci, Smṛti to Aṅgiras,
Prīti to Pulastya, and Kṣamā indeed to Pulaha.
To Kratu he gave Saṃtati, and likewise to Atri he gave Anasūyā; to Vasiṣṭha he gave Ūrjā, and to Agni he gave Svāhā.
And Svadhā belongs to the ancestors; hear from me now concerning their offspring.
All these highly fortunate beings remain following after their progeny.
Throughout all the Manvantaras until the dissolution of all beings, Śraddhā gave birth to Kāma; furthermore, Darpas is recorded as the son of Lakṣmī.
From Dhṛti, Niyama is the son; from Tuṣṭi, Saṃtoṣa is said to be born.
From Puṣṭi, Lābha is the son, and likewise Śruta is the son of Medhā.
Dama and Śama are said to be the two sons of Kriyā;
furthermore, Bodha and Apramāda are both the sons of Buddhi.
Vinaya was the son of Lajjā; Vyavasāya was the son of Vasu;
Kṣema was also the son of Śānti; and Sukha was born from Siddhi.
Yaśas was also the son of Kīrti; these were the sons of Dharma.
Harṣa, however, was born as the son of Kāma by the goddess Siddhi.
Thus, this creation of dharma characterized by sattva indeed results in happiness;
for from adharma, however, violence, deceit, and falsehood were born.
From Nikṛti and Anṛta were born Fear and Hell, as well as Māyā and Vedanā; these two pairs constitute their offspring.
Then from Māyā was born Mṛtyu, the destroyer of beings;
and from Vedanā was born Duḥkha, which arises from Raurava.
From Death were born disease, old age, grief, anger, and envy;
for all these are known to be characterized by suffering and are the marks of unrighteousness.
They have wives or sons, for all are remembered as being immortal;
such was this Tāmasa creation, born as the regulator of dharma.
Commanded by Brahmā to create progeny, Nīlalohita meditated upon his wife Satī and fashioned beings born from himself.
He created those mental sons, neither more nor less than himself and equal to him in mind;
and he also created a thousand times a thousand who were clad in animal skins.
Kapardin, who is blue-and-red in hue, saw them all as equal to himself in form, splendor, strength, and learning— tawny-complexioned and equipped with quivers.
They were shaven-headed and hairless, with eyes that put out vision; they were skull-bearers, possessing great forms, yet deformed, appearing in universal forms while having specific shapes.
Charioteers, armored warriors, archers, and those protected by defensive shields—
those with hundreds and thousands of arms, and those who move through the heavens, upon the earth, and in the intermediate space.
Those with large heads, eight tusks, two tongues, and three eyes;
those who eat food, those who eat flesh, those who drink clarified butter, and likewise those who drink soma.
They had massive and formidable bodies, blue throats, and fierce tempers;
they were equipped with quivers and armor, bearing bows, swords, and shields.
Whether they were sitting, running, yawning, or standing;
whether they were studying, muttering prayers, practicing yoga, or meditating.
[He saw] Buddhas and those who are most perfectly enlightened, blazing, raining, shining, and emitting smoke; they were the masters of Brahman, the perceivers of Brahman.
They have blue necks and a thousand eyes;
they all move upon the earth, yet are invisible to all beings—great yogis of immense power.
"Create these thousands of Rudras, the best of gods, who are thus endowed with weeping and running, and who are fresh and untiring."
Seeing this, Brahmā said to him: "Do not create such offspring;
one should not create offspring who are equal to oneself, nor indeed those who are superior."
"Create other offspring—blessings upon you—endowed with death;
for beings who are free from death do not undertake actions."
Thus addressed, he said to him: "I shall not create offspring endowed with death and old age; may it be well with you. I remain here; you, O Lord, create them."
"These indeed, who were created by me, are multiform and blue-and-red;
for thousands upon thousands of my own selves have issued forth."
These gods shall become the mighty ones named Rudras;
on earth and in the intermediate space, they are renowned as the Rudrāṇīs.
Those who are recited in the Śatarudra shall become worthy of sacrifice here;
they shall all become partakers of the sacrifice together with the hosts of gods.
Those gods born of the Vedic meters who will exist here during the various Manvantaras,
being worshipped together with them, shall remain here until the end of the Yuga.
Thus addressed by Mahādeva, the lord Brahmā,
the progenitor of creatures, being observed by him, replied in that manner to Bhīma.
"So be it; may you be blessed, O Lord, according to what has been declared by you.
When Brahmā had thus given his consent, everything indeed came to pass.
From that time forward, that god indeed did not procreate offspring; remaining as Sthāṇu with his vital seed drawn up, he remained so until the dissolution of all beings.
Because he said, "I am standing," he is therefore remembered as Sthāṇu by the wise;
for he is knowledge, austerity, truth, sovereignty, and indeed righteousness itself.
Dispassion and self-awakening— all these reside in Śaṅkara,
as do all the gods and ṛṣis together with the asuras.
He surpasses all by his splendor; therefore he is remembered as Mahādeva.
He surpasses the gods by his sovereignty and the great Asuras by his strength.
Through his knowledge he [perceived] all the sages, and through his yoga all beings in every way;
even so, Mahādeva, who is saluted by all the gods,
having created progeny throughout the heavens and the earth, desisted from further creation.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Rudra," in the second section (Anuṣaṅga-pāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
The Sage said:
"In this Kalpa, the manifestation of the Great-Souled One was not mentioned by you."
Together with the seers who were practitioners of Mahādeva Rudra.
Sūta said:
I have briefly described the origin of the primary creation;
I shall now declare in detail the names [of the beings] along with their bodies.
Mahādeva begot many sons upon his wives;
now hear of them in this present kalpa, after other kalpas have passed.
At the beginning of the kalpa, the Lord meditated upon a son equal to himself;
thereupon, a dark-blue and red youth appeared upon his lap.
Seeing the youth Nīlalohita suddenly weeping, he wept with a loud and terrible cry, as if burning everything with his splendor.
"Why do you weep, O youth? Brahmā replied to him.
He said, "O Grandfather, give me my first name."
"O God, you are named Rudra. When he was addressed thus, he wept again.
Brahmā spoke to him: "Why do you weep, O Kumāra? (Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 1.10.7)
"Give me a second name," he said to the Self-Existent One.
"By the name of the gods, you are Bhava," he was told; and he wept again.
To him who was weeping, Brahmā replied, "Why do you weep? When he said, "Give me a third name," Brahmā spoke again.
When he was told, "O God, you are Śarva by name," he wept again.
To him as he was weeping, Brahmā replied, "Why do you weep? (Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 1.10.10).
When he was told, "Give me a fourth name," he spoke again:
"By the name of the gods, you are Īśāna. Having been told this, he wept once more.
To him who was weeping, Brahmā spoke again, asking, "Why do you weep? He replied to the Self-born One, "Grant me a fifth name. (Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 1.10.12)
"You are the Lord of beasts, O God"—having been addressed thus, he wept again.
To him who was weeping, Brahmā spoke once more: "Why do you weep? (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.10.13).
When he was told, "Give me a sixth name indeed," he replied to him, "O God, you are Bhīma by name. Having been thus addressed, he wept again.
To him who was weeping, Brahmā spoke again, "Why do you weep?
Being thus addressed, he replied, "Give me a seventh name. (Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 1.10.15)
"O God, you are Ugra by name"; having been addressed thus, he wept again.
To that weeping youth, he said, "Do not weep. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 1.10.16)
He said, "O Lord, give me yet another name, the eighth.
Having been told, "You are named Mahādeva," he indeed ceased speaking.
Having obtained these names, Nīlalohita spoke to Brahmā: "Please assign the locations for each of these names."
Then, their subtle bodies were emitted by the Self-Existent One under these names:
the Sun, Water, Earth, Wind, Fire, and Space.
The initiated Brāhmaṇa is the Moon; thus your body is eightfold.
Among these, he is to be worshipped, saluted, and respectfully honored with effort.
Brahmā spoke again to that youth Nīlalohita:
"O All-pervading One, as for what was previously said by me to you—that your name shall indeed be Rudra."
"When it was said, 'This is the first [form] of you, the first, named Ādityatanu,' that splendor which was his became your eye, the illuminator."
He entered each respective sun; therefore, he is remembered as Rudra.
One should avoid looking at the sun when it is rising or setting.
Since it is born perpetually and since it remains perpetually,
one who desires long life should always remain pure and not look upon the sun.
For the Brahmins, reciting the Sāman, Ṛg, and Yajur Vedas while performing worship at both twilights, indeed cause Rudra— the Lord of the past and the future— to swell with power.
Rising, he abides in the Ṛg-verses; at midday, he is in the Yajus-formulas;
and in the Sāmans during the afternoon, Rudra gradually enters into rest.
Therefore, one should never urinate toward Rudra under any circumstances—whether he has risen or has set. ||| BndP_1,10.27 |||
The god Rudra does not indeed harm those twice-born ones who are thus disciplined;
then Brahmā spoke again to that blue-and-red (Nīlalohita) god.
That second name which was proclaimed for you by me as "Bhava," let this water be your second body by that name.
When this was said, that which existed within his body as the essence of rasa entered him; therefore, he is remembered as Bhava, whose nature is water (āpaḥ).

Because beings arise from them and they cause those [beings] to develop, and because of their coming into being (bhavana) and their causing to grow (rāvana), it is called "existence" (bhava) for beings.
Therefore, one should never void urine or feces in water;
nor should one spit, nor bathe, nor engage in sexual intercourse therein.
One should not despise these waters, whether they are flowing or standing still; for these bodies of water have been declared by the sages to be both pure and impure.
Those that are discolored, tasteless, foul-smelling, and scanty in quantity should be avoided in every respect;
for the ocean is the source of waters, and therefore they desire it.
Even the waters that are middling become immortal once they reach the ocean;
therefore, one should not obstruct the waters, for they long for the sea.
"The god Bhava does not harm one who conducts himself thus in the waters.
Then Brahmā spoke again to the youth Nīlalohita.

let this body be the physical form of that third name.

Therefore, one should perform the evacuation of feces and urine on cultivated ground;
one should not urinate in the shade, nor on a path, nor in one's own shadow.
One should cover one's head and perform [the rite] after covering the ground with grass;
Śarva does not harm him who conducts himself thus upon the earth.
Then Brahmā spoke again to the youth Nīlalohita:
"The fourth name for you, which was proclaimed by me here, is 'Īśāna'."
"But the fourth [syllable] of the fourth [quarter], 'vā', is your body named Vāyu.

The Lord Īśāna entered that wind of his;
therefore, one should not speak ill of this wind, the sovereign lord, when it blows.
Those who indeed engage with him through sacrifices and those who serve him—

therefore, the god who is remembered as being in space is nowhere obstructed.
One should not void urine or feces, nor eat or drink;
one should not engage in sexual intercourse, nor should one throw away food remnants.

therefore, this moon is indeed perceived as Mahādeva.

on one particular night, both the sun and the moon were to come together.

for all this world is indeed pervaded by Rudra through both bodies and names.

by the light of the Sun, living beings behold with their eyes.
Established as the liberated self, Rudra drinks the water with his rays;

That subtle element born of water indeed accumulates within bodies;

That virtuous earthly body of his sustains all creatures,
which resides within the bodies of living beings through the functions of their vital breaths.
This northeastern direction consists of wind; it is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of living beings here, which digests all that is drunk and eaten within the bellies of creatures here on earth.

indeed, those cavities which exist here within the bodies are his.

That [power] of his is of a fierce nature; therefore, he is remembered as the "Fierce One" (Ugra) who has been initiated.
As for that which is his volitional faculty (*saṃkalpaka*), it is established here among living beings.
That mental body of his is the moon, which dwells within living beings and becomes ever-new as it is born again and again.
This Mahādeva, whose nature is nectar, is drunk at the proper time by the gods together with the ancestors; he is remembered as the moon, consisting of water.
His first body, which is proclaimed by the name Raudrī, has Suvarcalā as her wife; and his son is Śanaiścara.

That which is known as the earth is remembered as the body of the third name of Śarva;

The daughter of the fourth [Prajāpati], Īśāna, was Vātastanu;
her wife was named Śivā, and her son was Manojava.
Furthermore, there were two sons of Anila whose course was unknown;
and that body of Paśupati which is remembered by the twice-born as Agni [was also among them].
Her wife is known as Svāhā, and Skanda is remembered as her son;
that which is called the sixth form of Bhīma is said to be the ether (ākāśa).
The quarters are remembered as his wives, and heaven is also remembered as his son;
that which is the seventh body, the foremost, is remembered as the initiated Brāhmaṇa.
Initiation (dīkṣā) is known as his wife, and their offspring is called the son;
that which is the body of the eighth great light by name is known as the Moon.
His wife was indeed Rohiṇī, and his son is remembered as Budha;
thus these are his incarnations proclaimed along with their names.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "Description of the Manifestations of Mahādeva," in the second section (Anuṣaṅga-pāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Khyāti bore to Bhṛgu two sons who were the lords of pleasure and pain.
They are the bestowers of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness upon all living beings here in this world.
The two gods Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ wander through the Manvantaras;
their elder sister is the goddess Śrī, the creator of the worlds.
That beautiful woman, having obtained the god Nārāyaṇa as her husband,
gave birth to two sons of Nārāyaṇa who were intoxicated by their own strength.
The son of Bala was Tejas, and the son of Unmāda was Saṃśaya;
he had other mind-born sons who moved through the sky.
Those who carry the celestial chariots of the gods of meritorious deeds—
Merukalpā and Smṛtā, the two wives of the Creator and the Ordainer respectively.
Āyati and Niyati were their two sons, firm in their vows;
Prāṇa and Mṛkaṇḍa were the two eternal repositories of the Veda.
Mārkaṇḍeya was born to Mṛkaṇḍa by his wife Manasvinī;
his son Vedaśiras was born to him by Dhūmrā.
The sons of Vedaśiras were born of Pīvarī; they are remembered as the Vaśakaras, the sages known as the Mārkaṇḍeyas, who had reached the further shore of the Vedas.
From Prāṇa, Dyutimat was born as his son in Puṇḍarīkā;
from Dyutimat were born both Unnata and Svanavāta.
The sons and grandsons of those two Bhārgavas passed away from one another during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara; now hear of the progeny of Marīci.
Saṃbhūti, the wife of Marīci, gave birth to Pūrṇamāsa, who was born of his own self; now learn of these daughters of the Prajāpati.
Kṛṣi, Vṛṣṭi, Tviṣ, and Upaciti Śubhā—
these two sons he begot upon Sarasvatī during the full moon.
Both Viraja and Dharmiṣṭha were indeed Parvaśas;
the learned son of Viraja was the renowned Sudhāman by name.
That Sudhāmā, the son of Virāj, is the world-protector who dwells in the eastern quarter; he is righteous-souled, the son of Gaurī, and possessed of great majesty.
Having entered into the calculation of the lunar fortnights,
that highly illustrious one indeed begot two sons month by month during each successive fortnight.
Yajurdhāman and Dhīmant, as well as Stambhakāśyapa—
two sons were born to them who established their lineages and were resolved upon renunciation.
It is remembered that you were born as the wife of Girasa; for she gave birth to her own offspring—four sons and four auspicious daughters who are renowned throughout the world.
Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and likewise Anumati;
and similarly both Bharata and Agni Kīrtimant.
Likewise, Sadvatī gave birth to Parjanya as the son of Agni;
Parjanya, whose hair was golden, was born from Mārīcī.
He is indeed remembered as a world-protector who remains until the dissolution of all beings; and at the sacrifice of Kīrtimān, Dhenukā and Vītakalmaṣā were also present.
Cariṣṇu and Dhṛtimat were both the best among the Aṅgirases;
their sons and grandsons have indeed passed away by the thousands.
Anasūyā, free from blemish, gave birth to five sons of Atri and a daughter named Śruti, who was the mother of Śaṅkhapada.
The wife of Kardama was the daughter of the patriarch Pulaha;
[their sons were] Satyanetra, Havya, Āpa, Mūrti, and Śanaiścara.
And Soma was the fifth among them during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara;
these five past descendants of Atri, together with the Yāmadevas, are thus celebrated.
The sons and grandsons of those high-souled Ātreyas passed away by the hundreds and thousands during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
From Prīti, the wife of Pulastya, Dāna was born; Agni became his son.
In a previous birth, during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, he is remembered as Agastya.
Madhyama, Devabāhu, and the one named Atri—these were the three;
their youngest sister was renowned by the name Sadvatī.
The auspicious Parjanyajanani is remembered as the wife of Agni;
she was also the daughter of the wise Brahmarṣi Paulastya, who was the son of Prīti.
And Dānā, the wife of Sujaṅgha, gave birth to many sons who were renowned and remembered as the Paulastyas during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
Kṣamā, however, gave birth to the sons of the patriarch Pulastya,
all of whom possessed the brilliance of the three sacrificial fires and whose fame is firmly established.
Kardama, Corvarīvan, and Sahiṣṇu—these were the three;
and there was the sage Kanakapīṭha, as well as the auspicious daughter Pīvarī.
Śruti, the wife of Kardama,
herself gave birth to a son named Śaṅkhapada and likewise a daughter named Kāmyā.
That glorious Śaṅkhapada, the world-protector and lord of creatures, is established in the southern quarter; O Priyavrata, he has been given to you as a desirable gift.
Kāmyā obtained from Priyavrata ten sons equal to Svāyambhuva Manu,
as well as two pairs of daughters, through whom the Kṣatriya order was established.
The slender-waisted Yaśodharā gave birth to a son of Kanakapīṭha, renowned by the name Sahiṣṇu, who was like the god of love himself.
From Kratu, Saṃnati gave birth to sons equal to Kratu himself, all of whom were auspicious; they had neither wives nor sons, for they were all perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas).
Those sixty thousand known as the Vālakhilyas go before Aruṇa, surrounding the sun.
Until the dissolution of all beings, they all shall be companions to the sun;
and their two younger sisters were the virtuous Satyavatī and [Gāndhārī].
From Parvaśasya were born the Snusvas; from Pūrṇamāsa, the Sutās; and from Ūrjā, seven sons of Vasiṣṭha were born, who were the Vāsiṣṭhas.
And their eldest daughter was Puṇḍarīkā, who was slender-waisted;
she was the mother of Dyutimat and the beloved queen of Prāṇa.
Her younger sons were the seven renowned Vāsiṣṭhas:
Rakṣa, Gartodarbāhu, Savana, and Pavana.
Sutapā and Saṃkṛti—these were all the seven Ṛṣis who had passed away;
Ratna begot them upon the illustrious Mārkaṇḍeyī.
In the western quarter, King Ketumān was the Prajāpati;
these were the lineages and names of those high-souled Vāsiṣṭhas.
"Listen now to the progeny of Agni during the past Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
Thus has this creation of the sages been proclaimed, along with its subsequent details.

Sūta said:
O Agni, he who was known as Rabhimānin during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara,
being the mind-born son of Brahmā— Svāhā was born from him.
Pāvaka, Pavamāna, and that which is known as Śuci Agni— the fire produced by friction is Pavamāna, while the fire from lightning is known as Pāvaka.
Śuci is to be known as the son of Saura; those three are the sons of Svāhā:
Nirmathya, Pavamāna, and Śuci, who is remembered as the son of Saura.
Abhyagni and Vaidyuta—these indeed are their stations;
and Pavamānātmaja is called Kavyavāhana.
The son of Śuci was Pāvaki, also known as Saharakṣas and Havyavāha;
Agni is the carrier of oblations for the gods and Kavyavāhana for the ancestors.
Together with the Rākṣasas and Asuras, there were three fires for each of the three [classes];
the sons and grandsons of these, however, numbered exactly forty.
I shall declare their names and their individual divisions:
Viśruta, the worldly fire, was the first son of Brahmā.
Brahmādatta’s son was the renowned Bharata;
his son was Vaiśvānara, who carried the sacrificial oblation for a hundred years.
Formerly, Atharvan collected the primordial sacrificial fuel (medhiti) in the ocean of the lotus;
that Atharvan is the worldly fire, while the one who destroys pride is known as the Atharvaṇa fire.
Atharvan was born from Bhṛgu, and Agni is remembered as the son of Atharvan;
therefore, that is the common (laukika) fire, while Dadhyañc is considered the son of Atharvan.
The Pavamāna fire is remembered as the Atharvan, produced by the sages through churning;
he is to be known as the Gārhapatya fire, and his two sons are remembered.
The one who is praised and worthy of worship, remembered as the carrier of oblations for Agni,
is the second son, declared to be Śukra, the fire that is led forward.
Likewise, both Savya and Apasavya were the two sons of Agni Śaṃsya;
moreover, Śaṃsya, the bearer of oblations, desired sixteen rivers as his wives.
That fire which is the Āhavanīya, remembered by the twice-born as its presiding deity,
[is located] at the Kāverī, the Kṛṣṇaveṇā, the Narmadā, and likewise the Yamunā.
The Godāvarī, the Vitastā, the Candrabhāgā, the Irāvatī, the Vipāśā, the Kauśikī, as well as the Śatadrū and the Sarayū; 1,12.15.
Having divided the sixteenfold self into distinct portions within the Sītā, Sarasvatī, Hrādinī, and Pāvanī rivers, [he entered them].
He then placed himself within those hearths (dhiṣṇīs), and he became [the fire];
the hearth that moves among the Kṛttikās was born, and they are known as the Dhiṣṇyas.
Because they were born from the *dhiṣṇīs*, they are celebrated as the *dhiṣṇayas*;
thus indeed these sons of the river were born from the *dhiṣṇīs*.
Listen now to a brief and accurate account of those fires which are to be maintained and those which are to be attended by them. BndP_1,12.19 //
Vibhu is the Pravāhaṇa, and the other Dhiṣṇya fires situated there are ordained according to their respective places in the sequence of the libations on the day of the Soma-pressing.
Listen now to the sequence of the fires that are to be established without specific designation:
the Samrāḍagni, the Kṛśānu, and the second, which is the Antarvedika.
The eight [sages] headed by Samrāṭ Agnimukha attend upon those twice-born ones;
the Pavamāna assembly is indeed the second, and it is designated after them.
Another is called Nabhah; he is perceived in the four [quarters].
Then Havya, being unpolished, is perceived in the Śāmitra fire.
Ṛtudhāman and Sujyotis are proclaimed as the Audumbaras;
Viśvavyacas, the ocean-like Agni, is celebrated in the station of Brahman.
He whose abode is the light of Brahman and the Vasus is said to dwell in the station of Brahman;
he whose feet and private parts are not exposed is indeed one who finds happiness in his own home.
