For Ahirbudhnya is to be praised; he is remembered as Agni Gṛhapati.
All these sons of Śaṃsyas are remembered as those who are to be worshipped by the twice-born.
Next, I shall describe those who were to dwell [there], as well as his eight sons:
Vibhu, Pravāhaṇa, Agnīdhra, Dhiṣṇya, and others besides them.
On the day of the Soma-pressing, they are assigned to their respective places in the sequence of the libations;
for the fire known as Hotrīya is indeed remembered as Vahni, the bearer of oblations.
The fire Praśānta is the first, while the second here is named Pracetas;
thereafter, the fire Vaiśvadeva is called Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
Agni the Uśij is the sage who is perceived as the Purifier;
Agni the Āvāri and the Vābhāri are perceived as the Vaiṣṭhīya.
Avasphūrja is Vivasvat, and he is said to be Āsthā;
the eighth is Sudhūmragni, who is called Yomārjālīya.
For these are indeed brought from their hearths and are worshipped by the twice-born on the day of the Soma pressing;
he is remembered as the source of the waters, for he is perceived as having the name "Ap" (Water).
Then, he who is named Pāvaka and who is called the lotus-womb (abja) embryo—
that Agni is to be known as being present at the avabhṛtha rite, where he is worshipped together with Varuṇa.
Tadricchaya was his son, for he is the fire that digests food within the bellies of men;
Vidvān is known as the son of the digestive fire Mṛtyumān.
That fire, arising from mutual friction, would utterly consume all beings here;
the son of that wrathful fire is known as the terrible Saṃvartaka.
Drinking the waters, he dwells in the ocean as the Mare’s Mouth (Vaḍavāmukha);
the son of Samudravāsī, he is known as Sāharakṣa.
The son of Saharakṣas is emaciated and burns the houses of men;
his son is Kravyādagni, who devours those who are dead.
Thus these sons of the purifying Agni have been proclaimed; thereafter Śuci was indeed the son of Sūrya, and Āyu was offered by the Gandharvas.
That fire which is produced by friction in the forest kindles one fire with another;
however, that venerable one who is carried forth is known by the name Āyu.
Mahiṣa was the son of Āyu, and his son was named Sahas;
Agni, who takes pride in the *pākayajñas*, is remembered as the son of Sahas.
And the son of Sahasāgni was the wonderful and highly illustrious Vivici;
and the son of that Vivici was remembered as the great Agni Tumas.
Free from pride regarding expiatory rites, he always consumes the offered oblation;
his son is indeed Arka, and these are the sons of that Agni.
Anīkavān, Vājasṛk, Rakṣohā, Caṣṭikṛt,
as well as Surabhi, Vasu, and Annāda— he who has entered [them] is Rukmarāṭ.
For this progeny belongs to the pure fire, and there are fourteen fires;
thus these fires have been declared, which are indeed led forth in the sacrifices.
In the primordial creation, during the Svāyambhuva interval, those fires along with the Yāmas and the best of gods were formerly endowed with self-consciousness.

In this world, these beings— both conscious and unconscious— who were worthy of being inhabited, formerly existed as the carriers of oblations, conceiving themselves to be established in their respective places.
Established in these ritual acts— both those performed for specific desires and those performed as regular obligations—
they passed away in the previous Manvantara along with their sacrifices of white oblations.
These places and their inhabitants have been described by me as belonging to the first interval of Manu, during the time of the high-souled and meritorious gods.
By these very [verses], however, the characteristics of the fires (jātavedas) throughout all the past and future Manvantaras here have been fully enumerated.
For all these are indeed ascetics, and likewise all are sustainers of the Veda;
they are all remembered as lords of creatures and as luminous beings.
In all seven Manvantaras beginning with Svārociṣa, they are to be known as Sāvarṇyas, according to their names, forms, and purposes.
The fires exist together with the present gods;
likewise, the future fires will exist together with the future gods.
Thus has this collection of fires been enumerated in due order;
it shall be described again in detail and in proper sequence for the ancestors.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Accumulation of Fire," in the second section (Anuṣaṅga-pāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
The son said: "Formerly, during the Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara, while Brahmā was creating his sons..."
From his limbs were born humans, asuras, and gods.
Regarding him as their father, the Pitṛs (Ancestors) also were born from him; hear again in brief their creation, which was previously described.
Having created the gods, asuras, and humans, Brahmā felt dejected;
indeed, they were born from his armpits as if he were thinking of them as his fathers.
Spring and the other six seasons are called the Pitṛs;
"The seasons are the Pitṛs, the gods"—this is the Vedic revelation.
Indeed, throughout all the past and future Manvantaras,
these were previously produced during the auspicious Svāyambhuva interval.
The Agniṣvāttas are remembered by name, as are the Barhiṣads;
among them, those who did not perform sacrifices were the householders.
Those ancestors who did not maintain the sacred fires are remembered as the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs;
among them, those who were performers of sacrifices are the Pitṛs who drink Soma.
Those ancestors who are remembered as the Barhiṣads are indeed the performers of the Agnihotra;
the seasons, the ancestors, and the gods—this is the certainty reached in this scripture.
Madhu and Mādhava are to be known as the two juices; Śuci and Śukra are the two full of vigor; and Nabhas and Nabhasya are the two that sustain living beings. BndP 1.13.9.
Iṣa and Urja are the two months of the Ārdrā constellation, rich in *svadhā*.
Sahas and Sahasya are the two terrible months of the Tapas constellation.
Tapas and Tapasya are the two months of the cold season; these six, which are full of fervor, are established as the names of the months within the six seasonal states.
And these seasons have indeed been declared among both sentient and insentient beings;
the seasons are to be known as the sons of Brahmā, who possess self-consciousness.
The seasons are considered to be the inhabitants of the places consisting of the months and half-months;
apart from these places, they should be known as the presiding deities of the locations.
Days and nights, months, seasons, solstices, and years are indeed the abodes of those who possess self-conceit regarding the name "Kāma. (Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 1.13.14)
Now, listen as I describe those who are established in these states, fixed in time and condition; they are of that very essence and of that very nature. BndP 1.13.15.
Therein exist the Pārvaṇī sacrifices, the junctions of twilight, the fortnights measured by half-months,
as well as the moments (nimeṣa), units (kalā), instants (kaṣṭhā), hours (muhūrta), days, and nights.
Two fortnights constitute a month, and two months are said to be a season (ṛtu).
Three seasons constitute an ayana, and there are two ayanas: the southern and the northern.
The year and its divisions are these abodes of those who dwell therein;
likewise, the six seasons are to be known as the sons of Nimi.
The five classes of beings are known as the sons of Ṛtu, characterized by their seasonal nature;
for it is from these seasonal [periods] that all things, both stationary and moving, are born.
Therefore, the ancestors are the seasons, and the grandfathers are the seasons;
united together, they bring forth the progeny of Prajāpati.
Therefore, the year is indeed remembered as the great-grandfather of all creatures;
for these inhabitants of their respective stations are proclaimed to be the very essence of those stations.
They are known by that name, they possess that existence, and they are considered to have that as their essence;
he who is remembered as Prajāpati is regarded as the year.
For Agni, the son of the year, is called "Ṛta" by the wise;
and because the seasons (ṛtu) were born from Ṛta, they are therefore called ṛtus.
The months are to be known as the six seasons; among them, five seasons are traditionally taught for bipeds, quadrupeds, and indeed for all winged creatures alike.
Among the five classes of stationary beings, the flower is known as the seasonal bloom;
its state as a season, its nature as a seasonal product, and its status as the progenitor have been proclaimed.
Thus these Pitṛs are to be known, as well as the Seasons (ṛtus) and those belonging to the Seasons (ārtavas); from them all beings were born according to the time of the seasons.
Therefore, we have heard that these are indeed the Pitṛs known as the Ārtavas;
yet here, throughout the Manvantaras, they remain as the deities presiding over time.
Endowed with the nature of cause and effect, they abide pervading all through their sovereignty;
for these are the presiding deities of the locations who remain here by virtue of their attachment.
Furthermore, from the various Agniṣvātta and Barhiṣad Pitṛs,
Svadhā gave birth to two daughters who were world-renowned.
Menā and Dhāraṇī—by these two this world is sustained;
both of them were exponents of Brahman and both were practitioners of yoga.
Your ancestors gave their two auspicious daughters for the sake of dharma;
Menā was the mind-born daughter of those who are called the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs.
And Dhāraṇī Mānasī was known as the daughter of the Barhiṣads;
he created that auspicious one named Dhāraṇī for Meru to be his wife.
Those ancestors of yours who are remembered as the Barhiṣads and the Somapāyins,
as well as the Agniṣvāttas— Mena gave them to Himavat as wives.
Listen now to those who are remembered as invited, namely his grandsons:
Menā was the wife of Himavat, and she gave birth to Maināka.
The Gaṅgā, the best of rivers and the wife of the salt ocean, [flows there];
Maināka’s son is Krauñca, from whom Krauñcadvīpa is said to derive its name.
Meru’s wife was Dhāraṇī, who gave birth to a son, Mandara, endowed with divine medicinal herbs,
as well as three renowned daughters.
They know Velā, Niyati, and Āyati as the third;
Āyati is recorded as the wife of Dhātṛ, and Niyati as the wife of Vidhātṛ.
In the previous Svāyambhuva Manvantara, when the progeny of those two had indeed been proclaimed,
Velā bore to Sāgara one faultless daughter.
Prācīnabarhiṣ had a wife named Savarṇā, who was of the Sāmudra lineage;
ten sons were born to Prācīnabarhiṣ by Savarṇā.
All of them were named Pracetas and were masters of the science of archery;
the lord Dakṣa, the son of Svayambhū, became their son.
"By the curse of Tryambaka, during the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara.
Having heard this, Śāṃśapāyani then questioned Sūta.
How did he, having been born, become so skilled despite the curse of Bhava?
Tell that to us who ask, concerning the period of Cākṣuṣa Manu in the past.
Thus addressed, the charioteer, having invited Śāṃśapāyani, related the story concerning Dakṣa and the cause of the curse from Tryambaka.
Sūta said: Dakṣa had eight daughters, who have been mentioned by me;
having summoned them from their own homes, their father honored them in his house.
Then, having been honored, they all dwelt in their father’s house;
among them, the eldest was indeed Satī by name, the wife of Tryambaka.
Hating Rudra, Dakṣa did not indeed invite that daughter of his;
nor did Maheśvara ever show deference toward Dakṣa.
The son-in-law remained steadfast in his own nature before that father-in-law who was possessed of such splendor;
then, having learned of this, all those virtuous women continued to dwell in their father’s house.
Although she had not been invited, Satī went to her father’s house;
however, her father offered her a dishonorable reception, providing her with less honor than the others.
Then that goddess, provoked by anger, spoke to her father: "O Lord, you have offered me an inferior honor, even lower than that given to my younger sisters."
"O father, you have treated me with contempt and committed a reprehensible act;
I am the eldest and the most excellent, and it is right for you to honor me."
Thus addressed, Dakṣa, his eyes bloodshot with rage, said to her:
"My young daughters are superior to you, most excellent, and worthy of honor."
And their husbands, O virtuous lady, were highly esteemed by me;
they were most devoted to Brahman, great ascetics, masters of yoga, and profoundly righteous.
O virtuous lady, all of them were superior in qualities and praiseworthy because of their devotion to the Three-Eyed Lord:
Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Pulastya, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, and Kratu.
"Bhṛgu and Marīci are likewise my most excellent sons-in-law;
yet Śarva constantly vies with me and always treats me with contempt."
"Therefore, I do not adorn you, for my disposition toward you is hostile," so spoke Dakṣa at that time with a completely deluded mind.
Having been addressed by the supreme ṛṣis regarding her own curse and those [others] who were mentioned, that goddess, being enraged, spoke thus to her father: *Bṛhaddevatā* 1.13.56.
"Since you reproach me, who am blameless in my speech, mind, and actions,
therefore, O father, I shall abandon this body born of you."
Then, due to that insult, Satī, filled with indignation from her grief,
spoke these words after bowing to the Self-Existent One (Brahmā).
And wherever I am reborn with a radiant body,
there too I am born from one who is righteous, though not born of a womb.
"May I become the lawful wife of the wise Tryambaka himself. Then, remaining right there, she composed her mind and concentrated her soul.
And she maintained within her mind the fire-element concentration (dhāraṇā) of the self. Then, the fire arising from her own body, impelled by the vital wind (vāyu),
issued forth from all her limbs and reduced her to ashes.
Having heard of that death, and having understood the conversation between those two exactly as it was, the divine Śaṅkara, the Lord and Master who bears the trident,
became enraged at Dakṣa and the sages.
Rudra said: "Of all the worlds, the world of Bhūr is said to be the first;
by the command of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), I shall always sustain it."
All the radiant worlds are supported by this earth and remain here;
I constantly sustain them here by her command.
"For the four castes belong to the gods, and they eat together in one place;
I shall not eat with them, for then they will give [the offerings] to you separately."
"O Dakṣa, because my innocent daughter Satī was thus insulted,
while all her other praised sisters were honored by their husbands."
Therefore, when the Vaivasvata [Manvantara] has arrived,
these great seers shall indeed be born again in my second sacrifice, for they are not born from a womb.
When the *śukra* had indeed been offered by Brahmā during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu,
he addressed all of them and then cursed Dakṣa once again.
You shall become a human king in the lineage of Cākṣuṣa,
the grandson of Prācīnabarhis and the son of the Pracetasas.
"In this very Vaivasvata Manvantara, you shall indeed be born from Māriṣā, the daughter of the Śākhis, by the name Dakṣa. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 1.13.70)
O evil-minded one, I shall also create obstacles for you there,
even regarding that single, difficult-to-attain task of yours which is joined with righteousness.
Sūta said: Having heard that, Dakṣa then cursed Rudra again:
"Since you have brought about this misfortune for the sages on my account..."
Therefore, the twice-born shall indeed not sacrifice to you in the ritual together with the gods.
O cruel one, after they have offered an oblation to you in their rituals, they will touch water;
thus you shall dwell right here, having abandoned heaven at the end of the age.
Then he was no longer worshipped by those gods, but was instead worshipped separately;
thereafter, Dakṣa was addressed by Rudra of immeasurable splendor.
Having abandoned his self-born body, he was born here among human beings.
Having recognized the Lord and Master of sacrifices, the skillful householder performed a complete sacrifice here together with the deities.
Then, when the Vaivasvata interval had arrived, the king of mountains begot that goddess Umā, who was the goddess Satī, upon Menā.
The goddess who was Satī in the past later became Umā;
she is forever the wife of Bhava, and Bhava is never released from her.
The goddess was devoted to Marīci Kaśyapa as Aditi is to him,
as Śrī is to Nārāyaṇa, and as Śacī is to Maghavan.
Kīrti never abandons Viṣṇu, Ruṣā never abandons Sūrya, nor does Arundhatī ever abandon Vasiṣṭha;
these goddesses never forsake their husbands.
Returning through the kalpas, they are born again together with them;
thus was Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, born indeed during the Cākṣuṣa interval.
Furthermore, O King, we have heard that due to a curse, a second king was then born from the ten Pracetasas through Māriṣā.
And those seven great sages, Bhṛgu and the others,
were born formerly in the first Tretā Yuga of Vaivasvata Manu.
"At the great sacrifice of the God, while bearing the body of Varuṇa"—
such was the lingering remorse that followed those two through their subsequent births.
And from Prajāpati Dakṣa and the wise Tryambaka;
therefore, one should never harbor resentment toward enemies in this world.

Even for a being who has entered another birth and is subject to auspicious and inauspicious [karmas], the soul does not abandon its manifestation; therefore, a wise person should not act [in such a way].
Thus has this discourse, which liberates one from sin, been related in its entirety—
the very one that was previously proclaimed by you here concerning Dakṣa.
This narrative has indeed been proclaimed in connection with the lineage of the ancestors;
following the succession of the Pitṛs, I shall hereafter speak of the gods.
Formerly, at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga in the Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara,
there were those known as the Āyāma gods, who were previously the sons of Sacrifice (Yajña).
These sons of Brahmā are renowned as "the Unborn" (Aja) because they are unborn;
these mind-born sons of Svāyambhuva are indeed named Śaktas.
Since these groups of theirs are remembered as three classes of gods,
there were thirty-three born of their own will during the creation of Svāyambhuva.
Yadu’s two sons were the two gods Vīvadha and Sraṃsana;
Mati, Vibhāsa, Kratu, Prayāti, Viśruta, and Dyuti.
Vāyavya, Saṃyama, and Yāma—these twelve are proclaimed [as the sons of Yama].
Also Asama, Ugradṛṣṭi, Sunaya, and Śuciśravas.
Kevala, Viśvarūpa, Sudakṣa, and Madhupa; likewise Turīya, Indrayuk, and indeed Yukta, as well as Grāvajit.
Canimā, Viśvadeva, Javiṣṭha, Mitavān,
Jara, Vibhu, Vibhāvasu, Ṛcīka, and then Durdaha.
Śruti, Gṛṇāna, and Bṛhat—these twelve are proclaimed as the Śukras;
they were the drinkers of Soma during the interval of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu.
For these hosts were radiant, heroic, and possessed of great strength;
among them, Viśvabhuk was the lord and Indra in that first age.
At that time, those who were the heirs and kinsmen of the Asuras were the Suparṇas,
Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
Those eight divine classes of beings, together with the Pitṛs,
were the progeny who passed away during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara by the thousands.
Endowed with majesty, beauty, longevity, and strength,
they are not described here in detail, lest there be excessive prolixity in this work.
The creation of Svāyambhuva is to be understood as being concurrent with the present;
that past [creation] is not seen within the Vaivasvata [manvantara] by means of the present.
Together with the subjects, the deities, the sages, and the ancestors, there were formerly the serpent-sages among them; learn of them now.
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Marīci, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
and Atri, as well as Vasiṣṭha— these were the seven [sages] in the Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
Āgnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Modha, Medhātithi, Vasu,
Jyotiṣmān, Dyutimān, Havya, Savana, and Sattra.
These ten sons of Svāyambhuva Manu, possessed of great luster,
great speed like the wind, and great strength, were the kings during the first interval (Manvantara).
It included the Asuras, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas;
it also contained Piśācas and humans, along with hosts of Suparṇas and Apsarases.
It is not possible to describe them in their proper sequence even in hundreds of years;
because the names are so numerous, how could there be a count of them within a single family?
Indeed, those beings known as the *yugas* who existed during the Svāyaṃbhuva interval have passed away through the long course of time, by means of the sequence of solstices, years, and *yugas*.
The sages said:
Who is this Lord Time (Kāla), the seizer of all beings?
Of what is he the source, what is his origin, what is his true essence, and what is his nature?
What is its eye, what is its form, and what are its limbs said to be?
What is its name, and what is its self? Tell me this truthfully.
Sūta said:
Listen to the true nature of Time; having heard it, let it be understood.
He is called the source of the Sun, the beginning of the *nimeṣa* (twinkling of an eye), and the eye of calculation.
Day and night are his physical form, and he consists of the parts of time known as the *nimeṣa*;
the year is his essential nature, and his name is composed of the *kalā* units.
That Prajāpati consists of the present, future, and past times;
now learn of the fivefold division of the states of time.
By means of half-days, fortnights, months, seasons, and likewise solstices,
there is the first year and the second, the *parivatsara*.
The third is Iḍravatsara, the fourth is Anuvatsara, and the fifth is Vatsara; that period of time among them is designated as a Yuga.
I shall declare their true nature; listen as it is being proclaimed.
That which is called the sacrificial fire is considered to be the year.
That Sūrya is the son of Aditi, the fire of time, the year,
the one whose path is both white and black, the essence of the waters, and the sky-goer.
That Soma, known as Iḍāvatsara, has reached a firm conclusion in the Purāṇa;
he who purifies the worlds with his seven-times-seven forms.
That wind which blows according to the world is the Anuvatsara;
Rudra, who was produced from the ego (ahaṅkāra) by Brahmā, is the Udag-vāyu.
That Rudra, who is blue-and-red (nīlalohita), should be known as their year;
I shall declare his true nature—listen as it is being proclaimed. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.13.120)
From the conjunction of the major and minor limbs [of the body], he became the Grandfather (Brahmā), the soul of time,
the source of the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus Vedas, the Lord and master of the five elements.
He is Agni, Yama, and Kāla; he is Saṃbhūti and Prajāpati;
and he is declared by the wise to be the year and the sun.
Because [he is the cause] of the divisions of time— of months, seasons,
and solstices— as well as of the planets, constellations, cold, heat, rain, lifespan, and karma.
He is the source of all divisions and the sun of the days;
he is the transformative one, the pure-souled Prajāpati, the son of Brahmā.
He is the One, not the many; he is the day, the month, and the season, O Grandfather;
he is Āditya, Savitṛ, and Bhānu; he is the source of life, honored by Brahmā.
Because he is both the source and the imperishable of all beings, the Sun (Bhāskara),
who presides over the stars, is to be known as the second year, Parivatsara.
Soma is the lord of all herbs, for he is the great-grandfather;
he is the life-sustenance of all beings, the Lord who provides their security and prosperity.
Constantly observing, he sustains the world with his rays during the lunar days, the junctions of the phases, and at both the full moon and the new moon.
Since he is the source, the maker of night, the one whose nature is nectar, and the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), Soma is therefore remembered as having a father; he is the essence of the year.
Through the functions consisting of prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, and udāna,
he is the initiator of all the activities of living beings in this world.
Even while accomplishing the simultaneous performance of the functions of the five senses, the mind, intellect, memory, strength, and the self, [he remains unattached].
He who is the self of all and the lord of all worlds exists through the seven sets of seven bodies, such as Āvaha, Pravaha, and the others, performing his beneficial services.
He is the ordainer of all beings, the eternal protector, and the wind that shatters; he is the source of fire, water, earth, the sun, and the moon.
Vāyu is Prajāpati, the manifested soul of the worlds, the great-grandfather;
because he creates day and night, that Vāyu is the year.
These four Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis), born from the armpits,
are proclaimed as the fathers of all worlds and the very selves of the worlds.
O Brahmins, as Brahmā was meditating, Bhava emerged from his mouth—
the seer, the great god, the soul of all beings, and the great-grandfather.
The Praṇava, which is recited as the Lord of all beings,
is the source of the limbs and minor members of beings through the infusion of the Self.
Rudra, the intoxicator and the bestower of grace, is called Vatsara;
likewise, he is Sūrya, Candramas, Agni, Vāyu, and Rudra.
The Lord Rudra, the soul of time who presides over the ages, the all-pervading one who eternally effects destruction, has entered this world with his own splendor.
Through the conjunction with me as his support, he likewise [manifested] by means of subtle forms;
then, by his power, he acted for the benefit of the worlds.
Since he possesses divinity, the state of being a progenitor, and that supreme nature of time,
Rudra is indeed worshipped in every way by those who possess true knowledge.
For he, the Lord, is the master of the lords of creatures, the Prajāpati;
he is the creator of all beings, the soul of all, Nīlalohita.
Rudra repeatedly restores the medicinal herbs that have been exhausted by the gods,
who have Prajāpati as their leader, when they seek the fruits of their sacrifices performed with complete correctness.
Because the Blessed One is worshipped with three skulls when the medicinal herbs have been exhausted by the Three-eyed One, he is therefore called Tryambaka.
The Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, and the Jagatī, which are remembered by name as the Tryambakas— these, out of affection, are the wombs of the Vanaspati.
Through those three types [of powers] which have become one with his own vigor,
that sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is traditionally known as having three means of accomplishment and three potsherds (trikapāla).
He has three eyes because of that sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa); for this reason, he is remembered as Tryambaka.
Thus, indeed, this cycle of five years has been proclaimed by the wise.
And that year, which is declared by the twice-born to be fivefold in nature,
was born as a single sixfold entity known by the names of the seasons beginning with spring (madhu).
The five seasons, beginning with *ṛtu*, constitute the creation in brief;
such indeed is the great delusion regarding the lives of living beings.
Time rushes on, withdrawing all things, like the irresistible current of a river. (Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 1.13.149)
Indeed, their offspring—
sons and grandsons, infinite in number— are impossible to enumerate due to their vastness.
By reciting this lineage of the lords of subjects, who were great performers of meritorious deeds and possessed of glorious fame, one shall attain great spiritual perfection.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Existence of Time," in the second section, the Anuṣaṅga-pāda, of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
The son said:
Now, regarding all the intermediate periods (*antaras*) that have passed and those yet to come here:
All are born with an equal conceit regarding name and form.
The eight classes of gods who were the lords during that Manvantara,
as well as the sages and the Manus— all had identical purposes.
The lineage of Svāyambhuva has been transferred to the creation of the great ṛṣis;
listen as it is being proclaimed in detail and in its proper sequence.
The son of Svāyambhuva Manu had ten grandsons equal to him,
by whom this entire earth with its seven continents and its cities was [governed].
In the first Tretā Yuga, during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, Karavatī was established together with the oceans every year.
By those sons and grandsons of Priyavrata— who were endowed with goodness and austerity— this [earth] was populated by the progeny of Svāyambhuva Manu.
O illustrious lord of creatures, that daughter of Kardama gave birth to heroic sons endowed with progeny and possessed of desirable qualities through Priyavrata.
O auspicious one, you had two daughters and ten sons, Samrāṭ and Kukṣi;
and those two had ten heroic brothers who were equal to Prajāpati.
Āgnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Medhā, Medhātithi, Vasu,
Jyotiṣmān, Dyutimān, Havya, Savana, and Sabhra.
Priyavrata duly consecrated those seven kings over those seven continents;
now learn of the other continents as well.
He made the very powerful Āgnīdhra the lord of Jambūdvīpa,
and he also appointed Medhātithi as the lord of Plakṣadvīpa.
On Śālmala, he consecrated Vapuṣmat as king;
the Lord made Jyotiṣmat the king in Kuśadvīpa.
Priyavrata consecrated Dyutimat as king in Krauñcadvīpa, and he also made Havya the sovereign of Śākadvīpa.
The Lord also performed a sacrificial session at Puṣkara;
from that sacrifice at Puṣkara, Mahāvīta was born as his son.
Dhātaki—these two were the excellent sons of that virtuous father;
the region known as Mahāvīta was named after that great-souled one.
And because of the name of Dhātaki, it is called Dhātakīkhaṇḍa;
the lord Havya begot sons who were the rulers of Śākadvīpa.
Jalada, Kumāra, Sukumāra, Maṇīvaka,
Kusumottara, Modāka, and the seventh, Mahādruma.
The first [manvantara] of the Manu Jalada is called Jalada;
the second of the Manu Kumāra is proclaimed as Kaumāra.
The third son was Sukumāra, and his hundred sons were likewise delicate; the fourth son of Maṇīvaka is here called Maṇīvaka.
The fifth region is Kusumottara, where there is a rain of flowers; the sixth region is proclaimed as Modaka, where even the sweetmeat is a source of delight.
And because of the name Mahādruma, that seventh region is called Mahādruma;
indeed, those seven regions there are named after them.
The son of Dyutimat, the lord of Krauñcadvīpa, was indeed Kuśala; his sons were Manonuga, Choṣṇa, Pāvana, and Andhakāraka.
Muni and Dundubhi were indeed the two sons of Dyutimat;
after them, the auspicious regions situated within Krauñcadvīpa were named for their own names.
But the region of Kuśala was known by the famous name Kauśala;
and the region of Manonuga is remembered as Mānonuga.
The region of Uṣṇa is known as Uṣṇa, and that of Pāvana is likewise Pāvana;
the region of Andhakāra is proclaimed to be Āndhakāra.
The region of the Sage is indeed Maunideśa, and that of Dundubhi is known as Dundubhi;
these are the seven radiant provinces within Krauñcadvīpa.
In Kuśadvīpa, there were seven sons of Jyotiṣmān who possessed great majesty:
Udbhijja, Veṇumān, Vairatha, Lavaṇa, and Dhṛti.
The sixth is Prabhākara, and the seventh is remembered as Kapila; the first region is Udbhijja, and the second is Veṇumaṇḍala.
The third is indeed Rathākāra, the fourth is known as Lavaṇa;
the fifth is the Dhṛtimat-varṣa, and the sixth is the Prabhākara-varṣa.
The seventh is named Kapila, which is proclaimed as belonging to Kapila; their countries in Kaśadvīpa bear those very same names.
Adorned by subjects engaged in the conduct appropriate for their respective stages of life (āśrama),
those seven sons of Śālmalī were endowed with great physical beauty and became the lords of that region.
Śveta, Harita, Jīmūta, Rohita,
Vaidyuta, Mānasa, and Suprabha as the seventh.
The region of Śveta was Śveta; that of Harita was Suhārita;
that of Jīmūta was Jīmūta; and that of Rohita was Rohita.
Vaidyuta was the son of Vaidyuta, and Mānasa was the son of Mānasa;
Suprabha was the son of Suprabha—these seven were the protectors of the regions.
I shall now describe Plakṣadvīpa, which follows immediately after Jambūdvīpa.
There were seven sons of Medhātithi who were the kings and lords of Plakṣadvīpa.
The eldest is named Śāntabhaya; the second is remembered as Śiśira;
the third is Sukhodaya, while the fourth is called Nanda.
Śiva was the fifth among them, and Kṣemaka is said to be the sixth;
Dhruva is to be known as the seventh—these are remembered as the sons of Medhātithi.
Indeed, those seven regions are named after those seven [sages];
therefore, they are Śāntabhaya, Śiśira, and Sukhodaya.
Ānanda, Śiva, Kṣemaka, and likewise Dhruva—
these are their seven regions, equal in size and divided accordingly.
These were previously established by those sons of Medhātithi, the kings who were lords of Plakṣadvīpa, during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
In Plakṣadvīpa and the other continents up to Śākadvīpa, the subjects have been established as being endowed with the conduct of the castes and stages of life.
Indeed, the Dharma among the five [elements] is to be known as that which distinguishes the social classes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas),
and it eternally bestows happiness, longevity, beauty, strength, and righteousness.
Among these five islands, Prakṣadvīpa is known to be common to all;
it has been described, so now learn of Jambūdvīpa.
Priyavrata consecrated Āgnīdhra— the eldest heir, the son of Kāmyā, and possessed of great strength—
as the king and sovereign of Jambūdvīpa.
He indeed had nine sons who were equal to the Prajāpatis;
the eldest was known as Nābhi, and his younger brother was Kimpuruṣa.
Harivarṣa was the third, while Ilāvṛta was the fourth;
Ramya was the fifth son, and Hiraṇvān is said to be the sixth.
Kuru is the seventh among them, and Bhadrāśva is recorded as the eighth;
Ketumāla is the ninth—learn now of their respective regions.
The father gave the region to the south of Nābhi, known as Himavat;
and he gave the region of Hemakūṭa to Kimpuruṣa.
He gave the region known as Naiṣadha to Harivarṣa,
and he gave that which was the central region of Sumeru, Ilāvṛta, to him.
The region known as Nīla was given by Ramyaka to Itarpta;
and the northern region, Śveta, was given by his father to Hiraṇvat.
He gave the region north of Śṛṅgavat to Kuru,
and likewise he assigned the region of Sālyavat to Bhadrāśva.
He assigned the region of Gandhamādana to Ketumāla;
thus have these nine regions been described by me according to their divisions.
That righteous-souled one consecrated those sons as Āgnīdhra among those regions in due order, and thereafter he remained established in asceticism.
Thus, by these seven sons of Priyavrata and the grandsons of Svāyambhuva, the entire earth consisting of seven continents was settled.
Thus, in all the ages, when a dissolution has occurred, the settlements are established again and again by the seven kings over each of the seven [continents].
Such is the nature of the eons and the arrangement of the islands,
including those such as Kimpuruṣa, whose eight colors have been heard of.
For them, success by its very nature comes easily and without effort;
for them there is no adversity, nor is there any fear of old age or death.
In those eight fields, dharma and adharma do not exist, nor are there superior, inferior, or middling [beings]; nor does the condition of the ages (yuga) exist in any way whatsoever in those fields.
I shall describe the lineage of Nābhi; listen to it in this account called Himavat.
Nābhi begot a son of great splendor upon Merudevī.
To Ṛṣabha, the best of kings and the first-born of all the kṣatriyas,
was born Bharata, a hero who was the eldest of a hundred sons.
Having consecrated his son as the preeminent ruler, he remained established in the great life of renunciation;
he then assigned the southern region known as Himāvat to Bharata.
Therefore, the wise know that this land of Bhārata is named after him;
Bharata’s son was the learned and righteous Sumati by name.
In that kingdom, Bharata consecrated him;
then, having transferred his royal fortune to his son, the king entered the forest.
The son of Tejas was also Prajāpati Amitrajit;
the learned son of Tejas is remembered as Indradyumna.
Parameṣṭhin was also his son, and upon his death, Pratīhāra became the head of that family; from him, the lineage known by that name was born.
From that wise one was born the one renowned as Pratihartṛ;
the son of Pratihartṛ is remembered as Unnetṛ, and Bhūman was his son.
Udgītha was his son, and Prastāvin was his son as well;
Vibhu was the son of Prastāvin, and Pṛthu was his son.
And Pṛthu’s son was Nakta; Nakta’s son was Gaya;
Gaya’s son was Nara; and Nara’s son was Virāṭ.
The son of Virāṭ was the wise and greatly heroic Dhīmān;
and the son of that Dhīmān was Mahān, and the son of Mahān was Bhauvana.
Tvaṣṭṛ was the son of Bhauvana, and his son was Virajas;
Rajas was the son of Virajas, and likewise Śatajit was the son of Rajas.
He had a hundred sons, all of whom were indeed kings;
they were headed by Viśvajyotis, and by them these subjects were caused to prosper.
By them, this Bhārata-varṣa consisting of seven islands was marked here;
and by those born of their lineage, this land of Bhārata was enjoyed in ancient times.
There are seventy-one cycles known as Yugas, consisting of the Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth;
together with those Yugas that have passed, there were those kings and their lineages.
Formerly, in the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, there were hundreds and thousands [of such beings];
thus was the creation of Svāyambhuva, by which this world was filled.
This creation of the ṛṣis, the deities, the ancestors, the gandharvas,
the rākṣasas, the yakṣas, the bhūtas, the piśācas, as well as humans, beasts, and birds,
has been described; it revolves together with the yugas.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Lineage of Priyavrata," in the second section (Anuṣaṅga-pāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said: Having thus heard the arrangement of the progeny, Śāṃśapāyani...
He questioned the Sūta with certainty regarding the extent of the earth and the oceans.
How many continents, oceans, or mountains are recorded? And how many regions are there within them, and what rivers are said to exist?

Tell us all this in detail and according to the truth: the dimensions of the great elements, as well as the world and the non-world, their synonyms, their measurements, and likewise the course of the moon and the sun.
Sūta said:
"Indeed, I shall proclaim to you the extent and dimensions of the earth."
He also [described] the number of oceans and the extent of the continents,
as well as the thousands of divisions of continents contained within the seven.
It is not possible to describe them here in their entirety, by which [beings] the world is constantly pervaded;
I shall, however, declare the seven continents along with the moon, the sun, and the planets.
Regarding these matters, humans set forth proofs through reasoning;
however, those entities which are truly inconceivable cannot be established by means of reasoning.
That which is beyond the primary elements is declared to be inconceivable;
I shall now describe Jambūdvīpa with its nine regions exactly as they are.
Learn from me its extent and its mandala:
it measures one hundred thousand yojanas in circumference.
It was filled with various provinces and diverse, auspicious cities;
it was crowded with *siddhas* and *cāraṇas*, and adorned with mountains.
And with [waters] bound to all the elements, arising from networks of stone,
and with rivers originating from mountains, [it was filled] from every side.
Jambūdvīpa is vast and glorious, with a wide circular perimeter on all sides; it is entirely encompassed by nine worlds that bring forth all beings.
It is surrounded on all sides by the salt ocean,
which is equal in extent to Jambūdvīpa on every side.
These six mountain ranges of the world-continents extend eastward, possess beautiful peaks, and are deeply immersed on both sides into the eastern and western oceans.
Himavān consists mostly of snow, as does Hemakūṭa which abounds in gold;
and the great mountain Niṣadha is pleasant in all seasons.
Meru is remembered as being four-colored and made of gold, most beautiful to behold;
it is thirty-two thousand [yojanas] wide at its summit.
It was circular in shape and proportion, square, and elevated;
its sides were of various colors, endowed with the qualities of Prajāpati.
Born from the navel of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, the first-born was white in complexion; therefore, he is called a Brāhmaṇa. (Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 1.15.18)
To his left was Raktavarman by nature;
because of him, his status as a Kṣatriya arose, for Meru is the cause of various purposes.
And because it is yellow on the right side, he is considered to belong to the Vaiśya caste;
moreover, it is covered on the west with a hue resembling the wings of a bhr̥ṅga bee.
"Therefore, his state as a Śūdra would arise"; thus were the castes proclaimed—defined by conduct, by inherent nature, by color, and by measure.
Nīla is made of lapis lazuli, Śveta is white and golden,
while Śṛṅgavān is the color of a peacock’s plumage and is made of śātakaumbha gold.
These are the kings of mountains, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas;
the distance between them is said to be nine thousand [yojanas].
In the center, however, is the region named Ilāvṛta, surrounding Mahāmeru;
it is nine thousand [yojanas] wide on all sides.
In its center stands the great Mount Meru, like a smokeless fire;
the southern half of the altar belongs to Meru, and likewise the northern half.
As for those six Varṣas and their mountain ranges,
each is two thousand yojanas in width and height.
The length of those two mountains is said to be equal to the width of Jambūdvīpa; they are each one hundred and twenty thousand yojanas long.
Nīla and Niṣadha; those others which are inferior to these two are Śveta, Hemakūṭa, Himavat, and likewise Śṛṅgavat.
Their length is two thousand nine hundred and eighty;
in their midst are the inhabited regions, which indeed consist of seven castes.
But those regions, surrounded by mountains rugged with precipices and covered by various rivers, are inaccessible to one another.
In them dwell beings of various kinds in every way;
this is the region of Haimavata, renowned by the name Bhārata.
Indeed, beyond Hemakūṭa is the region known by the name Kiṃpuruṣa;
and beyond Hemakūṭa is Naiṣadha, which is called Harivarṣa.
Beyond Harivarṣa and on the other side of Meru is Ilāvṛta;
beyond Ilāvṛta lies the region known as Somyaka, which is famous by that name.
Beyond Ramyaka lies the renowned Śveta, which is made of gold;
beyond Hiraṇmaya is indeed that which is known as Śṛṅgavān, O Kuru.
The two regions, the southern and the northern, should be known as being shaped like a bow;
among them, four are long, and the middle one is Ilāvṛta.
The southern half of the sacrificial altar is known as that which lies to the east of Niṣadha,
while the northern half is that which lies beyond Nīlavaṅta.
On the southern half of the Vedi there are three regions, and likewise three on the northern half;
between those two, Meru is to be known as the center, and [the region] Ilāvṛta is situated in the middle.
To the south of Nīla and to the north of Niṣadha,
there extends a great mountain named Mālyavat.
The distance from Ānīla to Niṣadha is one thousand yojanas,
while its length is proclaimed to be thirty-four thousand yojanas.
To its west, the mountain Gandhamādana is to be known; furthermore, the mountain renowned as Mālyavat is equal to it in length and breadth.
In the center of the circular [continents] stands Mount Meru, the golden mountain;
it is four-colored, made of gold, square, and lofty.
Sumeru, white and resplendent, shone like a king when occupied [by him],
glowing with the color of the young sun like a smokeless fire.
It rises eighty-four thousand yojanas high;
it enters sixteen thousand yojanas below the surface and is likewise sixteen thousand yojanas in width.
Because it is shaped like a shallow bowl, its width is thirty-two [yojanas] across the heads;
its circumference all around is three times that width.
By way of its circular circumference, its measurement is desired as being triangular;
it is forty thousand yojanas all around.
The measurement for a triangular [mandala] is proclaimed to be eight more [than that];
the circumference all around is measured by the square measure.
That great divine mountain is prescribed to be sixty-four thousand yojanas in extent, and it is endowed with divine medicinal herbs.
The entire world was covered with auspicious objects made of gold;
there, all the hosts of gods, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas [were present].
Upon the king of mountains, the auspicious hosts of Apsarases are seen;
that Meru is surrounded by the worlds that bring forth all beings.
Indeed, his four regions are established on the four sides:
Bhadrāśva, Bharatāśva, and Ketumāla in the west.
And the Northern Kurus are the refuge for those who have performed meritorious deeds;
on the slopes of Mount Gandhamādana, however, lies the other Aparagaṇḍikā.
It is delightful in all seasons, eternally joyful, and auspicious;
it measures thirty-two thousand yojanas from east to west.
In length it measures thirty-four thousand [yojanas];
there, those of auspicious deeds, the Ketumālas, are established.
There, all the men were of long life, great beings, and possessed of great strength;
and all the women had the luster of lotus petals and were lovely to behold.
There stands a divine great tree, a jackfruit tree (*panasa*) that is the source of the six flavors;
it is the lord, the son of Brahmā, who moves at will with the speed of thought.
Having drunk its fruit juice, they live for a thousand years;
moreover, on the eastern side of Mālyavat is the unprecedented Gaṇḍikā.
In length and breadth, just as this other secondary region (aparagaṇḍikā) is,
so should Bhadrāśva be known there, its inhabitants always joyful in mind.
And here is the Bhadraśāla grove, where there is a great tree, the Kālāmra;
there those men are white, possessed of great energy, and endowed with strength.
The women have the luster of white water-lilies, are beautiful and pleasing to behold;
they possess the radiance of the moon, the complexion of the moon, and faces resembling the full moon.
Those women have limbs as cool as the moon and the fragrance of blue lotuses;
their lifespan is ten thousand years, free from disease.
Having drunk the juice of the black mango, all [the inhabitants] possess stable youth;
[it lies] to the south of Śveta and to the north of Nīla.
In that age known as Ramanaka, human beings are born there who are devoted primarily to pleasure, pure, and free from old age and foul odors.
They were all born of pure lineage and pleasing to behold;
there too was a very great, vast, red *nyagrodha* tree.
Drinking the juice of that fruit,
they indeed subsist for ten thousand years and fifteen hundred years.
Those highly fortunate ones, the best of men, live there forever, being ever beheld on the southern side of Śṛṅgavān and also to the north of Śveta.
There is a region named Hairaṇvata, where the river Hairaṇvatī flows;
there human beings are born with great strength and radiant splendor.
The Yakṣas are heroes, great beings, wealthy, and pleasant to behold;
those of great majesty live for eleven thousand years.
They live for a lifespan of fifteen hundred years;
in that year, there is a great lakuca tree which is the repository of the six flavors.
Having drunk its fruit juice, they live free from disease.
Śṛṅgavān has three peaks that are lofty and vast.
One of them was made of jewels, another was made of gold,
and one was composed of all kinds of gems, adorned with celestial mansions.
To the north of Śṛṅgavān and to the south of the ocean lies that meritorious region, Kuru, which is frequented by the Siddhas.
There, the trees bear honeyed fruit and are always laden with flowers and fruit;
they produce garments, and within their fruits are found ornaments.
There, some charming trees that grant all desires exude the finest honey,
endowed with exquisite fragrance, color, and flavor.
There are other delightful trees there called Kṣīrin,
which constantly exude milk that possesses the six flavors and is like nectar.
The entire ground consists of jewels with fine golden sand;
it is endowed with the comforts of all seasons, free from mud, devoid of dust, and auspicious.
Falling from the world of the gods, auspicious men are born there;
they are endowed with pure lineage and all possess perpetual youth.
Pairs are born there, and women who are like celestial nymphs;
they drink the milk of those milch-cows, which is indeed comparable to nectar.
A couple is born at once, and they grow up together;
their character, appearance, and even their affection are equal.
Mutually affectionate like ruddy geese,
they were indeed free from disease and sorrow, constantly enjoying happiness.
Thirteen thousand one hundred and fifty of those great heroes live, and they do not consort with any other woman.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Extent and Dimensions of the Earth," in the second section (Anuṣaṅgapāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Such indeed is the natural configuration of the regions in the auspicious land of Bhārata.
It has been seen by those who know the supreme reality; what more shall I describe to you?
The sage said:
This is the land of Bhāratavarṣa, wherein these fourteen Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva, have repeatedly presided over the creation of progeny.
"We wish to know this; O best of beings, explain it to us.
Having heard these words of theirs, Romaharṣaṇa spoke.
In this regard, I shall describe to you the subjects in this land of Bhārata;
for this central region is wondrous, giving rise to both auspicious and inauspicious fruits.
That region which lies north of the ocean and south of the Himavat is named Bhārata, wherein this Bharata progeny resides.
Because he supported his subjects, Manu is called Bharata;
and according to the etymological definition, that region is likewise known as Bhārata.
From here, heaven, liberation, the intermediate state, and the end are reached;
indeed, for mortals, no other place on earth is prescribed for the performance of ritual action.
Learn now of the nine divisions of this land of Bhārata;
they are known to be separated by oceans and are inaccessible to one another.
Indradvīpa, Kaśerumān, Tāmravarṇa, Gabhastimān, Nāgadvīpa, Saumya, Gāndharva, and Vāruṇa.
But this ninth island among them is surrounded by the ocean;
this island extends for a thousand yojanas from south to north.
For its length extends from Kumārī to the source of the Gaṅgā,
and its width toward the north is exactly nine thousand [yojanas].
For this island is inhabited by Mlecchas on all its borders;
the Kirātas are known to dwell at its eastern edge, while the Yavanas are situated at the western.
The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras were established in their respective portions in the midst [of society], subsisting through sacrifice, weaponry, and trade.
Among them, indeed, mutual social interaction proceeds here,
joined with the aims of dharma, artha, and kāma, according to the specific duties of the social classes (varṇas).
And the resolve regarding the five stages of life according to the rules is for the sake of heaven and liberation in this world; it is within these that human activity proceeds.
As for this ninth island, which is said to extend across [the ocean],
he who completely conquers it is designated as a Sovereign (samrāj).
This world, O Emperor, is known as Samrāj; the intermediate space (antarikṣa) is remembered as Virāj; and that world [of heaven] is remembered as Svarāj. I shall speak of these again in detail.
In this [land], there are seven renowned principal mountain ranges:
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimān, and Ṛkṣaparvata.
The Vindhya and the Pāriyātra—these seven are the principal mountain ranges (kulaparvata). There are thousands of other mountains that are situated near them.
Avijñāta, Sāravant, Vipula, Citrasānu,
Sandara, the best of mountains Parvataśreṣṭha, Vaihāra, and likewise Durdura.
Kolāhala, Sasurasa, Maināka, Vaidyuta,
Vātandhama, Nāgagiri, and likewise Pāṇḍuraparvata.
Tuṅgaprastha, Kṛṣṇagiri, Godhana, and Girireva;
Puṣpagiri, Ujjayantau, and likewise the Raivataka mountain.
Śrīparvata, Citrakūṭa, Kūṭaśaila, and likewise Giri;
others besides these are unknown, being small and subsisting on meager means.
Interspersed with them, the noble and the barbarian peoples dwell in their respective regions,
by whom these rivers— the Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, and the Sarasvatī— are drunk.
The Śatadru, the Candrabhāgā, the Yamunā, and the Sarayū;
likewise the Irāvatī, the Vitastā, the Vipāśā, the Devikā, and the Kuhū.
The Gomatī, Dhūtapāpā, Budbudā, Dṛṣadvatī,
Kauśakī, Tridivā, Niṣṭhīvī, and likewise Geḍakī.
Cakṣu, Lohitā—these [rivers] have issued from the foot of the Himavat;
as well as Vedasmṛti, Vedavatī, Vṛtraghnī, and Sindhu.
The Varṇāśā, the Nandanā, the great river Sadānīrā,
the Pāśā, the Carmaṇvatī, the Anūpā, the Vidiśā, and also the Vetravatī.
For the Kṣipras and Avantis are likewise remembered as those who take refuge in the Pāriyātra mountains;
as are the Śoṇa, the Mahānada, the Narmadā, the Surasā, and the Kriyā.
The Mandākinī, the Daśārṇā, and likewise the Citrakūṭā;
the Tamasā, the Pippalā, the Śyenā, the Karamodā, and the Piśācikā.
The Citropalā, the Viśālā, the Bañjulā, the Vāstuvāhinī,
the Sanerujā, the Śuktimatī, the Maṅkutī, the Tridivā, and the Kratu.
Those auspicious rivers, with waters like jewels, were born from the Ṛkṣavat mountain:
the Tāpī, the Payoṣṇī, the Nirvindhyā, the Sṛpā, and the river Niṣadhā.
Veṇī, Vaitaraṇī, Kṣiprā, Vālā, Kumudvatī,
Toyā, Mahāgaurī, Durgā, and likewise Vānnaśilā.
Those auspicious rivers of meritorious waters originate from the foothills of the Vindhya;
they are the Godāvarī, the Bhīmarathī, the Kṛṣṇaveṇā, and the Vañjulā.
The Tuṅgabhadrā, the Suprayogā, the Bāhyā, and the Kāverī—
these rivers flowing toward the south have issued forth from the foot of the Sahya mountain.
The Kṛtamālā, the Tāmraparṇī, and the Puṣpajātyutpalāvatī—
these noble rivers, all possessing cool waters, flow auspiciously from the Malaya mountains.
Trisāmā, Ṛṣikulyā, Bañjulā, Tridivābalā,
Lāṅgūlinī, and Vaṃśadharā are remembered as the daughters of Mahendra.
The Ṛṣikulyā, the Kumārī, the Mandagā, the Mandagāminī,
the Kṛpā, and the Palāśinī are known as those originating from the Śuktimat mountain.
All those rivers are indeed Sarasvatīs and Gaṅgās that flow to the ocean;
they are all remembered as the mothers of the universe and the removers of the world's sins.
From those [rivers] flow hundreds and thousands of other rivers and tributaries;
along them dwell these peoples: the Kurus, Pañcālas, Śālvas, Mādreyas, and Jāṅgalas.
The Śūrasenas, the Bhadrakāras, the Bodhas along with the Paṭaccaras,
the Matsyas, the Kuśalyas, the Sauśalyas, the Kuntalas, and the Kāśis and Kośalas.
The Godhas, Bhadras, Karings, Magadhas, along with the Utkalas—
these are generally proclaimed as the countries of the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa).
And at the northern extremity of the Sahya mountain, where the river Godāvarī flows—
that region is the most delightful on the entire earth.
There, a city named Govardhana was built by Rāma;
furthermore, divine trees and medicinal herbs from heaven were brought there for the sake of Rāma’s beloved.
They were planted by the sage Bharadvāja for the sake of his beloved;
therefore, that region to the east became delightful to the mind.
The Bāhlīkas, the Vāṭadhānas, the Ābhīras, the Kālatoyakas,
the Aparāntas, the Muhmas, the Pāñcālas, and the Carmamaṇḍalas.
The Gāndhāras, the Yavanas, the regions of Sindhu and Sauvīra, the Cīnas, the Tuṣāras, the Pallavas, and those from mountain caves.
The Śākas, Bhadras, Kulindas, Pāradas, Vindhya-cūlikas, Abhīṣāhas, Ulūtas, Kekayas, and Daśāmālikas; 1,16.48.
The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, as well as the families of Vaiśyas and Śūdras;
the Kāmbojas, Daradas, Barbaras, Aṅgas, and Lauhikas.
The Atrayas, along with the Bharadvājas, the Prasthalas, the Daśerakas, the Lamakas, the Tālaśālas, and the Bhūṣikas together with the Ījikas; BndP_1,16.50.
These are indeed the northern regions; now learn of the eastern regions:
Aṅga, Vaṅga, Cola, Bhadra, and the various tribes of the Kirātas, as well as the Tomaras, Haṃsabhaṅgas, Kāśmīras, and Taṅgaṇas.
The Jhillikas, the Āhukas, and likewise the Hūṇas and Darvas.
The Andhravākas, Mudgarakas, those dwelling within the mountains and those outside the mountains,
as well as the Plavaṅgas, Maladas, and Malavartikas, are to be known [as such].
The Samantaras, Prāvṛṣeyas, Bhārgavas, Gopapārthivas, Prāgjyotiṣas, Puṇḍras, Videhas, and Tāmraliptakas; // BndP_1,16.54 //
The Mallas, Magadhas, and Gonardas are known as the eastern provinces;
furthermore, there are other provinces inhabited by those dwelling in the Deccan.
The Paṇḍyas, the Keralas, the Colas, and likewise the Kulyas;
the Setukas, the Mūṣikas, the Kṣapaṇas, and the Vanavāsikas.
The Mahārāṣṭras, the Mahiṣikas, and the Kaliṅgas in their entirety;
the Ābhīras together with the Aiṣīkas, the Āṭavyas, and likewise the Sāravas.
The Pulindas dwelling on the crest of the Vindhya, the Vaidarbhas along with the Daṇḍakas, the Paurikas, the Maulikas, the Śmakas, and the Bhogavardhinās.
The Koṅkaṇas, Kantalas, Āndhras, Kulindas, Aṅgāras,
Māriṣas, and those regions of the South— learn now of the others as well.
The Sūryārakas, the Kalivanas, the Durgālās along with the Kuntarūs,
the Pauleyas, the Kirātas, and the Rūpakas together with the Tāpakas.
Likewise, the Karītas, all the Karandharas, the Nāsikas, and others, as well as those who dwell within the Narmadā; BndP_1,16.61 //
The Sahakacchas, along with the Sārasvatas, are to be subdued;
as are the Kacchis, the Surāṣṭras, and the Ānartas together with the Arbudas.
Thus, O inhabitants of the Vindhya, hear these [names] of the western regions:
the Maladas, the Karūthas, and the Mekalas, together with the Aitkalas.
The Uttamas, Daśārṇas, and Bhojas together with the Kiṣkindhakas;
the Tośalas and Kośalas, as well as the Traipuras and Vaidiśas.
The Tuhuṇḍas and the Barbaras, along with the Ṣaṭpurās and the Naiṣadhas, as well as the Anūpas, the Tuṇḍikeras, the Vītihotras, and the Avantyas.
All these districts are inhabitants of the Vindhya ridges;
hereafter I shall describe those countries which are situated in the mountains.
The Nihīras, Haṃsamārgas, Kupathas, Taṅgaṇas, Śakas, Apaprāvas, Raṇas, Ūrṇās, Darvas, and Sahūhukas.
The Trigartas, the Maṇḍalas, and the Kirātas along with the Tāmaras—
these four, O sages, declare themselves to be the Yugas within the land of Bhārata.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Tiṣya ages—
I shall describe their creation in full further on.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Lineage of the Bhārata Dynasty," in the second section (Anuṣaṅgapāda) of the first part of the glorious *Bṛhad Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
The sages said:
And as for the region of Kimpuruṣa and likewise Harivarṣa—
explain these to us according to their true nature, just as the Bhārata region was described by you.
Sūta said:
O Brahmins, listen attentively to that which you wish to hear.
In the Kiṃpuruṣa region, there is a vast grove of Plakṣa trees that resembles the Nandana garden.
The lifespan in Kiṃpuruṣa is recorded as ten thousand years;
the men there are golden-colored, and the women are like Apsarases.
There, human beings are born free from disease and sorrow, with minds perpetually joyful, possessing the luster of refined gold.
In the meritorious Kiṃpuruṣa Varṣa, there is an auspicious tree that flows with honey;
indeed, all the Kiṃpuruṣas drink its supreme nectar.
Beyond that, they declare the regions of Kimpuruṣa and Harivarṣa;
there, human beings are born resembling great silver.
Having descended from the world of the gods, all those who resemble gods, O Lord of All, are the men in Harivarṣa; they all drink the pure juice of sugarcane.
In Harivarṣa, all live for eleven thousand years, free from disease and with joyful minds.
There, old age does not afflict them, nor do they die soon;
that which I have described as the middle region is called by the name Ilāvṛta-varṣa.
There the sun does not scorch, nor do human beings age;
when [the world] is enveloped, the moon and sun along with the stars are neither illuminated nor visible.
There, human beings are born with the radiance of lotuses, the complexion of lotuses, eyes resembling lotuses, and the fragrance of lotus petals.
Subsisting on the juice of jambu fruits, free from excrement, fragrant,
wise, having enjoyed their pleasures, they experience the fruits of their virtuous deeds.
And those best of men, clothed in garments of great silver, shall remain in the world of the gods for thirteen thousand years.
The lifespan of those who dwell in Ilāvṛta is one year;
and that region extending nine thousand [yojanas] in each direction from Meru is likewise described.
Its extent is thirty-six thousand yojanas;
it is square on all sides and shaped like a shallow bowl.
On the western side of Meru, measuring nine thousand [yojanas],
stands the Gandhamādana mountain, thirty-four thousand [yojanas] in extent.
Extending from north to south between Nīla and Niṣadha,
it rises forty thousand [yojanas] above the surface of the earth.
The Mālyavat mountain in the east is proclaimed to be one thousand [yojanas] deep and likewise extensive; its dimensions are said to be equal to those.
Nīla is to the south, while Niṣadha is to the north;
between them stands the great Meru, established according to its own dimensions.
The extent of all these mountains, as they are submerged, should be equal to their width; their length is recorded as one million [yojanas].
Due to the circular nature of the ocean and the spherical nature of the terrestrial globe, their lengths decrease; they are recorded as being equal to squares.
The river Jambūrasavatī, resembling crushed collyrium, flows from the central part, dividing Ilāvṛta which is four-cornered.
On the southern side of Meru and to the north of Niṣadha,
there is a great, eternal Jambu tree named Sudarśana.
Endowed with eternal flowers and fruits, and frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
that lord of the forest is known by the name Jambūdvīpa after him.
The height of that great-souled king of trees is one thousand and another hundred yojanas; it touches the heavens on all sides.
The sages who perceive reality have calculated the measure of the fruit to be eight hundred and sixty-one *aratnis*.
Falling upon the earth, they produce a great sound;
the juice of the fruit of that Jambū tree flows forth, becoming a river.
Having circumambulated Meru, they enter beneath the base of the Jambu tree;
having seen it, those dwelling in Ilāvṛta always drink its Jambu juice.
When the juice of the jambu fruit is drunk, neither old age afflicts them,
nor hunger, nor fatigue, nor death, nor even lethargy.
There, the gold known as Jāmbūnada, which serves as the ornament of the gods, is produced; it is radiant and resembles the color of the Indragopaka insect.
The auspicious juice of the fruits of all the rain-trees is praised;
when it falls, it becomes that bright gold which is the ornament of the gods.
By the grace of the Lord, the earth swallows up their urine and excrement in every direction and in all respects, as well as those who have died.
The Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and Yakṣas are all said to dwell in Haimavata;
on Hemakūṭa, however, the Gandharvas together with the hosts of Apsarases are to be known.
All the Nāgas—Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and the rest—are on Niṣadha;
and upon Mahāmeru, the thirty-three sacrificial gods sport.
On the blue mountain made of lapis lazuli dwell the pure perfected ones and the celestial rishis;
the white mountain is said to belong to the Daityas and Dānavas.
Śṛṅgavān, the best of mountains, is the place of reabsorption for the ancestors,
situated according to their respective portions within these nine regions.
Beings, both mobile and immobile, have settled down;
their growth is seen in many ways, whether divine or human. Their number cannot be calculated, yet it is to be believed by those who desire prosperity.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Varṣas such as Kiṃpuruṣa," in the second section (Anuṣaṅga-pāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
On the ridge of the Himavat mountains, there is a mountain named Kailāsa.
In that place dwells the glorious Kubera together with the rākṣasas.
Accompanied by apsarases, the king, the lord of Alakā, indeed rejoices;
for from the foot of Kailāsa flows that auspicious, cool-watered, meritorious stream.
From that divine lake named Kumudvatī, which resembles the ocean, flows the auspicious river Mandākinī.
And on its bank is the great divine Nandana forest;
to the northeast of Kailāsa is the divine Sarvauṣadhi mountain.
Facing the mountain Sabala, which is variegated and composed of a treasury of jewels,
there is a mountain named Candraprabha, very white and resembling a gem.
At its foot is that great divine lake named Svacchoda;
from that divine source flows the river named Svacchodā.
On its bank is the great, divine, and auspicious Caitraratha grove;
on that mountain dwells Maṇibhadra together with his followers.
The cruel Yakṣa general, surrounded by Guhyakas,
as well as the auspicious Mandākinī river with its clear waters.
Having entered the middle of the earth’s circle, they reached the great ocean and the mountain Śivasattvauṣadhi, located to the east of Kailāsa and to the south.
Near that divine mountain composed of realgar with its variegated slopes,
there is a great mountain, red-hued with golden peaks, possessing the brilliance of the sun.
At his foot is a great divine lake named Lohita;
from it flows that great and meritorious river, the Lauhitya.
On its bank is the great forest of Devāraṇya, free from sorrow;
on that mountain dwells the self-controlled Yakṣa Maṇidhara.
Surrounded by gentle and righteous Guhyakas,
on the southern side of Kailāsa is the mountain of cruel creatures and medicinal herbs.
It is said that collyrium was produced from the body of Vṛtra for the sake of Trikakud;
there stands a very great mountain of lightning, composed of all minerals.
At its foot is the meritorious Mānasa lake, frequented by the Siddhas;
from it flows forth the auspicious Sarayū, renowned throughout the world.
On its bank is a divine forest, renowned by the name Vaibhrāja;
there dwells the self-controlled Praheta, the son of Tanaya, who is a follower of Kubera.
The Rākṣasa Brahmapīta, possessed of infinite prowess, dwells there,
surrounded by hundreds of terrible Yātudhānas who roam through the atmosphere.
But on the other side of Kailāsa is the mountain Aruṇa, the best of peaks, auspicious and composed of golden minerals, which is a source of medicinal herbs for meritorious beings.
The glorious mountain, beloved of Bhava, resembles a cloud and is covered with networks of white rocks made of śātakaumbha gold.
With its hundreds of golden peaks that seem to scrape the heavens,
Mount Muñjavat is a great, divine, and inaccessible mountain covered in snow.
On that mountain dwells the Lord of the Mountain, Dhūmralocana;
from his foot originates that lake named Śailoda.
From that source flows the auspicious river named Śilodā;
it enters the salt ocean between the two eyes of Sītā.
On its bank is a divine forest renowned as Surabhi;
to the north-west of Kailāsa is the mountain Sattvauṣadhi, belonging to Śiva.
Facing the excellent mountain named Gaura, which consists of yellow orpiment,
stands the very great, divine mountain Hiraṇyaśṛṅga, made of jewels.
At her foot is the great, divine, and auspicious Bindusaras, beautiful with golden sands, where King Bhagīratha dwelt.
The royal sage dwelt for many years for the sake of the Gaṅgā;
those who are drenched by the waters of the Gaṅgā shall quickly go to heaven.
Having resolved, "She is mine," with a concentrated mind upon Śiva,
the Goddess Tripura first established herself there; having issued from the foot of Soma, she flows forth in seven streams.
There, sacrificial posts made of jewels and spread out with those made of gold were found;
having performed sacrifices there, Śakra, together with all the gods, attained perfection.
That luminous path of shadows seen in the sky at night, appearing without a circle of stars, is the goddess who flows through the three worlds.
Nourishing both the atmosphere and the heavens,
the celestial river fell upon the head of Bhava, where she was obstructed by the illusory power of Yoga.
Some drops of hers, falling to the earth while she was enraged, formed the Bidusaras lake;
therefore, it is known as Bindusaras.
Then, having been restrained by the smiling Bhava, that goddess reflected in her mind regarding Śaṅkara’s dismissal.
Having understood that cruel intention and what the Goddess desired to do, I shall pierce through to Pātāla and seize Śaṅkara by the stream [of his power].
Śaṅkara, having perceived her pride, became enraged at that river which had conceived the intention to vanish from his limbs.
And as she was falling violently to the ground upon Nyaru’s head,
at that very moment, the king saw her before him.
Emaciated, with veins standing out, his senses distressed by hunger,
he had already pleased me long ago for the sake of the river.
Having heard the words of Brahmā, "Hold back the celestial river," he, the Buddha, restrained both his granting of boons and his wrath.
Then, gratified by his fierce asceticism, he released the river that had been restrained by his own splendor for the sake of Bhagīratha.
Then, as it was being released, that stream split into seven parts:
three flowed toward the east and three indeed toward the west.
The stream of the Gaṅgā then divided into seven branches:
Nalinī, Hlādinī, and Pāvanī flowed toward the east.
Sītā, Cakṣus, and Sindhu were established in the western direction;
the seventh among them, however, followed Bhagīratha from the south.
Therefore, that Bhāgīrathī who has entered the salt ocean nourishes these seven [rivers] within this very region called Himavat.
Seven auspicious rivers were produced there from the Bindusaras lake;
flowing forth, they inundate various regions that are for the most part inhabited by Mlecchas.
All of them approach from wherever Vāsava sends rain:
the Śilīndhras, Kuntalas, Cīnas, Barbaras, Yavanas, and Aḍhakas.
Having divided Siṃhavana into three parts, the Puṣkaras, the Kulindas, and those who roam among the Acoṃlas, went from Sītā to the western ocean.
Then [he conquered] the Cīnas, the Marus, the Tālas, the Masamūlikas,
the Bhadras, the Tuṣāras, the Lāmyākas, the Bāhlavas, the Pāraṭas, and the Khaśas.
He sent his eye [his army] across these regions until it reached the ocean,
including the Daradas along with the Kaśmīras, the Gāndhāras, the Raurasas, and the Kuhās.
He passed through Śivaśaila, Indrapada, and Vasatī,
as well as Saindhava, Randhrakaraka, Śamaṭha, Ābhīra, and Rohaka.
And he frequents the Śunāsukhas, the Urdhvamarus, and the Sindhus;
as well as the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Vidyādharas, and Uragas.
He also conquered Kalāpagrāma, the Pāradas, their tribes, the Khaśas,
the Kirātas, the Pulindas, and the Kurus along with the Bharatas.
The Pañcālas, Kāśīs, and Matsyas, as well as the Magadhas and Aṅgas; the Suhmas, Uttaras, and Vaṅgas, and likewise the Tāmraliptas.
The auspicious Gaṅgā sanctifies these venerable regions;
thereafter, repelled by the Vindhya mountains, she entered the salt ocean.
Then the holy Hlādinī flowed toward the east,
causing the Upabhāgas, the Naiṣadhas, and the Trigartas to overflow.
Fishermen and ṛṣikas, as well as those with blue faces,
those with squinting eyes, those with lips reaching to their ears, and indeed the Kirātas.
He saw the sons of Kālodara, who were discolored, as well as those on the golden ground,
extending as far as the ocean's circle and vanished from the east.
Then the purifying river also proceeded toward the eastern direction,
sanctifying the fair paths here as well as the lake of Indradyumna.
Likewise, he traveled through rough paths and even paths marked by cane stakes,
with Jānaki in the middle, while they were covered with fine rugs and cloaks.
Having entered the salt ocean at Indradvīpa,
the Nalinī then proceeded with speed toward the eastern direction.
Nourishing the Tomara regions here, along with the Haṃsamārgas and the Haihayas,
she flows through the eastern lands after piercing the mountains in many places.
Having encountered the Karṇaprāvaraṇas and even the Śvamukhas,
and having gone to the Aru mountain of sand, he proceeded toward the Vidyādharas.
They entered the salt ocean through the middle of the circle of mountains;
and their tributary rivers numbered in the hundreds and thousands.
They all approach from wherever Vāsava sends rain;
on the banks of the Vakvaukasā, however, there is a forest renowned for its fragrance.
In Hiraṇyaśṛṅga dwells the wise Kubera, the self-controlled one;
he is endowed with sacrifice, exceedingly great, of immeasurable power, and of noble prowess.
Surrounded there by those learned brahmarākṣasas,
these four are indeed remembered as the equal companions of Kubera.
In this very way, the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of those dwelling on the mountains is to be understood:
it is doubled in relation to one another by virtue of their dharma, their desires, and their purposes.
On the back of Hemakūṭa, however, there is a lake named Varcas;
from it flow the rivers Manasvinī and Jyotiṣmatī.
For on the excellent mountain Niṣadha, there is a lake named Viṣṇupada, which plunges into both the eastern and western oceans.
From them two were born, Gāndharvī and Nākulī;
from the side of Mount Meru there issues forth the great lake Candraprabha.
There flows the holy river Jambūnadī, from which Jāmbūnada gold is said to originate;
and there is the lake Payoda on Mount Nīla, as brilliantly white as a lotus.
From that [lake] flow forth two rivers, Puṇḍarīkā and Payodā;
from Śveta proceeds the meritorious Sarayū, and from Mānasa flows the Dhruva.
From that [lake] two others were born: Jyotsnā and Mṛgākāmā;
and there arose a lake renowned among the Kurus, filled with lotuses, fish, and birds.
It is renowned as Rudrakānta, fashioned by Bhava himself;
and there are others also well-known there, abounding with lotuses, fish, and birds.
From those lakes named Jayā, which were like twelve oceans, two rivers emerged: Śāntā and Yamadhvī.
In those lands such as Kiṃpuruṣa and others, the god does not send rain;
there, excellent rivers flow with waters that spring forth spontaneously.
Ṛṣabha, Dundubhi, Dhūmra, and the very great mountain Sumahāgiri—
these mountains with their vast ridges extend toward the east and are submerged in the salt waters.
Candra, Kāka, and Droṇa, as well as very great mountain ranges,
rose up in the north and extended toward the northern region, plunging into the great ocean.
Somaka, Varāha, Nārada, and Mahīdhara extend toward the west; they indeed enter the salt ocean.
Cakra, Balāhaka, and the mountain Maināka—
these great mountains extend toward the southern ocean.
Between Mount Cakra and Maināka, toward the southern intermediate direction, there is the fire named Saṃvartaka; it drinks that water.
Samudravāsa by name, Aurva, and Vaḍavāmukha—
these twelve mountains indeed entered the salt ocean.
Formerly, terrified by the fear of Mahendra and fearing the severing of their wings,
[the stars] appeared in the white moon in the form of a black hare.
These nine divisions of the land of Bhārata have been proclaimed;
they are seen here as they were described, just as others are described elsewhere.
Each succeeding one among these is declared to be superior in qualities—
regarding health, lifespan, and measure— in terms of dharma, desire, and wealth.
Endowed with these merits in their respective portions, beings of various kinds dwell within those regions;
thus does this earth support the entire universe as it stands. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 1.18.84)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of Jambūdvīpa," in the second section (Anuṣaṅgapāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
I shall now describe Plakṣadvīpa here in summary, exactly as it is.
Listen to this, O best of the twice-born, as I speak it according to the truth.
Its width is twice that of Jambūdvīpa;
its circumference all around is twice its width.
By that island, the salt-water ocean is indeed enclosed;
there are holy regions there where people do not die for a long time.
Famine is indeed a thing of the past; whence could there be fear of old age or disease?
There too, seven meritorious mountains stand adorned with jewels.
Likewise, there are oceans of jewels and rivers; I shall state their names:
in these five continents, beginning with Jambūdvīpa, there are seven of each.
In Plakṣadvīpa, the rain-mountains (varṣaparvata) are situated straight and extended in every direction; I shall now describe the seven continents of great power within it.
The first mountain here is Gomedaka, which resembles a cloud;
it is after its name that the region is known as Gomedaka.
The second mountain is Candra, endowed with all medicinal herbs;
there the herbs were gathered for the sake of nectar by the two Aśvins.
The third is named Nārada, a massive mountain peak;
long ago, the mountains Nārada and Parvata were born upon that mountain.
The fourth mountain there is known by the name Dundubhi;
in ancient times, Chandamṛtyu was struck down upon it by the gods with a drum.
Rajjudāla, Urukāma, Śālmali who was the destroyer of the Asuras,
and the fifth named Somaka, where the gods formerly obtained the nectar of immortality.
Saṃbhṛta and Ahṛta were also born for the sake of their mother by Garuḍa;
the sixth is named Sumanas, and the seventh is called Ṛṣabha.
Hiraṇyākṣa was slain by the Boar on that mountain;
there, the seventh is Vaibhrāja, a great, radiant crystal peak.
Because it shines with rays of light, it is remembered as Vaibhrāja;
I shall now describe their regions in order, according to their names.
The first region is Gomeda, known by the name Śāntabhaya;
the second is named Śiśira, belonging to Candra; and the third is Sukhodaya, belonging to Nārada.
The rain of Ānanda is known as excellent; that of Somaka is auspicious;
that of Kṣemaka is also like a bull; and likewise, that of Vaibhrāja is constant.
In these [regions], gods, gandharvas, and siddhas, together with the cāraṇas,
dwell, take delight, and sport, being seen by them [the inhabitants].
O you whose wealth is asceticism, I shall now declare by name those seven rivers that flow to the ocean in each respective varṣa; they are known as the seven Gaṅgās.
Anutaptā, Asukhī, Vipāśā, Tridivā,
Kramu, Amṛtā, and Sukṛtā— these seven are the best among rivers.
Those rivers flow toward it, and from them, thousands of others—
abounding in water and surging with currents— flow forth wherever Vāsava sends down rain.
Those rivers of the region always flow with joy;
they are auspicious, free from fear, delightful in the cool season, and auspicious.
There were joys and pleasures, as well as security, along with the eternal ones;
and the subjects, endowed with the conduct of their respective castes and stages of life, were established under them.
