All his subjects were free from disease, possessed of great strength, and devoid of illness;
for them there was neither the aeon of decline (avasarpiṇī) nor likewise the aeon of increase (utsarpiṇī).
Therein, no state of the Yugas produced by the four ages exists anywhere;
at all times, a period equal to the Tretā Yuga prevails there.
In all five of these, beginning with Plakṣadvīpa,
it should be known that the divisions of time are recorded as following the divisions of space.
Human beings live for five thousand years in those [ages];
they are handsome, well-attired, free from disease, and likewise strong.
Happiness, long life, strength, beauty, health, and indeed righteousness—
these are to be known as existing in the islands beginning with Plakṣadvīpa and ending with Śākadvīpa.
Prakṣadvīpa is broad and glorious, abounding on all sides with wealth and grain;
it is endowed with divine medicinal herbs and fruits, and possesses every kind of herb and forest tree.
O best of the twice-born, it is surrounded by all kinds of domestic and wild animals by the thousands; in its center stands the Jambū tree, which is well-known.
There is a great tree named Plakṣa; it is called by that name, and it is indeed worshipped there in the center of the country.
And that Plakṣadvīpa is surrounded by the Ikṣurasoda ocean,
which is equal to Plakṣadvīpa in its breadth and extent.
Thus has the configuration of Plakṣadvīpa been described to you in due order and in brief; now learn of Śālmala[dvīpa].
Next, I shall describe the third, the most excellent island, Śālmala;
the ocean surrounding the island of Śālmala consists of sugarcane juice.
Surrounded by a circumference twice the width of Plakṣadvīpa,
there too seven mountains should be known as sources of jewels.
Likewise, there are jewel-mines and rivers within those seven regions;
the first mountain is named Kumuda, resembling the sun.
And here there is a second mountain, renowned by the name Uttama, which consists of peaks made of all kinds of minerals and is covered with networks of stone.
There stands a third mountain there, known as Balāhaka, which remains covering the heavens with its peaks made of yellow orpiment.
The fourth mountain, Droṇa, stands covering the heavens with its peaks made of native antimony; there indeed is that Sahāuṣadhi (the mountain of medicinal herbs).
Viśalyakaraṇī, Mṛtasañjīvinī, and Kaṅka as the fifth; there also is the mountain Sumahodaya.
The sixth mountain there is Mahiṣa, resembling a cloud, endowed with eternal flowers and fruits, and covered with trees and creepers.
On that mountain where that lotus-born fire named Mahiṣa dwells,
there is a seventh mountain called Kakudmat.
There, Vāsava himself personally guards many jewels for the sake of all creatures,
starting from Prajāpati, according to the prescribed rule.
Thus, these are the seven mountains on Śālmala, adorned with jewels;
O serpent, I shall now describe their auspicious regions.
The conch of Kumuda is remembered as white, and that of Uttama as red;
the conch of Balāhaka is Jīmūta, and that of Droṇa is remembered as green.
Kaṅka’s was named Vaidyuta, Mahiṣa’s was Mānasa, and Kakuda’s was Suprada; these seven [mountains] are thus divided into seven parts.
Learn now of the rains, the mountains, and the rivers among them:
Jyotis, Śānti, Tuṣṭā, Candrā, Śukrā, and Vimocanī.
The seventh among them is known as Nivṛtti; they are said to exist in every year, and there are hundreds and thousands of others situated near them.
No human being whatsoever would be able to calculate its number;
thus has this configuration of your Śālmalī tree been described.
In its center stands a great tree, reckoned as a Plakṣa;
it has massive branches and is called by the name Śālmalī.
The Śālmaladvīpa is surrounded by the Suroda ocean;
its extent is equal to that of Śālmaladvīpa itself, but not on all sides.
But as for the northern islands, O people, listen to me as I speak according to what has been heard and in accordance with the law; understand it from me.
I shall now describe Kuśadvīpa, the fourth continent, in brief:
it is surrounded on all sides by the ocean of excellent wine (suroda), which is encompassed by Kuśadvīpa.
Twice the width of the Śālmalī tree on all sides, there are seven mountains; listen now as they are described.
In Kuśadvīpa, however, the mountain known as Vidruma is to be recognized;
it is the first of that island, and the second is the Hemaparvata.
The third is the mountain named Dyutimān, resembling a cloud;
the fourth is named Puṣpavān, and the fifth is Kuśeśaya.
The sixth is named Harigiri, and the seventh is known as Mandara;
for "Manda" is the name of waters, and this Mandara is so called because it causes them to burst forth.
The interval between them is twice as large in its division;
the first region is Udbhida, and the second is Veṇumaṇḍala.
The third is indeed Rathākāra, the fourth is Lavaṇa,
the fifth is the Dhṛtimat region, and the sixth region is Prabhākara.
The seventh is named Kapila; all of them are the sustainers of the regions.
Within these, the gods and Gandharvas are the subjects, while the lords of the world are the progenitors.
They dwell and take delight, rejoicing in every way;
among them there are no bandits, nor any tribes of Mlecchas.
Almost all people there are fair-complexioned, and they die in due course;
furthermore, there are exactly seven rivers there, namely Dhūtapāpā and Śivā.
Pavitrā, Saṃtati, Vidyut, Daṃbhā, and Mahī,
as well as others unknown from them by the hundreds and thousands.
They all go toward wherever Vāsava sends rain;
Kuśadvīpa is surrounded on the outside by the Ghṛtoda ocean.
It should be known that, in its extent, it is equal to Kuśadvīpa;
thus has this configuration of Kuśadvīpa been described to you.
Hereafter, I shall describe the extent of Krauñcadvīpa;
it is indeed recorded as being twice the extent of Kuśadvīpa.
The ocean of clarified butter is indeed joined with Krauñca Island;
on that island stands the foremost of mountains, the first mountain, Krauñca.
Beyond Kraiñca is Vāmanaka; beyond Vāmanaka is Andhakāraka;
and beyond Andhakāraka is the mountain named Divāvṛt.
Beyond Divāvṛta is Dvividha, the best of mountains;
and beyond Dvividha is the great mountain Puṇḍarīka.
Beyond Puṇḍarīka, Dundubhisvana is also proclaimed;
these seven mountains of Krauñcadvīpa are composed of jewels.
Covered with various trees and creepers endowed with many flowers and fruits,
they are twice as wide as one another and increase one's joy.
I shall describe the regions there by name; listen to them:
the region of Krauñca is Kuśala, and that of Vāmana is Manonuga.
Beyond Manonuga is Uṣṇa; this is called the third varṣa.
Beyond Uṣṇa is Pīvaraka, and beyond Pīvaraka is Andhakāraka.
Beyond Andhakāra, the region of the Munis is remembered by the wise; and beyond the region of the Munis, the region called Dundubhisvana is proclaimed.
The people there are remembered as being fair-complexioned and crowded with Siddhas and Cāraṇas;
even there, seven auspicious rivers are recorded for each varṣa.
Gaurī, Kumudvatī, Saṃdhyā, Rātri, Manojavā,
Khyāti, and Puṇḍarīkā— these are remembered as the seven Gaṅgās.
And thousands of other rivers, which flow into their vicinity— all of them vast and carrying abundant water— join them.
The glorious Krauñcadvīpa is surrounded on all sides by an ocean of whey-water (dadhimaṇḍaudaka) that is equal in extent to Krauñcadvīpa itself.
Thus, these islands beginning with Plakṣadvīpa have been briefly proclaimed; [now hear] their natural formation and all about them in their proper sequence.
It is not possible to describe in detail, even in a hundred divine years,
the nature of living beings as well as their dissolution.
I shall describe Śākadvīpa here according to its true determination;
listen to me as I speak it exactly as it is and in accordance with reality.
Its extent is twice that of Krauñcadvīpa;
it stands surrounding the ocean whose waters are like the scum of curdled milk.
There, the regions are meritorious and people die only after a long time;
how indeed could there be famine, and whence could come the fear of old age and disease?
There too, there are seven bright mountains adorned with jewels, as well as oceans and rivers; hear their names from me.
The first mountain, joined by celestial sages and gandharvas, is called Meru;
extending toward the east, that golden mountain is named Udaya.
There, the clouds arise and move about for the sake of rain;
beyond that is the great mountain Jaladhāra.
Since Vāsava constantly takes up the supreme water,
rain consequently arises here among living beings during the rainy season.
To the north of that is Raivataka, where the constellation Revatī is eternally established in the sky; such is the ordinance ordained by the Grandfather (Brahmā).
To the west of that mountain is a very great mountain named Śyāma;
it is said that in former times these very creatures attained their dark complexion from it.
To its west is known the very great mountain Nājata,
and further west of that is the great mountain Ambikeya, a formidable peak.
Beyond Ambikā is the delightful Kesara, endowed with all medicinal herbs,
from which the wind-god Prajāpati [proceeds].
The first year after the rising [of the sun] is known as Mahat-jalada;
the second year of Jaladhāra is known as Sukumāra.
The region of Raivata is Kaumāra; that of Śyāma is Maṇīvaka;
and the auspicious region of Asta should be known as Kusumottara.
The sweetmeat of Ambikeśa, the great tree of Kesarin,
and the measurement of the island— both its breadth and its length.
It is renowned as Krauñcadvīpa; its banner is a great tree named Śāka, which is of immense height, and its great attendants are worthy of worship.
There, the districts are meritorious and endowed with the four castes;
there are also rivers of great merit, such as the sevenfold Gaṅgās.
Sukumārī, Kumārī, and Nalinī; Veṇukā, Ikṣu, and Veṇukā; and likewise Gabhastī as the seventh.
And there are thousands of other auspicious rivers with holy waters that carry cool currents, which are proclaimed to exist wherever Vāsava sends down rain.
Neither their names nor their extent can indeed be fully enumerated; for those supreme rivers are meritorious.
Those people of the countryside always drink from those rivers with joy;
that island, O Śāṃśapāyana, is broad and circular in shape.
It was covered by river waters and by mountains resembling clouds,
variegated with all kinds of minerals and adorned with jewels and coral.
It was surrounded on all sides by various flourishing cities and prosperous districts, as well as trees endowed with flowers and fruit, and rich in wealth and grain.
It is surrounded on all sides by the ocean of milk (Kṣīroda),
which is equal in extent to the breadth of Śākadvīpa on every side.

In that region, there are meritorious provinces, auspicious mountains, and beautiful rivers; those seven lands are indeed remembered as being filled with people of the various castes and stages of life.
There was never any confusion among them caused by caste or stage of life;
and because their dharma was never deviated from, the subjects were exclusively happy.
In them there is no greed or deceit, nor anything born of envy or malice; for them there is no error, as their supreme state is natural and arises from time.
For them there is no acquisition of property, neither punishment nor those deserving of punishment;
knowing the Dharma through their own duty alone, they protect one another.
Only this much can indeed be spoken regarding that island;
only this much is to be heard by the inhabitants of Śākadvīpa.
I shall now describe the seventh island, Puṣkara; listen attentively.
This island of Puṣkara is surrounded on the outside by the Ocean of Milk.
It is held that Puṣkara is twice the extent of Śākadvīpa; therein stands a single, glorious mountain of massive rock.
On the eastern half of that island stands the great Citrasānu, elevated with variegated peaks made of jewels and dense clusters of rocks.
It is twenty-five thousand yojanas wide,
and its height from the surface of the earth is thirty-four thousand yojanas.
Encircling the half-Dvīpa is the Mānasottara mountain;
it stands near the shore like the newly risen moon.
It rises fifty thousand yojanas upward and is just as wide, being perfectly circular on all sides.
That very mountain Mānasa, the support of the earth, exists in the western half of the continent;
though it is a single mass of great substance, its arrangement is divided into two parts.
It is surrounded on all sides by the ocean of sweet water,
and it is as extensive as the breadth of Puṣkaradvīpa in every direction.
On that island, two meritorious and auspicious regions are remembered,
situated on both sides of the Mānasa lake within the circle of the mountain.
The region called Mahāvīta lies outside of Mānasa,
while Dhātakīkhaṇḍa is said to lie within it.
There, human beings live for ten thousand years,
free from disease, abounding in happiness, and established in mental perfection.
In those two years, flesh, life-span, and form are said to exist;
among them there is no distinction of low or high, for they are equal in both appearance and character.
Therein there are no robbers, no tamers, nor likewise envy, malice, or fear;
there is neither restraint nor punishment, neither greed nor possession.
Therein, neither truth nor falsehood exists, nor likewise merit or demerit;
nor do the castes and stages of life, nor agriculture, cattle-rearing, or trade.
The threefold knowledge, the science of government, service, and even the arts—
all of this is not found in Puṣkara for two years.
There, neither rain nor rivers, nor even cold or heat, is found;
there the waters arise spontaneously from the earth and from mountain springs.
And the people of Uttarakuru are likewise equal in age;
there, they enjoy the happiness of all seasons and are free from the process of aging.
Thus, this entire procedure for Dhātakīkhaṇḍa and likewise for Mahāvīta has been proclaimed in due order; now that of Puṣkara is being described.
Puṣkara is surrounded by the ocean of sweet water;
it is equal to Puṣkara in both its extent and its circumference.
Thus the continents are surrounded by seven oceans;
each ocean that lies immediately adjacent to a continent is equal in extent to that continent.
In this manner, the increase of the continents and oceans should be understood relative to one another;
and because of the overflowing of the waters, it is designated as the "ocean" (sāmudra).
Because the four kinds of living beings enter into and dwell within it,
and because it bestows happiness upon those beings, it is therefore called a "Varṣa" (region).

The word *ṛṣi* is used here in the sense of "delighting" (*ramaṇe*) and "binding with the power of a bull" (*vṛṣa-śakti-prabandhane*). Because they have achieved the rain through the binding of passion (*ratiprabaṃdhana*), they are indeed called *varṣa* for that reason.
The ocean is always filled by the waxing of the moon during the bright fortnight;
it diminishes as the moon wanes during the dark fortnight until the bird [the moon] has set.
For just as the ocean, when being filled, is filled from within itself alone,
so too, when it is diminishing, it is withdrawn back into its own self alone.
Just as the water within a cauldron is seen to overflow due to contact with fire,
so too does the water contained within the great ocean overflow by its own nature.
Neither deficient nor excessive, the waters of the Varandvatī decrease during the rising and setting of the moon in both the bright and dark fortnights.
Furthermore, the waxing and waning of the ocean occurs due to the increase and decrease of the moon;
[the difference between these two states is] five hundred and ten finger-breadths.
The increase and decrease of the waters of the oceans is observed during the lunar phases;
because they are surrounded by water on all sides, these are remembered as "dvīpas" (islands), meaning "twice-watered."
Because it is the path (*ayana*) for water, it is therefore called the ocean (*udadhi*);
likewise, mountains that have no joints are known as *parvatas* because of their joints (*parva*).
In Plakṣadvīpa, however, there is the mountain Gomeda, and it is named after that;
in Śālmalidvīpa, the Śālmali tree is worshipped by those of great vows.
In Kuśadvīpa, there is a *kuśa* pillar; it is named after that and thus called [Kuśadvīpa]. In Krauñcadvīpa, there is the mountain Krauñca in the middle of the country.
In Śākadvīpa there is a tree called Śāka; it is named after that [tree].
In Puṣkaradvīpa there is a banyan tree (nyagrodha), which is venerated by those who dwell there.
Mahādeva is indeed worshipped as Brahmā, the lord of the three worlds;
within him dwells Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, together with the Sādhyas.
There the gods of the Thirty-three, together with the great seers, wait upon him;
and there that supreme among the supreme gods is worshipped by the gods.
Various kinds of jewels proceed from Jambūdvīpa to all those other continents in succession for the sake of the inhabitants.
Through complete celibacy, truthfulness, and self-restraint,
their measure in terms of health and lifespan becomes double that [of the previous stage].
In this Puṣkaradvīpa, regarding the two regions that have been described,
the Self-Existent One himself protects the subjects there— both the dull-witted and the wise.
The Lord who wields the raised staff, Brahmā, the sovereign of the three worlds—he is the divine minister of Viṣṇu; he is the father, he is the grandfather.
And there, food endowed with the six flavors and great potency appeared spontaneously before them without effort, which the subjects always consumed.
Beyond half of Puṣkara,
the great ocean of sweet water stands encircling it on all sides.
Beyond that, the vast arrangement of the world is seen;
the golden ground is double [the previous extent], entirely like a single solid rock.
Beyond that is the mountain Śaila, which encircles the region like a bracelet;
being both luminous and non-luminous, it is called Lokāloka.
Its lower part is illuminated, and beyond that it is without light;
its height is said to be ten thousand yojanas.
Its extent on earth is as vast as that, and it moves at will;
it is a light abiding within the conduct of the world, yet it is indeed a lightless, supramundane radiance.
The worlds are measured as half a world [in extent], but outside they are without light;
indeed, the non-world (aloka) extends everywhere beyond, equal in width to the entire world.
It is delimited on all sides and enveloped by water; beyond the light, the egg remains, having encompassed everything.
Within this cosmic egg are these worlds: the earth with its seven continents, as well as Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, and Maharloka.
Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka—this much is the collection of worlds;
this alone should be known as the limit of the worlds, as well as that which is beyond.
Just as the moon stands in the pitcher-like sign when it first appears in the western quarter at the beginning of the bright fortnight, such is the form of the cosmic egg.
It should be known that there are thousands of millions of such eggs,
extending horizontally, upwards, and downwards, from the imperishable Self who is the Cause.
Each of these is surrounded by its respective sevenfold set of material elements;
and each, increasing tenfold at each stage, mutually supports one another.
All are mutually enveloped and have arisen from one another;
surrounding this entire egg, however, is the dense ocean (ghanodadhi).
He remains supported on all sides by a forest-like downpour,
whose circular expanse is dense externally, extending both horizontally and upwards.
But that which remains being held on all sides by its own brilliance is like a mass of glowing iron,
a circular form of fire on every side.
Supported on all sides by the dense wind, it remains;
indeed, the space remains by supporting that dense wind.
Likewise, the ether and the origin of the elements, as well as that Great One (Mahat) which is the origin of the elements,
are indeed supported by the infinite Unmanifest.
It is infinite, unmanifest, and subtle in ten ways;
it is infinite, the unconditioned self, and that which is without beginning or end.
It is impermanent, not terrible from others, without support, and free from disease;
it extends for many thousands of yojanas, is far-reaching, and is unobstructed.
It is indeed darkness, devoid of light, without boundaries, without a guide, unknown even to the gods, and utterly devoid of worldly activity.
At the end of darkness is the all-pervading, and at the end of space is the non-luminous;
this is the great abode of the infinite God within the boundary.
The sacred tradition declares that this divine place is inaccessible even to the thirty gods;
it is the established boundary of the Great God of Gods.
Those worlds which are renowned by the wise as being beneath the moon and the sun are designated as "the worlds" (loka) of the universe; of this there is no doubt.
O twice-born ones, there are seven nether regions and likewise seven upper regions;
furthermore, there are the seven layers of wind, together with the abode of Brahmā.
From the netherworld (pātāla) up to heaven, there are five types of destinies here;
this is the measure of the world, and this is the ocean of saṃsāra.
Arising from many births, they indeed proceed through that which is without beginning or end;
for that manifold nature of the world is established as the Prakṛti of Brahman.
And whatever here is divine or natural, however extensive it may be,
has not been perceived even by the highly fortunate Siddhas who possess super-sensory faculties.
Of earth, water, fire, wind, and likewise of ether, darkness,
and the mental body, O best of the twice-born, [there is the dissolution] of the infinite one.
Neither destruction, nor transformation, nor even an end is found;
this is everywhere recited as infinite within all forms of knowledge.
And concerning him, I have previously spoken in that enumeration of names;
he who was proclaimed in his entirety by the name Padmanābha.
He alone is omnipresent and is worshipped in all places:
on earth, in the netherworld (rasātala), as well as in space, in the wind, and in fire.
In all the oceans and even in heaven there is no doubt;
likewise, this very one of great splendor is to be known within the darkness.
With his limbs divided in manifold ways, the great yogi Janārdana,
the Lord of all worlds, is worshipped in many forms as the Sovereign throughout all the worlds.
In this way, the modifications, having arisen from one another, support one another; through the relationship of container and contained, they are themselves unchanging.
Earth and the other elements are modifications; they are mutually limited, mutually superior, and have entered into one another.
Because those created beings were produced from one another, they attained stability;
previously they were without distinction, but distinction arose through the qualification of one by another.
Those three elements, beginning with earth and ending with air, are indeed unlimited;
however, their specific limitation arises from the predominance of the accumulation of qualities (guṇas).
But the delimitation of the remaining [elements] is not discerned here due to their subtlety;
that earth is remembered as extending beyond those elements, pervading all the way to the worlds.
All beings and the light in space are entirely contained within it,
just as smaller vessels are held inside a large vessel.
They exist as mutually dependent, each lacking the other,
for just as light exists in space, so too are distinctions considered to be contained within it.
Indeed, all these four are mutually superior;
as long as these elements exist, so long is their arising said to continue.
He is considered to have entered within all beings like the continuous thread in a web;
yet, having set aside the elements, there is no arising of any effect.
Therefore, those limited distinctions are known as being of the nature of effects;
likewise, the distinctions such as the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest are of the nature of causes, being one.
Thus, O twice-born ones, this arrangement consisting of the seven islands and oceans has been declared by me in its various divisions according to its true nature.
Indeed, through detailed enumeration, the mandalas are also [described];
for [this] is a partial exposition of the transformation of the Primal Substance (Pradhāna) which possesses all forms.
This entire world is presided over by the Blessed One;
thus, the seven classes of beings are situated in mutual relation to one another.
This much of the arrangement can indeed be described by me;
this alone is to be heard regarding the arrangement of the earthly realm.
These seven primary natures sustain one another;
however, I am not able here to enumerate them by their specific measures.
Innumerable are the natural formations— across, above, and below—
as well as the arrangement of the stars, extending as far as the divine celestial sphere.
Next, O wise ones, I shall describe the arrangement of the earth’s zones and the regions situated above it. BndP_1,19.197 //

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Islands beginning with Plakṣa," in the second section (Anuṣaṅga-pāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
"Now learn the measurements for the regions below and above, which shall be described."
Earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth.
For these elements are infinite and are proclaimed to be all-pervading;
she is the mother of all beings, the earth that sustains all creatures.
It was filled with various provinces, containing diverse capitals and towns;
it possessed various mountains, rivers, and forests, and was teeming with many different species of beings.
The goddess Earth is sung of as infinite and exceedingly vast;
she dwells within the great rivers, streams, and oceans, and resides in the subtle supports of the minute.
The waters, which exist upon mountains and in the sky, as well as those that have entered beneath the earth, are indeed to be known as infinite; likewise, fire pervades all the worlds.
He is recited as being infinite, all-pervading, and the source of all;
likewise, he is remembered as space—unpaintable, delightful, and the manifold substratum.
It is recited that it is indeed infinite; wind arises from space, and water is upon the earth, while the earth is established upon the water.
Space, and again earth, and again water—
in this way, the notion of a material entity belonging to Ananta does not exist.
Understand also that the earth is augmented by these elements in succession;
the sequence consists of earth, water, fire, and space.
This is renowned as the abode in this seventh subterranean realm;
one thousand yojanas deep is the first earthly region, Rasātala.
Each one has been described in detail by the virtuous;
first is that named Tattvala, and after that is Sutala.
From there is Talātala, and the Vidyāda-tala of great extent;
below that is the region named Tala, and beyond that is Rasātala.
Below these as well, the seventh is known as Pātāla;
and the first portion of the subterranean realm is proclaimed to be Kṛṣṇabhauma.
The second is of pale soil, the third is of blue clay;
the fourth is of yellow earth, while the fifth consists of gravel.
The sixth is to be known as made of stone, and the seventh is remembered as golden;
on this first level, the palace of the lord of the Asuras is renowned.
[He went] to the abode of Namuci, the enemy of Indra, and of Mahānāda;
and to the city of Śaṅkukarṇa and the palace of Kabandha.
And he saw the city of Niṣkulāda crowded with joyful people,
as well as the abode of the terrible Rākṣasa Śūladanta.
The city of Lohitākṣa and Kaliṅga, the city of Śvāpada,
and the city of Dhanañjaya, the high-souled lord of the Nāgas.
And [he conquered] the city of the nāga Kāliya and that of Kauśika;
in this manner, he subdued thousands of cities belonging to nāgas, dānavas, and rākṣasas.
O brahmins, these [residences] are to be known as belonging to the Daitya lord and the Rākṣasa in the first underworld, Kṛṣṇabhūmi; and in the second, Sutala, there is no doubt.
Likewise, there is the city of Mahājambha, the first [of them],
as well as the palace of Tryambaka, Kṛṣṇa, and Nikumbha.
And [he saw] the city of the Daitya named Śaṅkha, and that of Gomukha,
and of the Rākṣasa Nīla, and of Megha, and of Kathana.
The abode of Kukūlāda, the abode of Mahoṣṇīṣa,
and the city of the nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara.
And there was the city of the high-souled Takṣaka, the son of Kadrū;
in this manner, there were thousands of cities belonging to the Nāgas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas.
On this second level, O Brahmins, is the Pāṇḍubhauma; of this there is no doubt.
On the third level, however, is the renowned realm of the high-souled Prahlāda.
And the city of Anudrāda, and the city of Agnimukha,
the city of Tārakākṣa, and likewise the city of Triśiras.
And there was the city of Śiśumāra, as well as the city of Tripura,
and the city of the Daitya Purañjana, which was crowded with joyful and well-fed people.
One should know the abode of Cyavana and that of the Rākṣasa;
as well as the city of Kumbhila, the lord of Rākṣasas, and that of Khara.
And [he conquered] the city of the cruel Virādha, as well as that of Ulkāmukha,
of the Nāga Hemaka, and likewise of Pāṇḍuraka.
And the city of Maṇināga, the palace of Kapila, the city of Nedaka, the lord of serpents, and the palace of Viśālākṣa.
O brahmins, there is no doubt that thousands of such cities belonging to the nāgas, dānavas, and rākṣasas exist on this third level, the Blue Earth (nīlabhauma).
In the fourth [region] were the city and the capital of the great-souled Kālanemi, the lion among Daityas, as well as those of Gajakarṇa and Kuñjara.
And the very extensive city of Sumāli, the lord of the Rākṣasas;
the world of Muñja, the protector of the world; and the abode of Vṛkavaktra.
In this fourth subterranean realm (Asātala), there is the city of Vainateya, extending for many yojanas and teeming with many birds.
In the fifth subterranean realm, Śarkarābhūmi, there is the city of the wise Virocana, that lion among the Daityas, extending for many yojanas.
[He saw] the abode of Vaidyuta Agnijihva Hiraṇyākṣa,
and the city of the wise lord of the Rākṣasas, Vidyujjihva.
And [he went] to the city of Sahāmegha, the lord of the Rākṣasas Mālin,
as well as to that of the Nāga Kirmīra, Svastika, and Jaya.
In this same way, thousands of cities belonging to the Nāgas, Dānavas,
and Rākṣasas are always to be known as existing on this fifth layer, which consists of a mass of gravel.
On the sixth level, in the city of Kesara, is the preeminent city of the lord of the Daityas,
as well as the cities of Suparvan, Puloman, and Mahiṣa.
And there is the city of the high-souled Suroṣa, the lord of the Rākṣasas;
there dwells Śataśīrṣa, the son of Suramā, filled with joy.
The glorious Vāsuki, the king of the nāgas and friend of Mahendra,
likewise has thousands of cities belonging to the nāgas, dānavas, and rākṣasas.
In this sixth celebrated level, Rasātala, which is of stone;
and in the seventh level, Pātāla, which is to be known as the very last of all.
The city of Bali was filled with joy and crowded with throngs of men and women;
it was teeming with asuras who were like venomous serpents, those happy enemies of the gods.
Right there was the great city of the Daitya Mucukunda,
along with many flourishing great cities belonging to the sons of Diti.
Likewise, it was filled with thousands of radiant Naga cities and with the great,
flourishing cities of the Daityas and Dānavas.
O best of Brahmins, it was crowded with many rising abodes of Rākṣasas,
extending for many yojanas at the end of Pātāla.
The great-souled one, whose eyes are like red lotuses, who is indeed ageless and immortal,
whose body has the luster of a polished conch shell, who is clothed in blue garments, and who possesses great strength, remains there.
Possessing vast coils, radiant, wearing variegated garlands, and powerful,
he shone with a glowing face bright as gold-horned [light].
The Lord, adorned with a single earring, shines with a thousand faces;
he is radiant with a garland of tongues that possess the flickering flames and rays of fire.
Enveloped by garlands of flames, he appeared like Mount Kailāsa,
resplendent with his two thousand eyes.
The garland of eyes of him, who has the complexion of a jasmine flower or the moon, shines with a body that is pale and lustrous like the newly risen sun.
Like a garland of young suns upon the summit of the White Mountain, his body,
with its outstretched arms raised aloft, is seen upon his couch.
Like a mountain with a thousand peaks spread across the earth,
it was filled with great serpents of immense coils, who were highly wise and noble-souled.
The immensely radiant Śeṣa, the infinite and highly effulgent lord of all nāgas, himself worships the Great Lord of Great Splendor.
That established rule of conduct belonging to Viṣṇu is the boundary that has been fixed;
thus these seven netherworlds have been described as the spheres of worldly activity.
It is always inhabited by gods, asuras, great nāgas, and rākṣasas; beyond this lies a region of total darkness, inaccessible even to perfected beings and holy men.
O best of the twice-born, even that which is unknown to the gods is [known] through the desire to explain worldly conventions regarding earth, water, fire, wind, and space.
The greatness [of this] is thus described by the sages; there is no doubt in this matter.
Hereafter, I shall explain the course of the sun and the moon.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Description of the Nether Worlds," in the second section (Anuṣaṅgapāda) of the first part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
As long as these two, the sun and the moon, revolve,
they illuminate with their splendors and radiance, elevated by their two orbs.
The extent of the seven oceans and the continents is equal;
however, half of that extent belongs to the earth, while the remainder lies outside.
The extent of the surrounding space where the moon and sun shine is equal to the circumference of the earth; thus is heaven remembered.
Because the sun, revolving around these three worlds,
protects them by providing what is called light, he is known as Ravi, from the root *av*, meaning "to protect."
Hereafter, I shall declare the dimensions of the moon and the sun;
for it is from the principle of Earth (mahītattva) that the word "Earth" (mahī) is applied to this continent.
Now learn the number of yojanas of the solar orb, which is equal in extent to the diameter of this Bhāratavarṣa.
The diameter of the sun is nine thousand yojanas,
and its circumference in its orb is three times that diameter.
The moon is twice as large as the solar orb of Viṣkambha;
now I shall describe the measurement of the earth in yojanas.
The extent and the circumference of the earth consisting of seven continents and oceans—
this has been calculated here in the Purāṇa according to its measurement.
I shall explain that by relating it to those who are currently possessed of pride;
for those who have passed away while possessing pride are equal here to those of the present.
Since those gods who have indeed passed away can no longer be known by their forms or even by their names,
I shall therefore describe the surface of the earth with its present-day deities.
Indeed, the entire arrangement of the day has been described in its entirety;
the whole earth is recorded as having an extent of fifty crores [of yojanas].
Its height is equal to the extent of Mount Meru’s elevation;
its width across the earth is proclaimed to be half of that, measured from the summit.
From the center of Meru, it is recorded that there is one crore [yojanas] in each direction;
furthermore, there are eighty-nine thousand [yojanas].
The circle of half the earth is calculated at fifty thousand [yojanas],
while from the total extent of yojanas, it is recorded as eleven crores.
Likewise, there are one hundred and thirty-seven thousand [yojanas];
this much is declared here to be the extent of the mandala ending with the earth.
As far as the arrangement of the stars and the celestial sphere in the sky,
and as far as the circular extent of the earth's surface and its configuration.
The measurement of the celestial realm is said to be equal to the extent of the earth;
this is proclaimed to be the location for all seven continents as well.
By way of its successive dimensions and its conformity to the mandalas,
it is circular like an umbrella, situated higher and higher above the worlds.
The entire arrangement has been ordained for those within which living beings reside;
this is proclaimed to be the measurement of the shell of the cosmic egg.

Within this egg are these worlds: the earth with its seven continents, as well as the world of the living beings (bhūrloka), the world of the atmosphere (bhuvarloka), and the third, the world of the seers (svarloka).
Maharloka, Jana, Tapa, and Satya as the seventh—
these seven worlds are established in the shape of umbrellas.
Held apart by their own subtle veils,
they are externally surrounded by those primary elements increased tenfold.
And being filled with various things produced from one another,
the solid ocean (ghanodadhi) is situated all around this egg.
The entire circle of the earth is supported by dense water;
the dense ocean, in turn, is supported by dense fire.
On the outside, the dense mass of light forms a mandala extending horizontally and upwards;
it is supported and established by the dense wind as commonly agreed upon.
The dense wind is likewise enveloped by space, and all that space is enveloped by the Great Self (mahātman); the source of the elements (bhūtādi) is entirely enveloped by the Great One (mahat).
Enveloped by the great Pradhāna, the infinite and unmanifest Self,
I shall describe in due order the cities of the world-protectors.
For the purpose of establishing the measurement of the movement of the qualities of light,
[he was placed] in the eastern direction of Meru, likewise upon the summit of Mānasa itself.
The city of Mahendra, adorned with gold, is Vasvaukasārā;
it lies to the south of Meru, upon the very summit of Mānasa.
Yama, the son of Vivasvat, resides in the city of Saṃyamanī;
furthermore, he is on the western summit of Mount Meru, which is indeed part of Mānasa.
There is a delightful city named Sukhā belonging even to the wise Varuṇa;
Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, dwells in that city called Sukhā.
In the northern direction, upon the very summit of Mount Meru and Lake Mānasa,
the city of Soma, Vibhāvarī, is equal in splendor to the city of Mahendra.
But on the slopes of Mānasottara, the world-protectors stand in the four directions for the sake of establishing dharma and for the protection of the world.
Now, learn of that course of the sun when it has reached its limit during the southern transit, above the world-protectors and on all sides.
As the sun moves toward the south, it glides like a discharged arrow;
taking up the circle of luminaries, it revolves continually.
When the sun is situated in the middle of Amarāvatī,
its rising is seen there at the junction of the Vaivasvata Manvantara.
When the sun is situated in the middle of the Saṃyamana hell of Vaivasvata, it is midnight in Sukhā; it sets in Vibhā;
and as it rises, it is seen in Sukhā or in Vāruṇī.
When the sun sets in the northeast, it is midnight for the inhabitants of the north;
when it sets in the east, it is the afternoon for those in the south. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.21.39)
For those dwelling in the south-western regions, the forenoon is proclaimed as the auspicious time;
for those people who dwell further to the north, it is the latter part of the night.
Those regions which lie to the northeast, toward them shines the morning twilight; in this very same way, it shines upon the northern worlds.
When the sun rises in the city of Vibhā, either in Sukhāyāsa, Vāruṇī, or at midday in Āryamā, it emerges from the city of Soma.
When it is midnight in Amarāvatī and at sunset in the city of Yama,
the sun is at midday in the radiant city of Soma.
When the sun rises in Amarāvatī, the city of Mahendra,
it is midnight in Saṃyamana and it sets in Vāruṇī.
Like a whirling firebrand, that sun swiftly revolves;
indeed, as it rotates, the sun moves along the circular paths of the stars.
Thus, by means of that [wind], he glides toward the southern quarter among the four directions;
and at both sunrise and sunset, he stands there again and again.
In both the forenoon and the afternoon, he possesses two celestial abodes;
and at midday, the sun blazes with those very same rays.
The sun, having risen, heats with its delightful rays until midday; thereafter, as its rays diminish, it goes to its setting.
And by its rising and setting, the eastern and western directions are known;
as long as it shines in front, so too does it shine behind and on both sides.
Where the sun is seen rising, that is considered their sunrise;
where it goes to its destruction, that is called their sunset.
To the north of all [the continents] is Meru, and to the south is Lokāloka;
this is due to the great distance from the sun, which is enveloped by a belt of earth.
Because its rays are absorbed [within it], the sun is not seen at night;
yet there is the visibility of the planets, the lunar mansions, the moon, and the sun itself [during the day].
The setting and rising [of the sun] should be known by the measure of its height;
fire has white radiance, while the earth has black radiance.
Indeed, due to its distance from the sun, even when it has risen, there is an absence of radiance;
because of the absence of radiance, there is redness; and because of that redness, there is also a lack of heat.
Wherever the sun is seen situated upon its path,
it is seen at a height of one hundred thousand yojanas.
For when the sun sets, its solar radiance enters the fire at night;
therefore, it shines from afar.
For when the sun has risen again, the fiery heat enters it;
joined with fire, the sun then shines throughout the day.
Luminosity and heat reside in the solar and fiery splendors;
through their mutual interpenetration, they shine day and night.
When the sun rises over the northern half of the earth and likewise over that southern half,
night enters the waters.
Therefore, by the power of devotion, those waters become cool through their entry day and night;
when the sun sets, the light (tvaṣ) enters back into the day.
Therefore, the waters become warm due to the entry [of the sun] by day and night;
by this sequential process, [this occurs] in the southern and northern halves of the earth.
The day and night of the sun consist of its rising and setting;
that which is called the light of the sun is the day, while the night is said to be of the nature of darkness.
Therefore, night is established [as fixed], while day is known in relation to the sun;
thus, when the sun moves through the middle of Puṣkara, [it is day].
He traverses a fraction of a fraction of the earth in a single muhūrta;
learn now the calculation here regarding the number of yojanas covered in one muhūrta.
It is recorded as being one hundred thousand and thirty-one full [years],
with an additional fifty thousand more.
This course of the sun is indeed prescribed as that of the astrologer;
by this movement, when he reaches the southern limit (dakṣiṇā-kāṣṭhā), [he is said to be] in conjunction with that motion.
That sun indeed reaches the very end of the wood in the middle;
then, during the southern solstice, it revolves through the center of the Puṣkara continent.
On the Mānasottara mountain, however, there is that equinox;
listen now as it moves toward the southern quarter.
Its circumference is calculated at nine crores of yojanas,
as well as four hundred thousand and fifty thousand more.
This movement of the sun is ordained for a single day and night;
it occurs when the sun, having turned back from the southern course, stands at the equinox.
Moving from the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk,
learn now its equinoctial circle in yojanas.
The mandala of the equinox is calculated to be three crores,
and furthermore, one hundred and eighty-one thousand [yojanas].
And when the sun is in Uttarāṣāḍhā during the month of Śrāvaṇa,
it moves toward the northern direction of the sixth continent, Śākadvīpa.
O twice-born ones, the measurement of the northern limit and of the celestial sphere is calculated to be exactly one *koṭi* from the tip of the *yojana*.
It is eighty million yojanas here,
and likewise fifty-eight yojanas more.
The Nāgavīthī is the northern path, while the Ajavīthī is the southern;
likewise, Mūla and Āṣāḍhā are the three [asterisms] at the rising of the Ajavīthī.
Aśvinī, Kṛttikā, and the southern [asterism] (Bharaṇī)—these three are the rising of the Nāgavīthī;
furthermore, I shall describe again to you that which lies between the two solstitial limits (kāṣṭhā).
This [measurement] consists of one hundred and eight lakhs,
plus another three hundred and thirty-three yojanas.
Indeed, the distance between these two *kāṣṭhās* is proclaimed to be one *yojana*;
likewise, the distance between the two *kāṣṭhās*, that is, the two lines, is from south to north.
I shall declare that after careful calculation; listen to it from me.
Each of its intervals is seventy-one yojanas apart.
In addition to those thousands, seventy-five others are recorded for the two lines and the two wooden beams, both on the exterior and the interior.
During the northern course, it moves within the circles;
during the southern course, it moves constantly outside them, always according to their sequence.
The sun traverses one hundred and eighty-three mandalas to the north,
and it travels exactly that same number to the south.
Now learn the measurement of the mandala in terms of yojanas:
it is, in brief, seventeen thousand yojanas.
Furthermore, another two hundred yojanas are proclaimed,
increased indeed by twenty-one yojanas.
This measurement of the mandala has been declared in yojanas;
furthermore, its diameter is prescribed as being across the mandala.
The Sun indeed moves through those [regions] every day by way of his orb,
just as the rim of a potter's wheel turns rapidly.
During its southern course, the sun likewise moves swiftly;
therefore, it traverses a vast distance in a short period of time.
During the southern course, the sun moves through twelve muhūrtas with speed;
however, during the day, the sun traverses thirteen and a half constellations.
Moving through eighteen such asterisms in as many muhūrtas during the night, he glides slowly like a potter’s wheel spinning within its frame.
Likewise, during the northern course of the sun, it moves with slow velocity;
therefore, it traverses a small distance across the earth over a long period of time.
The final day of the northern course, however, consists of eighteen muhūrtas;
during that time as well, he moves with slow progress.
During the first half of the thirteenth [lunar day], the sun moves through the constellations;
during the night, it moves through as many constellations in twelve muhūrtas.
Then, just as the wheel revolves more slowly at the navel,
so too does Dhruva revolve, situated in the center like a lump of clay.
The eternal Dhruva, as he revolves, declares that a day and night consists of exactly thirty muhūrtas;
indeed, he revolves through the circles situated between the two poles.
And just as the hub of a potter’s wheel remains fixed right there,
so indeed should the Pole Star (Dhruva) be understood to revolve right there.
Between those two poles, it revolves in circles;
the motion of the sun is indeed slow by day and swift by night.
Moreover, during the northern course, the movement of the sun is slow by day;
likewise, at night, its movement is indeed swift.
By moving toward the south, the sun's course during the day is swift;
likewise, its movement at night is slow.
Thus, distinguishing between nights and days according to the specific course [of the sun],
he likewise traverses the path, whether even or uneven.
For these world-protectors are stationed in the four directions around the Lokāloka mountain;
Agastya, however, moves with great speed above them.
Thus, while consuming [the fruits of] their past actions, they pass through the night and day; this is the specific description of their course:
to the south of the Nāgavīthī and to the north of the Lokāloka mountain.
For this world-continuum lies outside the path of Vaiśvānara;
as far as the solar radiance shines behind, so far does it manifest in front.
Extending along both its sides and its back,
this mountain rises ten thousand yojanas high.
It is both light and darkness, perfectly circular in every direction,
together with the stars, the moon, the sun, and the hosts of planets and constellations.
Indeed, the worlds shine within the Lokāloka mountain;
this much alone is the world, and beyond that is the region of darkness.
This mountain possesses light for the world, yet it is without light from its own perspective;
nevertheless, because it encompasses the sun, it connects the world with the light beyond.
Therefore, they call that *sandhyā* (the twilight) which is the interval between dawn (*uṣas*) and daybreak (*vyuṣṭi*).
O Brahmin, *uṣas* is known as night, and *vyuṣṭi* is known as day.
Indeed, at the time of twilight, for those Rākṣasas who were swallowing the sun and fire,
there was this curse upon these evil-minded ones by the command of Prajāpati.
Furthermore, the body attains imperishability and likewise freedom from death;
there are three crores of well-known Rākṣasas named Mandehas.
Day after day, those evil-minded ones pray for the thousand-rayed sun as it rises,
wishing to devour that very sun which scorches them.
Then a most terrible battle took place between Sūrya and them;
thereafter Brahmā, the gods, and the most excellent Brāhmaṇas [intervened].
Those who perform the twilight worship always cast water [into the fire],
conjoined with the syllable Om and Brahman, and consecrated by the Gāyatrī mantra.
Then the sun, the maker of light, blazes forth with fierce rays and flashing brilliance;
thereafter, he of great splendor, possessing immense strength and prowess, [shines forth].
The Blessed One, protected by the Brāhmaṇas and by the Vālakhilya sages who maintain his radiant flames, rises upward a hundred thousand yojanas and proceeds swiftly.
Fifteen *nimeṣas* make one *kāṣṭhā*, and one should count thirty *kāṣṭhās* as one *kalā*.
Thirty *kalās* constitute a *muhūrta*, and thirty of those make up a day and night combined.
The decrease and increase [of the day] occur through the divisions of the days in their respective order.
The twilight (saṃdhyā) lasts for only one muhūrta; its decrease and increase are traditionally recorded as such.
Once the sun has risen from the first streak of light until three muhūrtas have passed, [the morning twilight ends].
Then, that time remembered as morning is the fifth division of the day;
from that morning time, the period of three muhūrtas is called saṅgava.
Midday consists of three muhūrtas; from that time [beginning] with saṅgava, and from that time of midday, the period known as aparāhṇa is reckoned.
The wise have declared that there are exactly three muhūrtas known as *kāla*;
when the afternoon has passed, that time is called *sāyāhna*.
The day consists of fifteen muhūrtas, and there are exactly three muhūrtas [of night];
indeed, the day at the equinox is traditionally held to consist of fifteen muhūrtas.
During the southern and northern solstices, days and nights respectively increase and decrease;
for the day swallows the night, and the night swallows the day.
The interval between autumn and spring is considered the equinox;
during the day and night, as well as the lunar phases, the moon partakes equally.
Likewise, fifteen days are designated as a *pakṣa* (fortnight);
two *pakṣas* constitute a *māsa* (month), and two months, produced by the sun, form a *ṛtu* (season).
Three seasons constitute two solstices, which indeed make one solar year; fifteen twinklings of the eye (nimeṣas) make a lightning-flash (vidyut), and ten such flashes make a kāṣṭhā.
Thirty *kalās* constitute one *kāṣṭhā*, and a *mātrā* consists of eighty-two [units]. Thirty-one plus two, that is thirty-three, *mātrās* make up thirty-six [units]. (BndP 1.21.127)
The kalā of twenty-three mātrās consists of sixty-two [parts];
and there are forty thousand and eight hundred [kalās] of lightning.
Know for certain that there are seventy-nine [hundred] there as well;
they say there are exactly four hundred, joined with two lightning-strikes.
This indeed should be known as the excellent portion; here the *nāḍikā* is the cause.
The five [periods] beginning with the year are conceived according to the four measures.
The determination of all time is designated as a *yuga*;
the first year is the *saṃvatsara*, and the second is the *parivatsara*.
The third is the Iḍāvatsara, the fourth is the Anuvatsara, and the fifth of them is the Vatsara; such is time as it is composed of the Yugas.
In a yuga of the sun, there would be a full three hundred parvans;
and from the rising of the sun, there are eighteen hundred and thirty [revolutions].
The seasons consist of thirty solar months;
there are ten [lunar] months, and three hundred and sixty-five [days] constitute the year of the Sun.
Thirty days and nights indeed constitute a month of the Sun;
sixty-one days and nights are understood to be one season.
One hundred and eighty-three days is to be known as the measure of a single solstice of the Sun.
The solar, the lunar, the sidereal, and likewise the civil—
these are the four measures of time by which the determination in the Purāṇas is indeed established.
To the north of Śveta is the mountain named Śṛṅgavān;
its three peaks seem to touch the very surface of the sky.
And because of those peaks, the mountain is called Śṛṅgavān;
one path across it is also celebrated as its width.
Its eastern peak is indeed golden, the middle one is made of gold,
the southern one is silver, and the [northern] peak has the luster of crystal.
And its northern peak, the most excellent, is composed entirely of all kinds of jewels;
thus, by means of these three summits, the mountain is renowned as Śṛṅgavān.
That which is the eastern peak, that indeed the sun attains,
situated in the middle course between the seasons of autumn and spring.
Therefore, the dispeller of darkness makes day and night equal;
and his divine green horses are yoked to his great chariot,
appearing as if anointed by rays as red as lotuses.
At the end of Aries and at the end of Libra, fifteen muhūrtas are traditionally reckoned from sunrise; day and night are of that same duration.
When the sun has entered the first quarter of the Kṛttikās,
then the moon should be known to be in the fourth quarter of the Viśākhās.
When the sun moves through the third portion of Viśākhā,
one should know that the moon is situated at the head of Kṛttikā.
One should know that to be the equinox; so say the great seers.
One should know the equinox by the sun and observe the time by the moon;
when day and night are indeed equal, that is the equinox.
Then, gifts should be given to the ancestors during the equinoxes, especially to Brāhmaṇas; for this [mouth] is the very face of the deity.
The deficient month and the intercalary month, as well as the units of time—kalā, kāṣṭhā, and muhūrta;
likewise, the full moon day (paurṇamāsī) and the new moon day (amāvāsyā) should be known;
and also Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and Anumati.
Tapa and Tapasya, as well as Madhu and Mādhava, together with Śukra and Śuci, constitute the northern course (ayana).
Nabhas and Nabhasya, those known as Iṣa and Ūrja, along with Sahas and Sahasya, constitute the southern course.
Then the Ārtavas should be known as the five sons of Brahmā, five years of age.
From that, the seasons are to be known; for it is from the seasons that the menstrual periods (ārtavāḥ) are said to arise.
Therefore, the new moon day (amāvāsyā) should be known as the mouth of the season for this lunar festival (parvan).

Therefore, the equinox should always be known as beneficial to the ancestors and the gods; having understood the sacred festival day (parvan), a person shall not be deluded regarding rites for the ancestors or the gods.
Therefore, it is remembered that for the wise, the Viṣuvat is always all-pervading; because it extends as far as light, it is called the Loka, and thus it is known as Lokāloka.
The world-protectors stand there in the middle of the Lokāloka mountain;
those four great-souled ones remain until the dissolution of all beings.
Sudhāmā, Vairāja, Kardama, Śaṅkhapa, Hiraṇyaroman, Parjanya, Ketumān, and he who is Rājasa; // BndP_1.21.157 //
Free from duality, free from pride, boundless, and without possessions,
these world-protectors indeed abide in the Lokāloka mountain in the four directions.
That which lies north of the Apas and south of the Ajavīthī is indeed the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna); it lies outside the path of Vaiśvānara.
There dwell sages endowed with progeny who maintain the *agnihotra* sacrifice;
they ensure the continuity of the world and stand upon the path of the ancestors.

Those who desire the world undertake actions performed through the elements and their initiations, with the officiating priests prepared for them; that is their path, which is accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Furthermore, they establish your dharma, which has wavered, age after age,
being themselves purified by austerity, by the observance of boundaries, and by sacred learning.
Indeed, those who were born previously are born here in the houses of those born later;
and likewise, those born later are born even in the deaths of those born previously.
Thus revolving, those eighty-eight thousand sages who were householders remain until the dissolution of all beings.
For those who have resorted to the southern path of Savitṛ and have frequented cremation grounds, this is the enumeration of the ritualists, lasting as long as the moon and stars endure.
And worldly conventions arise from the undertaking of physical elements,
from the activity of desire and aversion, and indeed from the pursuit of sexual union.
Likewise, through the pursuit of sense objects here driven by desire,
and by these various causes, those who have attained perfection have resorted to the cremation grounds.
Those sages seeking [the truth] were born here during the Dvāpara ages;
they were those situated north of the Nāgavīthī and south of the host of the Seven Sages (Ursa Major).
The northern path of Savitṛ is known as the way of the gods (devayāna),
where those pure ascetics dwell who have attained perfection.
They loathe the continuity of rebirth; therefore, death has been conquered by them—the eighty-eight thousand sages who have drawn up their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas).
For they have excessively resorted to the path of water due to the flooding of their dwellings;
yet, because of their association with the world, they avoid sexual intercourse.

And through the cessation of desire and aversion, by avoiding the initiation of actions toward beings, and furthermore, through the absence of attachment to sound and other objects due to perceiving their defects; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.21.172.
By these reasons, they are established as having indeed attained immortality;
for the immortality of those who remain until the dissolution of all beings is thus conceived.
For those who approach their wives for the sake of maintaining the continuity of the three worlds,
there are others who perform both merit and sin through the acts of foeticide and the horse sacrifice.
At the end of the dissolution of all beings, those whose vital seed is drawn upward (the *ūrdhvaretas*) indeed perish;
beyond the Ṛṣis, however, is that which is remembered as Dhruva, situated further upward.
This is the divine third station of Viṣṇu, radiant in the sky;
having gone there, they do not grieve— that is the supreme station of Viṣṇu,
where Dharma, Dhruva, and others who have perfected the worlds abide.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Array of the Sun," in the second section (Anuṣaṅga-pāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
"In the creation of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu, the intermediate periods have also been explained."
And I shall declare to you the sequence of all those things that are yet to come.
Having heard this, O sages, they questioned Romaharṣaṇa concerning the entire course of the sun and the moon, as well as that of the planets.
The sages said:
"How do these luminaries wander through the celestial sphere,
all of them without confusion and likewise without intermixture?"
Does someone cause them to revolve, or do they revolve by themselves? We wish to know this; tell us, O best of beings.
Sūta said:
Understand this which I am telling you, which deludes all beings—
even that which is directly perceived and visible— since it causes the confusion of living creatures.
This Dhruva, who is situated at the tail of the Śaiśumāra [constellation] facing the four quarters, is the son of Uttānapāda; he stands in the sky as its central pivot.
He indeed constantly causes the moon and the sun, along with the planets, to revolve;
and the constellations follow him as he revolves like a wheel.
And by his mind, this entire host of luminaries was established by Dhruva:
the sun and the moon, the stars, and the constellations together with the planets.
Bound by bonds consisting of the armies of the winds to the Pole Star (Dhruva),
their conjunction, their separation, their time, and likewise their movement [are described].
The rising and setting of the stars, as well as the portents at the southern and northern solstices,
and the colors of the planets during the equinoxes— all these proceed from the Pole Star (Dhruva).
The rainy season, the heat, the winter, night, as well as the twilight and the day—
all these, and the auspicious and inauspicious for living beings, proceed from Dhruva.
Presided over by Dhruva, the sun takes up the waters and rains them down;
thus this maker of day, with his blazing rays, is the fire of time.
O brahmins, as the sun, illuminating the quarters with its rays, moved according to the sequence of its revolutions, it scattered a net of light in every direction, impelled by the wind.
O best of the twice-born, Soma receives all the water from the entire world;
that which has been drunk by the Sun, Soma completely transmits back as water.
The sustenance of the world proceeds by means of the channels joined with the vital winds;
for the water that flows from the Moon indeed remains within the very foods.
Just as clouds release water upon the earth due to the obstruction by the wind,
so too is water repeatedly uplifted and then falls down.
There is no destruction of water; it is that very same substance which undergoes transformation.
This is an illusion created by the All-maker for the sake of sustaining the worlds.

The other [aspect] is the Lord of the Universe, the creator of the world, the thousand-eyed Prajāpati, the divine one by whom the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, are pervaded through his illusory power (māyā).
The Creator, the sovereign lord of the entire world, is the maker of day;
from the moon, that which is the water common to all the worlds has descended from the sky.
It is proclaimed as a truth that this entire world has the moon as its support;
from the sun heat flows forth, and from the moon coolness proceeds.
These two, possessing the powers of cold and heat, sustain the world through their union;
they are the river Gaṅgā, which has the moon as its source, pure and of stainless water.
And the great rivers, O best of the twice-born, headed by Bhadrasomā,
as well as those waters that permeate the bodies of all living beings.
While those moving and stationary beings are being consumed by fire,
those waters, having become smoke, emerge here from all sides.
From that, clouds are produced; this is known as the abode consisting of clouds.
The sun, through its rays, draws up water from all living beings.
From the ocean, through conjunction with the wind, the rays draw forth the waters;
that water is the life-giver of the crops and is like nectar.
Then, at the appropriate time according to the power of the seasons, the sun, having turned back,
draws up the waters from the clouds with his bright and white rays.
Impelled by the wind and mixed with it on all sides, the waters situated in the clouds fall down for the sake of the welfare of all living beings.
Then he rains for six months for the growth of all living beings,
accompanied by the wind, thunder, and lightning born of fire.
For from the root *mih*, meaning "to sprinkle," they derive the word *megha* (cloud);
and since the waters do not fall away from it, the wise know that to be *abhram* (a cloud).
Furthermore, the threefold origin of clouds is said to be their source:
those born of fire, those born of Brahmā, and those various kinds born of birds.
Clouds are declared to be of three kinds; I shall describe their origin.
Those born from heat are said to be fiery (āgneya); for them, smoke is set in motion.
The cold, the foul weather, and the winds—these qualities remain established [therein];
as do buffaloes, boars, and those in the form of rutting elephants.
Having become [clouds] and reaching the earth, they delight and move about;
these are indeed the clouds named Jīmūtas, for from them the origin of living beings arises.
Devoid of the quality of lightning, with suspended streams of water,
these massive-bodied silent clouds are subject to the power of Āvaha.
They rain from a distance of one krośa, or even from half a krośa;
they rain upon the peaks and slopes of mountains, and they roar as well.
The clouds named Brahmajas, born from the breath of Brahmā, possess embryos of cranes and carry embryos of cranes within them.
For they are endowed with the quality of lightning and possess the pleasant sound of thunder;
by their constant roar, the earth causes its own body-hairs to sprout.
Like a queen consecrated to the kingdom, this rainy season enjoys renewed youth;
it is attached to these [months], bringing forth the life of all living beings.
The clouds are supported by the second wind, Pravaha;
they are situated at a distance of one and a half yojanas from Niṣkṛta.
Rain, the embryo, and the downpour—these three are proclaimed as their forms;
those clouds born from their wings are named Puṣkarāvartakas.
By Śakra, desiring the welfare of all beings, the wings were severed from those mountains of great power— beings who could travel at will and had grown exceedingly large.
Those clouds, swelling with pride and envious of the water, are called Puṣkaras;
for that reason, they are designated here as Puṣkarāvartakas.
Assuming various forms and possessing most terrible voices,
they are the creators of the rain at the end of the eon and the controllers of the fire of universal destruction.
These rain down at the ends of the ages; they are proclaimed as the third [class], possessing many forms and shapes, filling the surface of the earth.
In the past, those who carried the wind were dependent upon it as they accomplished the cosmic cycle; these were the ones that existed at the beginning when the primordial egg was first split apart.
Those very shell-capsules of the cosmic egg, in which the four-faced Brahmā himself arose as the self-sovereign lord, are proclaimed to be all the clouds.
Smoke is the nourishment for all of them without distinction;
however, among them, Parjanya and the four elephants of the quarters are the most excellent.
The lineage of elephants, mountains, clouds, and serpents is one; though they have become distinct, their single source is said to be water.
In the winter season, when cold prevails, Parjanya and the elephants of the quarters pour down showers of frost for the growth of the remaining crops.
The sixth wind among them, named Parivaha, is their support;
it is that which causes the Blessed Gaṅgā to flow through the atmosphere.
The meritorious river Divyāmṛtajalā stands upon the path of the three Svātis;
the elephants of the quarters, with their broad trunks, [support] its flowing waters.
They emit a spray of mist, which is known as *nīhāra*;
to the south is that mountain which is known as Hemakūṭa.
To the north-east of Mount Udayāgiri, there is a mountain;
there, a city named Puṇḍra is said to be extensively spread out.
The rain that fell upon it was produced from frost;
then a powerful wind blew, carrying away the Himavat.
Drawing it up by his own power, he sprinkles the great mountain;
having crossed over the Himavat, he pours forth the remainder of the rain beyond that.
After that, it arrives here for the sake of increasing the western region;
two years are declared to be for the increase of the two types of crops.
The clouds and their nourishment—all this has been proclaimed;
yet the Sun alone is taught to be the creator of the rains.
Rain indeed has the sun as its root; water proceeds from the sun.
Presided over by Dhruva, the sun sets that rain in motion.
Presided over by Dhruva, Vāyu again withdraws the rain;
for the planet, having emerged from the sun, pervades the entire circle of the constellations.
Having traveled [through the zodiac], at the end it enters the Sun, presided over by Dhruva;
thereafter, learn of the arrangement of the Sun’s chariot.
With a golden wheel that was firmly established, having five spokes, three naves,
and likewise golden rims, the Blessed One [proceeded].
The Sun moves along in his chariot with a radiant wheel that has eight spokes, six parts, and a single rim.
It is recorded that its width and length are ten thousand yojanas;
the pole of its chariot, from the seat of the chariot, is twice that measure in size.
That chariot, created for him by Brahmā according to his purpose,
was indeed golden, divine, unobstructed, and yoked with horses that move as fast as the wind.
With horses in the form of Vedic meters stationed wherever the wheel was,
he appeared here like the very chariot of Varuṇa by its characteristic features.
By him, shining throughout the entire sky, he is indeed the sun;
now, these are the various parts of the Sun's chariot.
Of that solar year, which is conceived as having constituent parts,
the day is traditionally held to be the nave of its single wheel, arranged in due order.
Its spokes are the five seasons, its rim is known as the six seasons;
this chariot bed is known as the year, and both its poles are the two solstices.
His Muhūrtas are known as his beautiful limbs, and his Kalās are remembered as his lovely digits; his Kaṣṭhās are known as his nostrils, and his Kṣaṇas are indeed his axle-shafts.
The closing of his eyes is known as the *anukarṣa*, and his *hīṣā* are said to be the *lavas*;
the night is his *varūtha*, and Dharma is his banner raised high aloft.
The two ends of the axle-pole are known as his Artha (prosperity) and Kāma (desire);
the seven horses, which are the Vedic meters, carry the yoke from the left side.
The Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, the Anuṣṭubh, and likewise the Jagatī;
the Paṅkti, the Bṛhatī, and the Uṣṇik is indeed the seventh.
The wheel is fixed upon the axle, and the axle is joined to the pivot;
the axle revolves together with the wheel, and the pivot revolves together with the axle.
Driven by the pivot, that lord of wheels revolves together with the axle;
such is the arrangement of that chariot according to its functional requirements.
Likewise, the radiant chariot, perfected through the state of conjunction,
moves through the sky by means of that shining sun-god.
The two reins of the chariot are fastened to the tip of the axle;
those two reins revolve around Dhruva, as do the wheel and the yoke.
As that celestial chariot revolves through its circular orbits,
the two ends of its axle-joint indeed remain on the right side of that vehicle.
When Dhruva was indeed firmly grasped, they both moved about like two wheels;
those two followed Dhruva as he revolved by means of their two cords.
The axle-end of that chariot is bound by its rays,
like a rope fastened to a stake, so that it whirls in every direction.
As he moves through the solar orbits, his rays diminish during the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) and increase during the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana).
The two reins of the chariot are indeed attached to the end of the axle-pin;
held fast by Dhruva, those two reins lead the Sun.
When those two, established together with Dhruva, are drawn along,
then the sun revolves within them through its orbits.
It is taught that there are one hundred and eighty circles between the two poles (kāṣṭhā),
as they are released again by the two rays from the Pole Star (dhruva).
In the same way, the sun revolves externally through its orbits;
scattering heat with great speed, it traverses those circular paths.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Enumeration of the Planetary Deities," in the second section (Anuṣaṅga-pāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
[The Sun] was stationed in his chariot, presided over by the gods, the Ādityas, and likewise the sages.
By the Gandharvas and Apsarases, by the Grāmaṇīs, Sarpas, and Rākṣasas.
These indeed dwell in the sun for two months each in succession:
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Pulastya, and the progenitor Pulaha.
Erāvata and Vāsuki, Kaṃsa and Bhīma— both of these,
as well as Rathakṛt and Rathaujā, are proclaimed to be Yakṣas.
Tuṃburu and Nārada, as well as Susthalā and Puñjikasthalā,
and Rakṣas and Heti— these are declared to be the two Yātudhānas.
These indeed always dwell in the sun during the months of Madhu and Mādhava;
Mitra and Varuṇa, as well as the sage Atri, are proclaimed [as its presiding deities].
Likewise, Vasiṣṭha is renowned, as are Sahajanyā and Menakā;
the two Rākṣasas are also well-known, as is the slaughter of Pauruṣeya.
The two Gandharvas Hāhā and Hūhū, as well as Yajña, Rathasvana,
Rathacitra, and another known as Nāgasākṣaka.
And Rambhaka—these dwell during the two months of Śuci and Śukra;
thereafter, other deities reside here once again when the sun [is in its southern course].
Vivasvān, Aṅgiras, Bhṛgu,
Elāpattra, the serpent Śeṣa, and both Śaṅkhapāla— these were the ones.
Viśvāvasu and Ugrasena, as well as Śveta and Aruṇa;
and those two, Pramlocā and Anumlocā, are likewise renowned.
Then the Yātudhāna, the serpent, and the tiger—
these three dwell in the sun during the months of Nabhas and Nabhasya.
Furthermore, in autumn, other radiant deities of the sages dwell there:
Parjanya, Pūṣan, Bhāradvāja, and Gautama.
The Gandharva Parāvasu and likewise Suruci,
as well as Viśvācī and Ghṛtācī— both of these possessed auspicious marks.
Nāga, Erāvata, the renowned Dhanañjaya,
Śceñajit, Suṣeṇa, Senī, and those two grāmaṇīs.
Water and wind—these two are declared to be *yātudhānas*;
they indeed always dwell in the sun during the months of Āśvina and Kārtika.
And during the two months of winter, while the sun dwells there,
these two— Aṃśa and Bhaga— are the sons of Kaśyapa, as are Kratu and Ha.
The serpent Mahāpadma, Sarva, Karkeṭaka, the Gandharva Citrasena, and both of those known as Ūrṇāyu; BndP_1,23.17 //
Both Urvaśī and Pūrvacitti were likewise Apsarases;
Tārkṣya and Ariṣṭanemi were both the Senānīs and the Grāmaṇīs.
Vidyutsphūrja and Śatāyu are proclaimed as the two Yātudhānas;
these dwell in the sun during the months of Sahas and Sahasya.
Then, during the two months of the dewy season as well,
Tvaṣṭṛ, Viṣṇu, Jāmadagnya, and likewise Viśvāmitra indeed dwell there.
Likewise, the two Nāgas who are the sons of Kadrū, both Kambala and Aśvatara,
as well as the Gandharva Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Sūryavarcas.
Likewise Tilottamā and Rambhā; the Rākṣasa Brahmāpeta, and another, Yajñāpeta, who was the most excellent of Rākṣasas.
Ṛtajit and Satyajit are declared to be the two Gandharvas;
O best of sages, Tapas and Tapasya dwell in the sun.
O twice-born ones, the Lord Savitṛ, constantly nourishing the ancestors, gods, humans, and others,
revolves as the cause of day and night.
These gods dwell in the sun for two months each in succession;
they are indeed the presiding deities of the stations, numbering twelve times seven.
These sages cause the supreme splendor of the sun to swell with their own splendor,
and they praise the Sun-god with their composed words.
The Gandharvas and Apsarases attend upon him with songs and dances, while the Grāmaṇīs, Yakṣas, and Bhūtas hold the reins.
The serpents indeed carry the sun, and the Yātudhānas travel with it;
the Vālakhilyas, surrounding the sun, lead it to its setting upon the mountain of sunrise.
Of these very gods, according to their prowess, according to their austerity,
according to their dharma, according to their application, according to their truthfulness, and according to their strength.
"That sun shines with heat; he is Indra among these by his splendor"—thus do these [deities] dwell here in the sun for two months each.
The sages, the gods, the gandharvas, the hosts of pannagas and apsarases, as well as the grāmaṇīs, the yakṣas, and the leading yātudhānas; BndP_1,23.31 //
These, being thus proclaimed, scorch, rain down, shine, blow, and create; they dispel the inauspicious karma of living beings.
For these [sins] take away the merit of men who are evil-minded,
while they occasionally dispel the misfortune of those whose conduct is virtuous.
These, following the day, revolve together with the sun,
raining, scorching, and indeed gladdening all living beings.
And they protect all beings here until the destruction of the Manu-period;
for this is indeed the station of those who identify with their respective stations throughout the Manvantaras.
Those who belong to the past, the future, and those who exist at present—
these fourteen groups of seven indeed dwell thus in the sun;
they are all the hosts throughout the fourteen Manvantaras here.
Releasing heat in summer and cold in the rainy season, and likewise rain, day, and night,
he moves under the influence of the seasons with his rays revolving, truly gratifying the gods, the ancestors, and human beings.
The Sun pleases the gods with nectar after having increased the Soma with the Suṣumṇa ray;
it becomes full through the sequence of days during the bright fortnight, and the gods drink it during the dark fortnight.
And indeed, the nectar of immortality— the Soma that remains as a single digit and flows by its rays at the end of the dark fortnight—
that the ancestors drink, as do the gods and the Saumyas, and likewise the Kāvyas.
Mortals overcome hunger with food and drink produced by medicinal herbs that have been nourished by rain— water which was first released by the sun and its rays, and then drawn up once more.
The Sun provides satisfaction to the gods with nectar during the bright fortnight, and to the ancestors with nectar during the dark fortnight;
he constantly sustains mortals with food, and nourishes them well with his rays as he blazes.
Then, with his swift, tawny horses, Hari steals away the waters with his golden rays;
and at the time of emission, releasing them once more, the Sun-god perpetually sustains the world of the moving and the unmoving.
Hari is drawn by his bay horses; then he drinks water with his thousandfold bay steeds;
