thereafter, being carried along by those bay horses, Hari releases that very water once more.
Thus, with his single wheel and swift chariot, drawn by those auspicious, unhindered horses, the Sun reached the abode of the Vedas.
Indeed, revolving with a single-wheeled chariot day and night,
he traverses the earth bounded by the seven continents and oceans, drawn by seven horses for each of the seven regions.

By those horses in the form of meters, which could assume any shape at will, which were yoked once and for all, and which moved with the speed of thought, the chariot stood wherever the wheel was directed. To their left were those [other horses] swift as the mind.
Those horses, green, white, and tawny, accompanied by the lords who are exponents of the Veda, complete one hundred and eighty-three circuits in a year.
The outer and inner mandalas, joined at the beginning of the kalpa, flow according to the sequence of days until the dissolution of all beings.
Surrounded by the Vālakhilyas, he revolves day and night,
being praised with foremost, well-composed words by the great seers.
The Lord of Heaven, wandering about, is served by Gandharvas and hosts of Apsarases with songs and dances, as well as by Pataṅgas, Patagas, and horses.
The chariot of Soma has wheels made of weapons; his horses are of a dark-blue hue, yoked ten on the left and ten on the right, and with them he moves about.
The constellations resting upon the celestial path are impelled by the support of Dhruva;
likewise, the contraction and expansion of its rays are understood to be like those of the sun.
The chariot of the Moon should be known as having three wheels and horses on both sides;
it arose from the mass of waters, complete with horses and a charioteer.
It was equipped with three wheels, each having a hundred spokes,
and yoked to ten excellent white horses— divine, lean, unimpeded, and swift as thought.
Once yoked to that chariot, they carry it until the end of the age;
when the chariot is brought to a halt, both Śveta and Cakṣuḥśravas indeed [remain].
Eight horses of a single color, possessing the luster of conch shells, carry him;
they are Yajus, Caṇḍamanas, Vṛṣa, Vājī, Nara, and Haya.
Aśva, Gaviṣṇu, the renowned Haṃsa, Vyoma, and likewise Mṛga—
by these names all ten of the Moon’s horses are known.
These carry the divine Moon along with the consecration;
surrounded by the gods and the ancestors, Soma proceeds.
At the beginning of the moon's bright fortnight, when the sun is situated beyond [the equinox],
it is constantly filled day by day until the end of the subsequent [fortnight] while remaining fixed.
The Sun, with a single ray, constantly replenishes the moon— which has its body drunk by the gods and has waned for fifteen days.
Filling each respective portion day by day through the *suṣumṇā* [channel],
the white digits (*kalā*) indeed increase as he is nourished by the *suṣumṇā*.
"Therefore, indeed, they wane during the dark fortnight and swell during the bright fortnight;
thus, by the power of the sun, the moon is replenished. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.23.62)
On the full moon day, he is seen white with a perfectly full orb;
thus is Soma nourished during the bright fortnight through the succession of days.
Then, from the second day until the fourteenth of the waxing moon,
[the moon] consists of the essence of the waters, being composed solely of the element of sapid flavor.
The gods, being delighted, drink the pleasant nectar of *svadhā* consisting of water;
for that nectar has been gathered over half a month by the radiance of the sun.
For the sake of food, they partake of the nectar Soma for one night on the full moon day, together with all the gods, the ancestors, and the sages.
At the beginning of the dark fortnight of the moon, as it faces the sun,
its digits are gradually diminished by the gods and the ancestors who drink them.
Three, thirty, and likewise thirty-three;
and three thousand gods indeed drink the Soma.
Thus, as he is being drunk by these, the dark digits indeed increase;
therefore, the bright digits wane, while the dark ones cause him to swell.
In this manner, as the moon is drunk by the gods day by day,
the best of the deities reach the new moon after drinking it for half a month.
For on the new moon day, the ancestors indeed abide in the moon;
therefore, when fifteen units of time remain, consisting of a mere fraction [of the sixteenth], [the offering should be made].
In the afternoon, the hosts of ancestors wait upon him last;
they drink for two lava-periods, as do those who remain of his remaining kalās.
On the new moon day, that nectar of *svadhā* flows forth from their rays;
having drunk that *svadhā* for the satisfaction of the months, they go to the state of immortality.
The sun heats that *suṣumṇā* ray, and by means of it, the moon—
composed of nectar— is likewise drunk by the gods during the dark fortnight.
The Saumyas, the Barhiṣads, and the Agniṣvāttas— these three groups,
as well as those who are called the Kāvyas, are all indeed the Pitṛs.
The years are indeed the Kāvyas; those known as the two sets of five-year periods are the Saumyas; the seasons are to be known as the Ṛtus; and the months are remembered as the Barhiṣads.
O twice-born ones, the Agniṣvātta and Ārttava Pitṛs are indeed the creation of the Pitṛs;
on the fifteenth day, a digit of him who is being drunk by the Pitṛs [remains].
When his fifteenth part has been completely exhausted, that is the new moon; thereafter, another part begins to fill up for him.
Indeed, the waning and waxing of the moon are traditionally held to occur at the beginning of its fortnights on the sixteenth day;
likewise, this waning and waxing of the moon is caused by the sun.
I shall further describe the chariots of the lunar mansions, the planets, and of Rāhu.
The chariot of the son of Soma (Mercury) is indeed composed of light and is brilliant white.
The glorious chariot of Bhārgava, equipped with quivers and a flagstaff, resounded like a cloud and was equal to the sun in its splendor.
Yoked with excellent horses of various colors born from the earth—
white, tawny, dappled, blue, yellow, and crimson— [he set forth].
And Kṛṣṇa, Harita, Pṛṣata, and Pṛśni—
by those ten illustrious steeds, which were not lean and possessed the speed of the wind.
The glorious golden chariot of Bhauma was also excellent, drawn by eight horses that were unimpeded, crimson, all-pervading, and born of fire.
The boy indeed creeps along with straight, crooked, and winding gait;
then the learned Bṛhaspati, the descendant of Aṅgiras and preceptor of the gods, [perceives him].
He proceeds with white horses on a golden chariot,
drawn by eight divine steeds as swift as the wind.
Remaining in the lunar mansion for a year, he indeed proceeds by means of that conjunction;
thereafter, Śanaiścara also [proceeds] with his powerful horses born of the sky.
Having mounted a chariot made of black iron, he indeed proceeds slowly;
likewise, Svarbhānu’s horses are eight in number, black and as swift as thought.
The chariot of that [Rāhu] consists of darkness; once yoked, it carries him away.
Having emerged from the Ādityas, Rāhu approaches the Moon during the lunar nodes (parvan).
And Soma goes to the Sun during the solar parvan days;
furthermore, the chariot of Ketu has eight horses that possess the speed of the wind.
Having the color of straw-smoke, brindled, and reddish-brown like a donkey—
these are declared to be the steeds of the planets, together with their chariots.
All of them are fixed upon Dhruva; having grown great, they are bound by the rays of the wind.
Being heated, they indeed revolve according to their respective courses.
Increased by the invisible winds of the Vāyavya region and by the rays of the wind, the moon, sun, and planets revolve in the sky, having grown great thereby.
The hosts of luminaries follow him as he wanders,
just as a boat on the water is carried along by the water itself.
In this way, these divine abodes are indeed carried along by the rays of the wind;
moving through the sky, those hosts of gods are not seen.
As many as are the stars, so many are the wind-ropes;
all are fastened to Dhruva, and as they revolve, they cause those [stars] to revolve.
Just as oil-pressers cause a wheel to revolve by their own rotation,
so too do the luminaries, bound by the wind, revolve in every direction.
Driven by the wind-circles, the luminaries move like a whirling firebrand; because it carries them along, that wind is known as the Pravaha.
Thus bound to Dhruva, this host of luminaries moves;
it is to be known as that very Śiśumāra (the porpoise) composed of stars, which is Dhruva in the sky.
Whatever sin one commits by day, one is released from it upon seeing him at night;
and as many stars as there are in the sky, they are all supported by the Śiśumāra.
One should know that Sākāra and Śiśumāra live for exactly that many years, or even more, according to their respective divisions.
Then, Uttānapāda is to be known as his upper jaw;
Yajña is to be known as the lower jaw, while Dharma is situated upon his head.
Nārāyaṇa is to be meditated upon in the heart, the two Aśvins in the two fore-feet,
and Varuṇa and Aryaman in his two hind-thighs.
The penis is the year; Mitra is seated in its apāna. In the tail are Agni, Mahendra, Mārīca Kaśyapa, and Dhruva.
The stars of the Śiśumāra do not set; nor do the four—the lunar mansions, the moon, the sun, and the planets—along with the hosts of stars.
All of them, facing upward yet turned away, have become curved and are situated in the sky;
presided over by Dhruva, they revolve clockwise around Dhruva alone.
The supreme lord who revolves, the central pivot in the heavens, is Dhruva;
he is remembered as the last among Agni, Indra, and Kaśyapa.
Alone, with his face turned downwards, he wanders upon the summit of Mount Meru; indeed, drawing this wheel of luminaries toward himself with his mace,
he gazes at Meru while circumambulating it clockwise along its perimeter.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Glorification of Dhruva’s Conduct," in the second section (Anuṣaṅga-pāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, as proclaimed by the great sage Vyāsa.
Sūta said:
Having heard this, those wise sages were once again filled with doubt.
Then they again asked for a reply that caused their hair to stand on end.
Regarding that which was stated by you, "the houses," and explained at length:
how can they be the abodes of the gods? Describe how they are the luminaries.
"Explain all of this, as well as the definitive determination of the luminaries.
Vāyu said:
"Having heard their words, Sūta then became composed."
He spoke these supreme words, resolving their doubt,
concerning that matter which has been declared by those of great wisdom and enlightened intellect.
I shall declare this to you regarding the origin of the sun and the moon,
and how the temples of the gods here are traditionally known as the abodes of the sun and the moon.
After that, I shall describe the origin of the three kinds of fire:
the divine fire, the elemental fire, and the earthly fire born from the unmanifest.
When the night had passed for Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest,
this world was yet undifferentiated and enveloped in the darkness of night.
When this world was left with no beings remaining and all distinctions had perished,
the self-existent Blessed One appeared there to accomplish the purpose of the world's governance.
Like a firefly, he moved about with the desire to manifest himself;
then, he beheld the fire at the beginning of the world, resting upon the earth and water.
Having concealed it for the sake of manifestation, the Lord divided it threefold;
that which is wind in this world is called the earthly fire.
That which blazes as the sun is known as the pure fire (śuci), while that which is in the lightning is to be understood as the water-born (abja); now I shall describe their characteristics.
The three fires—the lightning fire, the digestive fire, and the solar fire—are indeed the embryos of the waters;
therefore, by drinking the waters with his rays, that sun blazes there in the sky.
Just as the summer fire entered by lightning is not extinguished by the waters of the rainy season,
so too the digestive fire residing within the bellies of human beings cannot be quenched by water.
Therefore, solar, electric, and even digestive fire are without fuel; some light is considered to exist within the waters, while some is seen as having water for its fuel.
The fire fueled by wood is produced by friction; that same fire is extinguished by water.
The blazing fire is known as Pavamāna, while the digestive fire is considered to be Niṣprabha.
And this white, heatless light that illuminates the mandala is the solar radiance;
indeed, it sets at the time of the gods' departure by one quarter.
Fire enters the night; therefore, it shines from afar.
And when the sun rises, that heat which is of the nature of fire enters it.
From the foot of the earthly Agni, therefore, that [celestial] Agni burns;
likewise, both luminosity and heat reside in the solar and fiery splendors.
Through their mutual interpenetration, they nourish one another;
for the northern half of the earth is thus [sustained] by water, and the southern half by fire.
When the sun rises again, the night indeed enters the waters;
therefore, the waters become heated by the entry of the day and night.
When the sun sets again, the day indeed enters the waters;
therefore, at night, the waters appear white and radiant once more.
By this sequential process, at the southern and northern solstices,
he enters the waters daily during day and night at sunrise and sunset.
And that sun which blazes, drinking the water with its rays,
is known as the divine and pure fire, mixed with the earthly fire.
That fire has a thousand feet; pure and resembling a jar of clarified butter, it draws [the essence] from all sides through its thousand channels.
The waters of rivers, of the ocean, and of wells on all sides;
those that are stationary and those that are mobile, as well as the waters of irrigation channels and the like.
He has a thousand rays that emit cool, rain, and heat;
four hundred of those channels rain down with diverse forms.
The Candanas, the Sādhyas, and likewise the Kūtanās and Akūtanās—
these are all rays known by the name Amṛtas, which bring forth rain.
And from those two, three hundred other rays emerge:
the visible clouds, the southern ones, the rain-bearing clouds, and those that produce snow.
They are declared by name as the Candrās, the Aṣṭās, the Mitābhās, the Gabhastis,
the Śuklās, the Kuhakās, the Gāvas, and likewise the Viśvabhṛts.
Those three hundred and sixty white [channels] by name are the creators of all phenomena;
having equally divided the channels, they belong to humans, the ancestors, and the gods.
In this world, he satisfies humans with herbs, the ancestors with the ancestral offering (svadhā),
and all the gods with nectar (amṛta)— thus he gratifies all three by means of these three.
In both spring and summer, he heats [the world] with three hundred rays;
then, during the rainy season and autumn, he rains down with four hundred.
In both the winter and the cool seasons, Indra, Dhātṛ, Bhaga, Pūṣan, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman discharge the frost in three ways.
Aṃśu, Vivasvat, Tvaṣṭṛ, Savitṛ, and Viṣṇu [are the presiding deities] in the month of Māgha; and Varuṇa and Pūṣan in Phālguna.
In the month of Caitra, the Sun is Dhātṛ; in Vaiśākha, he is indeed Tāpana;
in the month of Jyeṣṭha, he becomes Indra; and in Āṣāḍha, he is Savitṛ.
Vivasvat is remembered as the portion in the month of Śrāvaṇa;
Bhaga in the month of Prauṣṭhapada; Parjanya in the month of Āśvayuja; and Tvaṣṭṛ-Ravi in the month of Kārttika.
In Mārgaśīrṣa he becomes Mitra, and in Pauṣa he is the eternal Viṣṇu;
Varuṇa possesses five thousand rays in his solar function.
The god Pūṣan [is borne] by six thousand [horses], and likewise the Sun by seven;
Dhātṛ by eight thousand, and Śatakratu by nine.
Savitṛ travels with ten [rays], Bhaga travels with eleven;
Sūrya heats with seven, and Tvaṣṭṛ likewise heats with eight.
Aryaman moves with ten [rays], Parjanya heats with nine;
but Viṣaṇu heats the earth with six thousand rays.
In spring the sun is tawny, in summer the sun has the luster of gold;
in the rainy season it is white in color, and in autumn the sun is pale yellow.
In the winter the sun is copper-colored, and in the cool season it is red;
thus are declared the colors of the sun arising according to the seasons.

The sun bestows strength upon medicinal herbs, sustenance upon the ancestors through their own inherent power, and nectar even upon the immortals; there is no third thing that he does not grant to these three.
In this way, the sun's thousand rays, which accomplish the welfare of the world,
are differentiated according to the season, yielding water, cold, or heat.
This white, radiant orb known as the sun is the foundation and the very source of the constellations,
the planets, and the moon.
The moon, the stars, and all the planets are to be known as originating from the Sun;
Soma is the lord of the constellations, and the Sun is the king of the planets.
The remaining five planets are to be known as lords who move according to their will;
moreover, it is recited that fire is Āditya and water is remembered as Candramas.
Listen as the natures of the remaining [planets] are correctly described:
Skanda, the commander of the celestial army, is recited as the planet Aṅgāraka.
The wise who know the knowledge of the Vedas declare Nārāyaṇa to be the Buddha;
Rudra is Vaivasvata himself, Yama, the lord of the world.
The great planet Śanaiścara, the best of the twice-born, moves slowly;
and the two preceptors of the gods and asuras are both radiant, great planets.
These two, Śukra and Bṛhaspati, are the sons of Prajāpati;
the entire three worlds have the Sun as their root—of this there is no doubt.
From this arises the entire world, including the gods, asuras, and humans—
of Rudra, Upendra, Indra, Candra, and the foremost of Brahmins who dwell in the third heaven.
He is the splendor of all splendid things, the entire energy that is universal,
the soul of all, the lord of all worlds, Mahādeva, the Lord of Creatures.
The Sun alone is the supreme deity and the pillar of the three worlds;
from him everything is born, and into him everything is dissolved.
For in ancient times, O Brahmins, existence and non-existence for all people issued forth from the Sun;
the world is to be known as his planet, the radiant and brilliantly shining Ravi.
Here they go to their destruction and are born again and again—
moments, hours, days, nights, and all the fortnights in their entirety.
The months, the years, the seasons, and the yugas— indeed,
without that Āditya, this reckoning of time does not exist.
Without Time, there would be no Veda, no initiation, and no sequence of daily rites;
and due to the lack of division among the seasons, whence could there be flowers, roots, and fruits?

Whence would there be the production of grain, or even the multitude of grasses and medicinal herbs? There would be an absence of all worldly transactions for living beings, both in heaven and here on earth.
Except for the Sun, who scorches the world and draws up the waters,
he is Time, he is Fire, the twelvefold Soul, and the Lord of Creatures.
O best of the twice-born, this one heats the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile; he is that mass of splendors who scorches the darkness of the entire world.
Having ascended the supreme path, he heats this entire world on all sides— with his sides, above, and below— by means of the rays of the wind.
Just as a lamp that illuminates, when suspended in the middle of a house, equally destroys the darkness on all sides, above, and below; BndP_1,24.63.
In the same way, the thousand-rayed Sun, the king of planets and lord of the world,
illuminates the entire universe from all sides with his rays.
Of those thousands of rays of the sun which were previously enumerated by me, seven further rays are the most excellent; they are the planets and the leaders.
Suṣumṇa, Harikeśa, and likewise Viśvakarman;
then another, Viśvaśravas, and beyond him Saṃpadvasu.
Arvāvasu is proclaimed as one, and Svarāṭ as another;
Suṣumṇa, who is a ray of the sun, nourishes the waning moon.
This Suṣumṇā is proclaimed to have a horizontal and upward movement;
he who is Harikeśa is celebrated as being born from the womb of a bear.
To the south, Viśvakarman increases the ray Vudha;
and he who is behind is known by the wise as Viśvaśravas, whose source is Śukra.
The ray named Saṃpadvasu is the source of Lohita;
the sixth ray, Arvāvasu, is the source of Bṛhaspati.
Furthermore, the self-ruling Sun again nourishes the planet Saturn with his rays;
thus, by the power of the Sun, do the planets, lunar mansions, and stars [shine].
All those revolve in the sky, and this entire world returns [to them];
because they do not perish (*na kṣīyante*), they are therefore designated as *nakṣatra*s (stars/constellations).
These fields are indeed first reached by the rays;
then the Sun, the maker of the constellations, takes possession of those fields.

For those who have crossed over by means of their good deeds performed here, these stars are indeed "tārakās" because they deliver them at the end of their merit through their reliance on the planets; and they are also "tārakās" because of their whiteness.
The sun constantly takes away all divine, terrestrial, and nocturnal splendors, as well as the heat of ascetic penances.
Among these elements, the verbal root *svan* is perceived in the sense of moving;
because he causes the movement of fire and water, he is therefore considered Savitṛ.
This root *cadi*, which possesses manifold meanings, is said to signify "delight";
it is manifested in whiteness, in immortality, and in coolness.
The sun and the moon are in their divine, radiant, and celestial orbs;
they are composed of water and fire, white, circular like jars, and auspicious.
In that [egg], the orb of the moon is known to consist of condensed water,
while the white orb of the sun consists of condensed light.
All the gods,
taking refuge in the stars, the sun, and the planets, enter all these stations in every respect throughout all the Manvantaras.
Those very temples are known by those names;
likewise, the Sun shall enter the solar abode, and the Moon the lunar one.
Śukra shall enter the station of Śaukra, which has sixteen flames and is radiant;
likewise, Bṛhaspati enters Jaiva, and Lohita enters Lauhita.
The deity Śanaiścara likewise enters the station of Śanaiścara;
Budha enters the station of Budha, and Svarbhānu likewise occupies the station of Svarbhānu.
And all the constellations enter into the constellations;
all these houses are the luminaries of those whose nature is merit.
These places, created by the Self-Existent at the beginning of the kalpa, endure until the final dissolution of all beings.
In all the Manvantaras, those very abodes of the gods are indeed occupied by presiding deities; thus, the abodes of the gods remain constant.

Those who are past are associated with the past deities; those yet to be are associated with the future deities; and those existing now are associated with the present deities who occupy their stations. In this very Manvantara, these are remembered as the celestial bodies (grahas) involved in the sacrificial rites.
In the Vaivasvata interval, Vivasvat was the son of Aditi and the Sun;
Tviṣi, the son of Dharma, is remembered as the divine Soma, the Vasu.
The god Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu, should be known as the priest of the Asuras;
the god of great splendor, the preceptor of the gods, is remembered as the son of Agni.
Budha and Manohara are known as the sons of Tviṣīmat;
Śanaiścara, who is deformed, is the son of Vivasvat and Saṃjñā.
From Agni was born Yuvan in Vikeśī; he was the lord of the Lohitas.
Those known as the Ṛkṣas were the daughters of Dakṣa, and they are remembered as the Nakṣatras.
Svarbhānu, the son of Siṃhikā, is an asura who torments all beings;
for those who possess self-conceit (abhimānin) are indeed proclaimed [to reside] within the moon, the lunar mansions, the planets, and the sun.
These locations have been described, as well as the deities who occupy them;
the white location belongs to Vivasvat, the thousand-rayed sun.
The abode of the radiance of the thousand-rayed sun is watery and white;
that of the charming one with five rays is known to be watery and dark blue.
The watery white lotus of Śukra has sixteen rays;
that of the nine-rayed Bhauma is a red watery abode.
The vast abode of Bṛhaspati is yellow and consists of twelve parts;
that of the Sun is said to be red and made of rays, while that of Saturn is black and composed of water.
The abode of Svarbhānu is a realm of darkness, a dwelling place that torments all beings; all the stars should be known as consisting of water, yet their rays are of fire.
The supports for merit and fame, which are exceedingly white in color, should be known as consisting of condensed water; they were created at the very beginning of the kalpa.
Through contact with the rays of the sun, they are known to be of the nature of light;
the diameter of the sun is recorded as nine thousand yojanas.
The diameter of that mandala is three times its [the sun's] extent;
the diameter of the moon is recorded as being twice the diameter of the sun.
But Svarbhānu, having become equal to those two, glides below them;
he was fashioned in the shape of a disk by lifting up the shadow of the earth.
The third station of Svarbhānu is the vast realm consisting of darkness;
having emerged from the sun, it proceeds toward the moon during the lunar phases.
On the solar festival days (parvan), he goes from Soma back to the Sun;
because he drives away the light with his own radiance (svar-bhās), he is therefore called Svarbhānu.
Bhārgava is ordained to be one-sixteenth part of the moon,
both in terms of its orb and its measurement in yojanas from the Viṣkambha.
Bṛhaspati should be known as having one-quarter less than Bhārgava;
both Bhauma and Saura are recorded as having one-quarter less than Bṛhaspati.
The wise one [should know that] the extent and the mandala of those two are each reduced by one quarter;
and indeed, those forms which consist of stars and constellations are possessed of bodies.
The knower of reality should know that the lunar asterisms are generally equal in form to Mercury, both in width and in their mandalas, and are conjoined with the moon.
The forms of the stars and constellations are inferior to one another by five hundred, four hundred, three hundred, and two hundred yojanas respectively.
The clusters of stars, drawn out from east to west, measure at least half a *yojana* and so forth; nothing smaller than these exists.
Above them are three planets that travel far;
they are to be known as Saturn, Aṅgiras (Jupiter), and Vakra (Mars), which move slowly.
Below them, moreover, are four great planets:
the Sun, the Moon, Mercury, and Venus, who move with great speed.
There are as many millions of stars as there are constellations in every direction;
by rule and according to their fixed order, the movement of these constellations is established.
And the course of the sun among them follows the sequence of the solstices as its low and high points;
when the moon is at the new-moon phases while situated on the path of the northern transit (uttarāyaṇa), [it is so].
Due to its height, it is seen quickly by those clear rays of policy;
at that time, it is situated on the southern path, having resorted to a lowly track.
Enveloped by the earth’s shadow at both the full and new moons,
the sun is never seen at its proper time and swiftly sets.
Therefore, while situated on the northern path, the moon is seen on the new-moon day;
it is seen on the southern path by necessity, and yet it is not seen [there].
By the movement and conjunction of the luminaries,
the sun and the moon have simultaneous settings and simultaneous risings during the equinoxes.
In the northern paths,
the setting and rising of the Vyantara deities are to be known as following the movement of the circle of luminaries on the days of the full moon and the new moon.
When the sun, possessing rays, moves while situated on the path of the southern solstice,
then the sun glides beneath all the planets.
Having formed a vast mandala, the moon moves above it;
the entire circle of constellations glides above the moon.
Above the lunar mansions is Mercury; above Mercury is Venus;
above Venus is Mars; and above Mars is Jupiter.
Above that is Saturn, and above that is the circle of the Seven Sages;
and above the Seven Sages is Dhruva established.
The distances between the stars and the planets above are, in successive order, two thousand and one hundred yojanas.
The planets and the moon and sun, moving with divine splendor in the sky,
are eternally joined with the constellations as they proceed in their fixed order.
The planets, constellations, and suns— whether in their states of depression, exaltation, or rectitude— behold all living beings simultaneously during both conjunctions and separations.
For these exist in mutual dependence and are joined with one another; their conjunction, however, should be understood by the wise as being without confusion.
Such indeed is the arrangement of the earth and the celestial bodies,
as well as that of the continents, the oceans, and the mountains.
Regarding the years, the rivers, and those who indeed dwell within them—
it is within these very constellations that all the planets have arisen.
Vivasvān, the son of Aditi and indeed the Sun, was born under the Viśākhā constellation during the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara; he is the foremost of all the planets.
The radiant Dharmaputra, the divine Soma, the son of Vasu,
the cool-rayed maker of night, was born under the constellation Kṛttikā.
Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu, possessing sixteen rays, arose immediately after the Sun as the foremost of the stellar planets in the constellation Tiṣya.
The planet Bṛhaspati, the son of Aṅgiras, who possesses twelve rays and is the preceptor of the world, was born under the Pūrvā-phālgunī nakṣatras.
The planet Lohitāṅga, the son of Prajāpati, possesses nine flames;
according to the sacred tradition, he was born here under the Pūrvāṣāḍhā constellation.
In the Revatī asterisms, the seven-rayed planet Sauri Śanaiścara [is located];
and in Dhaniṣṭhā, the planet Saumya Budha is said to have risen with five rays.
Consisting of darkness, the son of Death, the consumer of progeny, the crested one,
born under Ārśleṣā, is a great planet that seizes all.
Likewise, the daughters of Dakṣa were established under their own names;
Rāhu, consisting of darkness and vigor, was by nature a black orb.
A planet born under the Bharaṇīs is one who oppresses the moon and the sun;
these stars and planets, beginning with Bhārgava, are also to be understood in this manner.

Since they fall into a state of deficiency during afflictions caused by the birth star (janmanakṣatra), they are touched by that defect; therefore, [one should perform rites] according to the division of the planets (grahabhakti).
Among all these planets, the Sun is said to be the first;
among the star-planets, Venus is the first, and among the comets, the one with smoke is the first.
Among the planets divided according to the four directions, Dhruva is the pivot;
among the lunar mansions, it is Śraviṣṭhā; and likewise, among the solstices, it is the northern one.
Of the five-year cycle, the first year is recorded as the initial one;
of the seasons, it is the cool season (śiśira), and of the months, it is indeed Māgha.
Among the fortnights, it is proclaimed as the bright fortnight; among the lunar days, as the first day (pratipad);
and among the divisions of day and night, it is also declared to be the day.
Likewise, O best among those who know time, the first of the muhūrtas has Rudra as its presiding deity;
and the first of the moments (kṣaṇas) and twinklings of the eye (nimeṣas) is also time.
The five-year cycle (yuga) begins with the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā and ends at Śravaṇā;
it revolves like a wheel according to the specific motion of the sun.
Therefore, the Lord Divākara is known by those who know him as Time (Kāla),
the initiator and the terminator of the four classes of beings.
"Even for that [system], the Blessed Lord Rudra himself is the manifest deity who sets it in motion;
thus is the arrangement of the luminaries established through the determination of their purpose."
Created by the Lord for the sake of worldly convention,
this [system] was condensed by Uttara, and likewise by Dhruva.
Extending everywhere among them, it stands as if circular;
at the beginning of the kalpa, it was set in motion by the Lord through the power of the intellect.
Having that as its support, possessing that conceit, and consisting of the essence of all light,
this is the wonderful transformation of the Pradhāna in its universal form.
It is not possible for any person with physical eyes to calculate, according to its true nature, the coming and going of the luminaries.
Having examined it skillfully with the intellect through scripture, inference, direct perception, and logical reasoning, it should be believed by the wise man.
O Brahmins, these five— optometry, the scriptures, water, writing, and arithmetic— are the means for those whose wealth is their intellect in discerning the multitude of luminaries.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Luminaries," in the second section (Anuṣaṅgapāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Having spoken this, the highly intelligent Vāyu, who is devoted to the welfare of the world, [continued].
The Blessed One performed his recitation when the sun had reached its meridian.
And all those sages who had assembled there likewise stood with their souls restrained and their palms joined in reverence.
"He who is the Lord, the life of all living beings, worshipped at the conclusion of his vow—
to him, O Nīlakaṇṭha, be my salutation," thus spoke Sadāgati.
Having heard this, the sages of purified soul and praised vows,
known as the Vālakhilyas, became companions to the sun.
Eighty-eight thousand sages of perpetual celibacy,
who subsist on air, leaves, and water, questioned Vāyu.
O best of wind-gods, that which was spoken by you as "Nīlakaṇṭha" is a secret among purifiers; O foremost of those who know merit, it is the nourisher of the virtuous.
Therefore, O best of beings, please narrate that to us;
we wish to hear all of it through your grace, O Wind-god.
O Lord, we desire to hear specifically from your mouth the reason why the throat of the husband of Ambikā is blue.
As long as any words are uttered, they are all impelled by you;
when the vital air has reached the locations of the phonemes, the process of speech proceeds.
O Vāyu, enthusiasm proceeds from you preceded by knowledge;
yet when you are purified, the remaining manifestations of the castes arise.
Where words turn back and even descriptions of the body are difficult to obtain—from you indeed comes the true nature of all colors; you are omnipresent, O eternal Wind.
O Wind, there is no other all-pervading deity besides you;
indeed, O Anila, this world of living beings is manifest to you everywhere.
"Do you know the Lord Vācaspati, the master of speech and the leader of the mind?
Tell me, what transformation of form has occurred there in the region of his throat?"
Having heard those words of the sages of purified souls,
the highly resplendent Vāyu, who is saluted by the worlds, replied:
In former times, during the Kṛta age, there was a virtuous brahmin named Vasiṣṭha, devoted to the determination of the Vedas, who was indeed a mind-born progenitor (prajāpati).
He indeed questioned Kārttikeya, who has the excellent peacock as his vehicle and who steals the collyrium from the eyes of the women of Mahiṣāsura.
To Mahāsena, the great-souled one, whose voice resounds like the thundering of clouds,
who takes the form of a cloud as a pretext to delight the heart of Umā.
This which is seen here, excellent, bright, and resembling white collyrium, is the snatcher of Krauñca’s life and the delighter of Gaurī’s heart.
For what purpose has this arisen on your throat, O you who possess the luster of a jasmine flower and the moon upon your throat?
Tell this to me, your devoted questioner, who is radiant and self-controlled.
O highly fortunate one, for the sake of my pleasure, you ought to relate in its entirety that discourse which is endowed with auspiciousness, purifying, and destructive of sin.
Having heard those words of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha,
the one of great splendor, the destroyer of the forces of the enemies of the gods, replied.
Listen, O best of speakers, to these words being spoken by me,
just as they were heard by me in the past while seated upon the lap of Umā.
O great sage, for the sake of your pleasure, I shall fully relate that dialogue between Pārvatī and the high-souled Śarva.
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, variegated with various minerals,
resembling the rising sun and possessing the luster of refined gold.
On a divine staircase made of diamond and crystal, with variegated stone slabs for steps, fashioned from Jāmbūnada gold and adorned with various minerals.
It was filled with various trees and creepers, endowed with diverse flowers and fruits,
crowded with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, and adorned by ruddy geese.
Abounding with the songs of six-legged bees, resounding with the falling of rain showers,
and with its caves echoing with the cries of intoxicated krauñca cranes and peacocks.
It was crowded with throngs of Apsarases, graced by Kinnaras,
and made resonant by the warbling of Jīvañjīvaka birds.
Abounding with the cries of cuckoos, frequented by *siddhas* and *cāraṇas*,
rich with the lowing of bulls, and echoing with the rumbling of clouds.
With caves resounded by the cries of elephants agitated by fear of Vināyaka,
and with the resonant sounds of lutes and musical instruments that were pleasing to the sense of hearing;
It was frequented by throngs of women suspended upon swings,
and filled with the resonant tinkling of bells attached to those swinging banners.
Abounding in lutes and flutes, crowded with thirty peacocks,
and filled with the sounds of mouth-drums and cymbals being struck and clapped.
Its caves were filled with the sounds of the clamor from the force of their play,
and it was inhabited at ease by swans, pigeons, and kingfishers.
And while the Lord of the Gaṇas was sporting with various bodily forms—[beings] with the faces of lions and tigers, making terrible roars, and possessing fierce speed—; BndP_1,25.34 //
Others had faces like those of deer and monkeys, as well as faces like elephants and horses; some had fierce feline faces, while others took on the forms and appearances of jackals.
With some short and others tall, some very thin and others with large bellies and broad chests; with short shanks, protruding lips, and others with shanks as thick as palm trees.
With those having cow-ears, single ears, large ears, and no ears at all;
with those having many feet, large feet, a single foot, and no feet.
With many eyes, great eyes, a single eye, or being eyeless;
with a single tusk, great tusks, many tusks, or being tuskless.

Surrounded by spirits of such forms— those with one head, great heads, many heads, or no heads at all; those with one tongue, great tongues, many tongues, or no tongues— the Lord of Spirits was encircled by these great yogis.

Seated comfortably upon a most beautiful golden stone surface adorned with pure pearls, gems, and jewels, the daughter of the King of Mountains addressed these words to the destroyer of the serpent of passion (Madana): *BndP_1,25.40*
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, whose teaching is marked by the bull!
O Mahādeva, that which resembles a cloud shines upon your neck.
"O Lord, destroyer of the body of Kama, what is this that shines upon your neck—neither too intense, auspicious and brilliant, resembling a cluster of blue lotuses? (BndP 1.25.42)
O Lord, what is the cause, what is the reason, or why is there this blueness in your throat? Tell me all this according to the truth, for I am filled with curiosity.
Then, having heard those words of Pārvatī, Śaṅkara, the beloved of Pārvatī, related a narrative filled with auspiciousness.
Maheśvara said: Formerly, while the nectar was being churned in the Ocean of Milk by the gods and the Dānavas,
a terrible poison first arose, possessing the radiance of the fire of universal destruction.
O lady of excellent countenance, having seen him, the hosts of gods and the Daityas were all dejected in face; they went into the presence of Brahmā.
Seeing the hosts of gods terrified, the immensely radiant Brahmā said:
"O highly fortunate ones, for what reason are you afraid and agitated in mind?"
I have bestowed upon you a sovereignty consisting of the three qualities;
therefore, O best of gods, you have been deprived of that sovereignty.
"You are all indeed the lords of the three worlds, free from all affliction;
in the creation of progeny, there is no one here who would transgress my command."
All of them travel in celestial chariots, all of them moving according to their own will,
constantly [engaged] with the internal self, with the elements, and with the divine powers.
"O subjects, you are capable of proceeding by virtue of the ripening of your own karma;
for what reason then are you agitated with fear, like deer tormented by a lion?"
"What is the evil omen? What is the cause of this distress? Or from where has this fear come? You ought to explain all of this quickly and according to the facts."
Having heard those words of Brahmā, the Supreme Soul,
the lords of the gods, daityas, and dānavas, together with the ṛṣis, spoke.
While the mass of nectar was being churned by the gods and the asuras, he said to his father:
"It resembles a serpent or a bee, and is like a dark blue cloud. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 1.25.54)
A terrible poison appeared, possessing a radiance like the fire of universal destruction;
it arose like Time and Death, with the splendor of the sun at the end of an eon.
Resembling the sun at the destruction of the three worlds, it flashed forth on all sides; with its rising poison, it possessed a brilliance equal to the fire of cosmic dissolution.
Janārdana, whose body was once red and fair, was made black by being consumed;
having seen Janārdana thus turned black after his red and fair body had been burnt— BndP_1,25.57.
Then we all, having heard the terrifying words of both the gods and the asuras, became afraid and sought refuge in you alone.
The immensely radiant Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, replied:
"Let all the deities and the sages whose wealth is austerity listen!"
That poison which first arose when the great ocean was being churned,
resembling the fire of universal destruction, is known as Kālakūṭa.
By the mere appearance of which the deities did not shine—
whether it be Viṣṇu, or I, or all the foremost of the gods.
"Indeed, none except Śaṅkara are able to endure his impetus.
Having spoken thus, he who has the luster of the interior of a lotus, whose source is the lotus, and who is not born from a womb, [departed].
Having recollected the syllable Oṃ and meditating on the light all around,
Brahmā, the best among those who know the Vedas, then began to offer praise.
Salutations to you, O Virūpākṣa; salutations to you, the one with divine vision.
Salutations to the one who holds the Pināka bow in hand, and indeed salutations to the one who holds the thunderbolt in hand.
Homage to the Lord of the three worlds; homage to the Master of all beings;
homage to the slayer of the enemies of the gods, whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire.
Salutations to Brahmā, to Rudra, and to Viṣṇu;
salutations indeed to Sāṃkhya, to Yoga, and to the multitude of beings.
Salutations indeed to Kālapṛṣṭha, who destroys the limbs of Manmatha;
to Suretas, to Rudra, to the God of gods, and to Raṃhas.
To Kapardin, to Karāla, to Śaṅkara, and to Hara;
to Kapālin, to Virūpa, to Śiva, and to the Giver of Boons.
Salutations to the destroyer of Tripura and the slayer of Makha, to the Lord of the Mothers; salutations to the aged, to the pure, to the liberated, and to the powerful.
Salutations to the sole hero of the three worlds, to Candra, and to Varuṇa;
to the foremost, to the fierce, to the wise, and to the one with many eyes.
Salutations to you who are both passion (rajas) and goodness (sattva), whose source is the unmanifest;
salutations indeed to the eternal, to the non-eternal, and to that which is both eternal and non-eternal.

Salutations indeed to the manifest and to the unmanifest, and to that which is both manifest and unmanifest; salutations indeed to the conceivable and to the inconceivable, and to that which is both conceivable and inconceivable.
To the destroyer of the suffering of the worlds, to the beloved of Nārāyaṇa,
to Śarva, the beloved of Umā, and to him who is marked by the face of Nandin.
Salutations to the one who consists of the fortnights, months, half-months, seasons, and years;
to the multiformed one, to the shaven-headed one, to the bearer of the staff, and to the protector.
Homage to him who holds a skull in his hand, who is clothed in the directions, who wears a topknot,
who bears a bow, who is a charioteer, who is a self-restrained ascetic, and who is a celibate student.
"Obeisance be to You, the Puruṣa, the Lord, who is the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas"— having praised You with such hymns and other deeds as these, O fair-faced one, Brahmā then prostrated himself.

Having perceived my devotion to the deities, O Lord Rudra, you— whose hair is disheveled by the waters of the Gaṅgā, who are subtle and inconceivable due to the excellence of your yoga— do not indeed manifest yourself, for you are beyond thought.
Thus was I previously praised by the Blessed One Brahmā, the creator of the world, with various hymns arising from the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Then, with my primary voice, I addressed the Grandfather:
"O Lord of the past, future, and present; O Protector of the worlds; O Master of the universe!"
"O Brahmā of noble vows, tell me what must be done for you by me; what is your purpose?
Having heard these words, the lotus-eyed Brahmā then replied:
O Lord of the past, future, and present, O Lord of Causes, O Lotus-eyed One, listen as the ocean was being churned by the gods and the asuras.
O Blessed One, a terrible poison has appeared, resembling a cloud, like a dark rain-cloud, with a radiance equal to the fire of universal destruction.
And seeing him, we were all terrified, our minds agitated;
therefore, O Mahādeva, drink it out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
O Lord, you alone are indeed capable and the enjoyer; you are the best of gods.
O Mahādeva, there exists no one other than you who can withstand this force.
O fair-faced one, having heard these words of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin and accepting his speech with the words "So be it," [they did as instructed].
Then I began to drink the poison, which was like the God of Death himself;
as I drank that most terrible poison, it produced great fear.
O woman of excellent complexion, his throat quickly became dark;
seeing it, which resembled the petal of a blue lotus and appeared like a serpent clinging to the throat, [he was struck with wonder].
To Takṣaka, the king of the nāgas, who stood there licking his lips as if risen up,
the immensely radiant Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, then spoke.
"O Mahādeva of noble vows, you shine with this throat.
Having heard these words of his, O daughter of the mountain king, I [acted].
Because I held that terrible poison in my throat, O lady of beautiful countenance, I am therefore called Nīlakaṇṭha (the Blue-throated One), while the hosts of gods, Daityas,
Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Bhūtas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas were looking on.
O daughter of the mountain king, when that deadly poison of fierce potency was held in his throat,
the hosts of gods and demons, beholding it being placed there, were struck with supreme amazement.
Then all the hosts of gods, along with the Daityas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas, spoke with palms joined in reverence to her who moves with the gait of an elephant in rut: BndP_1,25.92.
O Lord, how great is your strength, heroism, and prowess; oh, how wonderful is your body and the power of your yoga!
Oh, how great is your power, O God of gods, most wonderful destroyer of the body of Manmatha!
You alone are Viṣṇu, you are the four-faced Brahmā; you alone are Death, and you alone are the bestower of boons.
You alone are the sun and the maker of night; you alone are the manifestation of this world of moving and unmoving beings.
You alone are fire, you alone are wind, you alone are earth, and you alone are water.
"You alone are the creator and the ordainer of all that is moving and unmoving; you alone are the dissolution.

Having spoken these words and having grasped the Soma while bowing their heads, all the lords of the gods departed in their celestial chariots, swift as the wind, and reached Mount Meru, the great mountain.
This is the supreme secret, great, more meritorious than merit itself.
It is proclaimed as "Nīlakaṇṭha," renowned throughout the three worlds;
this sin-destroying narrative was spoken by the Self-born One himself.
But to him who constantly retains this auspicious hymn sung by Brahmā,
I shall declare a very vast and great reward.
O lady of excellent hips, whether it be stationary or mobile poison,
once it reaches his body, O fair-hipped one, it is instantly neutralized.
It pacifies terrible inauspiciousness and removes bad dreams;
it brings about favor among women and in the assembly of the king.
In dispute he attains victory, and in battle he achieves triumph;
he travels his path in safety, endowed with constant prosperity from his home.
O fair-faced one, I shall now describe here the destiny of that body:
he has a tawny beard, a blue throat, and hair marked by the crescent moon.
He has three eyes, holds a trident in his hand, has a bull as his vehicle, and wields the Pināka bow;
he possesses strength equal to Nandin, is illustrious, and has prowess equal to Nandin.
By my command, he wanders through all the worlds, the seven worlds;
his movement cannot be obstructed, just like that of the wind in the sky.
O lady of excellent hips, those men who listen with devotion to me shall remain equal in power to me until the dissolution of all beings.
I shall declare their destiny in this world and in the next:
a Brāhmaṇa attains the Veda, and a Kṣatriya gains the earth.
A Vaiśya shall obtain profit, and a Śūdra shall attain happiness;
one afflicted by disease is freed from illness, and one who is bound is released from bondage.
A pregnant woman obtains a son, and a maiden finds a virtuous husband;
one also recovers lost wealth, both in this world and in the next.
A mortal obtains that same fruit which results from the perfect gift of a hundred thousand cows by hearing this divine narrative.
He who constantly retains even a single quarter-verse, or half a quarter-verse, or a full verse, or even half a verse,
goes to the world of Rudra.
Alternatively, any man who should constantly recite all of this in the presence of gods and brahmins, with his inner self absorbed in me; ||| BndP_1,25.112 |||
The man who is always faithful and devoted goes to the world of Rudra;
O Goddess, such a person should always recite this with devotion and cause others to recite it as well.
Therefore, there has never been nor will there ever be a hymn superior to this.
Neither yakṣas, nor piśācas, nor bhūtas,
nor vināyakas shall create obstacles in the home where this praise resides.

O lotus-eyed one, being pleased with you, I have now declared the greatness of this hymn, which destroys the flood of sins and is endowed with meritorious fruits and other benefits; it was itself proclaimed by the Four-faced One.
Having related this tale, which is endowed with the fruits of merit and other virtues, to the Goddess, the Lord whose hair is bound with the moon,
together with Umā, mounted the back of his bull and departed for the cave of Kailāsa, he who is beloved by the Ganas.
I have heard that which destroys sin; it was then reported by me to Prajāpati.
Having studied all of it in its entirety along with its defining characteristics, the best of the twice-born attains the station of the Sun.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Origin of the Name Nīlakaṇṭha," in the second section (Anuṣaṅga-pāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
The sages said:
"Tell us of the majesty and the sovereign power of the great-souled Mahādeva."
We desire to hear the full and correct exposition of the qualities of sovereign power.
Sūta said:
Formerly, during the conquest of the three worlds, Viṣṇu bound Bali,
the immensely powerful lord of the three worlds, in ancient times.
When the Daityas had been utterly destroyed and the Lord of Śacī was greatly rejoiced,
then all the gods came to see the eternal Lord.
There dwells the soul of universal form, the Lord of Kṣīroda and Maṇidvīpa,
where perfected beings, Brahman-sages, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and hosts of Apsarases reside.
The Nāgas, divine sages, rivers, and all the mountains,
having approached the Great-Souled One, praise the Person Hari.
You are the sustainer and you are the creator; O Lord, you bring forth the worlds.
And through your grace, the imperishable triple-world has attained its auspicious state.
"All the Asuras have been conquered and Bali has indeed been bound by you.
Thus was Viṣṇu addressed by the gods, the Siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis.
Then Puruṣottama replied to all those gods:
"Listen, O best of the gods; I shall declare the reason."
He who is the creator of all beings, Time itself, the Lord who brings about the end of time;
by whom, through his power of illusion (māyā), I and Brahmā were created along with the worlds.
And by his very grace, I first attained the state of perfection,
long ago when the three worlds were swallowed up by me in unmanifest darkness.
While all beings were situated within my belly, I alone then lay there,
having become one with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet.
With conch, discus, and mace in hand, he was reclining upon the pure waters;
in that interval, I beheld from afar one of immeasurable splendor.
Resembling a hundred suns, blazing with his own splendor,
the four-faced one, the great yogin, a personage with the luster of gold.
That Supreme Person, wearing a black antelope skin and adorned with a water-pot,
arrived in the mere twinkling of an eye.
Then Brahmā, who is worshipped by all the worlds, said to me:
"Who are you? From where do you come? And why do you stand here? Tell me, O Lord."
"I am the creator of the worlds, the self-existent one whose face is turned everywhere.
When I was addressed thus by Brahmā at that time, I spoke to him.
"I am indeed the creator of the worlds and their destroyer again and again.
Thus they spoke, each desiring victory over the other.
Having turned toward the northern direction, they beheld a flame standing there;
then, O sinless ones, having gazed upon that flame, they were filled with wonder.
Then, with their splendor and strength, they joined their palms in reverence toward the light of Śarva,
as that most wondrous flame continued to increase.
Brahmā and I both rushed swiftly toward that flame; having pierced through heaven and earth, we reached the circle of flames standing there.
In the midst of that flame, we two behold a linga of immense radiance,
one span in size, indistinct, yet supremely brilliant.
And that gold was neither in the middle nor was it made of stone or silver;
it was indescribable and inconceivable, appearing again and again as both perceptible and imperceptible.
Abounding with thousands of garlands of flames, most wonderful and marvelous,
endowed with great splendor, and likewise swelling intensely.
Spread with garlands of flames and cast down, it was terrifying to all beings;
possessing a most dreadful form, it seemed as if it were splitting asunder both heaven and earth.
Then Brahmā said to me: "Go down quickly indeed;
let us find the end of this great-souled Liṅga."
"I shall go upwards as far as its end can be seen;
having made that agreement, I indeed went both upwards and downwards."
Then, for a thousand years, I descended further down;
yet I did not see its end, and I became terrified because of that.
In that very same way, Brahmā indeed ascended upwards, yet he did not find its end;
he encountered me right there in that great expanse.
Then, overcome with wonder and fear of that great-souled one,
they were deluded by his illusory power and remained there deprived of their senses.
Then, while absorbed in meditation there, [he beheld] Īśvara, who faces all directions,
the source and the end of the worlds, the imperishable Lord.
Bowing with palms joined in reverence, we offer our salutation to that Śarva,
the wielder of the trident, who possesses a terrifying roar, a fearsome form, and fangs;
to him who is unmanifest and yet supreme.
Homage be to you, O God, Lord of the world and lords of gods; homage be to you, O Great-Souled One, Lord of beings!
Homage be to you, the eternally perfected yogin; homage be to you, who are established as the foundation of the entire world.
You are Parameṣṭhin, the Supreme Brahman, the Imperishable, and the Highest State;
you are Jyeṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Rudra, Skanda, Śiva, and the Lord.
You are the *ya* [syllable], you are the *vaṣaṭkāra*, you are the *oṃkāra*, and the scorcher of foes;
you are the *svāhākāra*, the *namaskāra*, and the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of all ritual acts.
The utterance of *svadhā*, the sacrifice, the vows, and likewise the observances;
the Vedas, the worlds, and the gods—the Blessed One alone is all these in every respect.
And you are the sound of space; you are the origin and dissolution of the elements.
Maheśvara is the fragrance in the earth, the taste in the waters, and the form in fire.
O Lord of Gods, the touch belongs to Vāyu, and likewise the body belongs to the Moon.
O Lord of Gods, within the intellect (buddhi) reside knowledge and the very seed of primordial nature (prakṛti).
The destroyer of all worlds, Time, Death, and Antaka—
O Lord, you sustain the three worlds and you alone create them.
With your eastern face, you indeed exercise the office of Indra;
with your southern face, you again withdraw the worlds.
By your western face, you are undoubtedly Varuṇa;
by your northern face, you are Soma, O best of gods.
O God, you are manifoldly one and the source and dissolution of the worlds;
you are the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Maruts, together with the Aśvins.
The Sādhyas, Vidyādharas, Nāgas, Cāraṇas, and those whose wealth is austerity;
the high-souled Vālakhilyas, and those perfected in austerity who are firm in their vows.
O Lord of Gods, those others of restrained vows who have been born from you—
Umā, Sītā, Sinīvālī, Kuhū, and the Gāyatrīs as well.
O Lord of Gods, Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Dhṛti, Medhā, Lajjā, Kānti, Vapuḥ, Svadhā,
Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, and Kriyā, as well as Sarasvatī, the goddess of speech,
and likewise Sandhyā and Rātri, were all produced from you.
Homage be to you, whose splendor is like ten million suns; homage be to you, white as a thousand moons!
Homage be to you, the wielder of the thunderbolt and the bow; homage be to you, O God, clad in golden raiment!
Homage be to you, whose limbs are adorned with ashes; homage be to you, the destroyer of the body of Kāma. Homage be to you, O God of golden seed; homage be to you, O God clothed in gold.
Homage be to you, O God, whose origin is gold; homage be to you, O God, whose navel is gold;
homage be to you, O God, whose seed is gold; homage be to you, O God, wondrous with a thousand eyes.
Homage be to you, O God of golden hue; homage be to you, O God with golden hair;
homage be to you, O God of golden heroes; homage be to you, O God who bestows gold.
Homage be to you, O God Hiraṇyanātha; homage be to you, O God Hiraṇyanāda.
Homage be to you, O God who holds the Pināka bow in hand; homage be to you, O Śaṅkara, O Blue-throated One.
Being thus praised, the high-minded one became manifest—
the God of gods, the source of the universe, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Filled with compassion, the immensely radiant Mahādeva spoke,
appearing as if he were swallowing the sky with his thousands of millions of faces.
With a neck like a conch shell, handsome-bellied, adorned with various ornaments,
his limbs variegated with diverse gems, and anointed with various garlands and unguents.
The Blessed One, whose hand holds the Pināka bow, who is worshipped by the gods, who bears the trident,
who has a serpent as his sacred thread, and who grants fearlessness to the deities.
Then he let out a laugh, sounding like the roar of a drum and resembling the thunder of a rain-cloud, filling the entire world.
Terrified by that great sound of the Great-Souled One, we then spoke;
and Mahādeva said, "I am pleased, O best of gods."
Behold the great yoga; let everyone be liberated from fear.
You two, eternal ones, were formerly born from my limbs.
My right arm is Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds;
and my left arm is Viṣṇu, who is eternally unconquered in battles.
"I am pleased with you both; I shall grant you a boon exactly as you desire.
Thereupon, with hearts full of joy, they bowed at the feet of the Lord.
And they spoke to Mahādeva, who stood facing them with a gracious countenance: "O God, Lord of the Suras, if affection has arisen [in you] and if a boon is to be granted by you,
let there be eternal devotion toward you for us both."
The God of gods said:
"So be it, O highly fortunate ones; create abundant progeny.
Having spoken thus, the omnipresent Lord vanished right there.
This very power of that wise one has been described by me to you;
for this is the supreme knowledge, unmanifest, known by the name of Śiva.
Those with the eye of wisdom behold this subtle and inconceivable [reality];
to that God of gods, we offer our salutation.
O Mahādeva, homage be to you; O Maheśvara, homage be to you!
Sūta said:
Having heard this, all the gods returned to their respective abodes,
offering salutations to the high-souled Śaṅkara.
Whoever recites this hymn to the Great-Souled Īśvara obtains all their desires and is liberated from sins.
All this was then spoken by that powerful Viṣṇu through the grace of Mahādeva; indeed, it is the eternal Brahman. Thus has all this power of Maheśvara been narrated to you by me.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Origin of the Liṅga," in the second section (Anuṣaṅgapāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
The sages said:
"O one of great intelligence, tell us once more about that Great-Souled One."
We have a great curiosity to hear the majesty of Mahādeva.
How did he assume that distorted appearance in the Dāruvana forest, which is frequented by hosts of divine sages, such that even the great seers who are Buddhas [were affected]?
And having recognized Mahādeva, they then wandered about, deprived of their senses; yet, though they sought to propitiate him for the sake of grace, he did not find favor with them again.
O best among the wise, relate here to us all that which was performed by the God of gods exactly as it occurred.
Sūta said:
Listen, O unwearied ones; I shall declare this dharma, which was established by the God of gods out of compassion for his devotees.
Long ago in the Kṛta age, O brahmins, on a beautiful peak of the Himavat there was a delightful forest of Devadāru trees, filled with various kinds of trees and creepers.
Many sages were performing austerities there, observing the vows of sages;
some subsisted on water-moss, while others lay within the water.
Some dwell in the open air under the clouds, standing on the tips of their big toes;
others use their teeth as mortars, while still others grind with stones.
Others, being heroes of steadfast posture, delighting in hunting and wandering,
those of great intelligence pass their time with intense austerity.
Then, for the sake of inspiring faith in them, the Lord came to that forest,
his limbs smeared with white ashes, naked, and possessing deformed features.
With disheveled and falling hair, and likewise with formidable teeth,
he held a firebrand in his hand and had blood-red, tawny eyes.
His penis, along with the testicles, resembles red ochre;
his face is adorned with a color like glowing embers and white.
In one place he laughs fiercely; in another, he sings in wonder;
in another, he dances as a lover; and in another, he cries out again and again.
Dancing and utterly infatuated, their wives quickly obstructed him,
who had come repeatedly to the hermitage again and again.
A wife of such a form was created, adorned with ornaments of grass;
she let out a bellowing like that of a bull and also brayed like a donkey. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.27.15)
Thus he began to deceive them, making all embodied beings laugh;
thereupon those sages became enraged, their minds clouded by anger.
Deluded by her magic power, they all prepared to curse him:
"Since you sing with your hand, therefore you shall become a donkey."
Whether they were Rākṣasas, Piśācas, or Dānavas,
all of them became equally enraged at the sages, just as they had intended.
They struck that god, the Lord of the World, with various kinds of arrows;
yet the ascetic powers of them all were repelled by Śaṅkara.
Just as the stars situated in the sky do not shine by the light of the sun,
so too do all splendors [fade] before Śaṅkara.
It is heard that, due to the curse of a seer, the highly exalted Brahmā’s prosperous sacrifice,
which was rich in blessings, indeed met with destruction.
Moreover, by the curse of Bhṛgu, Viṣṇu became supremely distressed;
he underwent ten incarnations and was made perpetually sorrowful.
For even Indra’s penis, along with its testicles, was formerly cast down upon the earth by the wrathful sage Gautama, O knower of dharma.
Likewise, the dwelling in a womb was ordained for the Vasus by a curse;
and by the curse of the sages, Nahuṣa became a serpent.
The ocean of milk was indeed rendered undrinkable by the Brahmins,
and Dharma himself was cursed there by the high-souled Māṇḍavya.
These and many others have come to their torment,
with the exception of Virūpākṣa, the god of gods, Maheśvara.
Thus deluded by him, they did not recognize Śaṅkara;
then all those sages spoke to one another.
And this rule is not prescribed for us householders,
nor for those who delight in celibacy, nor for forest-dwellers in the wilderness.
Or likewise, this is not seen in any way to be the dharma of ascetics;
rather, O twice-born ones, this is a great injustice by which he has been deluded.
"Cast off this linga; this is not the dharma of ascetics.
Speak with sweet words and put on a single garment."
"And once you have been made to abandon your linga, you shall then receive worship.
Having heard those words of the sages, the Blessed One, the destroyer of Bhaga's eyes, [acted accordingly].
Śaṅkara, as if smiling, spoke with gentle words:
"It is not possible for us to cause this liṅga to fall by force."
O best of the twice-born, I could cause even this liṅga to fall by means of all the deities beginning with Brahmā, let alone by other ascetics rich in penance.
"Stay in the hermitage or go," they said these words to him.
Thus addressed, Mahādeva, whose senses and movements were restrained, [remained].
While everyone was looking on, the Lord vanished right there; when the Blessed One had thus disappeared and the world-linga had been made manifest, [the assembly remained].
In the three worlds, the manifestation of all beings does not occur;
everything then becomes chaotic, and nothing at all is visible.
The sun did not burn, nor was the fire deprived of its radiance;
even the stars and planets became disordered.
For those sages who were intent on the welfare of their lineages and whose nature was one of spiritual power,
their sacrifices did not cease as they approached their wives during the proper seasons.
They practice the Dharma again, free from possessiveness and free from egoism;
yet their power and vigor are lost, and their splendor is likewise destroyed.
At that time, their understanding of the Dharma did not remain firm;
they all gathered together and departed for the world of Brahmā.
Having gone to the abode of Brahmā and seen the one born from the Puṣpaka,
they all fell at his feet and related the account of Śiva.
He was hideous, with stiff hair and terrifying teeth;
his hands were occupied with an owl, and his eyes were reddish-brown.
His penis, along with the testicles, was red and adorned with red ochre;
and [he likewise appeared] before his daughters-in-law, daughters, and especially his granddaughters.
Then, because he was acting perversely at our side, we recognized him as a madman and treated him with contempt.
Though we were reviled, beaten, and even our lingas were torn away,
we have come to you for refuge so that you may appease his anger.
"We do not know what this task is; tell us that, O Grandfather.
Having heard those words of the sages, the Lord understood through meditation.
Then Brahmā, being well-composed, replied with these words:
"This god is to be known as Mahādeva, the Great Lord."
No supreme state whatsoever can be attained that surpasses him;
he is the lord of the gods, the sages, and the ancestors alike.
At the end of a thousand yugas, during the dissolution of all embodied beings,
the Blessed One, having become Maheśvara, withdraws everything as Time.
He alone creates all creatures by his own splendor;
he is the playful one, marked with the curl of hair on his breast and the śrīvatsa.
In the Kṛta age he is Yegī, in the Tretā he is called Kratu;
in the Dvāpara he is Kālāgni, and in the Kali age he is remembered as Dharmaketu.
The wise should also understand that Rudra has three forms:
Tamas is indeed Agni, Rajas is Brahmā, and Sattva is Viṣṇu, the illuminator.
One form of his is remembered as Digvāsas, named Śiva;
where he abides, he is indeed endowed with the yoga of Brahman.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, having conquered anger and subdued the senses, worship the Lord Īśāna, the God of gods, the immutable Sovereign.
Having fashioned an image exactly like the form that was seen of that great-souled one, he took refuge in the wielder of the trident.
Then you shall behold the Lord of Gods, who is difficult to be seen by those of unrefined self;
upon seeing him, all ignorance and unrighteousness perish.
Then, having circumambulated Brahmā of immeasurable splendor,
they remained in the Devadāru forest, free from sorrow.
When they began to propitiate him, Brahmā spoke as follows:
"Upon various sacrificial mounds, on mountains, and in caves..."
And on the various beautiful sandbanks of the rivers,
when the year was thus complete and the spring season had arrived,
the god assumed that very same form and came to that forest.

The Great Lord enters that forest hermitage, where many trees and creepers are in full bloom, where its groves are celebrated by swarms of bees, and which resounds with the full and beautiful calls of cuckoos.
Then all the sages, being well-composed, offered praise to him.
With water, fragrant garlands, and likewise with dense incense,
those highly fortunate ones, together with their wives, sons, and retinues, [honored them].
Then, with gentle words, they spoke thus to the Lord of the Mountains:
"Whatever has been performed by us out of ignorance regarding the God of gods..."
You ought to forgive all that— whether by deed, mind, or speech—
including the various, secret, and profound ways of conduct.
O Śaṅkara, these things are difficult even for the gods, beginning with Brahmā, to comprehend:
"Welcome to you! We do not know [your origin], nor indeed your destination."
O Viśveśvara, Mahādeva, whoever you are, you are indeed that; let there be salutation unto you!
The great-souled ones praise you, the God of gods, the Great Lord (Maheśvara).
Homage to Bhava, to Bhavya, to Bhāvanā, and to Udbhava;
homage to the Lord of beings, who possesses infinite strength and vigor.
Salutations to the Withdrawer, who has a tawny body, who is both imperishable and subject to transformation,
who is the stream of the Gaṅgā’s waters, the ultimate support, and whose self consists of the qualities.
Salutations to you, the three-eyed one with three eyes, who wields the excellent trident;
salutations to you, Kandarpa, and salutations be to the Supreme Self.
Salutation to Śaṅkara, who bears the bull as his emblem, the lord of the Gaṇas;
salutation indeed to Kāla, who holds a staff in his hand and a noose in his hand.
Salutations to you, whose tongue is a hundredfold, for whom the Vedic mantras are primary;
[to you who are] that which has been, that which is, and that which will be, both the stationary and the moving.
O Lord, this entire universe has arisen from your body;
protect it, may you be auspicious, and therefore, O Blessed One, be gracious.
Whether out of ignorance or through knowledge, whatever a person does,
all that is performed by the Blessed One alone through his yogic power (yogamāyā).
Having thus offered praise with a delighted inner self, the sages, endowed with ascetic power, entreated him: "May we behold you as before."
And let your physical form remain as it was before;
salutations eternally to you, the sky-clad one, who wears a garland of tinkling bells.
Salutations to you who are the formidable, the terrifying, and the one with a terrifying face;
to the formless, the well-formed, and the one whose form is the universe.
Salutations indeed to Kaṭaṅkaṭa, to Rudra, and to Svāhākāra;
salutations to you, the self of all living beings, whose body consists of the qualities (guṇas).
Salutations indeed to the one who possesses both foul odor and sweet fragrance, to the one with a trident in hand;
salutations again and again to the self-manifested Nīlaśikhaṇḍa, to Śrīkaṇṭha;
to the blue-throated god who has ashes from the funeral pyre as his body-unguent.
Salutations to you, whose self consists of the three qualities, the creator of the universe;
salutations indeed to you who eternally dwell in the cremation ground and possess the form of a ghost.
You are Brahmā among all the gods, and Nīlalohita among the Rudras;
you are the self of all beings, and by the Sāṃkhyas you are called Puruṣa.
Among mountains you are Mahāmeru, among the stars the moon,
among the sages Vasiṣṭha, and likewise among the gods Vāsava.
Oṃkāra among all the Vedas, and the Jyeṣṭhasāman among the Sāmans;
among all forest-dwellers, you, O Supreme Lord, are the lion.
And the Blessed One, the bull among the villagers, honored by the world,
will exist in every way as whatever state is to come to pass.
We see you alone there, just as it was described by Brahmā:
desire, anger, greed, despondency, and even pride.
We truly wish to restrain this; be gracious, O Supreme Lord!
O God, when the great dissolution has arrived, you who are of perfected soul— [BndP_1,27.85]
Pressing his hand against his forehead, you produced fire;
by that fire, the worlds were then enveloped on all sides with its flames.
Therefore, these many beings with transformed fires are indeed equal to fire;
so too are all other beings, whether stationary or moving.
Those living beings are being consumed by the fire arising from you;
O Lord of the Gods, become the protector of us who are being burned.
And you, O Maheśvara, highly fortunate lord who gazes upon auspiciousness, sprinkle living beings for the sake of the welfare of the world.
"Command us, O Lord; we shall carry out your word, even through thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of forms."
“O Lord, we were unable to reach the end; salutations be unto you!
Then the Blessed Lord Īśa spoke these words:

For those Brahmins who are devoted to the sacred ash, whose sins have been burnt away by the ash, who act according to what has been taught, who are self-controlled, and who are intent upon meditation— // BndP_1,27.92 //
A wise person should not revile them, nor should he transgress against them;
desiring their welfare both in this world and the next, he should not speak unpleasant words to them.
The foolish soul who reviles them reviles Mahādeva;
but he who constantly worships them worships Śaṅkara.
Conduct yourselves thus—may it be well with you—and you shall attain perfection through me.
Having understood this supreme method taught by Śiva, which brings about the destruction of incomparable and great darkness in this world,
those whose fear, greed, delusion, and anxiety had vanished bowed their heads together with their wives and bore it upon them with great splendor.
Then those brahmins were delighted that Maheśvara had returned to his natural state;
they [honored him] with very pure water mixed with perfumes, kusha grass, and flowers.
They bathe the god Maheśvara with waters from great jars,
and they sing various secret hymns as well as beautiful-sounding *huṃ* syllables.
Salutations to the sky-clad god, salutations indeed to the bearer of the small bell;
salutations to the one whose body is half-female, the promulgator of Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
To the one whose vehicle is the cloud, who is dark-hued, who dwells in an elephant hide,
who has a black antelope skin as his upper garment, and who wears a serpent as a sacred thread.

Salutations to you, Śaṅkara, who wear well-fashioned earrings of diverse and variegated designs, who are adorned with beautifully arranged garlands and ornaments, who are clothed in the skin of the best of beasts, and who possess a broad battle-axe.
Furthermore, once the Liṅga had been installed out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
those best of sages remained devoted to the duties of their respective castes.
Then Maheśvara, being pleased, replied to those sages:
"I am gratified by your austerity; choose a boon, O you of excellent vows."
Then all those sages— Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Vasiṣṭha, and likewise Viśvāmitra— having prostrated before Maheśvara, [spoke].
Gautama, Atri, Sukeśa, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Marīci, Kaśyapa, and Saṃvarta of great asceticism; BndP_1,27.104 //

Having prostrated before Mahādeva, they spoke these words: "O Lord, we desire to know this: the bathing in ashes, nakedness, left-handedness, acting contrary to the grain, and what is fit or unfit to be practiced."
The Blessed One said:
"I shall now truly declare to you this entire essence of the narrative:
for I am Agni joined with Soma, and Soma is dependent upon Agni."
People, having fully relied upon Agni, say that he consumes both what has been done and what has not been done;
indeed, the entire world, both mobile and immobile, has been repeatedly burnt by Agni.
For all that is to be accomplished by means of the sacred ash is achieved; this is the most excellent purifier.
By resorting to the power of the ash, one sprinkles [it] over all beings.
And whoever, having performed the fire-rite, shall perform the Tryāyuṣa rite with my ash through my power, is liberated from all sins.
Because it illuminates and because it purifies with auspiciousness,
it is proclaimed as "Bhasma" (ashes) for the instant destruction of all sins.
The Pitṛs are to be known as those who drink the warm [oblation], while the gods indeed originate from Soma;
