the entire world, both stationary and moving, consists of the nature of Agni and Soma.
I am Agni of great splendor, and Soma is this Ambikā of mine;
I am both Agni and Soma, being by nature the Self-existent Puruṣa.
Therefore, O highly fortunate ones, ash is called my own potency;
it is my established nature that I indeed sustain this as my own power through my very body.
From that time forward, for the sake of protection in the worlds against inauspicious things,
protection with ashes is performed in the houses of women who have recently given birth.
One whose self is purified by the ash-bath, who has conquered anger and subdued the senses,
having come into my presence, does not return again.
The Pāśupata vow, the Yoga, and the Kāpāla created by Yoga—
this Pāśupata was indeed fashioned first, and it is unsurpassed.
And all the other orders of life were created later by the Self-born One;
this creation was fashioned by me as consisting of shame, delusion, and fear.
For indeed, the deities and likewise the sages are born naked;
and all other human beings in the world are born without clothing.
Those whose senses are unconquered are naked even when covered by fine silk; those whose senses are restrained are truly clothed. It is taught that clothing is not the cause of modesty.
Forgiveness, fortitude, non-violence, and complete detachment,
as well as equanimity toward honor and dishonor— these constitute his supreme garment.
If one whose limbs are smeared with ash-white ashes meditates on Bhava with the mind,
even after having committed thousands of improper acts, he becomes purified by bathing in the ashes.
Just as fire consumes a forest with its brilliance, reducing it all to ashes,
so too does he who, becoming diligent, always performs [this] at the three times of day.
He who performs his bath with ashes attains the state of a leader of the Gaṇas;
having withdrawn all sacrificial rites and having grasped the supreme nectar.
Those who meditate upon Mahādeva, absorbed in him and permeated by his being,
shall attain immortality by means of the northern path.
Then, on the southern path, those who frequented the cremation grounds attained the powers of atomization (aṇimā), magnification (mahimā), levitation (laghimā), and extension (prāpti).
Greatness is the fifth, and the sixth is indeed pre-eminence;
they have attained lordship, mastery, and immortality.
Likewise, Indra and the other gods, having undertaken the vow that fulfills desires,
all attained supreme sovereignty and became renowned for their splendor.

Having understood this supreme humiliation, you who are free from intoxication and delusion, whose passion has been released, and whose very nature is devoid of the defects of darkness, pride, and ignorance— practice this vow beloved by Paśupati.
He who, having become pure, faithful, and with senses subdued, should recite this,
goes to the world of Rudra, his soul purified of all sins.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for Entering the Dāruvana Forest and Bathing in Ashes," in the second section (Anuṣaṅgapāda) of the Pūrva-bhāga of the Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa, as narrated by Vāyu.
The Sage said: "O King, how did he go to heaven every month on the new moon day?"
O Sūta, how did Purūravas, the son of Ilā, satisfy the ancestors?
Sūta said:
O Śāṃśapāyana, I shall describe to you the power of that Aila through his conjunction with Āditya and the high-souled Soma.

[He explained] the waning and waxing of the moon, which consists of internal essence, during its bright and dark fortnights, as well as the determination of the lunar day (tithi) pertaining to the ancestors.
And from Soma, one attains immortality as well as the satisfaction of the ancestors;
and there is the vision of the Kavyas, the Agniṣvāttas, the Aumyas, and the Pitṛs themselves.
Just as Purūravas indeed gratified his ancestors,
all of that I shall relate, along with the chapters in their proper order.
But when the moon and the sun are joined with a lunar mansion on the new moon day, they dwell together for one night within a single orb.
Then he goes to behold the sun and the moon,
and on every new-moon day, his maternal grandfather and paternal grandfather.
Having saluted them there, he waits,
awaiting the proper time for the libations that flow from the distilling Soma for the sake of the ancestors.
The wise Aila Purūravas, desiring to perform the monthly śrāddha,
remained stationed in heaven worshipping Soma, who is accompanied by the ancestors.
Having deliberated upon both Sinīvālī, who consists of two lava-s, and Kuhū,
who consists of a single mātrā, he worshipped Sinīvālī according to the prescribed measures for Sinīvālī.
Having understood the new moon (kuhū) as merely a digit (kalā), he worships that new moon;
thus, while worshipping it, he perceives it by awaiting the [proper] time.
That nectar of immortality indeed flows from the moon for the satisfaction of the months,
by means of ten and five streams of that flowing nectar of immortality.
While his arms were being scorched with affection by those rays during the dark fortnight,
he [the moon] immediately drenched them with that gentle nectar.
Then, O Indra among kings, in windless regions and on the lunar fortnights sacred to the ancestors,
that lord of kings indeed gratified the ancestors with nectar and ambrosia in heaven.
The Saumyas, the Barhiṣads, the Kāvyas, and likewise the Agniṣvāttas—
the fire that is called Ṛta is considered to be the year.
From him the seasons (ṛtu) were born; likewise, from the seasons came those belonging to the seasons (ārtava).
Those known as the half-months are the Ārtavas, for they are the ancestors (pitṛs), the sons of the seasons.
The seasons are the grandfathers (pitāmahas), and the months are the sons of the solstices and the year;
the gods are indeed the great-grandfathers (prapitāmahas), the five-year periods who are the sons of Brahmā.
The Saumyas should be known as born of Soma; the Kāvyas should be known as the sons of Kavi.
The gods known as Upahūtas are remembered as the Somajas, and they are remembered as the Soma-drinkers (Somapas).
The Kāvyas, known as the drinkers of clarified butter (ājyapa), are remembered as the three classes of ancestors (pitṛjāti).
These are the Kāvyas, the Barhiṣads, and the Agniṣvāttas; thus they are threefold.
Those householders who are performers of sacrifices, who sit upon the sacrificial grass during the seasons, are the Dhruvas;
likewise, those householders who do not perform sacrifices are the Agniṣvāttas and the Ārttavas.
Know those sons of Kavi, the lords of the Aṣṭakas, to be five years of age;
for their year is Agni, while Sūrya is the Parivatsara.
Soma is said to be the Iḍvatsara, Vāyu is the Anuvatsara, and Rudra is the Vatsara; these five years constitute the nature of a Yuga.
They are remembered as the Kāvyas, the Uṣmapās, and the Divākīrtis—
those who drink the nectar (sudhā) in heaven month after month on the new moon day.
With that [water], he gratified them as long as Purūravas existed;
for from it flows the soma, and month after month it nourishes them.
Therefore, that indeed is the nectar of immortality for the ancestors who drink the soma;
thus it is the gentle amṛta, the sudhā, and the madhu.
Just as during the dark fortnight the thirty-three gods drink the fifteen digits of the moon in succession, [so do they drink] that which consists of water. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 1.28.26)
Having drunk the nectar of immortality for half a month on the fourteenth day,
the maker of night is thus being consumed by all the gods.
He comes together [with the moon] on the fifteenth part of the new moon;
indeed, he is nourished by the *suṣumṇā* channel according to the sequence during the new moon.
Those ancestors drink the nectar of immortality for a period of two lava-measures;
then the Sun, with a single ray, dries up that consumed Soma.
While those soma-drinkers were being nourished from the Suṣumṇā,
he again replenished the soma once its portion had been entirely consumed.
As he is nourished by the *suṣumṇā* [nerve] day by day, his portions diminish part by part in sequence;
those dark digits (*kalā*) wane, while the bright ones nourish him.
Thus, by the power of the sun, the body of the moon is replenished;
on the full-moon day, it is indeed seen bright with its orb completely full.
Thus is the accomplishment of Soma during the two fortnights, the bright and the dark;
in this way, Soma is remembered as possessing the Pitṛs, consisting of the year.
He has traversed together with the fifteen [digits] that flow with the nectar of immortality;
henceforth, I shall declare the lunar phases (parvans), as well as the divisions of the year and their junctions.
Just as knotted joints occur in sugarcanes and reeds,
so indeed do the joints of the fortnights— the bright and the dark— occur.
The differences between the full moon and the new moon are indeed the knots and the junctions;
the half-months, however, are the lunar phases (parvan) beginning from the second day.
Since the rite of adding fuel (anvādhāna) is performed at the junctions of the lunar phases (parvasandhi),
therefore, at the beginning of each phase, on the first day (pratipad), at all such junctions— Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.28.37.
In the evening, for the Anumati and other rites, the time is said to be two lava-s;
for the Rākā, the time to be known is the afternoon consisting of exactly two lava-s.
When the time of the first day of the dark fortnight has passed during the afternoon,
and when the evening has arrived, that is the time for the full-moon rite.
When the sun is situated at Vyatīpāta in the half-portion of the crescent during the interval between the Yugas, and likewise when it has arisen in that interval,
it occurs sequentially in the half-portion of the moon.
When the full moon day and the *vyatīpāta* yoga should behold each other,
at whatever time those two should coincide, that very moment is indeed the *vyatīpāta*.
Seeing that time designated by the sun as it moves through its reckoning, that indeed is the time for the performance of the *vaṣaṭ* call; it is prescribed as the immediate moment.
On the full lunar fortnight, the conjunction of night occurs at the full moon;
thereafter, on the day of the full moon, the maker of night begins to wane.
When the moon and the sun,
full in essence, gaze at each other during the day on the occasion of Vyatīpāta in the afternoon, that is the full-moon day (Pūrṇimā).
Because the ancestors together with the deities give their approval (anumanyante) to her,
therefore this first full moon is remembered by the name Anumati.
Because the maker of night shines exceedingly in this sky,
and because of the delighting [of all beings] by the moon, the poets have called her Rākā.
When the moon and the sun are in conjunction with the lunar mansion of Amāvasyā, that fifteenth night is known as Rākā; therefore, it is remembered as Amāvāsyā.
When the moon and the sun, having emerged from the darkness of the new moon (amāvāsyā), are seen to have come together with one another, that is called a *darśa*.
Two *lava*s each at the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)—that is the time during the junctions of the lunar phases (*parvasaṃdhi*).
Two syllables and one *kuhū*-measure are recorded as the three durations of the *parva* periods.
The new moon day (amāvāsyā), during which the moon has vanished, begins at midday;
having reached the sun, the moon [reappears] after half a day and night.
Having gone to the ocean together with the sun, that sun indeed has two fixed times of conjunction: at dawn and at midday.
On the first day of the bright fortnight, the moon is indeed released from the solar disc in the space between those two discs.
That indeed is the time for the oblation of the New Moon sacrifice, when the *vaṣaṭ* call is uttered;
this should be known as the beginning of the season, the *amāvāsyā*, the lunar day of conjunction of this fortnight.
For the new moon (amāvāsyā) occurs during the day when the moon has waned in the dark fortnight;
therefore, on that new moon day, the sun is indeed grasped by it during the day.
But it is perceived during the day; therefore, on the new moon day, there is a waning in the sky of these very digits through their increase and decrease due to the nature of the water.
The names of the lunar days have indeed been designated by the learned;
on those days, both the sun and the moon reveal their true selves.
Then, emerging from the solar disc in that very same sequence,
the moon touches the sun during a day and night diminished by two lava-units.
At that time, the *vaṣaṭ* call for the oblation of Kālodara occurs;
that period which is called "Kuhū" by the cuckoo comes to an end.
Because the new moon (amāvāsyā) is reckoned according to that specific time, it is known as *kuhū*;
however, the moon (*niśākara*), when its remaining portion has waned, is measured by the standard of *sinīvālī*.
On the new moon day, she enters the sun; therefore, she is remembered as Sinīvālī.
She is distinct from Anumati, Rākā, Sinīvālī, and Kuhū.
The time for these [rites] is two lavas; *kuhū* is known as that which lasts only a *kuhū*.
It occurs at the conjunction of the moon and sun during the interval between full moons when there is a *vyatīpāta*.
One should observe the fast on the day of the new moon; the time for the festival lasts for two measures (mātrās).
The period between the two tides of the ocean constitutes the time for both Kāhū and Sinīvālī.
In the solar and fiery mandalas, as well as in the lunar one, the time of the parvan is equal to a kalā;
thus it occurs during the night at the junctions of the parvans in the bright fortnight.
The glorious moon, its orb fully complete, becomes eclipsed;
for it is from this [sun] that Soma is replenished on the fifteenth day, which is the full moon.
By means of ten and five digits (kalās) respectively according to the sequence of the days, there are thus fifteen digits belonging to the Moon; its sixteenth digit, however, is [the remainder].
Therefore, the depletion of Soma occurs on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight;
these are the Pitṛs, who are gods, drinkers of Soma, and the increasers of Soma.
The seasons are indeed the Ārtavas, and the gods nourish them;
therefore, I shall now describe the Pitṛs who partake in the monthly Śrāddha.
Indeed, the destiny and the true nature of their attainment, as well as that of the faithful one, cannot be known;
for the destiny of the deceased nor their return can be known.
This is true even by means of renowned ascetic power, let alone by the eye of the flesh;
these worldly ancestors are said to follow the gods and the ancestral spirits.
The gods who are gentle and wise, though they do not perform sacrifices and are not born from the sacrificial fire—
those gods are all the ancestors, and the gods indeed honor them.
The human ancestors, as well as others who are remembered as worldly [ancestors]—
namely the father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather.
Those who have performed sacrifices with the Sāman and possess the Soma are remembered as the Somavantas;
those who have performed sacrifices with the Havis-offering are indeed remembered as the Barhiṣadas.
Those who perform oblations but officiate at sacrifices for those for whom one should not officiate are remembered as the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs;
because of their similarity in dharma with those twice-born ones, they are said by the twice-born to attain union (sāyujya) with them.
And those who are established in the stages of the duties of the āśramas do not come to grief at the end, provided they are endowed with faith in their actions.
Indeed, [it is purified] in seven ways: by austerity, by celibacy, by sacrifice, by progeny, by ancestral rites, by knowledge, and by giving.
Those who remain engaged in these duties until the fall of the body [are united] with those divine ancestors, born of subtle [elements], who perform sacrifices to Soma.
Having gone to heaven, they rejoice in the celestial realm and attend upon their ancestors when the funeral offerings (nivāpa) are presented by the kinsmen and relatives of their lineage.
The inhabitants of the world of Soma obtain satisfaction by partaking of the monthly śrāddha;
these are the human ancestors who indeed partake of the monthly śrāddha.
But others besides them, who are also mixed in their origins through karma,
have fallen away from the duties of their stages of life and are devoid of the utterances *svadhā* and *svāhā*.
With their bodies shattered, these evil-minded ones become ghosts in the abode of Yama;
having reached the place of torment, they lament over their own past deeds.
Long-lived, yet exceedingly emaciated, with beards and without clothing,
they were overwhelmed by hunger and thirst and fled hither and thither.
Desiring rivers, lakes, ponds, and reservoirs,
and longing for the food of others, they were driven hither and thither.
And they are cast down again and again into various places of torment,
such as the Śālmalī tree, the Vaitaraṇī river, and likewise into the Kumbhīpāka hell.
And upon the sand of burning embers, likewise in the forest of sword-leaves,
and at the crushing of stones, they are cast down by their own actions.
For those who remain there— suffering and imperishable—
while dwelling in another world, their kinsmen [should offer oblations] by name and lineage.
Indeed, the three rice-balls offered upon the ground on the *darbha* grass to the left [of the performer] go forth and satisfy those who reside in the realms of the departed (*preta*).
Those who had not reached the place of torment, yet fell away in five ways,
were later born among the stationary beings at the end [of the world] due to their own lowly karmas.
They are born in various forms within animal wombs and even in non-wombs;
whatever their food may be, they take it in those various wombs here.

In each and every such food offering, that which is given with faith becomes established when it is bestowed at the proper time, acquired by righteous means, and offered according to the prescribed rite into the worthy recipient.
A living being obtains food exactly as it was given, wherever that being resides;
just as a calf finds its mother even when the cows have wandered away.
In the same way, the mantra conveys the food given at the śrāddha ceremonies to the ancestors;
for thus, the śrāddha offered with faith through the mantra is never fruitless.
Beholding with his divine eye, that prince,
who knew the comings and goings of the pretas, spoke regarding their attainment of the śrāddha together with them.
The Bāhlīkas, the Uṣmapās, and the Divākīrtyas are remembered as such;
for them, the dark fortnight is the day, and the night is for sleep during the bright fortnight.
Thus, these ancestors are indeed gods, and the gods are indeed ancestors;
the seasons, the half-months, and the months are remembered as being ancestors to one another.
Thus, these are the divine ancestors and those who are the ancestors of men;
when they are gratified through rites endowed with faith, they themselves are gratified.
Thus has this investigation into the ancestors who drink the Soma been declared;
for such is the true nature of the ancestors as established in the Purāṇa.
Thus occurs the conjunction of the Sun, the Ancestors, and the Moon,
as well as the attainment of the nectar of immortality and the satiation of the ancestors.
The times of the full moon and the new moon, as well as the place of torment, have been briefly proclaimed to you; this is the eternal creation.
Indeed, the manifold variety of creation has been described only partially;
it is impossible to enumerate it in its entirety, yet it must be believed by one who desires prosperity.
Indeed, this creation of Svāyambhuva has been traversed by me in detail and in its proper sequence; what more shall I describe?

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Investigation of the Ancestors at the Amāvāsyā Śrāddha," in the second section (Anuṣaṅga-pāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as narrated by Vāyu.
The Sage said: "Regarding those four Yugas that existed previously in the Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara..."
I wish to hear from you in detail their origin and their true nature.
Sūta said:
Regarding that which was previously mentioned by me in connection with the earth and the other elements, I shall now describe their four yugas; listen to it.
Having enumerated them here by number and in full detail from every perspective,
[he described] the Yuga, the divisions of the Yugas, and likewise the dharma of the Yugas.
The twilight of the age (yugasaṃdhyāṃśaka), as well as the junction of the ages (yugasaṃdhāna)— these six types known as the ages, I shall now explain according to their true nature.
A human year is established by worldly means of measurement;
by that year I shall here describe the calculation of the four yugas. One should know that a short vowel-syllable is equal in duration to the time of a blink of an eye.
Fifteen *nimeṣas* make one *kāṣṭhā*, and one should count thirty *kāṣṭhās* as one *kalā*.
Thirty *kalās* constitute a *muhūrta*, and thirty of those make up a day and night, which are equal in duration.
The sun divides day and night according to the human world.
There, the day is for the performance of ritual actions, while the night is intended for sleep;
among the ancestors, a month constitutes a day and a night, and their division is as follows.
For them, the dark fortnight is the day and the night is for sleep;
thirty human months are traditionally reckoned as one month of the ancestors (pitrya).
Indeed, three hundred and sixty months constitute a year of the ancestors (pitrya), as it is understood in human reckoning.
That which constitutes one hundred years by human measurement is indeed reckoned here as three years for the ancestors.
Ten months and ten days are designated here as the number of the ancestors; this is according to the worldly human measure known as the year.
This is established as the certainty in the scripture regarding this divine day and night;
furthermore, the division of those two, the divine day and night, constitutes a year.
The northern course (udagayana) is their day, and the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is their night;
such are their divine day and night, and now follows the calculation of those two.
Thirty human years are known as one divine month;
know that three hundred human years are equal to three such divine months.
Indeed, ten such days constitute a divine period; this is remembered as the divine rule. Those three hundred and sixty human years are proclaimed to be one divine year according to human reckoning.
Three thousand human years in measure,
plus another thirty years, are considered one year of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis).
Nine thousand human years,
plus another ninety, are recorded as one *dhruva* year.
Twenty-six thousand human years are to be known as one hundred [divine] years; this is indeed remembered as the rule for the divine reckoning.
They say that three hundred thousand human years indeed constitute [the duration].
And sixty thousand [years] are reckoned by calculation;
those who know calculation say that it is a thousand divine years.
Thus has it been sung by the sages here with divine reckoning;
the calculation of the number of yugas is indeed according to the divine measure.
Sages have spoken of four ages in the land of Bhārata:
the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali; such is the quartet.
First, the age named Kṛta is established; then Tretā is ordained;
and Dvāpara and Kali as well—these are the ages one should reckon.
They say that the Kṛta Yuga consists of four thousand years;
its dawn (saṃdhyā) lasts for as many hundreds of years, and the twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is equal to the dawn.
In the other three [ages], together with their twilights and their twilight-portions,
hundreds and thousands proceed according to the same principle.
In the Tretā and Dvāpara ages, the durations are respectively three thousand and two thousand years;
the morning and evening twilights (saṃdhyās) are each three hundred and two hundred years, and their transitional periods (saṃdhyāṃśas) are equal to those [twilights].
The best of the twice-born say that Kali consists of one thousand years;
its dawn (saṃdhyā) lasts for one hundred years, and its twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is equal in duration to the dawn.
The number of their ages (yugas) is proclaimed to be twelve thousand;
these four are the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali.
Here, the years have been observed according to human measurement;
now I shall speak of the years of the Kṛta age—listen to them.
Indeed, they say that fourteen hundred thousands,
as well as another forty thousand, constitute the Kṛta Yuga.
Likewise, the duration of the Tretā Yuga consists of one million years and eighty thousand years.
They say that the duration of the Dvāpara age is seven million and twenty thousand years by human reckoning.
Likewise, the duration of the Kali Yuga is three hundred and sixty thousand years in number.

Thus, in a cycle of four ages (caturyuga), time is said to consist of the ages along with their transitional periods (saṃdhyāṃśaka); indeed, the ages [of this cycle] amount to twenty-six million, nine hundred thousand, seven hundred and twenty-eight years.
In this reckoning, four hundred and three million,
plus twenty thousand years, constitute the period of the four yugas along with its transitional junctures (saṃdhyāṃśa).
Thus, seventy-one cycles of four yugas,
including the Kṛta, Tretā, and the others, are said to constitute the interval between Manus.
Now learn the number of years for a Manvantara according to the human year:
thirty crores of years are proclaimed in human reckoning.
Furthermore, this period consists of sixty-seven million,
twenty thousand, and some additional years, excluding the extra time.
This is the number of a Manvantara as recorded by the learned twice-born;
this duration of a Manvantara is proclaimed along with its associated Yugas.
The Kṛta Yuga consists of four thousand years;
I shall now describe the remaining Tretā, as well as the Dvāpara and the Kali.
The meaning cannot be expressed in two ways simultaneously;
for this reason, I have not told you these two pairs [of doctrines] all at once, but rather as they arrived in succession.
And likewise, due to being preoccupied with the lineage of the ṛṣis,
at the beginning of this Tretā Yuga, Manu and those who were the seven ṛṣis [were present].
The Vedic and Smṛti dharma has been proclaimed to you by Brahmā,
together with the connection to wives and the Agnihotra sacrifice, and the collections of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
The seven sages declared that dharma characterized by such [Vedic injunctions] is śrauta;
they also declared that dharma which has come down through tradition is smārta, characterized by right conduct (ācāra).
Manu Svāyambhuva declared that it is endowed with the conduct of the castes and stages of life,
and is indeed established through truth, celibacy, sacred learning, and austerity.
Indeed, through their heated asceticism and by means of the Ṛṣi’s ritual procedure,
this occurred for the Seven Sages and for Manu during the first Tretā Yuga.
Their [mantras] are not preceded by conscious deliberation, nor are they preceded by ritual action;
yet those mantras are manifested through examples such as the *Tāraka* and others.
In the first kalpa, those [mantras] which appeared spontaneously among the gods were the source for the attainment of the remaining siddhis and the initiation of others as well.
Those mantras which existed in thousands of past kalpas have indeed reappeared for them through their own inspired intuition.
The Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, the Sāman-chants, and the Atharvan-mantras were proclaimed by the Seven Sages; Manu, however, proclaimed the Smārta Dharma.
In the beginning of the Tretā age, the Vedas existed as unified collections (saṃhitās), serving solely as the bridges of dharma;
however, due to the contraction of the lifespan, they will indeed become fragmented during the Dvāpara ages.
In the Dvāpara and subsequent ages, the sages study the Vedas through the power of their asceticism;
these divine scriptures were created from the beginningless and endless past by the Self-born Creator himself.

Possessing the same dharma, the same vows, and the same constituent parts, the Vedic teachings— which have identical purposes— are modified according to the dharma in each successive age, in accordance with the requirements of that age.
The Kṣatriyas have sacrifices involving physical exertion, the Vaiśyas likewise have sacrifices of oblations,
the Śūdras have sacrifices of service, and the best of the twice-born have sacrifices of silent recitation.
Then, during the Tretā age, the social orders were joyful, protected by righteousness,
devoted to their duties, possessed of offspring, prosperous, and likewise happy.
The Kṣatriyas follow the Brāhmaṇas, the Vaiśyas follow the Kṣatriyas, and the Śūdras follow the Vaiśyas; thus they are devoted to one another in succession.
Their auspicious activities, as well as their duties according to caste and stage of life,
are performed through their mentally conceived intentions, their spoken words, and their own specific actions.
And in the Tretā Yuga, even a fruitless undertaking of action becomes successful;
[so too do] longevity, intelligence, strength, beauty, health, and virtuous conduct.
For these [duties] were indeed common to all during the Tretā age;
it was Brahmā who then established their system of social classes and stages of life.
Furthermore, those subjects, out of delusion, failed to protect even those very duties;
due to their mutual conflict, they approached Manu once again.
Furthermore, Svāyambhuva Prajāpati, having perceived the truth as it is and having meditated,
begot two sons upon Śatarūpā.
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were the first two to be seen as kings;
from that time forward, monarchs arose who wielded the rod of punishment.
Because they delighted the subjects, they became kings and lords of men;
yet those who were secretly wicked could not be restrained by those rulers.
Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is remembered as their Dharmarāja and their teacher;
and the divisions of the social classes were fully proclaimed during the Tretā age.
Then, from that [collection], the mantras were compiled by the sages, the sons of Brahmā;
and at that very time, the sacrifices were set in motion by the gods.
Together with Viśvabhū, who had acquired [merit] during the watches of the night, and with Devendra of great splendor, who had gathered all the necessary means for accomplishment; BndP_1,29.67.
In the Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara, sacrifice was first instituted by the gods;
truth, recitation, austerity, and charity are said to be the dharma of the Tretā age.
Then, at the end of thousands of ages, the dharma of non-violence prevails;
and at that time, heroes are born who are long-lived and possessed of great strength.
The highly fortunate ones have well-proportioned limbs, are most righteous, and are exponents of the Veda;
they have eyes as broad as lotus petals, broad chests, and are well-knit in their build.

In the Tretā age, there will be great beings who are free from the fear of lions, who possess the gait of rutting elephants, and who are wielders of great bows— these shall be the universal monarchs (cakravartins).
His arms are endowed with all the primary marks and are as well-proportioned as a banyan tree;
his two arms are remembered as being like a banyan, and thus he is called "Nyagrodha" (the Banyan-like).
When the height of an embodied being is equal to the span of his outstretched arms,
and his circumference is equal to his height, he is to be known as one with the "Nyagrodha-circle" (symmetry like a banyan tree).
The wheel, the chariot, the jewel, the wife, the treasure, the horse, and likewise the elephant—
these seven are the jewels common to all universal monarchs.
The wheel, the chariot, the jewel, the sword, and the fifth, the precious shield;
the banner and the treasure—these seven are said to be devoid of life.
The wife, the domestic priest, the army commander, the chariot-maker,
the counselor, the horse, and the young elephant— these seven are proclaimed as living beings.
These divine jewels, perfected for the high-souled ones,
are fourteen in number and are to be possessed by all universal monarchs (cakravartins).
By a portion of Viṣṇu, universal emperors are born here on earth throughout all the past and future Manvantaras.
Those who were in the past, those who will be in the future, and those who exist in the present—
all these Cakravartins are born here in the Tretā Yuga.
For those rulers of the earth, these four most wonderful blessings indeed come to pass here: strength, righteousness, happiness, and wealth.
Without mutual conflict, kings attain together wealth, virtue, pleasure, fame, and victory.
Indeed, by means of sovereignty such as the power of atomization (aṇimā) and the like, as well as by their lordly power,
sacred learning, and austerity, they surpass even the sages.
By means of their strength and austerity, as well as by superhuman bodily marks residing upon their bodies, gods, dānavas, and humans are born.
His hair is glossy, his forehead is high, and his tongue is long enough to wipe his face;
his lips and eyes have a coppery luster, he bears the Śrīvatsa mark, and the hair on his body grows upward.
Their arms reached down to their knees, their hands were as red as mangoes, their waists were slender, their girth was like that of a banyan tree, and they had the shoulders and testicles of lions.
He has the gait of an elephant and a camel; he has large jaws, and on his two feet are wheels and fish, while on his two hands are a conch and a lotus.
Those eighty-five thousand kings reigned without aging;
among them were four wheel-turning monarchs (cakravartins) who possessed unimpeded movement.
In the atmosphere, in the ocean, in the netherworld, and among the mountains—
sacrifice, charity, austerity, and truth are said to be the dharma of the Tretā age.
Then Dharma proceeds according to the divisions of social classes and stages of life,
and the science of government (daṇḍanīti) is put into operation for the purpose of establishing the boundaries of conduct.
All subjects were well-nourished, free from disease, and full of contentment;
during the period of the Tretā Yuga, it is recorded that the single Veda was divided into four quarters.
At that time, human beings live for three thousand years;
surrounded by sons and grandsons, they die in due course.
This is the dharma of the Tretā Yuga; now learn of the twilight (saṃdhyā) of the Tretā.
The twilight of the natural characteristics of the Tretā Yuga proceeds for one quarter (pāda);
that quarter of the twilight, being its inherent nature, persists by means of a single portion (aṃśa).
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Cycle of Numbers," in the second section (Anuṣaṅgapāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Śaunaka said:
How did the commencement of the sacrifice take place at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga?
Tell me that correctly, as it occurred previously during the Svāyambhuva creation.
When twilight had vanished together with the Kṛta Yuga,
and when that which is called Time had set in, the Tretā Yuga then arrived.
When the medicinal herbs had grown, when the release of rain had commenced,
and when the means of livelihood were established once more, people became devoted again to the householder's stage of life.
And having established the system of the castes and stages of life according to their enumeration,
and having gathered those necessary materials, how was the sacrifice set in motion?
Having heard this, Sūta said: "O Śāṃśapāyana, listen to how the commencement of the sacrifice took place at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga."
I shall describe that in due order from the former creation of Svāyaṃbhuva;
when the twilight period had vanished along with the Kṛta Yuga.
When the period known as Kāla had begun, and the Tretā Yuga had arrived,
when medicinal herbs had appeared and the release of rain had commenced.
When the means of livelihood were established and people were devoted to the life of householders,
he arranged the system of castes and stages of life, and then the Mantras in their collective form.
Then, having applied those mantras to rituals both here and in the hereafter,
the Lord Indra, the consumer of the universe, commenced the sacrifice.
When his horse sacrifice had been prepared, all the great seers arrived together with all the deities, bringing every kind of sacrificial provision.

While the officiating priests were intent on their duties and the sacrificial rite was proceeding continuously, all [the gods] assembled together said to me as I was sacrificing with animals and mental offerings: *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa* 1.30.11.
Then, while all the chanters of the Sāman were singing beautifully together,
and while the swift Adhvaryus, those bulls among priests, were moving about.

And while the sacrificial animals were being immolated, as well as when the flocks of beasts were likewise offered, and while the oblation was being poured into the fire by the Brāhmaṇas who maintain the sacred fires; ||| BndP_1,30.13 |||
And when all those entitled to share in the sacrifice had been invited in due order at that time,
those gods who consist of the senses then became the sharers of the sacrifice.
Then those who exist at the beginning of the kalpas seek out the gods;
at the time of the ritual summons, they are indeed the great seers who have emerged as the Adhvaryu priests.
Then the great sages, seeing those groups of animals distressed, gathered together and asked Indra: "What is this sacrificial rite of yours?"
"O best of gods, this dharma of yours is indeed powerful, for it proceeds from a desire for the dharma of violence; therefore, this slaughter of animals occurs in your sacrifice."
Unrighteousness was undertaken for the destruction of righteousness through the slaughter of animals;
this is not dharma, for this is adharma, since violence is never said to be dharma.
O Bhavānī, if you so desire, perform a sacrifice here according to the sacred tradition,
by means of a rite seen in the injunctions, which is righteous and free from obstacles.
O best of gods, the sacrificial seeds are those in which no violence exists,
which have remained for a maximum period of three years and have not sprouted.
O one of great wisdom, this dharma was ordained of old by Virañci;
thus it was established by Viśvabhuk, Indra, and the seers who perceive the truth.
At that time, a very great dispute arose between Indra and the great sages as to whether the sacrifice should be performed by mobile beings, immobile beings, or both.
But those great seers, weary of their dispute, stated the truth,
reached an agreement with Indra, and questioned the sky-dwelling Vasu.
O wise one, O King, how was the sacrificial rite observed by you at the sacrifice of Uttānapāda’s son? Speak, O Lord, and dispel our doubt.
Having heard their words and without deliberating upon their relative strengths or weaknesses, Vasu,
recollecting the Vedas and the Śāstras, spoke concerning the true nature of sacrifice.
"The sacrifice must be performed with whatever has been brought forth," said the king;
"it must be performed for me with pure animals, and also with seeds and fruits."
"Violence is the inherent nature of sacrifice; this is my view and my sacred tradition, for here the mantras addressed to the deities bear the marks of violence as perceived by the great seers."
"Because it was spoken by me on the authority of those such as Tāraka, who were endowed with long asceticism and [divine] vision, you ought therefore to attain that."
O twice-born ones, if those very mantra-sentences are indeed authoritative, then let the sacrifice proceed accordingly; otherwise, your word is false.
Having thus offered their responses, those ascetics, whose minds were disciplined,
seeing that which was destined to happen, then became silent.
As soon as this was said, the king entered the subterranean realm (rasātala);
having been a dweller above, he became a wanderer in the subterranean realm.
By those words,
King Vasu, the dispeller of doubts regarding all dharmas, descended to the surface of the earth.
Therefore, even by one who is highly learned, it should not be asserted with certainty regarding a matter of doubt;
for the course of Dharma, which has many doors, is subtle and its reach is exceedingly far.
Therefore, no one— beginning with the gods and the ṛṣis, except for Manu, the son of the Self-born— is able to declare the Dharma with absolute certainty.
Therefore, non-violence has been declared by the great seers to be the gateway to dharma;
thousands of millions of seers have gone to heaven by means of their own austerities.
Therefore, the great sages whose wealth is austerity do not praise either giving or sacrifice; rather, they value gleaning grains, roots, fruits, vegetables, and a vessel of water.
Having given this according to their means, they are established in the heavenly world;
likewise, freedom from malice, absence of greed, austerity, compassion for living beings, and self-restraint [are the means].
Celibacy, truthfulness, compassion, forgiveness, and fortitude—
this is the unassailable root of the eternal dharma.
For it is heard that the sinless ones such as the Brahmins and Kshatriyas attained perfection through austerity—
namely Priyavrata, Uttānapāda, Dhruva, Medhātithi, and Vasu.
Sudhāmā, Virajas, Śaṅkha, Pāṇḍyaja, Prājīnabarhis, Parjanya, and King Havirdhāna and others; (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.30.40).
These and many other royal sages of great being, whose fame is firmly established, have gone to heaven by means of their own ascetic penances.
Therefore, austerity is superior to sacrifice for all these reasons;
by means of austerity, Brahmā created this entire universe in the beginning.
Therefore, that sacrifice does not persist; this is remembered as having austerity (*tapas*) as its root.
Sacrifice consists of material substances and mantras, while austerity consists of fasting.
Through sacrifice one attains the state of the gods; through austerity, the state of Virāj;
through the renunciation of action, the state of Brahman; and through dispassion, victory over Prakṛti.
"Through knowledge one attains liberation; these five are declared to be the destinies.
Thus did a very great dispute arise among those who were ignorant regarding the process of manifestation.
Formerly, during the Svāyambhuva interval, this occurred among the deities and the ṛṣis;
then, seeing him slain by the power of Dharma, the ṛṣis [were amazed].
Having disregarded the words of Vasu, they all departed as they had come;
when the hosts of sages had gone, the gods completed the sacrifice.
For such was the commencement of sacrifice during the Svāyambhuva interval;
from that time forward, this sacrifice has evolved along with the Yugas.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Commencement of Sacrifice," in the second section (Anuṣaṅgapāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Hereafter, I shall again declare the rules for the Dvāpara age.
There, when the Tretā Yuga has waned, the Dvāpara Yuga begins.
The spiritual perfection that belonged to living beings at the beginning of the Dvāpara age, and that which existed in the Tretā age—
when that age has passed away, they perish along with those perfections.
Then, in the Dvāpara age, there arises again among those people the intermixture of castes and the reversal of duties.
Sacrifice, ascetic observance, punishment, intoxication, hypocrisy, forbearance, and strength—
this activity, joined with passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas), is recorded as characteristic of the Dvāpara age.
The dharma that existed when the Kṛta age was established continues in the Tretā;
having become disordered in the Dvāpara, it perishes in the Kali Yuga.
In that age, there will be a confusion of the castes and likewise of the stages of life;
both the Śruti and the Smṛti will fall into a state of duality.
Likewise, because of the duality of the Śruti and Smṛti, certainty cannot be attained;
and due to the failure to attain certainty, the true nature of Dharma is not known.
Due to the non-existence of phenomena, there will arise a divergence of opinion among friends;
and through their mutual discord and the confusion of their views, [the world will fall into ruin].
For the certainty that "this is dharma" or "this is not" is not attained,
because of the deficiency of causes and the uncertainty regarding effects.
Indeed, through a divergence of opinion among them, a confusion of views would arise;
and because of those who were thus divided in their views, this treatise became disordered.

The single Veda indeed consists of four quarters; it is prescribed here as threefold during the Tretā age, and due to the decline of the lifespan, it is divided into separate branches during the Dvāpara ages.
Furthermore, due to the divisions within the Ṛṣi-mantras, it is differentiated by errors of vision,
by the arrangements of Mantra and Brāhmaṇa, and by the transpositions of vowels and consonants.
The Saṃhitās of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas are recited by the great seers;
they are both common and modified, differing here and there in their various perspectives.
The Brāhmaṇas, the Kalpasūtras, and the Mantrapravacanās—
others indeed set out toward them, while some remained opposed to them.
In the Dvāpara ages they proceed, but in the Kali age they cease;
there was once a single Ādhvaryava [Veda], but it again became divided into two.
But this [Veda] has been rendered confused by treatises composed with meanings contrary to the general [tradition],
and it has been made disordered in many ways by the various systems of the Ādhvaryava ritual.
Likewise, in the Kali age, which is perpetually agitated by various interpretations and designations of the Atharva, Ṛg, and Sāman Vedas, it is rendered fragmented by diverse philosophical views.
Their divisions, subdivisions, and even their enumerations prevail during the Dvāpara age; thereafter, in the Kali age, they perish.
In the Dvāpara age, however, their opposites arise:
drought, death, and likewise afflictions of disease.
Furthermore, through the sufferings arising from the actions of speech and mind, world-weariness (nirveda) is born;
from world-weariness, there arises in them the contemplation of liberation from suffering.
From reflection comes dispassion; from dispassion, the perception of defects;
and from the perception of defects, ignorance arises in the Dvāpara age.
In the first age, the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, opponents of the scriptures indeed arise among those who lack knowledge during the Dvāpara period.
Furthermore, there were various branches of Āyurveda, as well as those of astrology,
various treatises on statecraft (Arthaśāstra), and the analysis of the sciences of logic (Hetuśāstra).
The grammatical systems, the ritual manuals (Kalpasūtras), the various interpretations of the commentaries,
the different branches of traditional law (Smṛti), and the distinct philosophical schools— each stands as a separate path.
In the Dvāpara ages, the various inclinations of men's minds prevail;
through thought, deed, and speech, their livelihood is accomplished only with great difficulty.

In the Dvāpara age, for all beings, their livelihood is preceded by physical austerity and characterized by greed, primarily through trade, and there is a lack of certainty regarding the principles of reality.
The promulgation of Vedic scriptures, the confusion of dharma, the destruction of the system of castes and stages of life, as well as desire and anger; BndP_1,31.27 //
In the Dvāpara ages, passion, greed, and likewise violence prevail;
during the Dvāpara and subsequent ages, the Veda is divided by Vyāsa into four parts.
When that Dvāpara age has completely ended, its twilight period, which is devoid of qualities, remains; such is the state of the dharma of the Dvāpara.
In the same way, the twilight [age] is considered to have one foot remaining;
now learn of the remainder of the Dvāpara and the Tiṣya [Kali] ages.
The commencement of the Dvāpara age is characterized by the non-observance of duties, and that of the Kali age likewise consists of violence, envy, falsehood, deceit, and the killing of ascetics.
These natures of Tiṣya indeed bring about the welfare of living beings;
this entire Dharma has been established, yet the Dharma is also declining.
Whether through thought, action, or praise, the livelihood of the people succeeds or fails;
in the Kali age, there is a plague that kills, as well as constant hunger and fears.
In the Tiṣya age among the worlds, there will be terrible fear of drought and the ruin of countries;
indeed, in that age, there is no authority for traditional law (smṛti).
In the Kali age, some of the people die while still in the womb, others in youth,
and some even as elders die in their childhood.
Through ill-performed sacrifices, poorly studied texts, evil deeds, and improper traditions— through these defects in the ritual actions of Brahmins, fear arises among the subjects.
Violence, deceit, as well as envy, anger, malice, and impatience toward men;
passion and greed—these prevail among living beings in the Tiṣya age in every respect.
When the Yuga has reached its extreme limit, great agitation arises;
indeed, when a full thousand years have passed, that is the maximum lifespan of men at that time.
At that time, the twice-born do not study the Vedas nor perform sacrifices;
men, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas likewise perish in succession.
In that Kali age, there will be social relations between Śūdras of the lowest birth and Brāhmaṇas through sharing beds, seats, and meals.
At that time, kings will consist mostly of Śūdras and will be promoters of heretics; likewise, the subjects will be devoid of virtue, and thus the age shall proceed.
Lifespan, intelligence, strength, beauty, and lineage itself perish;
Śūdras adopt the conduct of Brāhmaṇas, and Brāhmaṇas adopt the conduct of Śūdras.

When the end of the age has arrived, those who follow the conduct of kings will become thieves, and kings will adopt the behavior of thieves; indeed, these servants will become mere sustainers of their own lives.
O best of sages, at the end of the age, women will be devoid of virtue, untruthful, fond of liquor and meat, and full of deceit.
O best of sages, at the end of the age, women will not remain faithful to a single husband;
there will be an increase in the power of beasts of prey and a total destruction of cattle.
And at the end of that yuga, there shall be the withdrawal of the virtuous;
then, in that time of great calamity, dharma—rooted in generosity—is difficult to find.
The Dharma will be practiced with laxity regarding the four stages of life;
at that time, the earth will yield little fruit in some places and great fruit in others.
At the end of the age, kings will neither be protectors nor speakers of justice regarding the share of tribute; they will be solely intent on protecting themselves.
At the end of the Yuga, O best of the twice-born, kings will be non-protectors, Brahmins will live off Śūdras, and all will offer salutations to Śūdras.
When the end of the age has arrived, the countryside will have spears for its eyes, the twice-born will have spears for their auspiciousness, and women will have spears for their hair.
In this Kali Yuga, many of the best of the twice-born will become sellers of the fruits of austerity and sacrifice, and there will be many who merely profess to be ascetics.
When the god rains down variegated [treasures], then they say the end of the age has come;
and all will become mere merchants in that lowest age.
People sell their merchandise mostly by means of false measures;
it is surrounded by those of wicked conduct, heretics, and those appearing as hunters.
When the end of the age has arrived, there will be few men and many women; people will become beggars for the sake of their own arms [for protection] against one another.
In the waning age, there will be one who does not give a reply, who speaks harsh words, who is neither upright nor free from malice, and who does not return a favor for what has been done.
And there will be no fear when he falls at the end of the age; that is his characteristic.
Thereafter, the earth, the bearer of wealth, will become a void.
There will arise rulers who are protectors yet not protectors,
who seize the jewels of others and violate the wives of others.
For those of lustful nature, evil-minded, and base, who delight in rashness, whose efforts are ruined, who are rogues with disheveled hair, and who are pierced by the thorn of pride; BndP_1,31.58 //
At the end of the age, children are born who are less than sixteen years old;
they have white teeth, controlled senses, shaven heads, and wear saffron-colored robes.
When the end of the Yuga has arrived, Śūdras will practice the Dharma;
they will become thieves of grain as well as stealers of clothing.
From thief come thieves and plunderers, and likewise another who plunders the plunderer;
when the world has ceased from knowledge and action and has entered a state of inactivity.
Insects, mice, and snakes will harass human beings;
thus, security, health, and capability will be difficult to obtain at all times.
The regions will be inhabited by the Kauśikas, oppressed by the fear of hunger;
and for those overwhelmed by suffering, the maximum lifespan at that time will be one hundred years.
In the Kali age, all the Vedas are seen and yet not seen;
likewise, sacrifices perish, being oppressed solely by unrighteousness.
Then there were those wearing saffron robes, as well as the Nirgranthas and the Kāpālikas;
others were sellers of the Vedas, and still others were sellers of sacred fords.
And whatever other heretics arise as adversaries to the castes and stages of life, they indeed appear when the Kali age has arrived.
At that time, Śūdras who are experts in the meaning of dharma will study the Vedas,
and kings born of the Śūdra caste will perform the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Having committed the slaughter of women, children, and cows, and having killed one another,
as well as having plundered each other, the people will then seek their own ends.

In the Kali age, it is recorded that there is the proclamation of suffering, a short lifespan, and bodies afflicted by disease; due to the adherence to unrighteousness, conduct is shrouded in darkness.
Then, among living beings, the slaughter of embryos proceeds out of enmity;
therefore, upon reaching the Kali age, lifespan, strength, and beauty are diminished.
Then, O best of the twice-born, at the end of the age, men will attain perfection in a short time; blessed indeed, they shall practice the Dharma.
Those who, free from malice, practice the dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti—
dharma that lasts for a year in the Tretā age— is recorded as lasting for a month in the Dvāpara age.
Acting according to his capacity, a wise man may attain in a single day during the Kali age what was gained through long practice;
such is the condition of the Kali Yuga—now learn of its transitional period (saṃdhyāṃśa).
In each successive age, however, the accomplishments (siddhis) diminish by three-quarters;
due to the inherent nature of the ages, they remain here during the transitional periods (saṃdhyās) only to such an extent as is appropriate.
The natures of the junctions (saṃdhyā) are established within their own parts, remaining as one-quarter [of each];
thus, when the time of the junction-part has arrived at the end of the age (yugāntika).
The teacher of those wicked Bhṛgus, who arose from their destruction,
was indeed by lineage of the Moon and was called Pramati by name.
In the previous Svāyambhuva Manvantara, that [portion] of Mādhava,
having indeed wandered over the earth for a full twenty years, existed as a partial incarnation.
Leading his army, which consisted of horses, chariots, and elephants,
he was followed by hundreds and thousands of Brahmins who held weapons in their hands.
Surrounded by them at that time, he slaughtered the Mlecchas on all sides,
as well as those kings born of Śūdra origin, together with their entire retinues.
Then the omnipresent Lord completely exterminated all the Pāravaṇḍas;
he slew them all without exception, including those who were not particularly righteous.
And those born from the transposition of castes, as well as those who live off them—
the northerners, the people of the Middle Country, and likewise the mountaineers.
[He subdued] those from the east and the west, as well as those who roam the ridges of the Vindhya mountains;
likewise, he subdued the Southerners and the Dravidians along with the Siṃhalas.
The Gāndhāras, the Pāradas, the Pahlavas, the Yavanas, the Śakas, the Tuṣāras, the Barbaras, the Cīnas, the Śūlikas, the Daradas, and the Khaśas.
The powerful lord, whose wheel has been set in motion, will be the destroyer of the Mlecchas, including the Lampakas, Ārās, Katakas, and the various tribes of the Kirātas.
Unseen by all beings, he then wandered over the earth,
having been born here through a portion of the divine Mādhava.
In a previous birth, there was a powerful lord known as Pramati,
of the lunar lineage, who flourished in a former Kali Yuga.
When his thirty-second year had dawned, he set out for twenty years,
slaughtering all living beings, indeed all human beings, in every way.
Having reduced the earth to its very seeds by their cruel deeds,
they did so through mutual provocation and sudden outbursts of anger.
Having thoroughly subdued those mostly unrighteous śūdras,
he reached his end in the region between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, along with his followers.
Then, when that eon had passed, he, together with his army, having destroyed all the kings and thousands of mlecchas in general, [reigned].
Then, when the time of the twilight period had arrived at the end of the age,
and only a few remaining subjects were situated here and there, [the dissolution occurred].
Then those very ones, seized by greed, formed into groups;
they insulted one another and struck each other down.
When the destruction brought about by the power of the ages had arrived in a state of anarchy,
all those subjects were indeed afflicted by fear of one another.
Agitated and wandering about, having abandoned their wives and homes,
they disregarded their own kinsmen, being deeply distressed for no apparent reason.
When the dharma of the Śruti and Smṛti had perished, they then struck one another;
devoid of restraint, without anyone to cry out for help, lacking affection, and shameless.
When the Dharma had perished, they were despondent; being short-lived, they abandoned their sons and wives, their senses agitated by despair for twenty-five years.
Afflicted by drought and having abandoned their livelihoods, they will become miserable and,
leaving their own districts, will resort to the borderlands.
They frequent rivers, ocean shores, and likewise mountains,
subsisting on meat, roots, and fruits, and are exceedingly miserable.
Wearing garments of bark and leaves, inactive and possessing no belongings,
fallen from their caste and stage of life, they have entered into a terrible state of social confusion; having reached this ultimate limit, the people will then be reduced to a small remnant.
Afflicted by old age, disease, and hunger, they attained detachment from suffering;
indeed, from detachment comes discernment, and from discernment, the state of equanimity.
Awakening consists in the state of equilibrium; from perfect enlightenment comes the nature of righteousness.
This occurs when those [qualities] are joined with tranquility and remain as the residue of the Kali age, indeed by itself.
Then, at the end of the eon, their day and night revolved;
having caused delusion of mind in them, they were indeed like those who are asleep or intoxicated.
Then, by the power of the destiny that was to be, the Kṛta age commenced; and once that pure Kṛta age had indeed begun, [the world proceeded accordingly].
Then, those beings who were remnants of the Kali age became like those of the Kṛta age;
and the Siddhas who remained here moved about unseen.
Together with the seven ṛṣis, they were established there—
those who are remembered here as the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras for the sake of the seed.
At that time, they became indistinguishable from the Kali-yugas;
meanwhile, the Seven Sages proclaimed the Dharma both to them and to others.
Endowed with the conduct of the castes and stages of life, that [dharma] is twofold: based on the Vedas (śrauta) and based on tradition (smārta).
Consequently, during the Kṛta age, all subjects indeed abide by those who perform ritual actions.
And some remain here until the end of the age for the sake of establishing the dharma shown by the seven sages, consisting of both the Śrauta and Smārta rites.
Indeed, the sages remain during the periods of the Manvantaras,
just as grasses here are consumed by the heat of a forest fire.
Just as the first growth of forests occurs at their roots through rain,
so too does the birth of those belonging to the Kṛta Age occur here among those born in the Kali Age.
In this manner, here on earth, the succession of one age from another proceeds without interruption until the end of the Manvantara.
Happiness, longevity, strength, beauty, dharma, wealth, and even desire—
these all diminish by three-quarters in each successive age.
O twice-born ones, the accomplishments of dharma in the yugas diminish during the remaining periods of the twilights; such is this transition that has been described by me.
By this alone is the establishment of all the four yugas accomplished;
this cycle of the four yugas multiplied a thousandfold constitutes [a kalpa].
That is declared to be the day of Brahmā, and his night is remembered as being of equal duration;
during this period, until the end of the age, there occurs the straightening and the stiffening of all beings.
This indeed is recorded as the defining characteristic of all the Yugas;
and this [period] multiplied by seventy-one constitutes the cycle of the four Yugas.
The period that occurs as the sequence of revolutions is called a Manvantara;
it is that which happens here in this world during each of the four ages (Caturyuga).
And likewise, it occurs again in other [creations] in that same manner;
in each successive creation, the various distinctions arise in exactly that way.
It is recorded that there are exactly thirty-five, neither fewer nor more;
likewise, the kalpas together with the intermediate ages (yugas) and the primary characteristics (lakṣaṇas) constitute this very same measure for all the Manvantaras.
Just as the revolutions of the ages have proceeded for a long time according to the inherent nature of the ages,
so too the world of living beings does not remain stationary, revolving through decline and rise.
Thus, this definition of the Yugas has been declared in brief.
For indeed, all the past and future Manvantaras here,
as well as all the intermediate periods (Antaras), are [reckoned] by means of a single Manvantara.
Understand that these have been proclaimed here for each respective kalpa;
likewise, a wise person should apply such reasoning to those yet to come.
In all the Manvantaras, both past and future,
all beings here possess equal conceit regarding their names and forms.
For the eight classes of gods who are the lords of this Manvantara,
as well as the sages and the Manus, are all equal in their purposes.
Thus, in the ancient age, the Lord indeed always ordains the classification of the social classes and stages of life, as well as the inherent characteristics of the ages.
The divisions of the social classes and stages of life, the Yugas, and the accomplishments of the Yugas have been described as incidental matters; now learn of the creation and emanation.
I shall describe here, in detail and in due order, the maintenance of the world throughout the Yugas.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Account of the Four Yugas," in the second section (Anuṣaṅga-pāda) of the first part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said: "Learn from me those beings who are born during the various Yugas."
The demoness, the serpent, the Gandharva, the Piśāca, and the Yakṣa-Rākṣasa [forms].
In whatever age their birth occurred, and for as long as they lived—
whether they were Piśācas, Asuras, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, or Pannagas.
In the Kṛta Yuga, they are born equal in both circumference and height;
indeed, the stature of the eight classes of divine beings is ninety-six finger-breadths.
According to their own finger-measure and that which is produced from the *pauṣṭika* [rite],
they establish this as their natural measure.
But humans existing here during the transitional periods (saṃdhyāṃśa) of the yugas have a stature of seven times seven fingers, which is equal to the measure of the gods and asuras.
The height of the gods and asuras is recorded by those born in the Kali age as being one hundred and fifty-eight full finger-breadths.
It is recorded that [the height] from the feet to the head is eighty-four times one's own finger-breadths (aṅgula) measured by one's own fingers, according to the standards of the Kali age.
Thus, this increase of human stature diminishes here during the portion of the yuga;
so it is in all yuga-periods, both past and future, in this world.
A man is said to be eight *tālas* in height when measured by his own fingers; he whose measurement from the soles of his feet to the top of his head is nine *tālas* is likewise known.
One who has both knees and arms joined together is honored even by the gods;
so too are cows, horses, elephants, buffaloes, and those things that are immobile in nature.
By this [measure of] karma, the decrease and increase [of stature] are to be known in each successive age;
indeed, the hump of cattle has a height of sixty-seven finger-breadths.
The height of elephants is recorded as a full eight hundred finger-breadths;
however, that of horses is one thousand finger-breadths minus forty.
The height of the trees is recorded as being fifty barley-corns;
and the configuration of the human body is exactly as it is [described].
The body of the gods is said to possess the tallakṣaṇa due to their vision of reality, and it is endowed with an excellence of intellect.
Likewise, such a body of a human being is said to be possessed of excellence;
thus indeed have these states, both divine and human, been fully described.
Of all animals, birds, and indeed of all stationary beings—
cows, goats, sheep, horses, elephants, birds, and trees.
Those who have been employed in all sacrificial rites here on earth are born again in the abodes of the gods, assuming forms exactly like those [deities].

The gods, whose forms are auspicious, experience enjoyments according to their inclinations; these [enjoyments] correspond to their respective forms, whether stationary or moving, and in their appropriate dimensions.
There, through those delightful states of being, they indeed attained happiness;
therefore, I shall now describe the refined, the virtuous, and likewise the good.
"Sat" is the name of Brahman; those who possess that [name] are likewise called "santaḥ. Because they share this commonality with Brahman, they are therefore designated as "the good" (santaḥ).
Those who neither become angry nor rejoice regarding the tenfold objects of the senses and the eightfold causes are known as those who have conquered their own selves.
Because the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are joined with both general and specific duties, they are therefore called the twice-born (dvijātayaḥ).
One who is devoted to the duties of the castes and stages of life, who moves happily toward heaven,
and who possesses knowledge of the dharma revealed in the Vedas and the dharma prescribed in the Smṛtis, is called a knower of dharma.
Through the practice of knowledge, the celibate student who is devoted to his teacher is called virtuous;
and through the practice of household duties, the householder is likewise called virtuous.
One who practices austerities in the forest is known as a virtuous Vaikhānasa;
one who strives with self-restraint is known as a virtuous Yati because of his practice of yoga.
Thus, by the accomplishment of the duties of their respective stages of life (āśrama), they are remembered as virtuous:
the householder, the student, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic.
Then neither the gods, nor the ancestors, nor the sages, nor human beings,
perceive with divergent views whether "this is dharma" or "this is not."
In this context, these two terms "dharma" and "adharma" are said to consist of action;
merit and demerit are traditionally understood here as dharma and adharma.
The verbal root *dhṛ* is proclaimed in grammar to have the meaning of "holding" (*dhāraṇa*).
Furthermore, the lack of holding and the state of being small are called *adharma*.
Dharma, which brings about what is desired, is taught by the teachers;
and adharma, which has undesirable results, is indeed taught by the teachers.
Those who are aged, free from greed, self-possessed, devoid of hypocrisy,
properly disciplined, and upright— such ones they recognize as true teachers.
Because he practices conduct himself,
establishes [others] in conduct, and gathers the scriptures, he is therefore called an Ācārya.
The Dharma known by the twice-born who understand the Dharma is twofold: that revealed in the Vedas (śrauta) and that based on tradition (smārta).
The characteristic of the śrauta [dharma] is twofold, consisting of the marriage rite and the establishment of the sacred fires (agnihotra).
The Smārta [dharma] is declared to consist of the conduct of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśramācāra), along with restraints (yama) and observances (niyama);
having taught this here to the ancients, the Seven Sages proclaimed it as the Śrauta [dharma].
The Rig, Yajus, and Sāman verses, as well as the limbs of the Veda, constitute the Śruti;
and having remembered the practices of the past Manvantara, Manu proclaimed the Smṛti.
Therefore, the dharma based on the Smṛtis is that which distinguishes the social classes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas).
This very manifold dharma is here called the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra).
The word *śeṣa* means "remnant" (*śiṣṭa*); they declare that which remains to be a remnant.
Those righteous ones who remain here as the learned (*śiṣṭa*) throughout the Manvantaras [are the Śeṣas].
Manu and the seven sages, who act for the sake of the continuity of the world and who abide for the sake of dharma— they indeed are called the *śiṣṭas*.
And those who were unrefined, such as Manu and others whom I have previously mentioned—
by those refined ones, dharma was practiced perfectly in age after age.
The three Vedas, the means of livelihood, the science of government, sacrifice, and likewise the castes and stages of life,
are practiced by the learned and have been repeatedly enjoined by Manu.
Because it was practiced by the ancients and followed by those who have gone before, that conduct of the virtuous (śiṣṭācāra) is Sāttvata;
it consists of charity, truth, austerity, knowledge, learning, sacrifice, pilgrimage, and compassion.
These eight are the practices that constitute the characteristic of the conduct of the learned; for it is these that the learned, namely Manu and the seven sages, practice.
In all Manvantaras, the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra) is thus remembered;
that which is known through hearing is called Śrauta, and that which is known through recollection is called Smārta.
Consisting of sacrifice and the Vedas, pertaining to the Śruti and the Smṛti, and comprising the castes and stages of life—
I shall here describe the characteristics of Dharma, including its constituent parts.
But he who, having seen a fact as it truly is, does not conceal it when questioned,
speaking exactly as it occurred— this is the characteristic of truth.
Celibacy, recitation of mantras, silence, and even fasting—
this is the nature of austerity, which is most formidable and exceedingly difficult to practice.
The conjunction of sacrificial animals, material offerings, the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus verses,
as well as the officiating priests and the sacrificial fees, is called a sacrifice.
That even-minded vision which functions for the benefit and the harm of all beings as if they were oneself— this entire state is remembered as compassion.
Whether reviled or even struck, he who does not revile in return nor strike back, and who understands through speech, mind, and action—this is known as endurance; this is remembered as forbearance.
The non-seizure of another's property, whether it is being guarded by its owner or abandoned during a state of confusion, is proclaimed as non-greed.
The non-practice of sexual intercourse—neither thinking of it nor speaking of it—but rather its complete cessation, is celibacy; that which is without flaw is called austerity.
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, he whose senses do not function perversely in this world— this indeed is the characteristic of a tranquil man.
He who does not become angry when obstructed regarding objects consisting of the ten [senses] or the eightfold cause is recognized as one who has conquered his self.
Whatever object is most beloved and has been acquired through righteous means—that very thing should be given to one who possesses virtuous qualities; this is the defining characteristic of giving.
This gift is of three kinds: inferior, superior, and middling.
Among these, that which leads to the highest good is the superior; the inferior is for the sake of achieving one's own worldly ends.
Out of compassion for all beings, sharing [one's wealth] is the middling [duty];
the dharma consisting of the stages of life (āśrama) and the social orders (varṇa), ordained by the Śruti and Smṛti, is the highest.
And Dharma is that which is not opposed to the conduct of the learned, is approved by the virtuous and good,
consists in freedom from malice toward those who are disliked, and likewise rejoicing in what is liked.
Detachment is the turning away from joy, distress, and dejection;
renunciation is the relinquishing of actions performed along with those not yet performed.
The abandonment of both the wholesome and the unwholesome is called "renunciation" (nyāsa);
those specific qualities that are manifest exist within this insentient transformation.
Knowledge is said to be the consciousness that discerns between the sentient and the insentient;
this is remembered as the defining characteristic of the Dharma regarding its constituent parts.
O sages who know the truth of dharma, I shall now describe to you that procedure for a Manvantara which was formerly established in the Svāyambhuva interval.
In the same way, for each Manvantara, another Śruti is indeed prescribed for the Cāturhotṛ and the Cāturvidya.
The Ṛg verses, the Yajus formulas, and the Sāmans, according to their respective deities—
even until the dissolution of all beings— one must avoid only the Śatarudriya.
The ritual procedure, the weapon-mantra, and likewise the hymn proceed as before;
there is the hymn of substance, the hymn of quality, and likewise the hymn of fruit.
This fourfold hymn, which generates the fourth [state],
is that by which the gods who exist throughout all the Manvantaras come to be.
Brahmā indeed causes their fourfold hymn of praise to proceed;
thus, the origin of the groups of mantras is fourfold.
Then, among the Atharva, Gārya, and Yajus verses, and separately among the Sāman hymns within these Vedas,
the sages performed intense and most difficult penance.
Indeed, in former Manvantaras here, the mantras manifested in five ways: from dissatisfaction, fear, suffering, pleasure, and sorrow.
I shall here describe by their characteristics that which constitutes the state of being a seer (ṛṣi) among the seers, arising from the vision known as the Star (Tāraka) through chance.
The Sage is said to be fivefold with respect to the past and the future;
therefore, I shall describe the sages and the origin of the *ārṣa* [Veda] therein.

When the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas) prevails at the time of the universal dissolution, when the Vedas are undifferentiated, indescribable, and enveloped in darkness; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.32.71.
That which is not preceded by intellect indeed proceeds for the sake of consciousness;
but that which is preceded by conscious intellect proceeds by means of consciousness.
In the same way, these two proceed together like a fish and its water;
the being, whose nature consists of the qualities (guṇas), proceeds impelled by consciousness.
Likewise, because it is the cause, the effect then proceeds from it;
and because it is the object, the objectivity [proceeds] from the object, and likewise from the purpose, the purposiveness.
When the time for their attainment has arrived, the differentiated effects consisting of the instruments—
namely Mahat and the rest— become manifest and are gradually perfected.
From the Mahat arose the ego (ahaṃkāra), and from that, the elements and the senses;
and from the elements, their various modifications were born through mutual interaction.
Having accomplished his task, he departed immediately,
just as sparks fly forth from a firebrand at one and the same moment.
In that same way, by a single cause and through time, the individual souls (kṣetrajñas) emerge,
just as a firefly suddenly becomes visible in the darkness.
Thus emerged from the unmanifest, blazing like a firefly;
and while still possessing a body, he moved about right there.
Established right there at the entrance of the gate-hall, the all-pervading wise one is perceived as distinct due to his difference from that great darkness.
When that very [state] has been established, the scripture states: "The wise one is at the end of darkness.
For one whose intellect is undergoing transformation, a fourfold [intellect] has become manifest.
Knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, and virtue—
these four are indeed to be understood as the innate qualities of a person.
That Great Soul is said to be perfected through the transformation of the body,
because he lies latent within all things, or rather, because he possesses the knowledge of the field (kṣetrajña).
He is called Puruṣa because of his being the primordial person (puruṣatva), and he is said to be Kṣetrajña due to his knowledge of the field;
furthermore, because he dwells within through the intellect, he is indeed of the nature of consciousness.
For the sake of perfect accomplishment, he has fully understood that which is manifest and unmanifest, and that which is insentient;
thus the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) has unfolded himself, conjoined with the knowledge of the Field.
At the very moment of his manifestation, the Sage himself perceived the Unmanifest through his intellect; because he perceives that which is supreme, he possesses the status of a *paramarṣi*.
The name "Ṛṣi" is derived from the root *ṛṣ*, meaning "to go," from the very beginning;
and because he became [the truth] by himself, his state as an Ṛṣi is likewise remembered.
Spontaneously arisen from Īśvara, these were the mind-born sons of Brahmā;
by them, as they were being produced, the supreme Great One was encompassed.
