Because those wise ones possess greatness through their virtues in every respect,
they are therefore called "Great Sages" (Maharṣis) by the Buddha, the seer of the supreme.
The sons of those lords— both those born of their mind and those born of their loins—
possessing both ego and ascetic power, have attained the state of sages.
Therefore, those seven sages indeed [arose] at the beginning of the elements through their vision of reality;
whereas the sons of the sages and the ṛṣīkas were born from embryos resulting from sexual union.
Those of great majesty perceive both the subtle elements and the Truth;
they are the seven seers, and they possess the vision of the Supreme Truth.
They are to be known as the sons of the Ṛṣikās, the "sons of the sages" (ṛṣiputrakas),
because they perceive the Truth (ṛta) and the specific distinctions in their true essence.
Therefore, those seven sages also, through their vision of that which is beyond the Veda,
[perceive] the unmanifest self (avyaktātman), the great self (mahātman), and likewise the ego-self (ahaṅkārātman).
The self of the elements and the self of the senses—this is said to be their knowledge.
Listen now to these five classes of sages by their names.
Bhṛgu, Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Kratu,
Manu, Dakṣa, Vasiṣṭha, and Pulastya— these are the ten.
For these sages were born from the mind of Brahmā as lords in their own right;
because they are remembered as being superior [to others], they are therefore called Maharṣis (Great Sages).
For these sages are indeed the sons of the lords; learn of them:
Kāvya, Bṛhaspati, Kaśyapa, and likewise Cyavana.
Utathya, Vāmadeva, Apasya, Uśija, Kardama, Viśravas, Śakti, the Vālakhilyas, and likewise Arvata.
Thus have these sages been described, who attained the state of seers through their ascetic penance;
now learn of the sons of the sages, the Ṛṣikas, who were born from the womb.
Vatsara, Nagaṛhu, and likewise Bharadvāja;
the sage Dīrghatamas, and Bṛhaduktha Śaradvata.
Vājaśravas, Śuci, Vaśyāśva, Parāśara,
Dadhīca, Śaṃśapa, and likewise King Vaiśravaṇa.
Thus these are declared to be the ṛṣikas; they have attained the state of being seers through truth.
They are remembered as both lords and ṛṣis, and indeed as ṛṣikas.
Understand all these who composed the mantras in their entirety:
Bhṛgu, Kāvya, Pracetas, and the self-possessed Ṛcīka.
Aurva, Jamadagni, Vida, Sārasvata,
Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, Yudhājit, Vītahavya, and Suvarcas.
Vainya, Pṛthu, Divodāsa, Bādhyaśva, Gṛtsa, and Śaunaka—
these nineteen are indeed the Bhṛgus who are reciters of the mantras.
Aṅgiras, Vaidyaga, Bharadvāja, and Bāṣkali;
likewise Ṛtavāk, Garga, Śini, and Saṃkṛti.
Purukutsa, Māndhātṛ, and likewise Ambarīṣa;
Yuvanāśva, Paurakutsa, Trasaddasyu, and Dasyumān.
Āhārya, Ajamīḍha, Tukṣaya, Kapireva, Vṛṣādarbha, Virūpāśva, Kaṇva, and Mudgala; (these were the descendants of Aṅga). BndP_1,32.109.
And Utathya, Sanadvāja, as well as Vājaśravas,
Ayāsya the universal emperor, and likewise Vāmadeva.
Asija, Bṛhaduktha, the seer Dīrghatamas,
and Kakṣīvān— these thirty-three are remembered as the foremost among the Āṅgirases.
All these were composers of mantras; now learn of the Kāśyapas:
Kāśyapa, Vatsāra, Naidhruva, and Raibhya.
Asita, Devala, and Laṅga—these six were exponents of the Veda;
as well as Atri, Arvāvasu, Śyāvāśva, and Gaviṣṭhira.
Āvīhotra was a wise seer, and he was likewise Pūrvātithi;
these three are declared to be the great seers who were the authors of the mantras.
Vasiṣṭha, Śakti, and likewise Parāśara;
the fourth was Indrapramati, and the fifth was Bharadvāja.
The sixth was Maitrāvaruṇi, and the seventh was Kuṇḍina;
thus these seven Vaśiṣṭhas are to be known as exponents of the Veda.
Viśvāmitra, the son of Gādhi, Devarāta, as well as Udgala;
likewise the learned Madhucchandas, and another ṛṣi, Aghamarṣaṇa.
Aṣṭaka, Lohita, Kata, and Kola— both of them— as well as Devaśravas, Reṇu, Pūraṇa, and Dhanañjaya.
These thirteen most excellent descendants of Kuśika are to be known as righteous:
Agastya, Aya, Dṛḍhāyu, and likewise Vidhmavāha; 1.32.119.
For these three— Manu Vaivasvata, King Eḷa, and Purūravas— are most devoted to Brahman, possessors of ascetic heat (tapas), and possess supreme renown.
These two, Bhalandana and Vatsa, should be known as practitioners of mantra among the Kṣatriyas; together with Saṃkīla, those three are so designated.
These are remembered as the foremost *pravara* lineages of the Vaiśyas, created by these very mantra-authors.
Thus, these ninety sages who composed the mantras have been declared;
now learn of the sons of the sages among the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Characteristics of the Ages and the Progeny of the Preeminent Sages," in the second section (Anuṣaṅga-pāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Furthermore, the sons of the Ṛṣikas should be known as the Ṛṣiputrakas.
Learn now the names of those who are the expounders among the Brāhmaṇas.
The seers of the Śruti will be proclaimed together with their principal disciples and their lineages:
Paila of the Bhṛgu clan, a master of the Ṛgveda, as well as Sāṃkṛtya and Jājali.
Saṃdhyāsti, Māṭhara, Yājñavalkya, Parāśara, Upamanyu, Indrapramati, Māḍūki, and Śākali; // BndP_1,33.3 //
Bāṣkali, Śokapāṇi, Naila, Paila, and likewise Alaka;
the Pannagas and Pakṣagantas—these are the eighty-six ṛṣis of revealed knowledge.
These were the principal twice-born seers of revealed knowledge among the Bahvṛcas:
Vaiśampāyana, Lauhitya, Kaṇṭhakāla, and Aśāvaha.
Śyāmāpati, Palāḍu, Ālaṃbi, and Kamalāpati—
these were their disciples and grand-disciples, the eighty-six seers of revealed knowledge (śrutarṣis).
These are declared to be the twice-born sages, the Carakas and Adhvaryus:
Caimitri, Bharadvāja, Kāvya, and Pauṣyañji.
Hiraṇyanābha Kauśilya, Laugākṣi, Kusumi,
Laṅgalin, Śālihotra, and Śaktirāja Bhārgava.
Then the teacher of the Sāma-singers was King Purūravas, the son of Ilā;
there were indeed forty-six other disciples among them who were seers of sacred learning (śrutarṣis).
Kauśīti, Kaṅkamudga, Kuṇḍaka along with Parāśara,
Lobhālobha, the righteous-souled Dharmātman, as well as Brahmabala.
Kranthala, Madagala, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Dharmavit—
these are to be known as the ninety brahmacārins who were like Hotṛ priests.
Anukṛṣṇa, as well as Āyu, Anubhūmi, likewise; and similarly Aprīta, Kṛśāśva, Sumūli, and Bāṣkali.
Caraka, Adhvaryaka, Adhvaryu, Namasyu, and Brahmachārī; the learned Śuka, son of Vyāsa, as well as Lauki and Bhūriśravas.
Somāvirata, Antakya, as well as Dhaumya and Kāśyapa,
Āraṇya and Ilaka, as well as Upamanyu and Vida.
Bhārgava, Madhuka, Piṅga, Śvetaketu,
as well as Prajādarpa, Kahoḍa, Yājñavalkya, and Śaunaka.
Anaṅga, Niratāla, Madhyama, Adhvaryu, Sthūṇa, Aditi the mother of the gods, Jalāpa, and Mānavī.
Urvaśī, Viśvayōṣā, and the two most excellent and auspicious Apsarases,
Mudgalā, Ātujīvā, and the illustrious Tārā.
Prātimedhī, Mārgā, Sujātā, Mahātapā, Lopāmudrā who knows the Dharma, and she who is remembered as Kośītikā. (BndP 1.33.19)
And these women, who were expounders of Brahman, were equal in form to the Apsarases;
thus, O sons of sages, have these principal ones been described by me.
Because they brought forth the fourteen branches of the Veda, those sages are thus remembered;
for the lords who speak the mantras are the Ṛṣis and likewise the Ṛṣikas.
The sons of the sages were the expounders of the ritual manuals (kalpas) for the Brāhmaṇas,
as well as for the lords, the ṛṣis, and the female seers (ṛṣikās), together with their offspring.
Compose such discourses that the seers of these mantras may perceive therein non-duality, which is consistent with the injunctions, radiant, and endowed with profound words.
The sign that is absolutely beyond perception, as well as that which is likewise [unmanifest], all beings, the non-being, and whatever constitutes the final surrender; BndP 1.33.24.
In some places, they know the Svāyaṃbhuva statement to have the meaning declared by Nirukta;
whatever is joined with mantras therein is characterized by nominal case-endings.
And the word of the sages is considered to be directly stated in this way,
through various Vedic terms and numerous particles.
Furthermore, there are the great sayings remembered as the words of the ṛṣis,
which have indistinct words and which may give rise to many doubts.
Indeed, all those lamentations of the seer’s son were full of reasons and illustrations, yet possessed variegated words that were devoid of meaning.
But all [others] are incapable of darkness; this speech, however, is human.
Those known as the Miśras have attained the state of sages through their power.
Through the two types of attraction and repulsion, there arises the possibility of changing one's birth;
this is the knowledge of the past, future, and present, which is the remedy for the suffering of birth.
The combined statement of these [authorities] shall be the application of the Guru’s power;
for the authors of the Dharmaśāstras are indeed all-pervading by virtue of their majesty.
Those whose austerity is exceedingly great are remembered as Ṛṣis;
namely Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Vyāsa, and likewise Sārasvata.
The Vyāsas are known as Vedavyāsa because they are the authors of the scriptures;
being born from the waters, these virtuous ones surpassed their predecessors in wisdom.
And because they were endowed with sovereign power, those sages are so remembered;
in that time, neither age nor physical stature was a measure for the state of being a sage.
For it is observed that one man may be seen as superior, while another is most eminent in intellect;
thus, through his understanding, even a sage who is older in years may be surpassed by one who is younger, yet learned and wise.
Any verse that possesses feet and is composed of a sequence of syllables,
but which has its application at the end, they call that a Ṛc.
Whatever mantra is measured by its constituent syllables, yet is not defined by the number of its feet,
and concludes with an *atiyuk* meter— that indeed they call a *yajus*.
The syllable *hrīṃ* is sung as the *praṇava*, the *prastāva* is the fourth,
the *pratihotra* is the fifth, and they say the *upadrava* is the sixth.
The seventh part of the Sāman is the Nidhana; this is remembered as the "Seven Vindhyas.
That which is proclaimed as the "Five Vindhyas" is the syllable *hrīṃ*, excluding the *praṇava*.
When *dharma* was addressed to Brahmā, that which was then made known through its meaning was designated as *āśāsti*; lamentation is reckoned as *paridevanā*. (Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 1.33.40)
Whether arising from anger or from hatred, as well as the proclamation [of faults],
this is the prescribed characteristic of mantras for all vidyās.
Mantras are said to be of nine kinds, characterized as Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman;
likewise, there are those concerning form, censure, praise, abuse, and satisfaction.
Inquiry, permission, narration, hope, memory, and injunctions are considered [the first six];
I shall now describe the divisions of counsel, which possess twenty-four characteristics.
Praise and eulogy, reproach and censure, lamentation,
imprecation and exorcism, as well as question and answer.
The Āśīr-yajña, as well as the Akṣepa, the Arthākhyāna, and the Saṃkathā; likewise, the Viyoga, the Abhiyoga, the Kathā-saṃsthā, and the Vara.
Prohibition, instruction, salutation, longing,
and lamentation— these twenty-four types of mantras have been extracted.
In ancient times, the Brahmanas were ordained by the sages who knew the true nature of sacrifice;
they are the cause, the etymological explanation, the censure, the praise, the doubt, and the treasure-store.
The Purākalpa, the Purākalpa, the Vyavadhāraṇakalpanā,
and the Upamā— these ten indeed are the ritual injunctions for the Brāhmaṇa.
This is the characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa ordained by all the Vedic schools:
he is traditionally considered the etymological ground for the root *han* (to strike), because he strikes down [the faults] proclaimed by others.

Alternatively, when the meaning has been fully attained through the root *hī* in its sense of "going," one may provide an etymological explanation (*nirvacana*) for the determination of the sentence's meaning.
The noble ones call that "nindā" (blame) which is speech censuring a fault;
whereas from the verbal root *pra-śaṃs*, preceded by *pra*, it means praise on account of possessing good qualities.
Having reached a state of doubt by not deciding whether "this is this" or "this is not this," the rule that "this must be performed in this way" is called *vidhi*.
The narration by the wise of one thing as another is called *purākalpa*;
for that which concerns a matter entirely beyond perception is termed *purākalpa*.
Because it was spoken long ago, it is called a *purākalpa*;
it consists of mantras, brāhmaṇas, and ritual manuals (*kalpas*), as well as pure and extensive scriptural expositions (*nigamas*).
They say that a conceptualization of restriction is made without certainty;
for as this is, so indeed is that, and as this is, so indeed is that.
Thus indeed is this analogy; for the tenth [state] belongs to the Brāhmaṇa. This protection of the Brāhmaṇa has been ordained at the outset by the wise.
Its explanation has been declared by the twice-born who know it; I shall explain it word by word, as well as the ritual application of the mantras in rites observed according to the injunctions.
A mantra is so called from the verbal root *mantr*, and a Brāhmaṇa is so called from the root *brāhmaṇ*.

Those who know the Sūtras understand a Sūtra to be that which consists of few syllables, is free from ambiguity, is substantial, is comprehensive in its scope, is not redundant, and is irreproachable. (Bṛhad-yogiyājñavalkya-purāṇa 1.33.58)
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Sages," in the second section (Anuṣaṅga-pāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vāyu said:
Having heard those words, the sages spoke this reply to Sūta.
O Great-minded One, tell us how the Vedas were further divided.
Sūta said:
In ancient times, during the Dvāpara age within the interval of Svāyambhuva Manu, Brahmā spoke this to Manu: "O high-minded one, protect the Veda!"
The age has changed, my dear; the twice-born have become weak in vigor, and all have been affected by the defects of the age in due succession.
Its measurement is seen to be small indeed due to the power of the Yuga;
for only one-tenth of ten thousand parts remains as it has been declared.
Wind, fire, and strength will become diminished, and everything will utterly perish;
therefore, the Vedic rites must indeed be performed so that there may be no destruction of the Vedas.
When the Veda reaches destruction, the sacrifice will go to destruction;
when the sacrifice is destroyed, the Veda is destroyed, and from that, everything perishes.
The original Veda consisted of four quarters and measured one hundred thousand verses;
furthermore, Kṛṣṇa is the sacrifice multiplied tenfold, the granter of all desires.
Having been addressed thus, Manu, the lord devoted to the welfare of the world, replied "So be it," and divided the single Veda, which consists of four quarters, into four parts.
O dear one, at the word of Brahmā and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
I shall now describe to you the arrangement of the Vedas as it exists.
O best of beings, listen as I describe the calculation of the past Manvantaras through both direct perception and inference.
In that age, Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara and scorcher of enemies, was known as Dvaipāyana; he was the eternal portion of Viṣṇu.
Urged by Brahmā, he began to proclaim this Veda;
then, for the sake of the Vedas, he took four disciples.
Jaimini, Sumantu, Vaiśampāyana,
Paila as the fourth among them, and Lomaharṣaṇa as the fifth.
O twice-born ones, he duly appointed Paila as the reciter of the Ṛgveda,
and Vaiśampāyana as the expounder of the Yajurveda.
He approached Jaimini, who was reciting the meaning of the Sāmaveda,
and likewise the most excellent sage Sumantu for the Atharvaveda.
Indeed, the Lord, the Sovereign Master, received from me the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, as well as the Kalpa-texts.
The Yajurveda was originally one; he divided it into four parts.
From that arose the Cāturhotra, and by means of it, he fashioned the sacrifice.

He performed the duties of the Adhvaryu with the Yajus formulas, likewise the duties of the Hotṛ with the Ṛks, the duties of the Udgātṛ with the Sāmans, and the office of the Brahman with the Atharvans.
Then, having extracted the Ṛcas, the Lord of the World fashioned the Ṛgveda; with that, he fashioned the office of the Hotṛ priest and the Yajurveda.
With the *sāmans* he fashioned the Sāmaveda and thereby the office of the Udgātṛ; with the Ṛgveda he performed all ritual acts, and with the Atharvaveda he caused the King to perform them.
Skilled in the meaning of the Purāṇas, he composed the *Purāṇasaṃhitā* by means of primary narratives, secondary episodes, verses, and expressions originating from the Kalpas.
That which remained in the Yajurveda, with that they performed sacrifices;
because of this sacrificing (*yajana*), it is the Yajurveda—such is the definitive conclusion of the scriptures.
And because the feet [of the verses] were displaced, the sacrificial formulas (*yajus*) became irregular;
then, by means of a hundred officiating priests who had mastered the Vedas, his vigor was restored.
For by him the horse sacrifice was performed, or rather, he was nourished by it;
having taken up the Ṛgvedic verses, Paila then divided them into two parts.
Having divided it into two parts and joined them together, Vibhu gave them to his two disciples:
one to Indrapramati and the second to Bāṣkala.
Having composed the four Saṃhitās, Bāṣkala, the best of the twice-born,
taught them to his devoted disciples who were intent on service.
On the Bodhī tree, [he established] the first branch, the second as Agnimātara,
the third as Pārāśarī, and another as Yājñavalkyā.
Indrapramati, the best of sages, taught one *saṃhitā* to the illustrious and highly fortunate Māṇḍūkeya.
But that illustrious and powerful Satyaśravas taught his son Satyasrava, who was endowed with the totality of tranquility, the welfare of truth.
O twice-born ones, that Satyahita also once again instructed his son,
the high-souled Satyaśrī, who was devoted to truth and righteousness.
He indeed had three disciples of great splendor,
who were wise, possessed the glory of truth, and were devoted to the mastery of the scriptures.
Śākalya was the first among them, followed by another, Rathītara, Bāṣkali, and Bharadvāja; these are the founders of the [Vedic] branches.
O twice-born ones, Devamitra Śākalya, arrogant with the pride of his own knowledge, indeed met his destruction at the sacrifice of Janaka.
Śāṃśapāyana said: How did that sage, who was proud of his knowledge, meet his destruction?
And how did the dispute arise at Janaka’s horse sacrifice?
For what purpose did the dispute arise, and with whom?
Tell me all this exactly as it happened, for it is known to you.
Sūta said: At Janaka’s horse sacrifice, there was indeed a great assembly;
for many thousands of ṛṣis arrived there in great numbers.
Then, seeing that the Brahmins had arrived, desiring to behold the sacrifice of the royal sage Janaka, a desire for knowledge arose within him.
"Who among these is the best of Brahmins? How may I reach a certainty?
Having thus resolved in his mind, the lord of men applied his intellect.
Taking a thousand cows and even more gold,
as well as villages, jewels, and female slaves, the lord of men spoke to the sages.
"I have sought refuge with all of you, who are entitled to the best portion;
let this wealth that has been brought here belong to whichever one among you is the most excellent."
"O best of the twice-born, know that this wealth has been offered by me to him.
Having heard these words of Janaka, those sages, who were capable of hearing [the truth], [responded].
Seeing that wealth of great value, those greedy for riches and desiring to seize it challenged one another, who were not arrogant in their knowledge of the Vedas.
In their minds they have already claimed this wealth as theirs, saying, "This is my property.
Tell me, why do you boast, "This is mine, not yours"?
Thus, on account of the fault regarding wealth, they engaged in disputes many times;
then another learned man, a wise son of Brahmā, was present there.
The highly effulgent Yājñavalkya, an ascetic and the foremost among the knowers of Brahman,
born from a portion of Brahmā, spoke these words in a melodious voice.
"O best among the knowers of Brahman, accept this wealth as my disciple;
take it to your home, my child, for this is mine—of this there is no doubt."
"In all doctrines I am the speaker; there is no other whatsoever who is my equal. Or, if any learned man is not pleased [with this], let him challenge me without delay. (BndP 1.34.47)
Then, like the ocean agitated during the dissolution of the world, the ocean of Brahmā was stirred;
yet Yājñavalkya, composed as before, spoke to them as if smiling.
"O wise ones, you who are speakers of truth, do not be angry;
we speak according to our ability, desiring to know one another."
Then their doctrines were accepted through various words,
in a thousand ways, by means of auspicious meanings arising from subtle insight.
In the world, in the Veda, and likewise in the fields of knowledge adorned with spiritual science,
there are examiners of the king who are endowed with the highest virtues.
There, debates arose among those great-souled ones for the sake of wealth;
on one side were all the sages, and on the other side was Yājñavalkya.
Then all those sages were questioned one by one by that wise Yājñavalkya, and they could not provide an answer.
Having completely conquered all the sages, that highly intelligent mass of Brahman spoke thus directly to Śākalya, the proponent of debate: *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.34.54.
"Śākalya, speak what must be said: upon meditating on what do you remain?
For the stake has been bound by the sacrificer and led away, just as it was held."
Thus insulted by him, his face and eyes copper-red with rage, he spoke to Yājñavalkya and his attendants in the presence of the sages: BndP_1,34.56.
Having treated us, as well as other best of the twice-born, like blades of grass,
you yourself desire to seize for yourself the highly precious wealth of knowledge.
Thus addressed by Śākalya, Yājñavalkya said to him:
"Know that the strength of those most devoted to Brahman is the vision of the true meaning of the principles of knowledge."
Because it is connected with the purpose of desire, we desire that purpose;
the Brahmins, whose wealth consists of the inquiry into desire, declare the inquiry into desire.
"And because of that debt, I have taken this wealth from the royal sage.
Upon hearing these words of his, Śākalya was overcome with rage.
Then he spoke to Yājñavalkya with words intended for the purpose of asking questions according to his desire:
"Now, speak truly about the questions on matters of desire as they have been proposed by me."
Then a great debate arose between those two knowers of Brahman;
at that time, Śākalya posed more than a thousand questions.
Then, while all the sages were listening, Yājñavalkya spoke;
Śākalya became silent, and Yājñavalkya addressed him.
"O Śākalya, answer this one question of mine as you wish;
for in this debate, where a wager must be won, death indeed awaits the speaker."
Whether it be Sāṃkhya conjoined with extremely subtle knowledge, or Yoga, or the primary course of the inner self, or even the path of meditation; ||| BndP_1,34.65 |||
Then, having been thus challenged with a question by the wise Yājñavalkya,
Śākalya, failing to understand it, met his death in that manner.
Thus was Śākalya remembered, tormented by the answering of the questions;
in this way, a very great dispute arose among those who were seekers of wealth.
Indeed, together with the other sages, Yājñavalkya took his leave of the ṛṣis;
and having received wealth and established his own fame, the self-controlled Yājñavalkya,
surrounded by his disciples, went to his own pure home.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Vyāsa’s Disciples," in the second section (Anuṣaṅgapāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
And Devamitra Śākalya, a high-souled bull among the twice-born—
The wise one, the best among the knowers of the Vedas, composed five Saṃhitās.
He had five disciples: Mudgala, Gokhala, Khalīyan, Sutapas, and Vatsa Śaiśireya as the fifth.
Śāka, Vaiṇya, and Rathītara recited three Saṃhitās;
moreover, that best of the twice-born composed the Nirukta as a fourth.
He had four disciples, O best of the twice-born: Paila, Ikṣvalaka, the wise Śatabalāka, and Gaja.
Bāṣkali Bharadvāja taught three *saṃhitās*;
he had three disciples who were high-souled and endowed with virtues.
Dhīmat, Tvāpanāpa, Pānnagāri, and the wise Buddhimat—
these three, along with Ārjava, were praised for their vows through their ascetic penance.
Free from passion, possessed of great splendor, and having reached the further shore of the knowledge of the Saṃhitās—
these are declared to be the Bahvṛcas, by whom the Saṃhitās were set forth.
This disciple of Vaiśampāyana compiled the Yajurveda;
by him were proclaimed the auspicious eighty-six Saṃhitās of the Yajus.
He gave them to his disciples, and they received them according to the prescribed rules;
however, one was excluded there: Yājñavalkya, the great ascetic.
Likewise, there were eighty-six disciples who composed various recensions (saṃhitās);
indeed, it is proclaimed that all of them have threefold divisions.
In this ninth auspicious division of the Vedas, there are three types of subdivisions:
those of the North, those of the Middle Country, and those of the East, each being distinct.
Śyāmāyani became the preeminent leader of the northern regions,
while Āsuri is remembered as the first founder of the Middle Country.
Ālaṃbiri and others belong to the Easterners, while Trayodaśya and the rest are those [of the West];
these, O twice-born ones, are declared to be the Carakas, the disputants of the Saṃhitās.
The sages said: "O Carakas, Adhvaryus, tell us truly for what reason this happened;
what was performed, or for what cause did they indeed come to be known as Carakas?"
Sūta said:
O best of Brahmins, there was a certain task for the Ṛṣis;
having reached the summit of Mount Meru, they then deliberated thus.
"Or, O best of the twice-born, whichever one among us does not return here within seven nights shall indeed commit the murder of a Brahmin; such is the covenant proclaimed by us."
Then all of them, together with their attendants— with the exception of Vaiśampāyana—
proceeded for seven nights until they reached the place where the junction had been made.
At the word of the Brahmins, he committed the murder of a Brahmin;
then, having gathered his disciples together, that Vaiśampāyana spoke to them.
"O best of the twice-born, perform the penance for the murder of a Brahmin on my behalf;
all of you, having assembled together, speak words that are both desirable and beneficial."
Yājñavalkya said:
"I alone shall wander; let these sages remain.
Purified by my own austerity, I shall raise [the world] up by my power."
Thus addressed, he then became enraged and abandoned Yājñavalkya, saying:
"Return everything that has been learned by you to me!"
Thus addressed, those best among the knowers of Brahman vomited up similar sacrificial formulas (*yajus*) smeared with blood and gave them to their guru.
Then that twice-born man, having resorted to meditation, propitiated the Sun;
for the Brahman that was produced from the Sun remains established within him once he has gone there.
Then, being pleased, Sūrya indeed gave those *yajus* mantras which had gone upward as far as the solar orb to that Brahmarāti.
To the wise Yājñavalkya, who was in the form of a horse,
Mārtaṇḍa imparted those Yajus formulas which Brāhmaṇas study by means of him.
They were given to him in the form of horses, and from that they became known as *vājinaḥ*;
however, those by whom the killing of a Brahmin was committed are remembered as *carakāḥ* because of their conduct.
Those disciples of Vaiśampāyana are declared to be the Carakas;
thus these Carakas have been described—now learn of the Vājins.
The disciples of Yājñavalkya were Kaṇva and Baudheya,
as well as Madhyandina with his progeny, Vaidheya, and Āddhabauddhaka.
Tāpanīya, Vatsa, as well as Jābāla and Kevala, Āvaṭī, Puṇḍra, Vaiṇoya, and Parāśara; // BndP_1,35.29 //
Thus these fifteen excellent Vājinas have been declared;
they should be known as one hundred and one, being the various alternatives of the Yajus formulas.
Then Jaimini taught his son Sumantu;
and Sumantu, in turn, taught his son Sutvana.
Then Sukarman again taught his son Sunvan;
and having quickly mastered the thousand Saṃhitās, Sukarman likewise [completed his study].
Then Sukarman, the performer of a thousand good deeds, who possessed the splendor of the sun, spoke;
and Śatakratu struck down those who were studying during times when study is forbidden.
Then, seeing him enraged, Śakra again granted him a boon; thereupon, he undertook a fast unto death (prāyopaveśa) under the pretext of being a disciple.
"Your two future disciples, of great heroism and incomparable splendor,
both being highly wise, shall study a thousand *saṃhitās*."
"O best of the twice-born, these highly fortunate gods are enraged," having said this,
the illustrious Vāsava addressed the renowned Sukarman.
Seeing the twice-born one with his anger appeased, the Lord quickly entered within him;
O best of the twice-born, the wise Pauṣyañji became his disciple.
Hiraṇyanābha, the king of Kośala, was the second ruler;
Pauṣya’s son Añji taught him five hundred Saṃhitās.
Those auspicious disciples of Pauṣyañji, known by the name Udīcyasāmānas,
studied the five *sattvas* of the *kauśilya-saṃhitā*.
The disciples of Hiraṇyanābha are known as the Prācyasāmagās;
Laugākṣi, Kuśumi, Kuśīdi, and Lāṅgali—these four were Pauṣyañji’s disciples; learn now their divisions.
From Nāḍāyanīya was born Sahataṇḍiputra; from him came Anovaina by name, who was very learned.
From Kotiputra were born Susaha and Sunāman; these were the branches of Vittalaugākṣi.
Traya was his disciple, and Parāśara was his legitimate son.
Nābhi and Vittas were both radiant; these three are remembered as the descendants of Kauśuma.
Śauriṣu and Śṛṅgiputra—these two were long-vowed observers of religious observances.
The son of Sumitrā, a follower of the Rāṇāyaṇīya school and an expert in the Sāmaveda, spoke: "O great-souled sons of Śṛṅgin, there exists a third Saṃhitā."
Vaina, Prājīnayoga, and Surāla, the best of the twice-born,
as well as Pārāśarya and Kauthuma, proclaimed six Saṃhitās.
Āsurāyaṇa and Vaiśākha, both devoted to the Vedas and the elders,
as well as Prācīnayoga’s son and the wise Patañjali.
The divisions of Kauthuma are six, as are those of Pārāśarya; Lāṅgala and Śālihotra are the six who recited the Saṃhitās.
Hālinirjyāma, Mahān, Jaimini, Lomagāyani,
Kaṇḍu, and Kohala— these six are remembered as the Lāṅgalas.
These were the disciples of Lāṅgalin by whom the Saṃhitās were promulgated;
one disciple of Hiraṇyanābha was a prince.
That best of bipeds composed twenty-four *saṃhitās* and taught them to his disciples; learn now from whom he taught them.
Rāḍi, Rāḍavīya, Pañcamauvāhana, Talaka, Māṇḍuka, Kālika, and likewise Rājika; // BndP_1,35.51 //
Gautama, Ajabasta, Somarājāyana,
Puṣṭi, Parikṛṣṭa, and Ulūkhalaka.
The youngest were Śālī, Aṅgulīya, Kauśika,
Śālimañjaripāka, and Śadhīya Kānini.
The righteous-souled Pārāśarya was the last of the Sāma-ga singers;
among all the Sāma-gas, two are proclaimed to be the most excellent.
O twice-born ones, Pauṣyañji and Kṛta were the compilers of the Saṃhitās; having divided the Atharvaveda into two parts, Sumantu gave them away.
He, the wise one, gave Kṛṣṇa back to Kabandha according to what he had heard;
but Kabandha, having divided [Kṛṣṇa] into two parts, gave one part again to Pathya.
The Lord divided Devadarśāyasa into four parts:
Moda, Brahmabala, and likewise Pippalāda.
And Śaulkāyani, the knower of Dharma, was the fourth, established in austerity;
these four were indeed the disciples of Devadarśa, firm in their vows.
Furthermore, know that there is a supreme threefold division of those who follow the path:
Jājali, Kumuda and others, and the third is remembered as Śaunaka.
But Śaunaka, having divided [the text] into two parts, gave one to Babhru;
the wise one gave the second Saṃhitā to those known as the Saindhavāyanas.
Saindhava and Muñjakeśya again divided the Bhinnā into two parts:
the Nakṣatrakalpa, the Vaitāna, and thirdly, the Saṃhitāvidhi.
The fourth is the Aṅgiras-kalpa, and the fifth is the Śānti-kalpa;
these are the most excellent among the Atharvan Saṃhitās, serving as their various supplements.
O best of ancient sages, Khaḍga, having performed what was appropriate for me,
[was joined by] the wise and intelligent Ātreya Sumati and Kāśyapa Akṛtavraṇa.
Bhāradvāja, Agnivarcas, Vāsiṣṭha, and he who is Mitrayu; Sāvarṇi, Somadatti, Suśarman, and Śāṃśapāyana.
"These disciples of mine, firm in their vows, are proclaimed in the Purāṇas;
by three of them, indeed, the three Saṃhitās were composed once again."
Kāśyapa shall be the author of the first Saṃhitā, Sāvarṇi that of the Śāṃśapāyana; the fourth shall be mine own—these are the four root Saṃhitās.
For all of them consist of four quarters and all express the same meaning;
like the various branches of the Veda, they become redundant in their different recensions.
All [these Purāṇas] consist of four thousand verses, with the exception of the Śāṃśapāyanika;
the Laumaharṣaṇika is the root, and after that comes the Kāśyapika.
The third is the Sāvarṇikā, adorned with the meaning of straightforward sentences;
another is the Śāṃśapāyanikā, embellished with the purpose of injunctions.
There are eight thousand and six hundred Ṛg verses;
these are fifteen others, and ten others likewise with ten each.
These seven, together with the Vālakhilyas and Suparṇa, are proclaimed;
there are eight thousand Sāmans and fourteen Sāmas.
The Sāmaga chanters sing this as the *sāraṇyaka* and the *sahoha*;
the *chanda* for the Adhvaryu is recorded as consisting of exactly twelve thousand [verses].
Vyāsa likewise compiled the Yajus formulas and the Brāhmaṇas,
including those pertaining to the village and the forest, as well as the ritual procedures accompanied by mantras.
Beyond this, however, the designation "ancient" (pūrvā) applies to the narrative portion;
that which is village-based or forest-based, together with the mantras, is remembered as the Ṛgveda, Brāhmaṇa, and Yajurveda.
Likewise, the *khilas* and *upakhilas* of those belonging to the Hāridravīya school,
as well as the *parakṣudras*, are recorded as belonging to the Taittirīyas.
In the Vājasaneyaka Veda, the collection of Ṛg verses is calculated to be two thousand less one hundred; the Brāhmaṇa, however, is four times that amount.
Eight thousand, eight hundred, and eighty-two additional verses— this is the extent of the Yajus and Ṛcs, including the Śukriya and the Khilas, according to the tradition of Yājñavalkya.
Likewise, hear the measure of the *cāraṇa* sciences along with their authorities:
six thousand *ṛcs* have been declared, and furthermore, twenty-six *ṛcs*.
In addition to that, some Yajus will be spoken by them;
there are eleven thousand Ṛks and another ten more.
Ten thousand verses, plus eighty-three thousand,
and one thousand mantras— this is declared to be the measure of the Ṛgvedic verses.
Such is the extent of the Ṛgveda; indeed, there is much more belonging to the Atharvaveda.
It is certain that the Ṛks of the Atharvans number five thousand.
Another thousand [verses], excluding twenty, are to be known by the sages;
this is declared to be the *Āraṇyaka* of the Aṅgirases.
Thus has the enumeration been fully recounted, as well as the various divisions of the branches,
the authors of those branches, and likewise the causes of their differentiation.
In all Manvantaras, these divisions of the branches are thus established;
the Śruti pertaining to Prajāpati is eternal, while these [divisions] are remembered as its various alternatives.
Because the gods are impermanent, the origin of mantras occurs again and again;
furthermore, in the Dvāpara ages, the divisions of the Śrutis are proclaimed.
Thus, at that time, the Blessed One, the best of sages, having bestowed this Veda upon him and his disciples, went to the forest to perform austerities.
By his disciples and grand-disciples, however, these divisions of the branches were made:
the six auxiliary limbs (aṅgas), the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, and the extensive Nyāya.
The Dharmaśāstra, the Purāṇas, and these fourteen sciences— namely,
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda, which makes three— [along with the four Vedas].
The science of polity (Arthaśāstra) is the fourth; thus, indeed, there are eighteen branches of knowledge.
First, the Brahman-sages were known, and from them, moreover, the divine sages (Devarṣis).
Furthermore, among them, the royal sages (rājarṣis) were of three types of ṛṣi-nature:
those among the descendants of Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, as well as Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Atri.
In these five lineages, the exponents of the Veda (brahmavādins) are born;
because they revere Brahmā, they are therefore known as Brahmarṣis.
Then [the daughters] of Dharma, Pulastya, Kratu, and Pulaha,
as well as of the god Pratyūṣa and again of Kaśyapa.
The sons of those [sages] were the divine seers (devarṣis); learn their names:
Devārṣi and Dharma were both the sons of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
The Vālakhilyas were the sons of Kratu; Kardama was the son of Pulaha;
Kubera was the son of Paulastya; and Dala was the son of Pratyūṣa.
Both Nārada and Parvata were the two sons of Kaśyapa;
because they have mastered the Vedas, they are known as devarṣis (divine sages).
Those kings who belong to the lineage of Manu, those in the lineage of Aila,
and those of the Ikṣvāku and Nābhāga lineages— these are to be known as the royal sages (rājarṣis).
Because subjects delight in them, they are therefore called *rājarṣis* (royal sages);
those stainless *brahmarṣis* (brahmin sages), however, are established in the world of Brahmā.
The auspicious celestial sages (devarṣis) are to be known as those established in the world of the gods;
all royal sages (rājarṣis), however, are considered to be established in the world of Indra.
Those who are declared to be Brahman-sages by virtue of their noble birth, as well as those divine celestial sages, through austerity and the recitation of mantras; BndP_1,35.99.
Likewise, there are the royal sages; I shall describe their characteristics:
they possess knowledge of the past, the future, and the present, and are likewise endowed with truthfulness.
Those who are themselves content, those who are indeed self-enlightened,
those who have attained perfection here through austerity, and those by whom [the truth] was realized even within the womb.
Those who utter mantras, those who are all-pervading through their sovereignty,
these are the royal sages (rājarṣis), as well as the gods, the twice-born, and the kings who are disciplined.
Those who have indeed attained these states are considered to be the Ṛṣis;
these seven are known as the Saptarṣis because of their seven qualities.
Those who are long-lived, creators of mantras, lords, and possessors of divine vision— the Buddhas, who perceive the dharmas directly and are the initiators of the lineage.
Constantly devoted to the six duties, modest householders conducted their affairs with equals through blameless actions based on the principle of karma.
Those intelligent householders dwelling in the depths of the forest sustained themselves with refined flavors prepared by their own hands.
In each of the ages known as Kṛta and the others, the establishment of the system of castes and stages of life is indeed performed by all [the Manus] again and again at the very beginning.
When the beginning of the Tretā Yuga arrives once again, the seven ṛṣis here shall establish the social classes and the stages of life in every respect.
In their very lineage, heroes are born again and again;
indeed, when a father and son are born, the son is born in the father and the father likewise in the son.
Thus, by continuing without interruption until the end of the eon,
eighty-eight thousand householders are said to have lived.
Those who have resorted to the southern path of Aryaman, the way of the ancestors,
are indeed those who possess wives and maintain the sacred fire, and are remembered as the causes of progeny.
"Though householders are innumerable, they resort to cremation grounds;
eighty-eight thousand [of them] are stationed in the northern region."
Those sages who are heard to have reached heaven, having their vital energy drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas),
and who were the authors of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, are born again at the end of the Yuga.
Thus revolving again and again through the Dvāpara ages,
they [attain mastery] over the Kalpas, the Vedic sciences of the sages, and those composed as various Śāstras.
By these [sages], the distinction of Vedic rites was established again and again during the Dvāpara ages within that Vaivasvata Manvantara.
Indeed, twenty-eight times were the Vedas divided by the great seers;
however, in the seventh Dvāpara age, the Vedas were divided by the Self-born One himself.
In the second Dvāpara, Prajāpati was the Vedavyāsa;
in the third, Uśanas was the Vyāsa; and in the fourth, Bṛhaspati.
Savitṛ is remembered as the lord in the fifth [period], Mṛtyu in the sixth;
likewise Indra in the seventh, and Vasiṣṭha is remembered in the eighth.
Sārasvata is remembered as the ninth, Tridhāman as the tenth,
Trivarṣā as the eleventh, and Sanadvāja follows after that.
In the thirteenth [generation] was Antarikṣa, and Dharma was also in the fourteenth;
Traiyyāruṇi was in the fifteenth, while Dhanañjaya was in the sixteenth.
Kṛtañjaya was [the son] in the seventeenth [generation], and Ṛjīṣa is recorded in the eighteenth;
from Ṛjīṣa came Bharadvāja, and from Bharadvāja came Gautama.
From Gautama came Uttama, and from him Haryavana is remembered;
after Haryavana came Vena, and from him Vājaśravas is remembered.
And after Vājaśravas came Somamukhyāyana;
from him came Tṛṇabindu, and from Tṛṇabindu came Tataja.
From him was born Śakti, and from Śakti came Parāśara;
from him was born Jātūkarṇa, and from him Dvaipāyana is remembered.
These twenty-eight are the ancient Vedavyāsas;
and in the future Dvāpara age, there will likewise be Droṇa and Dvaipāyana.
When this Vedavyāsa has passed away, there will arise one of great ascetic power;
and in the future, there will indeed be the pruning of the branches [of the Veda].
From that very Brahman, the imperishable Brahman was attained through austerity;
through austerity, action was attained, and through action, O you, your glory was attained.
Furthermore, by means of splendor, truth is pervaded; by truth, the imperishable bliss;
the immortal Brahman is the pure semen, and Brahman alone is called the nectar of immortality.
This single, imperishable syllable "Om" is established as eternal;
because of its greatness and its power to expand, it is designated as Brahman.
Salutations to that Brahman, who is established as the source of proof and is known as Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svar, and who resides within the Atharva, Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Salutation to that Subrahman, who is designated as the cause of the dissolution and origin of the world, and who is the supreme secret beyond the Great Principle (Mahat).
The world, which arises from the awakening [of beings], is unfathomable, boundless, and inexhaustible;
it has as its purpose the welfare of persons through both manifestation and activity.

The final goal and destination of those who possess Sāṃkhya knowledge and whose nature is tranquility and self-restraint is that which is unmanifest, inconceivable, primordial matter (prakṛti), and the eternal Brahman.
Pradhāna, the self-source (ātmayoni), the grasped (gṛhya), and sattva are praised;
likewise, the undivided, the semen, the imperishable, and that which possesses manifold natures.
Salutations again and again, eternally, to that Supreme Brahman;
once it has been accomplished, there is no further action to be done—how much less so for those whose actions are uncreated?
Whatever is done or left undone in the world, whether it be what ought to be heard or has already been heard, and likewise whether it be good or bad— all that is accomplished by this alone.
Whatever is to be known, or to be sown, or to be reflected upon, or to be questioned, or indeed to be eaten;
or whatever is to be seen, or heard, or smelled in any way whatsoever—[all this is to be abandoned].
Whatever has been shown by him alone is indeed known by the celestial sages;
as for that which he has not shown, who is capable of seeking it out?
The Blessed One alone has declared all things, everything, and all of them:
that whatever is done by whomsoever at any time, he conceives himself as being that very thing.
That which is performed here first was not spoken by anyone else;
and when something is performed by someone, in whatever manner or at whatever place.
Indeed, that very deed performed appears to the agents as either deficient or excessive,
whether it be through knowledge or ignorance, and whether it be pleasant or unpleasant.
Dharma and adharma, happiness and suffering, death and immortality,
as well as existence above, across, and below— all these belong to that very one who acts through the unseen (adṛṣṭa).
Then, for the self-existent Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, the eldest,
this becomes individually perceivable here again and again during the Tretā ages.
For indeed, that which was to be known as a single Veda is divided again and again during the Dvāpara ages;
Brahmā spoke these [divisions] at the beginning of this Vaivasvata interval.
Revolving again and again through the ages called yugas, these sages, being born in succession to one another, indeed compose the *saṃhitās*.
Indeed, eighty-eight thousand celestial sages (śrutarṣis) have passed away in the past; they continue to pass away again and again as time goes on.
Those who, following the southern path, resorted to the cremation grounds—
by them those branches were arranged again and again in age after age.
In all the Dvāpara ages here, the Saṃhitās were [compiled] by the Śrutarṣis;
indeed, within their lineages, these branches arise again and again.
Those branches and those creators shall exist here until the end of the age;
indeed, they are to be understood in this very same way regarding the past and future ages as well.
In all the past Manvantaras, the promulgations of the Vedic branches have indeed passed away; those that exist now belong to the current interval.
And those which are yet to come and will exist in the future as well—
by means of the former, the latter is to be known, and by means of the present, both.
By this sequential method, the determination of the Manvantaras is established;
thus indeed are the gods, along with the Pitṛs, the Ṛṣis, and the Manus.
Accompanied by the mantras, all the gods go upward from Janaloka and return with them again and again for ten kalpas.
When the time for their transition has arrived, those who have come into being meet with your destruction;
at that time, they are joined with that which is inevitable.
Then, perceiving that birth is fraught with defects and preceded by disease,
their activity ceases at that time due to their perception of those defects.
Thus, having revolved ten times through the ages of the gods here,
they go from Janaloka to Tapoloka, from which there is no return.
In this manner, thousands of divine ages have passed here,
and [the ancestors] have indeed gone to their end in the world of Brahmā along with the sages.
It is not possible to describe their extensive details in successive order,
because time is beginningless and because their enumerations are likewise infinite in every respect.
The past Manvantaras, along with the Kalpas of old,
together with the Pitṛs, the Munis, the Devas, and the Ṛṣis.
In due time, the dissolution and the evolution of the ages (yugas) occur;
by this sequential process, so too do the kalpas and the intermediate periods (manvantaras).
Hundreds and thousands of world-ages, along with their progeny, have passed away;
at the end of a Manvantara comes dissolution, and at the end of dissolution comes creation.
It is not possible, even in hundreds of years, to describe in their proper sequence [the lineages] of the gods, the sages, Manu, and the assembly of ancestors.
But learn now the full extent of both the creation and the dissolution in every respect, as well as the duration of a Manvantara according to human reckoning.
The Manvantaras have been calculated by the twice-born, who are experts in the science of numbers; they are reckoned as exactly thirty crores by those skilled in calculation.
Sixty-seven lakhs and twenty thousand years— this is the duration of time for the remaining [kalpas], excluding the additional period.
The number of a Manvantara has been proclaimed according to the human reckoning; now I shall declare the subsequent [duration] of the Manu according to the divine year-measure.
By divine reckoning, it is recorded as eight hundred thousand,
plus another fifty-two thousand additional years.
Indeed, this period of fourteen [yugas], lasting until the dissolution of all beings, constitutes a full thousand yugas;
that is recorded as one day of Brahmā.
Then all beings, having been scorched by the rays of the sun,
placed Brahmā at their head and stood together with the celestial sages and the Dānavas.
They enter the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the foremost of gods;
he is the creator of all beings again and again at the beginnings of the kalpas.
Thus, this duration of the stay has indeed been considered by the divine sages;
now learn of the transition between all the Manvantaras.
O sinless ones, that which was previously designated by me as "Yuga" is traditionally known as the four yugas, consisting of the Kṛta, Tretā, and the others.
And that [text], having been recited seventy-one times with a slight addition,
the Lord, the Master, proclaimed as this *Manoreta* section.
Thus, the characteristics of all the Manvantaras—
those past, those future, and the present one— have been proclaimed.
Thus has this creation of Svāyambhuva Manu been described to you;
now I shall speak of the transition between him and the next.
Just as in former times, a manvantara, together with the ṛṣis and deities,
comes to an end in due course through the inevitable force of destiny.
In the meantime, those who were previously the lords of the three worlds—
the seven ṛṣis, the gods, the ancestors, and likewise the Manus— [appeared].
Then, when the time of the manvantara had become full and exceeded its limit,
and her authority was exhausted, she became distressed, realizing the change in her own status.
They all turned their minds toward Maharloka;
then, when that Manvantara had come to an end, those deities—
When the period of the complete duration has passed, one Kṛtayuga remains;
those who are to become the lords of the Manvantara shall then be born.
The deities, the ancestors, the sages,
and Manu himself likewise come to an end when the Manvantara is complete, as do they in the Kali Yuga.
When those remnants of the Kali age have been brought to completion, then the continuity of the Kṛta age is indeed established;
thus it is remembered by the wise that the Kṛta age follows after the Kali.
Likewise, at the ends of the Manvantaras and at the beginning of a Manvantara—
when the previous Manvantara has expired and the next one has commenced once again.
Then, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, those who remained among them—
the Seven Sages and Manu— stood there awaiting the proper time.
Those ascetics, though wasting away, await the next Manvantara;
they do so always for the sake of the festival of the Manvantara and for the sake of their progeny.
As before, they proceed once the release of rain has begun,
when the pairs [of opposites] have come into operation and the medicinal herbs have arisen.
When the world had become joyless, when all things mobile and immobile had perished, and when there were no villages or cities, and it was devoid of the social classes and stages of life;
In the previous Manvantara, those who were righteous here remained as the Seven Sages and Manu, established for the sake of the lineage.
While they perform most difficult austerities for the sake of the subjects,
[the Manus] arise here at the end of the previous [Manvantaras], just as before.
The gods, asuras, hosts of ancestors, sages, and likewise humans; serpents, bhūtas, piśācas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas.
Then, among those who remained, the Seven Sages and Manu— indeed, at the beginning of the Manvantara— observed the practices of the virtuous.
And men undertake their activities together with the gods;
having then discharged their debt to the sages through the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya), they proceed.
Through offerings to the ancestors, through progeny, and likewise through sacrifices to the gods,
they remained established for a hundred thousand years in the dharma consisting of the [four] castes.
Having established the three Vedas, the means of livelihood, the science of government, as well as the duties of the castes and stages of life,
and having likewise established the hermitages, they set their minds upon heaven.
When those former gods were thus intent upon attaining heaven,
those very former gods remained entirely established in righteousness.
When the previous Manvantara has passed away, they abandon all their abodes and,
together with the mantras, ascend to the healthy Maharloka.
Having ceased their offices and attained mental perfection,
those self-controlled ones remain gazing [upon the world] until the dissolution of all beings.
Then, when those former gods had passed away,
the abodes of the gods throughout the three worlds were entirely empty.
Other gods who dwell in heaven have indeed arrived here;
then, endowed with ascetic power, they fill their respective stations.
Endowed with truth, celibacy, and sacred learning,
[they dwell] together with the Seven Sages, Manu, the gods, and the ancestors.
Herein are the endings of the past and the beginnings of those yet to come;
their lineage shall remain uninterrupted until the end of this Manvantara.
Thus, in this sequential order, their station remains established throughout all the Manvantaras, until the dissolution of all beings.
The characteristics of the transition between former Manvantaras of both the past and the future were indeed proclaimed by Svāyambhuva.
This is the means for those yet to come throughout the past Manvantaras;
in this way, there shall be no interruption of the lineage until the dissolution of all beings.
Indeed, the revolutions of the Manvantaras are entirely dependent upon the Mahā;
both the Mahājana and the Janāntapa arise within the Satya-yuga as being exclusively directed toward it.
But for those destined for that state, by means of vision there and through the cognition of manifoldness,
they remain eternally established in their permanence even when transformation has occurred at the time of re-absorption.
The revolutions of the Manvantaras release the truth, yet beyond that lies the ultimate limit;
from there, through diligent application and the abandonment of sense-objects, they enter the god Nārāyaṇa alone.
As the cycles of the Manvantaras have proceeded for a long time according to the nature of destiny,
the world of living beings does not indeed stand still for even a moment, revolving through decline and rise.

Thus, having perceived from the visible world these intermediate accounts of the Manus— those of divine vision, righteous souls, and celestial power— who were praised by the Ṛṣis, [Vyāsa] composed them through both detailed expansions and concise summaries, as directed by Vāyu.

All these revolutions are fully endowed with royal sages, gods, and seekers; likewise with Brahman-sages, gods, and serpents; and joined by the lords of the gods, the seven sages, the ancestors, and the lords of creatures.

For the merit that dispels all calamities belongs indeed to the lords who are born of noble lineage and ancestry, whose learning has been further increased by preeminent intelligence, and who are honored by fame, splendor, and renown.

This is conducive to heaven, supremely purifying, and beneficial for one’s sons; it is this supreme secret that should be chanted during the great festivals, which is foremost in granting the pacification of suffering and bestowing long life.

O lords of creatures, may you, being diligent, grant me success as I briefly proclaim this meritorious and celebrated lineage of the Unborn, which is preeminent among those who have attained the age of a hundred years through progeny.
Thus has been declared this interval of Svāyambhuva Manu, in detail and in proper sequence; what more shall I describe?

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Vedas' Distress and the Description of the Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara," in the second section (Anuṣaṅga-pāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Śāṃśapāyana said: "I desire to hear, in due order, the accounts of the remaining Manvantaras."
And also the lords of the Manvantaras, headed by Indra and the gods.
Sūta said: Listen as I describe, both concisely and in detail, those Manvantaras which have passed and those yet to come.
First was Svāyambhuva Manu, then Svārociṣa Manu,
as well as Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, and Cākṣuṣa.
These six Manus have passed away; I shall now describe the eight who are yet to come:
Sāvarṇi, Raucya, Bhautya, and likewise Vaivasvata.
I shall describe these later on, starting from the time of Vaivasvata Manu; first, however, learn of those five Manus who have already passed away, who were born of the mind.
I have related to you the Manvantara of Svāyambhuva;
hereafter, I shall describe the Manu Svārociṣa.
In brief, regarding the creation of progeny for the second high-souled Manu,
the gods were indeed the Tuṣitas during the interval of Svārociṣa Manu.
The Pārāvatas and the Vidvāṃsas are remembered as the two groups;
they were born in Tuṣitā as the sons of Kratu, the son of Svarocis.
The Pārāvatās and the Vāsiṣṭhas are recorded as two groups of twelve;
and the Chandajas are recorded at that time as twenty-four gods.
Divasparśa, Jāmitra, Gopada, Bhāsura,
Aja, Bhagavat, and the very powerful Draviṇa.
Āya, who is mighty-armed, possessed of great energy, and heroic;
and he who is known as Cikitvān, who is celebrated and is recited as Aṃśa.
The twelfth among them was Ṛta, who is celebrated as Tuṣita;
these were the sons of Kratu, and they were all drinkers of Soma at that time.
And the god Pracetas, as well as Viśvadeva; and he who is renowned as Samāñja, as well as Ajihma, the crusher of enemies.
Āyurdāna, Mahāmāna, and likewise Divyamāna;
Ajeya, the illustrious Mahābhāga, and Yavīyān, who is possessed of great strength.
The Hotṛ and the Yajvan; for thus these have been traversed from afar—these indeed were the deities during the interval of Svārociṣa Manu.
At that time, these twenty-four deities were indeed the Soma-drinkers;
their Indra was then Vipaścit, renowned throughout the worlds.
Ūrja, the son of Vasiṣṭha, Staṃba Kāśyapa,
Bhārgava, Prāma, and likewise Ṛṣabha Aṅgirasa.
Paulastya, Datta, Atri, Ātreya, Niścala, Paulaha, and Arvarīvat— these are likewise the seven ṛṣis.
Caitra, Kiṃpuruṣa, Kṛtānta, Vibhūta, Ravi,
Bṛhaduktha, Nava, Setu, and Śruta— these are remembered as the nine [sons].
O Lord, these sons of Svārociṣa Manu,
enumerated in the Purāṇa as the founders of his lineage, belong to that second interval.
The seven ṛṣis, Manu, the gods, and the ancestors— these four constitute the root of a manvantara, as do their lineages and progeny.
The deities are the sons of the sages, and the ancestors are the sons of the gods;
the sages are the sons of the gods—such is the settled conclusion in the scripture.
The Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas of Manu, as well as the twice-born from the seven ṛṣis—
this is declared to be the Manvantara in brief, and not in detail.
The detailed account of Svāyambhuva and of Svārociṣa is not to be known [in full];
it is impossible to recount its extent even in hundreds of years.
Furthermore, due to the great multiplicity of rebirths among living beings in every family,
this occurs during the third period within the interval of the supreme Manu.
Five classes of gods have been mentioned; listen as I describe them:
those gods who are the Sudhāmans, and those others who are the Vaśavartins.
The Pratardanās are known as the auspicious and truthful groups of twelve:
Satya, Dhṛti, Dama, Dānta, Kṣama, Kṣāma, Dhvani, and Śuci.
Iṣu, Arka, Śreṣṭha, and likewise Suparṇa as the twelfth—
these are declared to be the twelve Sudhāmans by name.
Sahasradhāra, Viśvāyu, Samitāra, Vṛhadvasu,
Viśvadhā, and Viśvakarman were born from Mānasa, who was himself born from Virāja.
Jyotis and Vibhāsa are also proclaimed as belonging to the lineage;
likewise Avadhya, Avarati, Deva, Vasu, Dhiṣṇya, and Vibhāvasu.
Vitta, Kratu, Sudharmā, Dhṛtadharmā, Yaśasvin,
Rathormi, and Ketumān are celebrated as the Pratardanas.
Haṃsa and Svāra were both generous, bringing fame to Pratardana;
Sudāna and Vasudāna were both endowed with excellent splendor and vigor.
Yama, Vahni, Yati, Sucitra, and likewise Sutapas—
these twelve others are to be known as the auspicious ones worthy of sacrifice.
Learn also the names of the Satyas exactly as they are:
Dikpati, Vākpati, Viśva, and likewise Śambhu.
Svamṛḍīka, Divi, Varcodhāman, Bṛhadvapu, Aśva, Sad-aśva, Kṣema, and likewise Ānanda.
For these twelve others, who are worthy of sacrifice, were indeed perfected as truths;
for these were the deities during the interval of the last Manu.
Among those gods, the one renowned as Indra was named Suśānti;
they were the sons of Aṅgiras, who was himself the son of the patriarch Uttama.
The seven sons of Vasiṣṭha were renowned as the Vāsiṣṭhas;
they were all the seven ṛṣis during the interval of Manu Uttama.
Ācaśca and Paraśuśca, Divya and Divyauṣadhirnaya, Devāmbuja and Apratimau, Mahotsāha and Gaja likewise.
Vinīta, Suketu, Sumitra, Sumati, and Śruti—
these were the thirteen sons of the high-souled Uttama Manu.
These were the leaders of the Kṣatras; this third interval was reckoned as the Auttamamanvantara by Svārociṣa.
Learn now in detail and in due order concerning the period of Tāmasa;
specifically, during the fourth cycle, in the interval of the Manu Tāmasa.
The Satyas, Surūpas, Sudhiyas, and Haris are remembered as the Gaṇas;
these gods were the sons of Pulastya during the Tāmasa Manvantara.
The sages declare that the host of those gods consists of twenty-five for each of the sense organs.
Together with their respective measures, the seven organs of perception— of which the mind is the eighth— and likewise the deities, are recorded as having existed within that Manu.
Among those gods, the powerful Indra was their commander-in-chief;
O best of beings, learn now who the seven ṛṣis were during that interval.
Kāvya and Āṅgirasa, Kāśyapa and Pṛthu, Atreya who is indeed Agni, and Jyotirdhāman of the Bhṛgu lineage.
Paulaha, Caraka, Vāsiṣṭha, Pīvara, Caitra, and likewise Paulastya— these were the sages during the Tāmasa Manvantara.
Jānujaṅgha, Śānti, Nara, Khyāti, Śubha,
Priyabhṛtya, Parīkṣit, Prasthala, and Dṛḍheṣudhi.
Kṛśāśva and Kṛtabandhu were the sons of Tāmasa Manu;
then, in the fifth cycle, during the interval of Svārociṣa Manu.
Now learn of those qualities which are proclaimed as belonging to the gods:
the Amitābhas, the Bhūtarayas, the Vaikuṇṭhas, and the Sasumedhas.
The most excellent and auspicious sons of the progenitor Vasiṣṭha were fourteen; they formed four groups that were brilliantly radiant.
Ugra, Prajña, Agnibhāva, Prajyotis, and likewise Amṛta;
Sumati or Virāva, Dhāman, Nāda, and likewise Śrava.
Vṛtti, Āśī, Vāda, and Śabara— these fourteen gods are remembered as the Amitābhas in the Svārociṣa Manvantara.
Mati and Sumati, as well as Ṛta, Satya, and Edhana;
Adhṛti and Vidhṛti, as well as Dama and Niyama.
Vrata, Viṣṇu, Sahas, Dyutimat, and Suśravas—
these, they know, are the names of the Ābhūtas here.
Vṛṣa, Bhettā, Jaya, Bhīma, Śuci, Dānta, Yaśas, Dama, Nātha, Vidvān, Ajeya, Kṛśa, Gaura, and Dhruva.
The Vikuṇṭhas have indeed been described; now learn of the Sumedhas:
Medhā, Medhātithi, and likewise Satyamedhās.
Pṛśnimedhas, Alpamedhas, and he who is the lord Bhūyomedhas;
likewise Dīptimedhas, Yaśomedhas, and Sthiramedhas.
Sarvamedha, Sumedha, and he who is remembered as Pratimedha;
Medhaja and Medhahantṛ—these are celebrated as the Sumedhas.
Vibhu was their Indra, possessed of surpassing prowess;
there were also Paulastya Dvivāhu and Sudhāman, the son of Kaśyapa.
Hiraṇyaroman was of the Aṅgiras lineage, Vedaśrī was of the Bhṛgu lineage,
Ūrdhvabāhu was of the Vasiṣṭha lineage, and Parjanya was likewise of the Pulaha lineage.
Satyanetra, Tathātreya, Mahāvīrya, Susaṃbhāvya, Satyaka, Hara, Hā, and Śuci were the sages in the Raivata Manvantara.
Balabandhu, Nirāmitra, Kaṃbu, Śṛṅga, and Dhṛtavrata were the sons of Raivata; that indeed was the fifth Manvantara.
Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, and Raivata—
these four Manus are remembered as belonging to the lineage of Priyavrata.
Furthermore, in the sixth cycle, those gods who were in the Cākṣuṣa interval—
the Ādyas, the Prasūtas, and the Bhāvyas— were the broad-minded inhabitants of heaven.
The five classes of gods are known as the Mahānubhāvas and the Lekhas;
all of them, being inhabitants of heaven, are addressed by the names of their mothers.
The grandsons of Atri, the Prajāpati Āraṇya, are indeed the Gaṇas;
each one of those groups of gods is traditionally remembered as consisting of eight members.
Antarikṣa, Vasu, Havya, Atithi, Priyavrata,
Śrotṛ, Mantṛ, and Anumantṛ— these are indeed proclaimed as the primordial ones.
Śyenabhadra, as well as the highly illustrious Śvetacakṣus, Sumanas, Pracetas, Vanena, Supracetas, and [Supracetas].
And Muni, as well as Mahāsattva, are proclaimed as his offspring;
likewise Vijaya, Sujaya, and Manasyuda.
Mati, Parimati, Vicetās, and Priyaniścaya—these are indeed known as the Bhavya gods; now learn of the Pṛthukas.
Ojiṣṭha, Śakuna, Deva, Vānaddṛṣṭa, likewise Satkṛta, Satyadṛṣṭi, Jigīṣu, and Vijaya.
Ajita, Mahābhāga, Pṛthuka, and those who are the inhabitants of heaven (divaukasas)—I shall likewise declare their fragments (leśas) by name; learn of them.
Manojava, Praghāsa, the highly illustrious Pracetas,
Dhruva, Dhruvakṣiti, and the heroic Atyuta.
Yuvan and Bṛhaspati were proclaimed as the Lekhas;
Manojava, of great heroism, was then their Indra.
Uttama and Bhārgava, Haviṣmat the son of Aṅgiras, Sudhāman the son of Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, and likewise Viraja.
Atināman, Paulastya, Sahiṣṇu, Paulaha,
and Madhura Ātreya— these were the seven [sages] in the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara.
Ūru, Puru, Śatadyumna, Tapasvin, Satyavāk,
Kṛti, Agniṣṭut, Atirātra, and Sudyumna— these are the nine.
And Abhimanyu was the tenth; these were the sons of Manu Nāḍvaleyā.
These indeed were the sons of Cākṣuṣa, and that was the sixth interval.
This creation was enumerated by Vaivasvata, the current Manu,
in detail and in proper sequence during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu.
The sages said: Whose son was Cākṣuṣa born? In whose lineage did he arise? And who were the others in his lineage? Tell us this exactly as it happened.
Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, hear now in brief the creation of Cākṣuṣa,
in whose lineage was born the powerful Pṛthu, the son of Vena.
The other lords of creatures were Dakṣa Prācetasa and others;
likewise, the patriarch Atri took Uttānapāda as his son.
That son of his, however, was Dattaka; for he was a king and a lord of subjects, given by Svāyambhuva Manu to Atri on account of a specific cause.
O twice-born ones, having reached the Manvantara of the future Cākṣuṣa, I shall now describe that sixth period by way of introduction.
From Uttānapāda, the beautiful Sūnṛtā, the daughter of Dharma renowned by the name Sūnṛtā and possessed of shapely hips, gave birth to four sons.
She who was born from the Dharma was the auspicious mother of Dhruva;
she of the pure smile was indeed born from Lakṣmī, the wife of Dharma.
Uttānapāda begot Dhruva, Kīrtimant, Āyuṣmant, and Vasu, as well as two daughters of pure smiles.
Svarā and Manasvinī are proclaimed as their two daughters;
and the heroic Dhruva remained for ten thousand divine years.
In the first Tretā Yuga, the grandson of Svāyambhuva performed austerities without food, seeking great renown.
Sustaining himself through yogic practices and seeking great renown,
Brahmā, being pleased, granted him the supreme station among the luminaries.
Having beheld his divine majesty and his extraordinary power, which remains undisturbed by rising or setting until the dissolution of all beings; Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.36.93.
The preceptor of the Daityas, Uśanas, sang this verse concerning the gods: "Oh, the power of his austerity! Oh, his learning! Oh, his vow! (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.36.94).
Having placed him above as the fixed pole, the Seven Sages remain there; and upon that Dhruva, the Lord, the master of the day, has fixed the triple heaven.
From Dhruva, Bhūmi gave birth to two kings, Sṛṣṭi and Bhavya;
the Lord indeed addressed his own shadow as Sṛṣṭi and called her Bhavanārī.
As soon as he uttered the word "Satyā," she immediately became a woman, possessing a divine frame and adorned with celestial ornaments. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.36.97)
In Chāyā, Sṛṣṭi begot five stainless sons:
Prājīnagarbha, Vṛṣabha, Vṛka, Vṛkala, and Dhṛti.
The wife of Prācīnagarbha, Suvarcā, gave birth to an incomparable son named Udāradhī, who was Indra in a previous birth.
Taking food only once at the end of a thousand years,
the Lord, thus disciplined throughout a Manvantara, attained the status of Indra.
Bhadrā gave birth to a son, Divañjaya, from Udāradhi; and Varāṅgī bore Ripu to Divañjaya, who was himself the conqueror of enemies.
From Ripu, Bṛhatī bore Cākṣuṣa, who possessed all splendor and was endowed with great strength.
His son was the wise Manu, the progenitor of the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas; he begot Cākṣuṣa Manu upon Puṣkariṇī, the daughter of Varuṇa.
The sages said:
"O sinless one, why is the daughter of Prajāpati called Vāruṇī?
Explain this in truth, for you are indeed skilled in detailed exposition."
Sūta said:
Araṇya’s son was Udaka, who attained the state of Varuṇa;
because of him, she became known as Vāruṇī, having acquired that fame through her brother.
Ten auspicious sons of great heroism were born to the maiden Naḍvalā from Viraja, the Prajāpati, by Manorā.
Ūru, Puru, Śatadyumna, Tapasvin, Satyavāk,
Kṛti, Agniṣṭut, Atirātra, and Sudyumna— these indeed were the nine.
And Abhimanyu was the tenth; these were the sons of Manu born of Naḍvalā.
Then Āgneyī bore to Ūru six sons of great splendor.
From Aṅga, Sumanas gave birth to Khyātiṅgaya, Śukra, Vraja, and Ajina; and from Aṅga, Sunīthā bore a single son, Vena.
Due to that offense of Vena, a great wrath arose;
he from whose right hand the sages churned for the sake of the subjects.
When his hand was churned, the handsome Pṛthu was born;
having begotten that son Pṛthu of celebrated prowess, [he departed].
"O sages, this king shall be the ruler of you and your subjects"; thus they spoke, and he was born joyful, equipped with bow and armor, as if burning everything with his splendor.
"This lord of men, Pṛthu the son of Vena, shall be the provider of livelihoods for you;
as the first-born of the Kṣatriyas, he will then protect the worlds."
He was the first lord of the earth among those consecrated by the Rājasūya sacrifice;
for the purpose of praising him, two skillful bards, a Sūta and a Māgadha, were born.
Thus, O Great King, this cow was milked by the wise one for grains,
by the gods together with the hosts of ṛṣis who desired a means of subsistence for their subjects.
By the ancestors, the Dānavas, the Gandharvas, the hosts of Apsarases,
the serpents, the Puṇyajanas, the mountains, and the trees and creepers;
As the Earth was milked into those various vessels, she yielded the desired milk; by means of that, they sustained their lives.
Śāṃśapāyana said: O observer of great vows, recount in detail the birth of Pṛthu,
and how in former times the earth was milked by that high-souled one.
Just as in former times with the gods and the nāgas, with the brahman-sages, and with the yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, and apsarases.
And in whatever manner, O Sūta, and by whichever specific rite, [the milk was obtained] from those particular vessels, the milker, and the milk itself— BndP_1,36.119.
Likewise, please tell us who are asking you about the specific types of calves,
as well as all the specific types of milk, in their proper sequence.
And for what reason was the hand of the forest [the sacrificial wood] churned by the ancient great sages in their anger? Tell us that reason indeed.
Sūta said:
O Brahmins, I shall relate to you the origin of Pṛthu, the son of Vena;
listen with one-pointed attention and self-restraint, O best of the twice-born.

This Brahman must never be imparted to one who is impure, nor to a sinner, nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who seeks his own harm, nor to one who observes no vows, under any circumstances whatsoever.
Blessed, conducive to fame and long life, meritorious, and equal to the Vedas—
let him who is free from malice listen to this secret proclaimed by the sages.
And whatever mortal, having paid homage to the Brahmins, should thus cause others to hear the account of the origin of Pṛthu, the son of Vena, shall not grieve over what has been done or left undone.
That lord Aṅga, a protector of dharma and equal to Atri,
was born into the lineage of Atri as a Prajāpati.
His son was Vena, who was not particularly righteous;
he was born as a lord of creatures (prajāpati) from Sunīthā, the daughter of Mṛtyu.
Due to the fault of his maternal grandfather, Vena— the son of the son of Kālātmaja—
placed righteousness beneath his feet and acted according to his own desires toward the worlds.
That king established this law for the sake of dharma;
yet, transgressing the Vedic scriptures, he became devoted to unrighteousness.
While he ruled that kingdom, which was devoid of Vedic study and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*,
the deities did not drink the Soma at the great sacrifices.
"No sacrifice is to be performed, no gift is to be given"— this was the cruel vow of that Prajāpati when his own destruction was at hand.
"I am the one to be sacrificed to and the one to be worshipped by the gods and the twice-born at the sacrifice;
sacrifices are to be performed for me, and offerings are likewise to be poured into me. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.36.132)
Then all the great seers, headed by Marīci, spoke to him who had transgressed the bounds of propriety yet remained well-restrained by his own virtuous conduct: *BndP_1,36.133*
"O King, we shall enter upon a consecration for a hundred years;
do not commit unrighteousness, for this is not the eternal dharma."
Born at the end [of the age], you are undoubtedly Prajāpati;
"I shall protect the subjects"—this was the vow formerly made by you.
Then Vena, the evil-minded one, who was skilled in deceit, laughed and spoke to all those brahmin-sages as they were speaking thus.
Who else is the creator of dharma, or whom should I listen to?
Who on earth is equal to me in heroism, austerity, and truth?
"O dull-witted ones, you certainly do not know me in truth— me,
the source of all worlds and especially of all dharmas."
If I so desired, I could flood the earth with water;
I could create it or swallow it up—of this there is no need for deliberation.
When he could not be persuaded, despite being firmly restrained by the noble ones who had seized him by the pillar,
then the great seers became enraged at Vena.
Having seized that one of great strength as he struggled with their arms,
they, being intensely enraged, then wrung his left hand.
From that which was being churned, indeed, the ancient one was born; thus says the Śruti.
A Puruṣa exceedingly short in stature and black in color also came into being.
Terrified, with palms joined in reverence and his senses unagitated, he stood there; seeing him thus distressed and overwhelmed, they reportedly said to him, "Sit down."
He, possessed of infinite prowess, became the founder of the Niṣāda lineage;
he also produced the fishermen who were born from the impurity of Vena.
Know that those others who dwell in the Vindhyas— the Taṃburas, Tuburas, and Khaśas—
as well as those who delight in unrighteousness, are the impure descendants of Vena.
Again, the great seers, filled with intense fervor and provoked to anger, vigorously churned the right hand of Vena as one would churn a fire-drill.
From that hand, which resembled a lotus, Pṛthu was born;
and because he was born from the palm of Pṛthu’s hand, he was therefore called Pṛthu.
Blazing with his physical form like a fire manifest in flames,
he took up the primordial bow named Ājagava, which produced a great roar.
Bearing arrows for the sake of protection and armor of great luster,
all beings everywhere were then filled with joy at his birth.
Vena went to the third heaven, O great king, while the royal seer attained union with the divine through his high-souled and virtuous son who had been born.
Then that tiger among men was rescued from the hell named Put;
and the rivers and oceans, taking all kinds of jewels from every side, [approached him].
And all stood ready with water for the consecration,
as did the blessed Grandfather (Brahmā) together with the Aṅgirases and the immortals.
Then all beings, both stationary and moving, having assembled from every side, consecrated the son of Vena as the lord of men.
That great king was consecrated by the sons of Aṅgiras, the gods, as a protector of subjects of great splendor by the mighty King of Kings.
The illustrious and powerful Pṛthu, son of Vena, was the first king;
his subjects, who had been alienated by his father, were brought to affection by him.
From that, the name "Rāja" arose for him indeed because of his [people's] affection;
even the waters solidified as he was about to march against the ocean.
The mountains split apart, yet there was no breaking of banners;
the earth yielded crops without being ploughed, and food was prepared by mere thought.
At that very time, during his sacrifice, there were cows that yielded all desires, and in every single leaf-cup there was honey. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.36.158)
On that very day of the Sautya sacrifice, a Sūta was born from a Sūta woman;
when he had thus been born, a Māgadha was then born again.
And while the chanters of the Sāmaveda were singing the auspicious Vaiśvadevika hymns, he was born from that [conjunction]; therefore, he is called Māgadha.
Then, having offered an oblation mixed with the oblation of Bṛhaspati by means of the divine oblation of Indra, he was born as a Sūta from Indra.
In that regard, negligence arose concerning the ritual acts and their expiations;
for the teacher's oblation was defiled and overwhelmed by the sacrificial offering of the disciple.
Through the practice of inverse intercourse, that corruption of caste arose;
