as did that which was born from a Kṣatriya father upon a Brāhmaṇa mother, due to the inferiority of the womb.
The Sūta is proclaimed to have qualities similar to those of the former [castes] due to their common characteristics;
indeed, this livelihood by means of the field (agriculture) is the duty of the middle-ranking Sūta.
The science of chariots, elephants, and horses, as well as the lowest form of medicine—
these two were summoned there by the great sages for the sake of Pṛthu’s praise.
Then all those sages said: "Let this king be praised;
this deed is worthy of him, and this lord of men is a fit recipient."
Then the Sūta and the Māgadha said to all those ṛṣis:
"We two please both the gods and the ṛṣis by means of our own respective duties."
"O twice-born ones, we do not know his deeds, nor his characteristics, nor his fame,
by which we might offer a hymn of praise for this radiant one," they said.
He is constantly devoted to his duties, truthful in speech, and has his senses restrained;
he is characterized by wisdom, is generous, and remains unconquered in battles.
The sages, however, commissioned them, saying, "Let [the deeds] of the mighty Pṛthu be praised as they will come to pass. (Bṛhaddevatā 1.36.170)
The Sūta and Māgadha then praised those [deeds] set to song;
thereupon, at the conclusion of that, Pṛthu, the lord of subjects, being well-pleased, bestowed gifts.
He gave instruction in the *sūta* [genre] to Sūta and instruction in the *māgadha* [genre] to Māgadha;
from that time forward, the protectors of the earth have been praised by *sūtas* and *māgadhas*.
Awakened by the benedictions of the bards, chroniclers, and panegyrists,
the subjects beheld him with supreme joy, as did the great seers, who spoke thus.
"This Vainya shall be the king who provides for their livelihood.
Thereupon, the subjects flocked to the highly fortunate Vainya.
"Provide us with a means of livelihood"— at these words of the great Ṛṣi,
he was then impelled by his subjects out of a desire to act for their welfare.
Taking up his bow and arrows, the powerful one rushed toward the earth;
then, terrified by the son of Vena, the earth fled away, having assumed the form of a cow.
Taking up his bow, Pṛthu pursued her as she fled;
at that time, out of fear of Vainya, she went through the worlds, beginning with the world of Brahmā.
He beheld Vainya before him, with bow raised in hand,
possessing unshakable splendor and blazing with sharp, flaming arrows.
Finding no protection anywhere, she sought refuge with Vainya alone— the great-souled Mahāyoga, who was invincible even to the immortals.
With palms joined in reverence, the goddess—who is always to be worshipped by the three worlds—spoke to him: "One does not perceive any unrighteousness in the killing of a woman."
"And how will you support the subjects whom I have nurtured?
O King, the worlds are established in me; by me this entire universe is sustained."
O King, let not these subjects, whom I have nurtured, perish on my account;
it does not behove you to kill me, for you desire to act for my welfare.
O protector of the earth, listen to these words of mine regarding all living beings:
all undertakings succeed when they are commenced through the proper means.
"O King, even having slain me, you will not be capable of protecting your subjects; I shall enter within them. Cast off your anger, O one of great splendor! (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.36.184)
O protector of the earth, they say that women are not to be killed, even among beings belonging to the animal realm; you ought not to abandon this dharma.
Having heard these various words of hers, the high-minded and righteous-souled one restrained his anger and spoke thus to the Earth: BndP_1,36.186 //
Whoever would kill even a single living being— whether for his own sake or for the sake of another—
even if it be many beings, that person incurs the sin of that act.
But when that one is slain, O auspicious lady, by whose death many live in happiness,
there is no sin or secondary offense in slaying him.
Therefore, O Earth, for the sake of my subjects, I shall slay you if you do not today carry out my word for the welfare of the world.
Having swiftly slain you with an arrow for turning away from my command,
he will establish himself here and personally sustain the subjects.
Therefore, O best among the upholders of dharma, abide by my word and constantly restore the living beings to life, for you are indeed capable; of this there is no doubt.
"Enter into the state of being my daughter, so that I may restrain this arrow of terrible appearance which has been raised for the purpose of killing you."
Then the Earth, having been addressed thus, replied to the son of Vena:
"O King, I shall perform all this; of this there is no doubt."
"Behold that calf of mine, so that I, out of maternal affection, may flow with milk;
and you, O best among the upholders of dharma, make me level everywhere,
so that my quivering milk may nourish all things."
Sūta said:
Then Vainya cleared away the masses of rocks in every direction with the tip of his bow; by that means, the mountains were leveled.
In the past manvantaras, the earth was uneven;
by its very nature, it possessed both level and rugged places.
For indeed, in the previous creation, when the surface of the earth was uneven, no division of cities or even villages existed.
In the former period of Cākṣuṣa, it is said that in ancient times there were no crops, no cattle-rearing, no agriculture, and no trade routes.
In that Vaivasvata interval, there was the origin of all this;
indeed, wherever there was any levelness of the earth, it occurred only in certain places.
In those various places, indeed, all those subjects dwelt everywhere;
it is said that the food of the subjects consisted of fruits and roots.
We have heard that from the time of Vainya onwards, the origin of all this in this world occurred for those [beings] only with great difficulty.
Having appointed Cākṣuṣa Manu as his calf,
the lord Pṛthu then milked the earth for grain upon his own surface.
By that food, those auspicious creatures indeed sustained themselves;
furthermore, it is heard by the sages that the Earth was milked once again.
Soma became their calf, and Bṛhaspati was the milker;
the Gāyatrī and all the other meters were the vessel.
At that time, their austerity and the eternal Brahman became milk;
then, by the hosts of gods led by Purandara, [it was churned].
Taking a golden vessel, the Earth was milked;
Maghavan was the calf, and the all-pervading Savitṛ was the milker.
By means of that, the deities subsist on milk, nourishment, and honey;
furthermore, it is heard that the Earth was milked again by the ancestors.
Taking up a silver vessel for the swift satisfaction of the *svadhā* offering,
the majestic Vaivasvata Yama became their calf.
The powerful lord Antaka became the milker of the ancestors;
moreover, it is heard that the Earth was milked again by the Asuras.
Having taken an iron vessel, Māya and Virocana, the son of Prahrāda, who was highly illustrious among them, likewise [took one] from all sides.
The son of the Daityas, Dvimūrdhan, became the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the milker for the Daityas;
and all those illusory asuras were skilled in the use of magical powers (*māyā*). They [milked] milk-rice (*pāyasa*) by means of their illusions.
Those of great heroism cause it to flow; that indeed is their supreme power.
It is heard that they milked [the earth] by means of serpents, having made Takṣaka the calf.
Then the earth took up an earthen vessel and poured forth poison as milk;
indeed, it was the powerful Vāsuki, the son of Kadrū, who had incited them.
O best of the twice-born, those fierce, large-bodied, and intensely venomous nāgas and serpents subsist entirely upon that very [substance].
Having that as their food, that as their conduct, that as their vigor, and that as their refuge,
they milked the earth— which is fond of concealment— into an unbaked clay vessel.
Having made Vaiśravaṇa the calf, along with the Yakṣas and Puṇyajanas,
Rajatanābha— who was the father of Maṇidhara— acted as the milker.
Born of sacrifice, possessed of great splendor, self-controlled, and of immense renown—
it is by him that they subsist, both in terms of worldly practice and according to the ultimate truth.
The earth was milked again by the Rākṣasas and Piśācas;
Brahmā was their milker, and Kubera was the vessel for them.
The powerful calf Sumālī milked blood indeed as its milk into a skull-bowl, while the Rākṣasas remained invisible.
With that milk, the *rakṣasas* subsist here in every way;
furthermore, it is milked by the Gandharvas and hosts of Apsarases into a lotus vessel.
Having made Citraratha the calf, the earth then yielded pure fragrances;
Vasuruci, the auspicious son of the sage, was their milker.
The Gandharva king Atibala, a great-souled one resplendent like the sun,
is heard to have milked the goddess Vasundharā once more with mountains as the milking vessels.
Then the medicinal herbs in embodied form and various kinds of jewels were the milk;
Himavat was the calf, and the great mountain Meru was the milker.
The vessel was indeed made of stone, and by it the mountains were established;
it is heard that the Earth was milked again by trees and creepers.
Taking a vessel made of *pālāśa* wood— which sprouts again even when cut or burnt—
the flowering *śāla* tree is the wish-fulfilling cow, and the *plakṣa* tree is the calf for those who possess glory.
The Earth, the source of all beings, is the milch-cow that yields all desires;
she alone is the nurse, the creator, the sustainer, and the bearer of treasures.
We have indeed heard that she was milked by Pṛthu for the benefit of the worlds;
she is the foundation and the very source of the world of moving and non-moving beings.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Remaining Description of the Manvantara and the Milking of the Earth," in the second section (Anuṣaṅgapāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
"As I have heard it, this earth was once bounded by the ocean."
Because she holds wealth (vasu), she is therefore celebrated as Vasudhā.
In ancient times, she was completely saturated with the fat (medas) of Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
therefore, she is called "Medinī" by those who discourse on Brahman according to its etymological derivation.
Then, because of the acceptance by the wise King Pṛthu, the son of Vena,
the Earth is thereafter recited as having attained the status of his daughter.
In ancient times, the division of the earth was accomplished by Pṛthu;
it belongs to that king who possesses mines and is garlanded with cities and mines.
Filled with members of the four castes and protected by that wise one,
such was the power of King Vainya, O best of the virtuous twice-born.
He is to be saluted and honored in every way by the entire multitude of beings,
and by the highly fortunate Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Only Pṛthu, the eternal source of Brahman,
is to be saluted by illustrious kings who seek great glory.
The first king, the majestic Pṛthu, son of Vena,
is to be saluted even by warriors who desire victory in battle.
Indeed, Pṛthu alone is to be saluted as the first creator of all things;
for whatever warrior goes forth to battle having invoked King Pṛthu [is victorious].
That renowned royal sage, having established himself here in the livelihood of a Vaiśya, emerges safely from that terrible battle even with the assistance of Vaiśyas.
The highly illustrious Pṛthu alone is to be honored for granting a means of subsistence;
these are the specific calves, the milkers, and the milk itself.
And all the vessels have been described by me in their proper order;
in ancient times, the earth was first milked by the high-souled Brahmā.
Having made the wind the calf, [he placed] the seeds upon the surface of the earth;
then, once again in the previous Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
Having made Svāyambhuva the calf and likewise all the crops,
this was done when the present Manvantara of Svārociṣa had arrived.
Having made Svārociṣa the calf, the earth was milked for crops;
and by that very Uttama, the younger brother of the gods, it was likewise milked.
Having made Manu the excellent calf, all the crops were [collected] by the wise one;
and again, during the fifth interval of the Tāmasa Manu, the earth was [prepared].
Having made this Tāmasa cow her calf by means of Balabandhu, she was milked when the sixth interval of Manu had arrived. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 1.37.17)
In former times, the Earth was milked by the Ancient One, with Āriṣṭa as the calf;
and again, when the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara had arrived.
In former times, the Earth was milked by the Ancient One, having made Cākṣuṣa his calf;
and when the interval of Cākṣuṣa had passed and the Vaivasvata interval arrived once again...
In former times, this earth was milked by Vainya, just as I have told you;
indeed, in previous aeons that have passed, the earth was milked by these very ones.
Thus, by gods and others, by humans, and likewise by spirits and so forth— all these are to be understood here in this manner regarding the past and the future.
The gods remained in their own abodes during the Manvantara; now hear of the progeny of Pṛthu.
Two valiant sons were born to Pṛthu, Antardhi and Pāṣaṇa.
Śikhaṇḍinī gave birth to Havirdhāna and Antarddhāna;
from Havirdhāna, Dhiṣaṇā, the daughter of Agni, gave birth to six sons.
Prācīnabarhis had two sons, Śukla and Kṛṣṇa, who were progenitors of offspring.
The venerable Prācīnabarhis was a great lord of creatures (prajāpati).
By virtue of his strength, learning, austerity, and heroism, he was the sole sovereign on earth;
because his *kuśa* grass blades were pointed toward the east, he was therefore called Prācīnabarhis.
Having taken the daughter of the Ocean as his wife, that lord,
the Prajāpati, at the conclusion of great ascetic penance, begot offspring upon Savarṇā.
Sāmudrī bore ten sons to Prācīnabarhis of the same lineage,
all of whom were named Pracetas and were masters of the science of archery.
Practicing their religious duties without deviation, they performed great austerities for ten thousand years, dwelling within the waters of the ocean.
While those trees were performing penance and thus scorched the earth, they covered it over as it remained unprotected; consequently, there occurred a destruction of living beings.
Then, when that Cākṣuṣa Manvantara had been withdrawn,
the wind was unable to blow, and the sky became filled with trees.
For ten thousand years the subjects were unable to move;
hearing of that, all the Pracetasas applied themselves to ascetic penance.
With their anger aroused, they emitted wind and fire from their mouths;
then the wind, having uprooted those trees, dried them up.
The terrible fire consumed them; thus occurred the destruction of the trees.
Then, perceiving that the destruction of the trees was nearly complete when only a few branches remained, [he spoke].
Having approached them, King Soma spoke to those wise ones,
having seen the true necessity for the sake of the continuation of the world.
"O kings, all you descendants of Prācīnabarhis, abandon your anger!
Trees shall spring up upon the earth; let Agni and Māruta be appeased."
This maiden of excellent complexion is a jewel among trees;
indeed, this future generation has been held by me within my womb.
She is named Māriṣā by name, fashioned indeed from trees;
let her become your wife, for she was nourished while bearing the embryo of Soma.
"By half of your splendor and by half of my own splendor,
a wise Prajāpati named Dakṣa shall be born from her."
He, who is himself like fire, shall further cause these subjects— who have been mostly consumed by the fire consisting of your own splendor— to flourish once more.
Then, at the word of Soma, those Pracetasas restrained their anger toward the trees and took Māriṣā as their wife according to dharma.
Then, indeed, they placed an embryo in Māriṣā by means of their minds;
from the ten Pracetas, Prajāpati was born of Māriṣā.
The highly energetic and powerful Dakṣa was born from a portion of Soma;
at first, Dakṣa created offspring through his mind, and then by means of sexual union.
Having first created, by means of his mind, those that move not and those that move, as well as bipeds and quadrupeds, Dakṣa subsequently created women.
He gave ten to Dharma, three to Kaśyapa,
and twenty-seven, who were engaged in the guidance of time, to Indu.
Having given these to them, he then gave four others to Ariṣṭanemi,
two to Bahuputra, and likewise two to Aṅgiras.
To Kṛśāśva they gave one daughter, and from them offspring was born;
this is celebrated as the sixth interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu.
Even for Manu Vaivasvata, the seventh Prajāpati,
there were the Vasudevas, birds, cows, nāgas, and the sons of Diti and the Dānavas.
The Gandharvas, Apsaras, and other species were likewise born;
from that time forward, offspring in this world have been produced through sexual union.
It is said that the creation of the earlier beings occurred through mere intention, sight, and touch.
The sage said:
"The auspicious origin of the gods, the dānavas, and the divine sages, as well as that of the high-souled Dakṣa, has been previously recounted to you."
The birth of Dakṣa from Prajāpati Prāṇa has been described by you;
but how did that great ascetic again obtain you as his wife?
O Sūta, you ought to explain this doubt of ours here:
how did he, who was the daughter's son of Soma, come to become his father-in-law?
Sūta said:
O best of beings, the wise sages and those people who possess true knowledge do not grieve over the constant arising and ceasing that occurs among living beings.
In every age, all these twice-born ones, beginning with Dakṣa, come into being; and again they are dissolved. The wise man is not deluded by this.
O best of the twice-born, among them there was formerly both seniority and juniority;
however, austerity alone became weightier, and spiritual power was the determining factor.
He who knows this creation of Cākṣuṣa, including all that moves and is stationary,
becomes possessed of progeny, lives out his full span of life, and is glorified in the heavenly world.
Thus has the creation of Cākṣuṣa been briefly described;
these six creations, consisting of the Manvantaras, have now been traversed.
O best of the twice-born, these creations, beginning with that of Svāyambhuva and ending with that of Aśvaśiras, have been described in brief and in their proper order by the wise.
The detailed account of them should be known through the creation of Vaivasvata;
all those creations of Vivasvat are neither deficient nor redundant.
He who recites this without malice attains these very qualities: health, longevity, and the fulfillment of his aims according to the Dharma, his desires, and his purpose.
I shall describe the creation of the high-souled Vaivasvata, who presides over the present age; listen as I speak of it both in brief and in detail.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Cākṣuṣa Creation," in the second section (Anuṣaṅga-pāda) of the first part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Now, in the seventh cycle of Manu Vaivasvata...
From Mārīca Kaśyapa, the gods and the supreme ṛṣis were born.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, the hosts of Maruts,
the Bhṛgus, and the Aṅgirases— these are remembered as the eight classes of gods.
The Ādityas, Maruts, and Rudras are to be known as the sons of Kaśyapa;
the Sādhyas, Vasus, and Viśvedevas are the three groups who are the sons of Dharma.
The Bhṛgus were the gods of Bhṛgu, and the Aṅgirasas were the sons of Aṅgiras;
in this Vaivasvata Manvantara, these are considered the eternal Chandas-born sages.
And these too shall pass away after the lapse of a great period of time;
thus is the present auspicious creation of Mārīca to be understood.
The radiant one among them, known by the name Mahābala, is now their Indra;
he is the lord of those who have passed away, those yet to come, and those who exist at present.
All those Indras of the Manvantaras are to be known as having identical characteristics;
they are the lords of the past, the future, and the present, possessing a thousand eyes and being Purandaras.
All of them were possessed of horns, with horn-tips like thunderbolts;
each had performed a hundred sacrifices, each multiplied by a hundredfold.
Whatever beings there are in the three worlds, whether mobile or immobile, they abide surpassed by [the Buddha] through causes such as the Dharma and other qualities.
In splendor, austerity, wisdom, strength, learning, and valor,
they were as powerful as the lords of the past, future, and present.
I shall declare all of this; listen to me as I speak.
This triple world, consisting of the past, the future, and the present, is considered by the twice-born to be eternal.
This world is known as Bhūrloka; the intermediate space (antarikṣa) is known as Bhuvah;
and heaven is known as Bhavya. Now I shall describe the means for attaining them.
While meditating upon the names of the worlds, Brahmā first uttered "Bhūḥ"; at that time, this became the world of Bhūrloka. (Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 1.38.13)
The root *bhū* is traditionally understood to mean "existence," and likewise, it signifies "beholding" in the context of the world.
Because of its state of being (*bhūtatva*) and because of beholding (*darśana*), this world became known as Bhūrloka.

Therefore, because it is the first world and is real, it is remembered as *Bhūr* by those born of the twice-born; furthermore, Brahmā declared that because one exists (*bhavati*) within this reality (*bhūte*), it is called *Bhuvaḥ*.
The word "bhavat" is used to denote the time of being born;
however, the world is called "bhuvaḥ" because of its existence, as it is etymologically defined by that very derivation.
The intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) came into being; therefore, it is called the second world.
When that second world had thus arisen, Brahmā once again [created].
After he was addressed as "Bhavya," the world thereafter became Bhavya;
in the future, this word "Bhavya" will be understood here [in this sense].
Therefore, that world is called "Bhavya," and it is known by the name Tridiva; this earth is remembered as Bhūḥ, and the intermediate space (antarikṣa) is remembered as Bhuvaḥ.
"Divam," "Smṛtam," and likewise "Bhavyam"—this is the determination of the three worlds;
through these utterances associated with the three worlds, the three *vyāhṛtis* came into being.
O Lord, this verbal root *nāth* is indeed recorded by those who know roots as signifying protection,
because [you protect] the world of the past, the future, and likewise the present.
Therefore, those lords of the three worlds are remembered by the twice-born as being both the primary Indras and likewise the subordinate ones.
Indeed, those gods who partake in the sacrificial offerings during the various Manvantaras, as well as the Gandharvas, Rakṣasas, Piśācas, Rākṣasas, and non-human beings; BndP_1,38.23 //
For these are remembered as the glories of all the lords of the gods;
indeed, those lords of the gods are your gurus, protectors, kings, and fathers.
"For these best of gods protect these subjects here by means of dharma";
this is declared to be, in brief, the characteristic of the lords of the gods.
I shall now proclaim the Seven Sages who have currently taken their place in heaven:
the wise Viśvāmitra, son of Gādhi and descendant of Kuśika, of great ascetic power.
Bhārgava Jamadagni, the powerful son of Aurva,
and also the highly illustrious Bharadvāja, the son of Bṛhaspati.
The wise Gautama, known by the name Śaradvān, was a righteous descendant of Autathya; and the fifth was the venerable Atri, the self-born, who is the treasury of the Veda.
The sixth son of Vasiṣṭha was Vasumān, renowned throughout the world;
and Vatsara was the son of Kāśyapa—these seven are esteemed as virtuous.
These seven sages have been mentioned as those who exist in the present interval;
and Ikṣvāku, Nṛga, Dhṛṣṭa, and Śaryāti as well.
Nariṣyanta was renowned, as were Nābhāga and Diṣṭa;
Karūṣa, Pṛṣadhra, and Pāṃśu is recorded as the ninth.
These nine very righteous sons of Manu Vaivasvata have indeed been proclaimed; this is the seventh interval (antara).
"Thus, O twice-born ones, this second quarter has been recounted by me in detail and in its proper sequence; what more shall I tell you?"

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manvantaras," in the second section, the Anuṣaṅgapāda, of the first part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu;
here concludes this first part of the *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
